20082-warrior-gap-a-story-of-the-sioux-o:
Warrior Gap tells a story of the Sioux outbreak of 1868, on the western frontier. A young lieutenant leads his column toward home after hard service. Barely two years an officer, he rides with a light heart. Each mile brings him closer to the home he longs for.

He had spent one hard year as a plebe at the military academy. At twenty-five, most of his years had seemed bright and glad. War on the plains will test that bright outlook soon enough. Readers get a frontier tale of troops, Sioux resistance, and a young man's trial.
4185-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-61-jan:
January 1667 to 1668 opens with Pepys in his chamber all morning, making up accounts against the new year. About noon he goes abroad with his wife, who is to dine with Hewer and Willet at Mrs. Pierce's, though he has no mind to join them.

He finds his wife troubled at his ways, and the volume follows a marriage under strain beside office work and inquiry. Accounts, dinners, and jealousies share the page. Readers get a new year that starts with sums and ends, as always with Pepys, in human complication.
4186-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-62-feb:
February 1667 to 1668 sends Pepys to the office pretty betimes, but the Board does not meet as soon as he wishes. Forced to Whitehall in expectation of a Tangier committee, he finds it put off and comes home to sit at the office till past two.

High words at the Board follow, in a month of delayed meetings and sharp talk. The volume follows inquiry winter, when committees slipped and tempers rose. Readers get Pepys waiting, walking, and arguing, in the diary's most procedural and human key. Put-off committees and high words mark an inquiry winter.
4187-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-63-mar:
March 1667 to 1668, a Lord's day, sends Pepys very betimes by coach to Sir William Coventry's, carrying all his notes and papers. There he runs over their whole defense in the business of tickets, in order to answer the House on Thursday next.

Pepys thinks the defense will hold unless the House judges without reason, a clerk's hope before a political storm. The volume follows the ticket inquiry, where sailors' pay became a parliamentary weapon. Readers see Pepys preparing, paper by paper, for a hearing that could end his career. Notes and papers, carried by coach, are his armor for Thursday.
4188-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-64-apr:
April 1668 finds Pepys dressing himself and calling, as he uses, Deb to brush and dress him, then working at his office till noon. Out to bespeak things against his wife's going into the country tomorrow, he comes home to dinner alone with her.

She is mighty busy getting her things ready, and the house hums with packing. The volume follows a household on the edge of a country trip, with office hours and domestic bustle side by side. Readers get a spring month of farewells, fittings, and a wife's departure.
4189-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-65-may:
May 1668 holds Pepys to office business all morning, then to Westminster Hall, where Sir William Pen labors to have his answer to impeachment read by the Commons. The Lords have sent it down, but the House is so busy on other matters that Pen cannot get a hearing.

The volume follows the Navy's men under parliamentary fire, with impeachments hanging over old officers. Pepys watches a colleague wait for a reading that never comes. Readers see Restoration politics as delay and procedure, where a man's name waits on a crowded agenda.
4190-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-66-jun:
June 1668 sends Pepys with Sir John Minnes to Westminster, where in the Hall he meets Harris and Rolt. He carries them to the Rhenish wine house, where he has not been in a morning, nor any tavern, these seven years and more.

There he gets the words of a song of Harris that he wanted, a small prize for a music-loving diarist. The volume mixes Hall business with tavern song, as Pepys returns to old haunts after years away. Readers will enjoy a summer month where a song matters as much as a committee.
4191-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-67-aug:
August 1668 fills Pepys's morning with office business, then after dinner to the King's house with his wife and Deb. Coming too late yesterday to hear the prologue, they like the play better now, finding true wit in it beyond the common sort.

The volume mixes office days with theater nights, as Pepys judges plays with the same care he gives accounts. His wife and Deb share the pit and the talk home. Readers get a summer of stage pleasure late in the diary, when Pepys still loved a good comedy.
4192-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-68-sep:
September 1668 keeps Pepys at the office all morning and again after dinner till about four, then abroad while his wife goes to Hales's about drawing her hand anew in her picture. He goes to see Betty Michell, but her husband is within, and there is no pleasure in the visit.

So to other company and home, in a month of work, portraits, and small disappointments. The volume follows late diary days, when office hours lengthen and pleasures narrow. Readers get Pepys near the end, still busy, still watching, still frank about a spoiled call.
4193-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-69-nov:
November 1668, a Lord's day, keeps Pepys with Hewer in his chamber all morning, going further into his great business for the Duke of York. At noon comes dinner, then Hewer writes fair what he had written, while Pepys's wife reads to him all afternoon.

Mr. Gibson joins them later, and the day closes in work and reading. The volume follows Pepys's late diary rhythm: dictation, fair copy, and a wife's voice reading aloud. Readers see the household as an office, with family labor carrying a Navy man's great business. Dictation, fair copy, and reading aloud fill the whole day.
4194-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-70-dec:
December 1668 keeps Pepys at the office all morning, at noon with his people to dinner, then at the office very busy till night. Home, he has his boy read to him Wilkins's Real Character, which pleases him mightily, and after supper he goes to bed with great pleasure and content.

The volume follows a working December lit by evening reading, as Pepys tests a scheme for a universal language. His content comes from work done and a book enjoyed, a quiet close to a hard year. Readers get Pepys the reader, ending days with ideas rather than accounts.
antony-and-cleopatra-pg2268: Enobarbus describes the barge in this edition: Cleopatra on the Cydnus, "the barge she sat in, like a burnished throne, burned on the water." The serpent of old Nile beguiles Antony to ruin. The richest love tragedy ever written.
arxiv-2509-00168:
James Cranch, Georg Struth, and Jana Wagemaker build convolution Kleene algebras on a broad class of structures in 2025. Convolution combines functions on monoids, groups, or categories into an algebra used across math and science. Kleene algebras add a star operation, which captures repeated action, to an idempotent semiring, a number-like system where adding twice changes nothing.

A suitable star was the missing piece for such algebras on wide structures. A generalized Möbius category, joined with a classic star for formal power series, now allows the build. Instances cover algebras with tests, modal and concurrent forms, and higher forms on strict higher categories. The unified build widens algebraic tools for program reasoning.
arxiv-2509-00468:
Mingwei Wang and one co-author, Xiaokui Yang, prove new formulas on compact Kahler manifolds, curved spaces that carry both geometry and a complex structure. Their formulas extend the Bochner-Kodaira type, identities that link curvature to the behavior of differential forms, mathematical objects used to integrate over spaces.

Wang and Yang add quadratic curvature terms, terms that involve curvature squared, to these identities. The new linearized curvature term, a simpler first-order form, yields vanishing theorems, results that force certain quantities to be zero, and bounds on Hodge numbers, counts that describe a space's shape. They also derive related Weitzenbock formulas, curvature identities, on both Riemannian and Kahler spaces under weak curvature rules.
arxiv-2509-00768:
Lee Hyun leads a team of fourteen authors on reasoning models for materials search. Automated experiments need recipe-to-property predictors. Those predictors must be accurate and well calibrated. They must also respect basic physics. Training often curates reasoning traces from a teacher model. But picking traces by correctness alone reflects physics poorly.

The team introduces Physics-aware Rejection Sampling, or PaRS. PaRS favors traces that agree with fundamental physics. It also favors traces close to numeric targets. Light halting rules control the compute cost. A large student model is fine-tuned on the chosen traces. It improves in accuracy and calibration over baselines. It also breaks physics rules less often. Sampling cost falls at the same time.
arxiv-2509-01068:
Mobile apps are shaped by what users need, and many teams now mine app data to find those needs with less hand work. Chong Wang, with four co-authors, surveys the tools and methods built for that job. Their review maps what is known about how these aids work and which tasks they support.

The team ran a systematic mapping study and selected seventy-three papers to examine. Semi-automated methods were the most common, and most tools were open source and built by others. Analysis, mining, and sorting of needs were the tasks studied most. Wang and the co-authors note steady growth in the field and point to gaps where better tools are still needed.
arxiv-2509-01168:
Rug pulls are scams where a token's creators drain its funds and vanish, leaving buyers with worthless holdings. Dmitry Yaremus, with four co-authors, builds a machine learning system to spot such scams early on decentralized exchanges, markets with no central operator, on the TON blockchain. TON's design and its large Telegram user base make it a fresh setting for fraud study.

The team merged data from the two largest TON exchanges and tested two ways to define a rug pull: a sudden drain of funds, or a sudden halt in all trading. Gradient boosting models flagged scams within the first five minutes of trading. The fund-based method scored higher overall, while the halt-based method caught more cases, though data patterns differed sharply between exchanges.
arxiv-2509-01368:
A photon surface is a boundary that traps light rays moving along it. Such surfaces shape what distant watchers can see of a collapsing star. Roberto Giambo and Camilla Lucamarini work out the equations for these surfaces. They assume spherical symmetry and use the most general dynamic setting. Their starting point is a known earlier formulation.

The condition for a timelike surface to be a photon surface can be recast in a new way. It becomes a dynamical system. The same condition holds when a light ray moving outward traces the surface. The team then studies a spherical dust cloud in collapse. The marginal case becomes an exact planar system. Its analysis shows a sharp split. The outer surface extends into the cloud in one lightlike way when the central singularity is covered. Timelike options open otherwise.
arxiv-2509-01568: Thomas F. Bloom, Jakob Fuhrer, and Oliver Roche-Newton measure how much additive structure a convex set can hold. Convex sets curve outward with no dents, which might seem to limit patterns such as arithmetic progressions inside them. Their main result builds a convex set packed with three-term arithmetic progressions, at a count growing as the set size to the power three halves.
arxiv-2509-01668:
Spiral arms shape disc galaxies, but whether they are lasting waves or passing patterns is still debated. Miguel Querejeta, with thirty co-authors, measures offsets between molecular gas peaks and star formation peaks across twenty-four nearby galaxies from the PHANGS survey, all with clear spiral structure. If gas crosses a steady arm, the youngest stars should sit ahead of the gas in the rotation direction.

Offsets were measured in radial bins and showed substantial scatter, implying star formation is not triggered only at one coherent spiral shock. Fourteen galaxies had positive mean offsets, typically a few hundred parsecs. In four, the offsets shrank with radius as a single steady density wave predicts. Ten showed positive offsets with no radial trend, fitting several overlapping modes, and ten showed no clear positive offsets, pointing to transient arms.
arxiv-2509-01768:
Alessandro Pinzi and Giuseppe Savare solve a transport problem for laws that govern random measures. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to reshape one spread of mass into another. Here the mass itself is random, so the objects are laws over measures in a broad space. The cost lacks smoothness, and the space bends in ways that block standard tools.

The authors build a notion of fully convex functions and their slopes for this setting. With those tools, they find a natural class of laws where the direct transport task has one unique solution. That class covers laws made by pushing smooth bell shaped laws through maps. The work mirrors deep links known from the classic Euclidean case.
arxiv-2509-02068:
G Aymerich leads fifty-two co-authors in constraining cosmology from a Planck cluster catalog with added lensing and X-ray data. Galaxy clusters weigh the universe through their counts and masses. Weak lensing shear profiles from a wide survey and Chandra X-ray views calibrate those masses. Hydrostatic masses are corrected for bias using the shear profiles.

Counts and calibration are fit together, yielding tight values for matter density and fluctuation strength. Results sit close to most late time probes, in mild tension with early universe data. A notable tension appears against a rival cluster analysis sharing the same calibration data. Direct mass comparisons for shared clusters rule out calibration as the cause. Center definition choices for shear extraction receive special robustness checks.
arxiv-2509-02168:
Ken Shiozaki gives a way to count the groups that sort topological phases when many order two point symmetries act at once. Topological phases are states of matter sorted by their symmetry class. Each point symmetry of order two adds its own set of types to the count. Pair rules add bits for which pairs swap cleanly and which pairs pick up a sign.

The sort turns out to rest on flip counts and flip counts alone in the end. Counts track how many space and momentum terms each symmetry flips, and how many a pair flips at once. That cut makes any count of symmetries fair game for the method. A full table for the two symmetry case shows the method at work. The result puts a wild corner of phase taxonomy in order.
arxiv-2509-02568:
Mohammad Mehedi Hasan, Pedro G. Lind, Hernando Ombao, Anis Yazidi, and Rabindra Khadka present a 2025 biomedical AI paper on detecting dementia early from EEG, the scalp recording of brain electrical activity. Standard methods miss the brief, shifting patterns that EEG contains.

Their EEG-MSAF pipeline works from microstates, short-lived stable voltage maps on the scalp. Stages extract microstate features automatically, classify them with machine learning, then rank features with SHAP explanations so clinicians can see what drove each call. Tests cover a public Korean dataset and a hospital cohort from Thessaloniki. Accuracy reached high levels on both, beating a deep learning baseline on one. Feature ranking highlighted disruption in an attention-linked microstate, plus a new default-mode pattern marking early decline.
arxiv-2509-02768:
Liyan Xie and Ruizhi Zhang present a 2025 statistics paper adding privacy to sequential change detection, the task of spotting a distribution shift as data streams in. The classic CUSUM procedure is optimal in a precise sense, but publishing its statistics can leak individual data points.

Their DP-CUSUM variant adds calibrated Laplace noise both to the running statistic and to its alarm threshold, giving per-sample differential privacy while keeping the simple recursive update. The authors derive closed-form bounds on false alarm run length and worst-case detection delay, spelling out the trade-off among privacy, false alarms, and speed. Under weak privacy demands, the method matches the classical procedure's first-order optimality. Simulations across privacy levels agree with the theory.
arxiv-2509-02868:
Lachezar Simeonov wrote a 2025 physics paper that takes a fluid-like view of quantum mechanics. In that view, a particle's behavior is described with flow ideas borrowed from the study of moving fluids. Simeonov starts from a quantity called osmotic velocity, which tracks a kind of diffusive drift.

From a rate of change of that drift, he derives the quantum potential, an extra energy term that sets quantum motion apart from classical motion. He builds a model with two interacting fluids and shows it can reproduce known core equations. The approach also stretches to magnetic and electric fields and to fast, relativistic cases for particles without spin. It offers a physical picture for terms often left abstract.
arxiv-2509-03868:
A 2025 physics letter by Alois Altenburger and two co-authors surveys jets crossing the earliest, anisotropic stage of the plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. Right after impact the plasma is stretched along the beam direction, far from equilibrium. Jet partons ploughing through lose energy, and measurements of that loss could expose this pre-equilibrium phase.

Predictions hinge on the jet-medium potential, usually handled with a harmonic approximation. The authors go past that approximation for the first time, extracting the potential from QCD kinetic theory simulations and supplying a compact small-distance form. Early on, the potential departs from thermal expectations, in momentum space and position space alike, and varies with angle. Gluon splitting rates, evaluated with a new computational method, then reveal tensions inside current kinetic theory implementations at these early times. Sharper potentials mean sharper readings of the plasma's first instants.
arxiv-2509-04068:
Mikhail Muzychuk and two co-authors classify a special family of abstract patterns called thin Jordan schemes in a 2025 mathematics paper. Association schemes are tables that record how objects relate, used across combinatorics, the study of counting and arrangements. Jordan schemes loosen the rules of those tables, much as Jordan algebras loosen ordinary algebra. The thinnest cases have the highest possible rank compared with their size, and those are the ones sorted here.

Thin association schemes turn out to match groups exactly, a known result the authors extend. For regular Jordan schemes, they find a match with a special family of loops named Ring Alternative loops. Loops are group-like systems where the usual rules partly relax.
arxiv-2509-04768:
Where should reflecting surfaces be placed to help both communication and sensing? Yilong Chen, lead author with three co-authors, study that placement problem in a 2025 wireless paper. Smart reflecting surfaces can redirect signals from a base station toward target areas for integrated sensing and communications.

Their design uses a channel knowledge map, which gives channel data for candidate surface sites. They jointly tune surface placement, base station beamforming, and reflective beamforming to minimise cost. Constraints guarantee minimum illumination power for sensing areas and signal quality for communication areas. Two cases cover dynamic and fixed reflective settings during operation.
arxiv-2509-04968:
Flows in a thin layer of conducting nanofluid can go unstable through rotation, magnetism, or heat. M. I. Kopp and one co-author review recent theory work on those instabilities in a 2025 paper. The fluid layer rotates at uneven rates under axial, azimuthal, or helical magnetic fields. Brownian diffusion and thermophoresis shape how its tiny grains behave.

Without temperature gradients, three forms of magnetorotational instability are weighed, with growth rates tied to the spin profile and wave number. With temperature gradients, steady convective modes are examined and formulas for the critical Rayleigh number are derived. The review identifies the mechanisms that calm or stir convection.
arxiv-2509-05168:
Green bonds promise environmental benefit, but their market structure could concentrate risk. Xinyue Zhang and one co-author uncover the network geometry of green bonds in a 2025 finance paper. They apply minimum spanning tree and hierarchical tree methods, where distances come from correlations between monthly price changes.

Green bonds show tighter distances on average than stocks and conventional bonds, indicating a highly interconnected market. Strong sector clustering appears, and utility sector bonds are the most central by betweenness measures. The authors argue those central nodes matter for risk propagation, and they offer guidance on monitoring concentration and transparency.
arxiv-2509-05268:
A full wrap-around view of a metal part while it is being printed is offered by James Taylor and seven co-authors in a 2025 manufacturing paper. Directed energy deposition builds and repairs large metal parts, but a defect at any layer can ruin the piece if nobody spots it in time.

Their system uses several camera and projector pairs around the print surface, taking shape measurements in a single shot from many angles. Cross-polarised filters cut glare from shiny alloy surfaces, and the views are joined into one complete reconstruction. In early tests inside a real printer, depth precision beat sixty micrometres. That speed and accuracy could support layer-by-layer correction during printing.
arxiv-2509-05368:
Robots learning long tasks from human videos need to check both their plans and their code, Quan Chen and eight co-authors propose in a 2025 robotics paper. Demonstrations with many steps strain visual imitation learning, especially where timing and object positions interact.

Their agent first drafts an action sequence, then a plan reflection module checks it against the video for timing and spatial fit. A code module turns the plan into commands, and a second reflection module verifies and fixes that code. To test such systems they built a benchmark of three hundred human demonstrations with sequences up to eighteen steps. Existing methods did poorly there, while their framework set a strong baseline.
arxiv-2509-05768:
Electricity forecasting is benchmarked on a decade of data from hundreds of European power stations by Chen Shao and seven co-authors in a 2025 energy paper. Reliable forecasts keep grids stable and operations efficient, but older benchmarks cover small regions, short spans, and few energy features.

Their Real-E dataset spans more than seventy stations in over thirty European countries across ten years, with rich station metadata. Benchmarking more than twenty baseline methods exposes trouble: a new metric for shifting correlation patterns shows the data's correlations change in complex, non-stationary ways that current methods handle poorly. The findings offer a hard, realistic test bed for more robust forecasting models.
arxiv-2509-05968:
Uniform subconvexity bounds for a family of L-functions are proved in a 2025 paper by Zhao Xu. L-functions package deep arithmetic information, and subconvexity bounds, estimates slightly beating the trivial convexity bound, are prized tools in analytic number theory. Xu studies second moments of products of two GL(2) L-functions at their central point, in the spectral aspect.

The moment estimate yields a bound that stays uniform in the spectral parameters of both forms. When either form is a dihedral Maass newform, or one has level one, the bound sharpens to Burgess type, the strongest classical shape. As an application, Xu also establishes a shrinking result for quantum unique ergodicity in the dihedral Maass case.
arxiv-2509-06168:
Every closed orientable three-dimensional shape can be folded into a stack of four-spheres, prove Shital Lawande and Kuldeep Saha in a 2025 paper. Their tool is the codimension-one spun embedding, a way of placing a space inside a space one dimension higher while preserving its open book structure, a decomposition like pages around a spine.

Explicit constructions use sphere twist maps and push maps, and the authors give planar open books for several three-manifolds with their embeddings. A side result proves simply that the twist map along a nonseparating sphere is nontrivial among orientation-preserving symmetries of the ambient space, relative to the boundary. The paper adds concrete embedding recipes to low-dimensional topology.
arxiv-2509-06568:
Electron-positron annihilation at high temperature, inside a modified theory of electromagnetism, is calculated by D. S. Cabral and three co-authors in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Podolsky electrodynamics adds a higher-derivative term to the photon sector. That change introduces a massive mode for light while keeping gauge invariance, a core symmetry of the theory.

Heat is included through thermo field dynamics, a real-time method for quantum systems at finite temperature. The authors compute the total cross section, a measure of how likely the annihilation is, and separate the influence of the Podolsky parameter from the influence of temperature itself. Comparing the two effects shows how each one shifts the scattering process. Results of this kind test whether modified electromagnetism would leave visible traces in hot settings, such as the early universe or high-energy collisions.
arxiv-2509-06668:
Fast follow-up of cosmic explosions with a new gamma-ray telescope is reported by Monica Seglar-Arroyo and eleven co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. The telescope, LST-1, is the first of its array at the northern Cherenkov Telescope Array site on La Palma. It is now in advanced commissioning and is built for rapid response to fleeting events.

Recent detections of gamma-ray burst afterglows at very high energies opened a new window on extreme accelerators, and neutrino and gravitational-wave alerts add more targets. The authors describe the observing strategies and the transient handler software, which manages alerts that are poorly located on the sky. Results from campaigns so far and lessons learned are presented, along with plans for joint work with the MAGIC telescopes. The program aims at quick, wide-energy coverage whenever the sky flashes.
arxiv-2509-06768:
Mobile robots that spot hazards and act on them using vision-language models are demonstrated by Oluwadamilola Sotomi and three co-authors in a 2025 robotics paper. Robots in changing environments should notice anomalies and report them. Adding proactive mitigation, where the robot responds rather than only observing, improves safety and keeps operations running.

The system combines vision-language models with large language models so the robot can perceive a scene, interpret hazards and conflicts, report them in real time, and respond when possible. Hazardous and conflict states are built directly into the decision framework, each triggering specific mitigation strategies. In user studies with thirty participants, the system detected anomalies with about ninety-one percent accuracy and responded with low latency using an edge computing setup. The authors target urban and environmental anomalies as the proving ground.
arxiv-2509-06868:
Blurry license plates are sharpened before recognition in a hybrid system by Behnoud Shafiezadeh and three co-authors in a 2025 intelligent transportation paper. Automatic plate recognition underpins smart city traffic systems, but plates vary widely and motion blur defeats many pipelines. Deep learning helps, at the cost of careful preprocessing.

A selective generative adversarial network deblurs only when needed, avoiding manipulations that can hurt clean images. Detection then uses a YOLOv5 model for both plate location and character recognition, with segmentation integrated. Detection is fast enough for real-time use, and accuracy reached the mid-ninety percent range in the reported tests, with the deblurring step lifting accuracy on blurred plates by nearly forty percent. The authors generated and released blur and plate datasets based on Iranian plates, chosen to reflect messy real-life captures.
arxiv-2509-06968:
Wireless systems that sense their surroundings and communicate on the same hardware are reviewed by Murat Temiz and six co-authors in a 2025 survey article. Integrated sensing and communication is seen as a key enabler for 6G networks, serving cars and factory robots that need both functions. Sharing hardware cuts complexity, spectrum congestion, and energy use, but the joint design is hard for conventional methods to compute.

Deep learning offers efficient, near-optimal options that fit limited computing budgets and low-latency real-time settings. After introducing the network designs and the basics of integrated systems, the survey organizes recent deep learning approaches by task. Tasks include waveform design, channel estimation, sensing signal processing, demodulation, and interference mitigation. Strengths, open challenges, and future directions are laid out for each area, giving designers a map of a fast-growing field.
arxiv-2509-07068:
Javier Mariño Villadamigo and 4 co-authors present FASTColor in a 2025 paper on accelerating particle physics model runs. High-multiplicity events remain a bottleneck for Large Hadron Collider model runs due to their computational cost. Matrix element reweighting, adjusting event probabilities to a more exact calculation, is a key step where approximations are commonly used.

Their machine learning surrogate approach accelerates reweighting from leading-color to full-color accuracy, building on recent advancements in leading-color event generation. Color here refers to the quantum chromodynamic charge structure of quarks and gluons. Comparing a variety of modern network architectures for representative processes, they achieve a speed-up of around a factor of two over the current benchmark. They also show how transformers learn and exploit underlying symmetries to improve generalization.
arxiv-2509-07168:
Simranjeet Bilkhu and 1 co-author give a short 2025 mathematics paper that breaks a familiar rule once sets grow without bound. Continuity of measure says the measure of a union of growing sets equals the limit of their measures. The rule holds for countable unions, meaning lists that can be counted off one by one. The authors test the uncountable case, where no such list exists.

Their first counterexample is built on the ordinal numbers, an extended counting system that runs past infinity. They then show that counterexamples also exist among the real numbers, provided the continuum hypothesis is assumed. That hypothesis is a well-known statement about sizes of infinity that standard mathematics can neither prove nor disprove. The paper is a clear warning that a trusted rule can fail quietly when its counting condition is dropped.
arxiv-2509-07268:
Galaxy clusters must be found reliably before the Legacy Survey of Space and Time can do precision cosmology. Ethan K. Steelberg and colleagues set out validation tests for cluster-finding algorithms in a 2025 note. The upcoming survey, LSST, will map the sky in great depth, and errors in cluster catalogs would flow straight into measures of how the universe expands and clumps.

The tests compare clusters found in optical images against catalogs built from X-ray data and from the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, a shadow that hot cluster gas casts on background microwave light. As a worked example, the pipeline runs two finders, redMaPPer and WaZP, on Dark Energy Survey data. Comparing finders across wavelengths shows where each one misses clusters or invents false ones. Such checks will matter even more once LSST data arrive.
arxiv-2509-07568:
Amine Chabane and 3 co-authors model the suppression of the K*(892) resonance in nucleus collisions in a 2025 paper. The K*(892) is a short-lived particle whose yield drops when it forms inside a dense collision fireball, because its decay products rescatter before escaping. Comparing proton-proton and argon-scandium collisions at CERN SPS energies shows how strong that suppression is.

Using the UrQMD transport model, the team computes multiplicities, rapidity and momentum distributions, and the K*/K yield ratio across energies and collision centralities. They also estimate the time between chemical and kinetic freeze-out, the moments when particle types and then momenta stop changing. The model captures the essential features of recent NA61/SHINE data. However, the very strong suppression seen in central collisions is stronger than the model reproduces, a gap the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2509-07668:
E. Barre leads a 7-author team in 2025 engineering the electronic bands of a bismuth layer on silicon. Atomically thin metal layers on semiconductors can host superconductivity, charge density waves, topological phases, and strong Rashba splitting, where spin and motion couple. To use such phases, researchers must tune the energies of the electronic states without wrecking them.

Using modulation doping by boron segregation at the surface, the team shifts the bismuth-induced Rashba bands by up to 200 millielectronvolts while keeping their strong Rashba parameter intact. The silicon valence states stay essentially fixed, ruling out simple band bending as the cause. Density functional theory traces the shift to changed hybridization of silicon states near the surface, induced by the boron atoms. The selective shift halves the bands' distance to the Fermi level, opening transport and spintronic uses.
arxiv-2509-07768:
Michele Joshua Maggini and 5 co-authors benchmark language models in 2025 on detecting hyperpartisan, fake, polarized, and harmful content. Online platforms struggle with such content, and language models look promising, but no proper benchmark had compared models, usage methods, and languages together. The study spans 10 datasets and 5 languages, from English and Spanish to Arabic and Bulgarian, in binary and multiclass settings.

Strategies range from parameter-efficient fine-tuning to many in-context learning setups: zero-shot prompts, codebooks, few-shot examples chosen randomly or for diversity, and chain-of-thought prompting. The headline discovery is that in-context learning often underperforms compared with fine-tuning a model. That finding, detailed across the full grid of tests, argues that adaptation by training still matters for content moderation, despite the convenience of prompting alone.
arxiv-2509-07868:
Where turbines should stand inside a wind farm is an optimisation puzzle taken up by Mehrshad Gholami Anjiraki and 6 co-authors in a 2025 engineering paper. Turbines steal wind from neighbours behind them, so layout decides total yearly energy. Accurate wake simulations are costly, while fast simplified models lose detail.

The team blends both worlds. High-fidelity large-eddy simulations and a cheaper Gaussian-curl hybrid model feed an autoencoder-based neural network that predicts the wake flow field reliably at low cost. With quick predictions available, the search over layouts can aim directly at maximum annual energy production. Better layouts squeeze more electricity from the same land and wind, a practical gain as wind farms spread.
arxiv-2509-07968:
Lukas Haas and 4 co-authors release a cleaned-up factuality test for language models in a 2025 benchmark paper. Their set, SimpleQA Verified, contains one thousand short-answer prompts built from OpenAI's earlier SimpleQA. The original had noisy and wrong labels, topical biases, and repeated questions, which distorted model rankings.

A multi-stage process deduplicated questions, balanced topics, and reconciled answers against sources, and the automatic grader's prompt was improved too. On the new set, a leading model still answers only a little over half the questions well by the reported score. A trustworthy yardstick matters because short factual answers are easy to check in principle, and inflated benchmarks hide how often models simply do not know.
arxiv-2509-08068:
Shining a laser on bismuthene can flip the material between topological states, predict Zhe Li and 2 co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Bismuthene is a two-dimensional bismuth sheet, and its trigonal form hosts topology centred at the Gamma point of its band structure. Light offers a reversible knob that chemical changes cannot match.

As laser intensity grows, the calculations show two successive transitions. A quantum spin Hall or metallic state first becomes a quantum anomalous Hall state, then converts into a compensated Chern-insulating state. A trigonal warping model explains the sequence. Optical switching of topology could underpin fast, low-power electronic devices whose conducting edge channels are turned on and reshaped by light alone.
arxiv-2509-08168:
Fluid equations can misbehave below a sharp regularity threshold, prove Jan Burczak and Antonio Hidalgo-Torné in a 2025 analysis paper. For the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations on a torus, they start from any smooth initial state and construct several different nonzero solutions whose gradients live in Hardy spaces with exponent below one.

That multiplicity means uniqueness fails in that regime, while exponent one marks the borderline between non-uniqueness and uniqueness for the vorticity path space. Reaching the result required developing Hardy space theory on periodic domains. Knowing exactly where fluid equations stop determining their own future matters for turbulence theory and for judging which weak solutions physics should accept as real.
arxiv-2509-08368:
Magnetic nanotubes of vanadium diselenide host swirling states with unusually high winding, report Jia-Wen Li and 4 co-authors in a 2025 spintronics paper. Curved magnets have rich phase diagrams, and these high-order vortex states, where magnetisation wraps around several times, enable magnonic functions that conventional magnetic systems cannot reach. Tube diameter decides which state wins.

The states arise from competition between nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic coupling and longer-range antiferromagnetic couplings, checked with density-functional calculations and Heisenberg model phase diagrams. Magnons, the waves of the magnetisation, hybridise in ways set by the vortex order. Diameter becomes a design dial: grow the tube to a chosen size and the magnetic texture, and its wave spectrum, follow predictably.
arxiv-2509-08768:
Qingyou He studies sharp power concavity for two free boundary problems in a 2025 paper. Free boundary problems involve a region whose edge moves over time. One case is a porous medium reaction-diffusion equation, the other is the Hele-Shaw problem, its incompressible limit.

For the porous medium case, one-half concavity of pressure holds for all time, but other powers do not persist. For Hele-Shaw, a range of powers up to one-half all persist, with one-half the largest. The contrast comes from Hele-Shaw no longer being a degenerate equation. Concavity also yields a sharp regularity estimate for the porous medium pressure.
arxiv-2509-09068:
Silicon photonic chips guide light well but barely respond to its intensity, limiting active functions like pulsed lasers. Maria Carolina Volpato and 5 co-authors add that response with a two-dimensional material, in a 2025 research paper. They added a single layer of a molybdenum telluride crystal to a silicon microring resonator. The combined device was built on a standard, factory-ready platform.

Tests under varying input power showed clear saturable absorption. The effect saturates at very low power, a few microwatts. A simple model reproduced the readings accurately. Saturable absorbers are the workhorse inside pulsed and mode-locked lasers. Showing one this small and this frugal points toward built-in lasers, ultrafast signal handling, and photonic computing parts that sip power. Hybrid sheet materials may supply the nonlinear functions silicon photonics has always lacked.
arxiv-2509-09568:
V. G. Kupriyanov and 1 co-author lay early groundwork for gauge theory on Snyder spacetime in a 2025 theoretical paper. Snyder space and its relatives, including Yang and Snyder-de Sitter spaces, are noncommutative geometries that keep Lorentz symmetry visible. Working in the semi-classical regime means treating the theory through Poisson structures, which first requires a concrete realisation of the algebra.

The authors give a general method that writes the Snyder algebra and its extensions with ordinary canonical phase space variables. Known representations come back out, and new ones appear as well. From those constructions they obtain an explicit realisation for Snyder-de Sitter space, a deformed derivative, plus remarks on free-fall motion and the shape of the geometry.
arxiv-2509-09868:
Yunhao Zhang and 8 co-authors extend ordered consensus in 2025 so that blockchain ordering must offer equal opportunity, not merely resist cheats. In state machine replication the final order of commands is usually left open, yet on a blockchain that order decides who earns what. Existing ordered consensus limits damage from Byzantine nodes, while real advantages often come from faster networks or living closer to the machinery.

Borrowed from social science, equal opportunity says two equally qualified candidates for a slot should stand an equal chance of taking it. The authors show randomness can hold bias in check and introduce a secret random oracle to supply it. The result is a fairness guarantee aimed at ordinary speed advantages, not just at outright attackers.
arxiv-2509-09968:
J. Giacomoni and 2 co-authors look for solutions of fixed mass to a Choquard equation that mixes nearby and faraway diffusion in a 2025 analysis paper. Choquard equations carry a nonlocal self-interaction, and here the diffusion itself blends a local operator with a fractional one, a combination that models systems pulled by both close contact and long-range influence. Normalised solutions, whose overall size is prescribed in advance, are the natural objects for such problems.

The authors prove such solutions exist and establish how smooth they must be. They then close a conceptual loop by showing that having a normalised solution and having a normalised ground state, a lowest-energy representative, amount to the same thing in this setting. That equivalence lets later work hunt whichever form is easier to reach.
arxiv-2509-10068:
Thomas Naimer and 3 co-authors compute the spin textures inside twisted double layers of transition-metal compounds in a 2025 condensed matter paper. When two sheets are stacked at a commensurate twist, a purely radial Rashba spin-orbit field can appear, fanning electron spins outward like spokes. The team studies three materials in that family with first-principles calculations, reading band structures and spin fields near the key symmetry points of the combined lattice.

Simple effective models with two mass terms, spin-orbit coupling, and interlayer tunnelling reproduce the main patterns. Fitted parameters reveal the radial field's strength varying with twist angle in a pattern symmetric around several special angles, while coupling between the layers' valley points fades as the repeating cell grows. Flat shifts between the layers complete the picture.
arxiv-2509-10268:
Siegfried Hörmann and Daniel Strenger-Galvis propose a new way to measure dependence when one variable is a category in this 2025 statistics paper. Their coefficient links a categorical variable, such as group membership, with a second variable that can live in any metric space, not just on a number line.

The authors derive the coefficient's main theoretical properties and show how its sample version behaves when data grow large. They also build an independence test whose distribution under independence follows the familiar chi-square shape, and they prove the test catches any real dependence. The same machinery covers the classic problem of comparing several groups, even when the underlying distributions are high-dimensional or infinite-dimensional, with a variant for conditional dependence as well.
arxiv-2509-10368:
Xuan Chen and nine co-authors quantify a stubborn uncertainty in Higgs boson physics in this 2025 paper. At the Large Hadron Collider, one prized channel makes Higgs bosons by vector boson fusion. A second channel makes them by gluon fusion, with two jets beside them. In the detector, the two look the same. The second channel is thus a background that cannot be removed.

Sharp predictions for that background are notoriously hard. Simulation programs disagree with each other. The team takes the best fixed-order calculations as a reference point. It compares existing event generators in detail. It also sets up shared simulation settings, so different programs reach the same precision in their inputs. The verdict is firm. No prediction for the two-jet outcome can be trusted without next-to-leading-order work behind it.
arxiv-2509-10468:
Yifan Liu and seven co-authors propose DECOR in this 2025 paper. DECOR is a framework for generative recommendation. Such systems work in two stages. A pretrained tokenizer turns each item into semantic ID codes. A language model then learns to generate the next item's code. The two stages chase different goals, though. Token assignments stay static. Pretrained meaning gets overwritten.

DECOR learns new token representations instead. They are decomposed, and they adapt to context. One step adjusts token embeddings to the user's situation. A fusion step keeps pretrained codebook knowledge. It sits beside fresh signals from clicks and purchases. On three real-world datasets, DECOR beat strong baselines again and again. The point for designers is plain. Do not throw away what pretraining knew. Do not freeze how items are described.
arxiv-2509-10568:
Muhammad M. Roomi and 2 co-authors specify a modeling language for smart grid cyber ranges in this 2025 paper. A cyber range is a safe copy of a real system where attacks can be rehearsed. Building one for a smart grid by hand is slow, so the authors define SG-ML, a language for describing a grid completely enough that software can build the range automatically.

SG-ML is written as XML schemas covering both the power system and its cyber network in one model. It reuses established standards for substation and controller files, and adds its own schemas for gaps those standards miss, such as attack settings and scenario data. A processor program reads a finished model and sets the range up.
arxiv-2509-10868:
Ian M. Musson connects Catalan numbers to the internal structure of Kac modules in this solo-authored 2025 paper. Kac modules belong to the Lie superalgebra gl(r|r). A standing question concerns their composition factors. How many can such a module have, when its atypicality is at its maximum? Atypicality measures how far the module sits from generic behavior.

Musson encodes the problem in diagrams. A pattern of marks runs along the integers. The pattern dictates rules for a set of non-intersecting arc diagrams. He gives a recursive way to count them. The recursion echoes the fundamental recurrence for the Catalan numbers. That is the famous sequence counting bracketings and paths. The payoff is a proof of the conjecture. The maximum number of composition factors is exactly a Catalan number. An algebraic maximum ties to a beloved counting sequence.
arxiv-2509-10968:
Swarm robotics needs rehearsal space, and Leo Cazenille, Loona Macabre, and Nicolas Bredeche built it in this 2025 software paper. Their subject is the Pogobot, a small open-source, open-hardware robot designed for swarm research, with vibration and wheel locomotion and fast infrared communication. Testing algorithms on physical swarms is slow and laborious, and tuning parameters on hardware alone is prohibitive.

Pogosim simulates Pogobots quickly and at scale, with a deliberate design promise: exactly the same user code runs in simulation and on the real robots. The paper walks through the architecture, configuration files, and user programs, and is candid about where simulation approximates or departs from experiment. It also covers launching large parallel batches of runs, analyzing the results, and optimizing code parameters automatically, cutting the cost of developing swarm behavior.
arxiv-2509-11068:
Zan-Kai Chong and 2 co-authors design a cheap way to check that a language model really did the work in this 2025 paper. In multi-agent systems, one agent may claim an answer came from a strong model while quietly using a cheaper one. Proving otherwise sounds expensive, since the checker might have to redo the whole computation.

Their framework leans on deterministic replicability: on identical hardware and software, the same model repeats its output exactly. Validators can then re-run small random slices of an answer instead of the whole thing. Simulations found targeted checking ran more than twelve times faster than full regeneration, with dials to trade speed against the chance of catching a cheat.
arxiv-2509-11168:
Peihong Zhang and six co-authors wrote this 2025 audio machine learning paper on acoustic scene classification, the task of labeling a recording by the place it was made. Models stumble when the test recordings come from devices they never trained on, especially when labeled data are scarce.

Rather than change the model, the authors change the order of training examples. An auxiliary classifier guesses which device made each recording, and the uncertainty of that guess, measured by entropy, ranks examples from device-neutral to device-specific. Training starts with the neutral ones and adds the specific ones later, teaching general features first. Across several standard baselines from the DCASE 2024 challenge, the strategy reduced the damage from device changes at no extra cost when the model runs.
arxiv-2509-11268:
Hyunbae Park and five co-authors build a fast recipe for a tricky signal in this 2025 astronomy paper. Lyman-alpha light from distant galaxies scatters in the gas between galaxies. Mapping its faint glow promises a new view of the cosmic web. Heavy simulations usually model the scattering.

Detailed photon-tracking experiments showed a simplifying fact. The gas of the later universe is highly ionized. Cosmic expansion shifts the light out of resonance quickly. Scattering stops early as a result. Photons last scatter on a thin, nearly spherical shell. The authors built closed-form formulas on that picture. The formulas need only the source spectrum, gas density, and gas motion. Against full simulations at redshift three, the recipe matched well. Averaged brightness profiles agreed within a few percent.
arxiv-2509-12268:
Jan Kuncewicz tests a dark matter model built from general relativity in a 2025 paper. Galaxy rotation curves, the speeds of stars at different distances from a center, provide strong evidence for dark matter, but its nature remains unresolved. Kuncewicz treats the halo as a perfect fluid with a specific anisotropic equation of state set by one parameter.

That framework yields two families of static, spherically symmetric solutions, called the Power-Law and Logarithmic metrics. Fitting their predicted speeds to representative galaxies from the SPARC database gave a split result. The logarithmic form matched large radii well, while the power-law form fit the inner curve. The model also favored a shallow central density, aligning with cored halo models.
arxiv-2509-12368:
Playful names can hide serious machinery. In a solo 2025 paper, Evan Sundbo introduces balloon animal maps. The maps run between broken toric varieties. Those are shapes assembled from simpler toric pieces. He uses the maps to build long exact sequences. The sequences relate the cohomology of the spaces involved.

The machinery pays off on hypertoric Hitchin systems, a family of spaces tied to graphs. Sundbo gives a fresh proof of a known relation for these systems, the deletion-contraction relation. He also sharpens it. He lands on an exact formula for the Poincaré polynomial of one class of these systems. The class is those whose graph has first Betti number two. A recipe extends the computation to all cases, from finitely many base cases.
arxiv-2509-12668:
Oguzhan Kurnaz, Tomi Kinnunen, and Cemal Hanilci investigate multi-stage score fusion for spoofing-aware speaker verification in a 2025 paper. Automatic speaker verification confirms a person's identity from voice, but spoofing attacks remain a major vulnerability. Integrating a verification system with a countermeasure system is a common defense.

Standard fusion joins scores in a single stage. The authors instead use the verification and countermeasure outputs in many stages, revising the fusion classifiers with the original scores. They combine named subsystems for verification and countermeasures and test classifiers including support vector machines and logistic regression. An auxiliary score from another countermeasure model further improved results. Their approach reached a low equal error rate on the SASV2022 challenge scoring set.
arxiv-2509-12968:
Marta Kwiatkowska, Gethin Norman and David Parker survey 25 years of probabilistic model checking in 2025. The method builds formal models of random systems. It checks traits with math proof, not just trials. That proof base is what sets it apart from plain simulation.

Main use fields are traced over time, from networks to bio systems and more. Core theory lines and tools that drove growth are summed up. Worked cases show gains such as faults found before build. The survey aims to guide new users to the right tools. It also points to where the field should go next and which open problems matter most.
arxiv-2509-13168:
Antonio De Benedittis and 3 co-authors report optical evidence of cesium release from a photomultiplier tube in a 2025 paper. Photomultiplier tubes are sealed sensors that amplify faint light, and their photocathode, the light-sensitive coating, can degrade over time. Understanding that degradation matters for tests that rely on these sensors.

During controlled heating of a tube, a laser scanned across a certain cesium absorption line. Absorption features appeared only above sixty degrees Celsius, indicating thermal desorption, the release of cesium atoms from the bialkali photocathode as it warmed. The absorption correlated with temperature and with quantum efficiency, the sensor's effectiveness at converting light to signal. The authors present the method as a non-invasive way to monitor photocathode degradation in sealed sensors.
arxiv-2509-13468:
Sihun Baek, Zhehan Qu, and Maria Gorlatova built an AR test to learn how distinct kinds of distraction change what users do in a 2025 paper. Head-worn AR is now used in jobs where a lapse can cause harm, yet no one had mapped how each kind of distraction acts. Their tool adapts the Trail Making Test, where users tap numbered targets in order, to a Magic Leap 2 headset.

They built three kinds of distraction, guided by a model of search. Some steer the mind from the top down. Some grab the eye from the bottom up. Others are tied to place. A study with thirty-four people tracked scores, gaze, hand moves, and felt load. Top-down noise hurt scores through clashes of meaning. Bottom-up noise broke the first grip of focus. Place-based noise made gaze jump about in a loose, scattered way.
arxiv-2509-13568:
Mihir Chaudhari and 10 co-authors test how much heat a thin-film platform can take in a 2025 paper. The platform is lithium niobate, a crystal used in tiny devices that sense or move by electric charge. Such devices may have to work in harsh heat, where films can crack or drift as layers expand at distinct rates.

The team made small acoustic resonators on a thin film of the crystal, with platinum top contacts. They baked the devices in rounds, step by step, up to eight hundred degrees Celsius, with a close watch on the range from five hundred fifty degrees up. After each round, they gauged shifts in the pitch of each device and in its quality factor, a gauge of how cleanly it rings. The work maps where this platform holds up and where it starts to fail.
arxiv-2509-13668:
Ankur Dhar and nine co-authors report experiments in a 2025 superconductivity paper on rare earth barium copper oxide, a high-temperature superconductor, under strong radio-frequency fields. How these materials switch out of the superconducting state under microwave power matters for devices from particle accelerators to dark matter searches.

The team tested two forms of the material, an electron-beam deposited film and commercial conductor tapes soldered to copper, inside a hemispherical cavity shaped to maximize the surface magnetic field. They recorded steady behavior at low power and, for the first time in this setting, fully time-resolved switching dynamics on microsecond scales under strong surface fields. The results give device designers direct data on how fast and how these coatings fail.
arxiv-2509-13868:
Manal Binkhonain and Reem Alfayaz ask whether prompts are all you need in a 2025 software engineering paper. Classifying written requirements into classes such as functional and non-functional is normally done by supervised models that demand large, costly labeled datasets and retraining for each new task. Prompted large language models might skip that burden.

The pair benchmarked several models and prompting styles, zero-shot, few-shot, persona, and chain-of-thought, across tasks on the PROMISE and SecReq datasets, then compared the best setups with a strong fine-tuned transformer. Prompt-based models, especially with few-shot examples, matched or beat the baseline, and persona prompting, sometimes with chain-of-thought, added further gains. They conclude prompting is a practical, scalable alternative.
arxiv-2509-14368:
Michael W. Healy-Kalesh and eight co-authors announce in 2025 the first nova super remnant found in the Large Magellanic Cloud. A nova is a bright eruption on a white dwarf star. Repeated eruptions sweep gas outward into a huge dense shell, the super remnant.

The shell surrounds the recurrent nova LMCN 1971-08a and looks circular in narrow band images. It glows in hydrogen and sulfur lines but stays very faint in oxygen, as models expect. Hydrogen data may show a matching structure as well. With a width near two hundred parsecs, it is the largest such remnant yet found. Only four were known before, so a fifth, and the second outside our Galaxy, sharpens tests of nova history.
arxiv-2509-14468:
James Holehouse and seven co-authors present a generative model in 2025 for how complex systems gain functions over time. Genomes, ecosystems, bureaucracies and cities all grow by adding new function types and expanding old ones. A single simple process may explain the shared pattern.

Their model generalises the Yule-Simon process in two ways. The chance of a new function depends on system size, and existing functions grow by a flexible preferential attachment rule. Real systems often depart from the classic Zipf rank pattern, the authors show. Sublinear attachment, where popular functions gain less than proportionally, fits cases such as bacterial proteomes, United States federal agencies and urban economies, while abundance still follows a power law.
arxiv-2509-14568:
Hai Siong Tan, Kuancheng Wang and Rafe McBeth present evidential physics informed neural networks in 2025, adding calibrated uncertainty to equation solving networks. Standard physics informed models give one answer with no honest error bar. Scientific discovery needs to know when a model is guessing.

Their E-PINN uses evidential deep learning losses to estimate output uncertainty directly. Unknown equation parameters are also inferred as a learned posterior distribution. Tests on a one dimensional Poisson problem and a two dimensional Fisher-KPP problem show coverage probabilities calibrated better than Bayesian and ensemble rivals. Real world demonstrations follow in the study. Uncertainty aware solvers can flag where new data would teach the most, guiding experiments rather than merely fitting them.
arxiv-2509-14768:
Dominik John and sixteen co-authors present stain mapping with numbers in 2025 for X-ray virtual histology, three dimensional tissue imaging with X-ray micro tomography. Classic histology gains its power from targeted stains that mark tissue parts. Virtual histology lacks that power, and where stain sits inside a volume was largely unknown.

Their method takes electron number density and X-ray attenuation at once, through modulation based imaging with a structured phase modulator. The two paired measures split stain amount from tissue background. Firm stain maps let biologists trust virtual sections as they trust stained glass slides. Hard numbers for three dimensional histology could cut destructive slicing while keeping the chemical marks pathologists rely on.
arxiv-2509-14868:
Qianyang Li, Xingjun Zhang, Shaoxun Wang, and Wei Jia propose DPANet for long-term time series forecasting in a 2025 machine learning paper. Long-range forecasts are hard because patterns repeat at several time scales and frequencies at once. Earlier Transformer and multilayer perceptron models often fail to capture that mix in one structured design.

DPANet builds two pyramids side by side. A temporal pyramid progressively downsamples the series to catch slow and fast dynamics, while a frequency pyramid splits the signal by band-pass filtering to catch cycles of different lengths. A cross-pyramid fusion block exchanges information between matching levels through cross-attention, working from coarse to fine. Experiments on public benchmarks report state-of-the-art accuracy, ahead of earlier models across the tested forecasting tasks.
arxiv-2509-15068:
Joy Jia Yin Lim leads a team of ten authors personalizing school content with language models in a 2025 education paper. Standard materials speak to no one in particular, and students disengage when examples ignore their backgrounds and interests. Their framework, PAGE, rewrites educational content around each student's context, such as major and hobbies.

PAGE was deployed inside a semester-long intelligent tutoring system and tested in a real course. Students receiving personalized materials learned measurably more than peers with standard content. They also reported higher engagement, stronger perceived relevance, and more trust in the system. Beyond the headline gains, the study draws design lessons for personalization tools: how much adaptation helps, where it can misfire, and how teachers might supervise it. The work shows personalization working in an authentic setting rather than a laboratory demo.
arxiv-2509-15168:
Michela Rigoselli and six co-authors hunt for TeV halos hiding among unidentified gamma-ray sources in a 2025 astrophysics contribution. New observatories have multiplied the known sources of very-high-energy gamma rays, yet many remain unidentified because the instruments resolve them poorly. About half coincide with a pulsar, a spinning neutron star.

Some of these extended sources may be TeV halos: clouds of high-energy particles that escaped a pulsar or its nebula and now diffuse through space. A halo's radial brightness profile differs from supernova remnants and pulsar wind nebulae, so resolving that profile is the key test. The authors gather every pulsar coinciding with an unidentified extended source and check whether its spin-down power and age can sustain a halo, sorting likely halos from impostors.
arxiv-2509-15768:
Herve Goeau leads a team that reports on a 2024 contest to name plants in plot photos. Field photos of small plots are key for ecology: they standardize sampling and let surveys scale. Botanists name every species in each plot by hand, which is slow. The contest asked whether AI could speed that work.

The test set holds thousands of plot images, labeled by experts across more than eight hundred species. Training data hold over a million single plant images, plus pre-trained vision models. The task is to list all species in a high resolution plot photo. The paper details the data, the scoring, the entrants' methods, and the scores they reached.
arxiv-2509-15868:
Johannes Leonhardt, Juergen Gall, and Ribana Roscher map land cover from satellite images using sparse expert labels. Large land maps guide many Earth science uses. Survey based label sets are principled and scalable, but their labels cover the ground sparsely. Standard deep models trained on them give fragmented, noisy maps.

Their frame, LC-SLab, labels whole objects instead of single pixels. Objects are coherent regions, which sets a smallest mapping unit and cleans the output. The frame is the first to explore object based deep learning for this task in a systematic way. It supports grouping at the input stage with graph networks, and at the output stage by merging pixel model results. Traits from images round out the input.
arxiv-2509-15968:
Shiyu Fang leads a team that improves self driving in rare, risky scenes. Such long tail cases are uncommon yet cause a share of crashes far above their frequency. Vision language action models reason well and could help, but data for rare scenes is scarce and learning there is inefficient. Their frame, CoReVLA, learns in two stages: collect, then refine.

First the model fine tunes on a mix of open driving question sets to learn the basics. It then drives in a cave like simulator where human takeovers flag scenes it mishandles. Each takeover marks a long tail case. Last, preference based training teaches it from those human choices. That avoids the reward gaming that hand made scores invite.
arxiv-2509-16368:
Maps that bend quantum states can expose entanglement when they pass some tests and fail others. Hajir Al Zadjali and Farrukh Mukhamedov study one family in between, the Kadison-Schwarz maps, which obey an inequality that sits between plain positivity and full positivity. They describe a subset of these maps on the smallest matrix space, for maps that keep the identity fixed.

From that description they derive clear conditions for such a map to count as Kadison-Schwarz, and give nontrivial examples. The class covered is wider than the well-known bistochastic maps. Sharper maps could sharpen entanglement tests in quantum information.
arxiv-2509-16868:
Matthew Harper, Ben-Michael Kohli, Jiebo Song, and Guillaume Tahar study patterns in link invariants in a 2025 math paper. A link invariant assigns numbers to a knotted link. One invariant, Links-Gould, generalizes a classic polynomial with two variables. For alternating links, its coefficients seem to alternate in sign and form a smooth, single-peaked pattern.

The team gather experimental and computational evidence for that pattern. They also link a related guess to Lorentzian polynomials, a class with strong shape traits. After a suitable scaling, the classic polynomial itself seems to sit in that class. Evidence, not proof, is the paper's offer, pointing to deep structure.
arxiv-2509-17068:
Chen Wang, Sarah Erfani, Tansu Alpcan, and Christopher Leckie detect odd trajectories over long spans in a 2025 paper. A path can look normal step by step yet be odd in intent. Past detectors miss either the high-level goal or the low-level detail. Their model joins a goal-aware layer with a detail layer, both built on diffusion.

Subgoal transition knowledge feeds the combined model. It captures the diverse spread of normal paths. Tests show anomaly scores improved by up to a third over top baselines, on a key measure. Better long-term detection serves fleet tracking, security patrols, and wildlife movement studies.
arxiv-2509-17368:
V. V. Enaldiev, writing alone, models what happens when a twisted two-layer material is sealed under a cover. His 2025 arXiv paper deals with van der Waals stacks, where encapsulation shields thin functional layers and keeps the stack stable. The cover also presses on the layers, so it changes how their atoms settle and shift against each other.

The model folds that cover effect into one parameter: the rigidity of the interfaces. Inside the bilayer, atoms relax in the plane, and the two layers sit at a set distance apart. Enaldiev tracks how the shift from weak to strong relaxation depends on twist angle. Stiffer covers push the crossover to larger twist angles. By tuning that one parameter, the model matches published lab results on twisted transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers well.
arxiv-2509-17468:
Ce Xu, writing alone, studies the parity of two families of cyclotomic Euler sums. His 2025 arXiv paper uses contour integrals and residue calculus, tools that turn sums into questions about poles in the complex plane. One family multiplies cyclotomic harmonic numbers; the other uses their odd counterparts.

Xu derives explicit formulas for the parity in the linear and quadratic cases. Worked examples show the formulas in action. The results unlock parity formulas for cyclotomic multiple T-values and S-values up to depth three, cousins of the famous multiple zeta values. He also states general theorems on the parity of both sum families at any order. Under broader conditions, the same contour method yields full linear and quadratic formulas, not just parity. The paper adds order to a corner of number theory rich in such sums.
arxiv-2509-17768:
Jessica Ojo, Zina Kamel, and David Ifeoluwa Adelani test how well tools can tell which tongue a text is in. Their 2025 paper calls that task language identification. It is a first step for most tools that work across tongues, yet tests tend to use clean, single-tongue text.

Their bench, DIVERS-Bench, checks speech text, web text, social posts, kids' tales, and mixed text. Top tools did well on clean sets but fell hard on noisy, casual text. A new mixed set with ten tongue pairs also tripped tools up. The work shows a need for tools that cope with real, messy use.
arxiv-2509-17868:
Ethan Ackelsberg and Vitaly Bergelson give a deep study of a classic number pattern and where it holds. Their 2025 paper rests on a theorem about dense sets of whole numbers. In such a set, two points can be found whose gap is a value of a fit polynomial.

The pair place that result in a wider algebra frame: rings of whole elements of global fields. They give exact tests for which polynomials keep the trait there. For finite rings, they also sort which chains of rings give the right pair counts. Old sums over finite fields serve as a key tool.
arxiv-2509-18168:
Dong Liu and Yanxuan Yu parse long texts by cutting them into segments and graphing each part. Their 2025 frame deals with a cost wall: pair-wise work on a whole long text grows as the square of its length. Memory grows just as fast, which blocks very long inputs.

Each segment gets a local sense graph, and a summary node stands for that graph. Summary nodes form a global memory graph for the whole text. New segments can be added with just local work. Queries first find the right segments by summary, then reason in their local graphs. Tests show large speed and memory gains.
arxiv-2509-18368:
High above the South Pole ice, detectors listen for radio pulses from rare, ultra-strong neutrinos. Pawan Giri reports on upgrades to the Askaryan Radio Array, known as ARA, in this 2025 conference paper. The array hunts neutrinos by the radio burst made when one hits the ice. It has run for over a decade as a test bed for new detector ideas.

The report centers on ARA-Next, the planned next data system. New chips would let stations process data on the spot and use smarter triggers. Planned triggers hunt double pulses, match known cosmic ray shapes, check for matches with the IceCube detector, and cut human-made noise by direction. In 2024, two of the five stations got upgraded electronics. The paper also covers the 2024-2025 season updates to the current system. Radio chip systems are set to follow in coming years.
arxiv-2509-18468:
Family and friends give much of the daily care received by older adults with dementia. Mohammad Abdullah Al Faisal examines what that informal care does to thinking skills and health care use. His 2025 paper uses a large United States survey of adults over fifty, tracked from 2010 to 2022. Care choices may reflect the patient's state, so plain comparisons can mislead.

To handle that bias, he uses the number of children as an instrument, a stand-in that shifts care but not outcomes directly. Plain estimates linked more informal care to worse cognition. The instrument-based estimates found no real causal effect on cognition once traits and past cognition were counted. But informal care did cut nursing home use and nights in institutions. No firm effects showed for hospital use or doctor visits. The findings matter for long-term care policy.
arxiv-2509-18668:
Folding a surface in space with flat faces is the idea behind origami constructions in geometry. Zhengyu Zou settles a minimum-vertex question for a hyperbolic surface in this 2025 paper. The surface is a genus two surface, like a two-holed donut, equipped with hyperbolic geometry. He builds a triangulation of it with just ten vertices.

Ten is the least number of vertices that can triangulate such a surface at all. Zou then embeds the surface in hyperbolic three-space so each triangle maps to a geodesic triangle. That kind of map is called a hyperbolic origami embedding. Since the vertex count hits the combinatorial floor, no smaller example can exist. The question of the minimum is thus closed. The result is a neat existence proof in discrete hyperbolic geometry.
arxiv-2509-18768:
Digital life looks weightless, but chips depend on materials purified to extreme levels. Gauthier Roussilhe, Thibault Pirson, David Bol, and Srinjoy Mitra trace that hidden material base in this 2025 paper. Talk of digital impact often stops at a few famous mined metals like cobalt and lithium. The authors argue purity is the sharper lens for semiconductors.

They study a few firms worldwide that supply ultra-high purity inputs for chip making. Those firms emerge as critical actors in tangled supply chains. The chains lean hard on mass-production chemical industries, not just mining. That dependence has stayed mostly out of view in debates on digital impact. The authors call for deeper study of the chemical side of chip supply. Purity, they show, reshapes who holds power upstream of every microchip.
arxiv-2509-18868:
Memory in a language model is more than its training text: it is any stored state that later shapes answers. Dianxing Zhang and six co-authors survey that broader idea in this 2025 paper. They sort memory into four kinds: built into weights, held in context, stored outside, and procedural or episodic. Each kind is tagged by where it lives and how it is written and read.

The survey links mechanisms to tests and to governance, the rules for updating and forgetting. A three-setting protocol keeps comparisons fair across systems with different information access. Layered tests cover recall, editing, privacy, and cross-session consistency. A governance loop coordinates retraining, patch edits, and retrieval, with audits and rollback. Four testable propositions close the paper. The authors aim to give the field one coordinate system for memory research. Comparable, governable memory is the stated goal.
arxiv-2509-19068:
At the center of many dwarf galaxies sits a dense nuclear star cluster, and nobody is fully sure how it got there. Mélina Poulain and ten co-authors study such clusters in 41 dwarf galaxies from the MATLAS survey, using sharp Hubble Space Telescope images. The leading idea is that globular clusters spiral in and merge at the center, with some extra stars born in place from infalling gas. The sample leans toward large, faint dwarfs, including ultra-diffuse galaxies.

Hubble's clarity revealed 13 nucleated dwarfs not known before, plus two galaxies with double nuclei. Modeling each cluster's light profile, the team found brighter clusters tend to have steeper profiles and bluer centers, a hint of mixed origins. Several clusters are heavier than counterparts in similar galaxies elsewhere. The authors suggest tidal disruption or unusually rich merger histories may explain the excess.
arxiv-2509-19568:
Every chip hides a secret map that scrambles memory addresses before they reach the memory chips. Antoine Plin and three co-authors recover that map from outside the chip, with no insider knowledge. Timing clashes in the memory reveal which addresses share a bank. The authors model the scrambling as linear math over bits and prove how the clash pattern exposes the map.

Their algorithm rebuilds the full bank mask in polynomial time and tolerates noisy timing data. Older heuristic hunts were partial and slow. A full map helps engineers tune software to the memory layout. It also helps security teams judge attacks such as Rowhammer, which hammer one memory row to flip bits in the next. The method works across platforms, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-19868:
Frustrated magnets can refuse to order, forming classical spin liquids with flat bands and emergent gauge fields. Naïmo Davier lays out recipes for building such systems from clusters of spins. Interactions are rewritten as rules on clusters, and symmetry guides how clusters decorate a parent lattice. Vertices and bonds can both host clusters.

A design trade-off appears: fewer cluster types mean more flat bands and stronger spin-liquid character, but denser links that are harder to build. The framework is tunable across many parent lattices. Quick characterization tools accompany the recipes. Such blueprints help experimentalists aim synthesis at lattices with the right frustration. The work turns scattered known examples into a general construction kit.
arxiv-2509-19968:
Catalysts change shape and make-up in hot reaction gases, so the stable form depends on the gas around it. Jon Eunan Quinlivan Dominguez and four co-authors speed the hunt for those stable forms. Their search checks shape and make-up at once, under set gas pressure and heat. A learned force model, trained as the search runs, stands in for costly quantum math.

Only the best candidates earn a full quantum check. A smooth fingerprint of each atom layout feeds the learner. The point is to judge catalysts as they work, not as they sit in empty space. Cutting the quantum load makes that real-world test cheap enough to run. The team tests the scheme on chosen systems.
arxiv-2509-20468:
Two-color quantum chromodynamics can be simulated where ordinary QCD cannot, because its sign problem vanishes. Manato Sakai and Daiki Suenaga explore its cold, dense phases in a 2025 arXiv paper. They use a version with two light and two heavy flavors. The focus is the axial anomaly, a quantum effect that mixes flavors in subtle ways.

Their linear sigma model describes both parities of hadrons and the superfluid phase where light pairs condense. Inside that phase, the strange chiral condensate grows stronger, an effect traced to the anomaly's flavor mixing. A second model confirms the enhancement. The analysis also predicts a new superfluid phase of heavy pairs at high density. A complete inverted mass ordering for negative-parity pairs emerges when anomaly effects are strong.
