Within the system, the authors obtain exact dynamical generalizations of several well-known regular black hole answers. Those give theorists analytic models of collapse that avoid singularities without sacrificing motion.
arxiv-2602-11068:
Strong lenses bend light, but their surroundings may bend the models too. William J. Gottemoller and thirteen co-authors measure eighty-nine confirmed lenses from the AGEL survey, pairing each deflector's Einstein mass with its halo setting from galaxy density maps. Nearly half sit in cluster settings, while only a small share have cluster-scale Einstein masses.

Einstein mass and density correlate only weakly, which the authors link to selection bias toward galaxy-scale lenses and to faint arcs that hide large radii. AGEL deflectors also sit in denser fields than control fields. The study offers a way to flag setting effects in lens models and publishes lens settings and sky maps for all eighty-nine systems.
arxiv-2602-11468:
Robot task planners usually assume every needed object is already known. Raihan Islam Arnob and five co-authors build a planning frame for missing objects using learning-informed object search actions. Each such action is a policy to find and retrieve one object, informed by model-based expected costs.

High-level planning treats those actions as fixed, interleaving search and execution into plans that are effective, sound, and complete despite doubt. The design stays compatible with current full-knowledge solvers. Tests in simulated homes and in the real world beat non-learned and learned rivals on recall and meal preparation tasks. The work lets planners ask what is needed and when to look for it.
arxiv-2602-11968:
Tracking how word meanings shift over time needs corpora spread across years and languages, yet multilingual resources beyond a dozen major languages remain scarce. Mariia Fedorova and two co-authors present DHPLT, an open collection of diachronic corpora in 41 diverse languages, built from web-crawled datasets with crawl timestamps as approximate creation dates. The collection covers three periods, 2011 to 2015, 2020 to 2021, and 2024 to the present, with 1 million documents per period for each language.

Alongside the texts, the authors provide pre-computed word and token embeddings plus lexical substitutions for chosen target words, while leaving other researchers free to pick their own targets from the same data. DHPLT aims to fill the gap in multilingual diachronic resources and open new experimental setups for semantic change research. All resources are publicly available, sorted by language.
arxiv-2602-12268:
AI agents now handle real tasks through long chats and tool calls, but training them by reinforcement learning is awkward when goals lack checkable rewards. Zhen Zhang led this work with 13 co-authors, presenting CM2, a frame that swaps outcome rewards for checklist rewards. Each turn's intended behaviour is split into fine binary criteria with evidence grounding and structured notes, turning open judging into steadier classification.

Rewards stay sparse while evaluation criteria stay dense, balancing stability and signal. Training runs in a scalable language-model-simulated tool world, avoiding costly real tool engineering. From an 8-billion-parameter base on 8,000 examples, CM2 beats supervised fine-tuning by 8 points on tau-Bench, 10 on BFCL-V4, and 12 on ToolSandbox, matching or beating similar open baselines.
arxiv-2602-12468:
Diffusion language models generate text globally rather than word by word, but their continuous latent dynamics make discrete rules hard to enforce. Jinwoo Kim led this work with two co-authors, asking how to guarantee outputs such as a JSON file matching a given schema. Their training-free guidance method steers continuous diffusion models to satisfy formal syntactic constraints expressed as regular expressions.

The method builds an analytic score estimating the chance that a latent state decodes to a valid string accepted by a given regular expression. It then uses its gradient to guide sampling, with no auxiliary classifiers to train. Denoising targets the base model conditioned on syntactic validity. Implemented as Diffinity on the PLAID model and tested on 180 regular-expression constraints, it reaches 68 to 96 percent satisfaction. It incurs only a small perplexity cost, beating autoregressive constrained decoding on both satisfaction and quality.
arxiv-2602-12668:
Computing a sparse subgraph of a directed graph that proves connectivity is central to streaming and distributed graph methods. Ho-Lin Chen led this work with three co-authors, studying space cost of that job in terms of independence number. A k-node strong connectivity certificate is a subgraph H. For every pair of distinct nodes s and t, the count of pairwise internally node-disjoint paths from s to t in H is at least k. Otherwise it matches the count in the original graph.

Prior work focused on narrow graph classes, since directed connectivity problems are hard in general. This paper gives space bounds for certificates in graphs of bounded independence number, in both streaming and distributed models, with matching upper and lower bounds in key regimes. Results show independence number is a useful gauge for taming directed connectivity certification.
arxiv-2602-12868:
Spencer's six standard deviations theorem says signs can be chosen to keep many sums small, and a complex analogue has been conjectured. Tomasz Kobos and Marin Varivoda state the conjecture precisely. For vectors in complex n-space with entries bounded by one, a sign vector with unit-modulus entries should keep every inner product within the square root of n. That bound is sharp, as Hadamard matrices show.

Should the conjecture prove true in dimension n, it would also fix the Banach-Mazur distance between complex l1 and l-infinity spaces at the square root of n. The authors prove the conjecture for dimensions two and three, settling those distances, and verify a related conjecture about distances between complex lp spaces in dimension two. The result completes the picture for all such distances in two dimensions.
arxiv-2602-12968:
Chatbots that recommend without being asked must guess intent from behaviour and context, a zero-query task where semantic gaps hurt. Junhua Liu and five co-authors propose RGAlign-Rec, a closed-loop framework pairing a language-model semantic reasoner with a query-enhanced ranking model. The gap between discrete user features and knowledge-base intents, and the mismatch between generic model outputs and ranking goals, are tackled together.

Ranking-guided alignment, a multi-stage training paradigm, feeds downstream ranking signals back to refine the model's latent reasoning. On a large Shopee industrial dataset, the framework gains 0.12% in GAUC, cutting error rate by 3.52% relatively and lifting Recall@3 by 0.56%. Live A/B tests add up: the ranking model alone lifts click-through rate by 0.98%, with alignment adding 0.13% more, validating the closed-loop design in production.
arxiv-2602-13068:
Hot plasmas at kinetic scales, where small-angle Coulomb collisions rule, are modelled by the Vlasov-Poisson-Landau system. Daniel Finn and three co-authors present a structure-preserving number system combining particle-in-cell discretisation with discrete gradient time integrators. The scheme conserves mass, momentum, and energy by construction, plus monotonic mess production, in both continuous and discrete forms.

The conservative integrator serves both the Hamiltonian Vlasov-Poisson part and the dissipative Landau part, implemented with the PETSc library to show the preserved traits. For plasma mock run, structure preservation is not cosmetic: schemes that leak mass or energy, or reverse mess, can produce plausible-looking but unphysical results. This system aims to keep long kinetic mock runs honest by construction.
arxiv-2602-13268:
AI systems that decide for people need more than accuracy; they need a sense of what is right, and that sense is still poorly measured. This paper compares ways to build ethical skill into decision models, then adds a new yardstick called Expected Moral Shortfall. The yardstick models the risk of loss in the least moral cases, and the model is steered to shrink that shortfall while keeping its performance up.

The measure is tested on two data sets against rival methods, and the paper closes by weighing performance, complexity, and the scale of ethical skill against real social impact. Trade-offs are the point: a model can look strong on paper while still failing the cases where morals matter most. Aisha Aijaz leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13368:
Beauty judgments often favor average faces, a finding shown for women's faces in earlier work. This study tests whether the same holds for men's faces. It uses faces from the Chicago Face Database, morphed into average faces for low, medium, and high width-ratio groups, each built from 96 or 97 photos. Each average face was then shifted in width ratio across levels in both directions, yielding 21 faces for comparison.

In forced-choice trials, participants picked the more beautiful face in each pair, and a Bayesian analysis inferred which width ratio was judged most beautiful. Results support averageness as attractive in male faces too, with care taken to control image artifacts and to note ethnicity as a possible moderating factor. Theresa Tennstedt leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13568:
Language models increasingly meet social information: other agents' answers, tool outputs, or human recommendations. Humans weigh such inputs by source credibility and consensus strength, and this paper asks whether models do the same, and whether they favor human feedback over feedback from other models. Four instruction-tuned models faced three binary decision tasks, reading comprehension, multi-step reasoning, and moral judgment, with prior responses attributed to friends, human experts, or other models.

Across tasks, models conformed far more to responses labeled as human experts, even when those signals were wrong, and revised answers toward experts more readily than toward other models. Expert framing thus acts as a strong prior for current models, a credibility-sensitive social influence spanning decision domains. Anooshka Bajaj leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13768:
Relativistic spin-momentum locking was proven in materials with broken time order and zero net pull in the slow limit, such as altermagnets and tilted magnets. Using density functional theory, this paper shows the effect in ferromagnets, covering a broad class of magnetic matter with magnetic sites linked by rotation sameness and set beside fcc nickel. In strontium ruthenate, lopsided exchange yields spin canting at right angles to the easy axis. In all other cases spin canting is forbidden, yet relativistic locking still adds sizably in momentum space.

Sample ferromagnets including strontium ruthenate, chromium telluride and chromium arsenide, half-Heusler manganese platinum antimonide, and fcc nickel show strong effects. Minor parts of these ferromagnets host locking similar to altermagnets, while lopsided manganese platinum antimonide hosts relativistic p-wave patterns. Ferromagnets' larger bandwidths promise an even-wave platform. Xujia Gong leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13868:
Udhaya Srinivasan and one co-author present a 2026 arXiv paper on an AI helper for next-generation radio networks. AI-native radio access networks are hard for engineers to run in real time, and small firms often lack local expertise. Prior tools helped plan radio and core parts, but not joint control of radio and edge AI.

Their assistant handles turn-based chats about layered AI-RAN problems, with a user dashboard, an intelligence layer, and a knowledge layer. In validation it scored 78% on service design, 89% on operating AI-RAN tools, and 67% on tuning performance, with a mean reply time of 13 seconds. The authors note hallucination risks, but see lower running costs for small enterprise users.
arxiv-2602-13968:
Ngoc Cuong Nguyen, writing alone, offers a 2026 arXiv paper on the fine local behavior of functions in complex Sobolev spaces. The setting is a bounded open set in complex n-space, and the main tool is a functional capacity inspired by a global version due to Vigny in 2007.

The author proves a sharp inequality linking this capacity to the Bedford-Taylor capacity for plurisubharmonic functions, shows the new capacity is a Choquet capacity, and proves an Alexander-Taylor type inequality. Those steps strengthen results of Dinh, Marinescu, and Vu, and of Vigny and Vu. A Moser-Trudinger type inequality in the space is then characterized by a volume-capacity inequality.
arxiv-2602-14168:
Guilherme S. L. Fabris and four co-authors study a 2026 arXiv carbon material called hydrogen-substituted graphdiyne. This porous three-dimensional framework has drawn interest for tunable properties, yet how its stacking order shapes behavior was largely unexplored. The paper runs first-principles calculations across stacking sequences.

The AA and ABC stackings prove most favorable in energy, with AA as the global minimum, matching recent experiments. The material is an indirect semiconductor with a band gap of 0.89 eV, governed by interlayer coupling and van der Waals forces. Its optical absorption spans visible to ultraviolet light, pointing to uses in optoelectronic devices.
arxiv-2602-14468:
Chang Liu and five co-authors propose a 2026 arXiv reinforcement learning method that controls response length. Reward-driven training has strengthened language models, but it can also produce excessively long responses, inflating latency and compute costs. Older length controls lean on set heuristic reward shaping, which can clash with task goals and need fragile tuning.

LACONIC enforces a target token budget during training through an augmented objective combining task reward with a length-based cost. The cost scale adapts throughout training to balance brevity against task performance, with a theoretical guarantee supporting the method. Across math reasoning models and datasets, LACONIC preserved or improved pass@1 while cutting output length by over 50%, and held out-of-domain performance with 44% fewer tokens.
arxiv-2602-14968:
Wang and colleagues address a gap in automatic 3D scene building for robot training. Most methods place objects but ignore ties such as contact, support, balance, and containment. Their system, PhyScensis, pairs a language-model agent with a solver run by a physics engine. The agent puts forward assets with spatial and physical tags. The solver builds them, and solver feedback drives more rounds.

Chance-based code keeps scenes steady, while a second rule weighs steadiness against spatial ties. The system stays easy to steer through text and numbers such as relative spots. In tests it beats prior methods on scene richness, visual quality, and true-to-life accuracy, giving one pipeline for dense, lifelike scenes for robot hand work like shelves and packed boxes.
arxiv-2602-15768:
Reymondet and colleagues quantify how fine-scale sea surface temperature shifts drive latent heat flux shifts over the Southern Ocean. Latent heat flux is a main path for ocean-air exchange of heat and moisture. Yet the role of shifts at scales of 100 kilometres or less remains poorly known. The team uses a year-long, global, fully coupled ocean-air run at kilometre-scale resolution.

Year-mean flux in eddy-rich regions hits about 215 watts per square metre. That is roughly three times the eddy-poor value. Ocean mesoscale and submesoscale shifts account for up to about 80 percent of total flux variance in eddy-rich sectors. In eddy-poor ones, the share falls to 10 percent. Strong submesoscale fronts force a local secondary circulation reaching into the mid-troposphere. ERA5 reanalysis largely misses those fine ocean scales, muting the air response.
arxiv-2602-15868:
Boman models language model failure with a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine. Each tape stands for one stage of the pipeline. The stages are input text, tokens, word lists, model weights, activations, chance scores, and output text. This frame lets each fault be traced to the stage where it starts.

Token splits can hide letter patterns that counting needs. That shows one plain cause of a slip on a trivial task. Chain of thought helps by moving work out onto the output tape. But that move has hard limits too. Boman offers the model as a testable rival to shape metaphors. It adds principled error study to plain scaling laws.
arxiv-2602-16068:
Yanni Bills and J. S. Wettlaufer connect a stripped-down chaotic model to real wind reversals in lab convection. The Lorenz equations are a severe truncation of the equations for Rayleigh-Benard convection. The authors study a stochastic form of those equations. It models how warm boundary layers interact with the core flow in the lab setup. Long runs, out of reach for the full equations, yield a spread of times between lobe switches with a skewed, multifractal shape.

In the Gaussian frequency range, the runs mirror lab measures, and classic checks show Brownian second-moment stats. Closer looks reveal a nonlinear moment-exponent function, hence multifractality. A simple two-scale Cantor-cascade check reproduces these traits. The authors conclude that multiplicative intermittency, a hallmark of turbulence, strongly shapes the stats. That makes the stochastic Lorenz system a faithful low-dimensional stand-in for mean-wind reversals.
arxiv-2602-16168:
Supravat Sarkar proves a conjecture of Miyanishi about endomorphisms of varieties. The setting is a quasi-projective variety over a field, with a birational endomorphism that is injective outside a closed subset of codimension at least two. Sarkar shows such a map must be an automorphism, a result that generalizes an old theorem of Ax and settles Miyanishi conjecture. The statement is short, but its force lies in how little it assumes.

A key step is a finiteness result on class groups, interesting in its own right. For readers in algebraic geometry, the proof turns a local injectivity condition, failing only on a small subset, into a global conclusion that the map is invertible everywhere. The paper thus closes a long-standing question with a clean theorem, while supplying a finiteness tool that may serve other problems about varieties and their endomorphisms.
arxiv-2602-16468:
Jung Min Choi, Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi, and Lars Schmidt-Thieme propose HPMixer, a layered patching mixer for time series work. In long-term forecasting, capturing both repeat patterns and rest dynamics matters. HPMixer models cycles and rest in a split yet complementary way.

The cycle part uses a learned cycle module enhanced with a nonlinear channel-wise multilayer perceptron for greater expressiveness. The rest part passes through a learned stationary wavelet transform to extract stable, shift-invariant frequency-domain representations. A channel-mixing encoder then models explicit inter-channel dependencies, while a two-level non-overlapping patching mechanism captures coarse- and fine-scale rest variations. By combining split cycle modelling with structured, multi-scale rest learning, HPMixer offers an effective framework. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show it achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance against recent baselines.
arxiv-2602-16568:
Ziyun Chen, Jerry Li, Kevin Tian, and Yusong Zhu separate two models of sparse recovery. The task is finding the support of a sparse signal from few measurements. In the oblivious model, the guarantee need hold only for each fixed signal in turn. In the adaptive model, it must hold for all signals at once. The distinction matters for variable selection, where the goal is to name the right variables.

Under the oblivious model, the optimal error is reachable in near-linear time with a modest sample count. Under the adaptive model, far more samples are necessary for any algorithm to reach the same bound. That split contrasts with the standard squared-error setting. There, the smaller sample count suffices even adaptively. The paper also opens a partially adaptive model with nontrivial guarantees.
arxiv-2602-16868:
Joheen Chakraborty and co-authors present the first systematic study of minute-to-hours stochastic variability in the X-ray light of tidal disruption events, using XMM-Newton data and Fourier methods. They measure spectral traits, power spectral densities, fractional variability amplitudes, and energy dependence for eighteen events spanning fifty-four observations, split between thermal disk-dominated states and nonthermal hard X-ray corona states.

Events with coronae prove more variable with steeper power spectra, indicating longer correlation timescales. That state-transition behavior resembles X-ray binaries, which vary more in the hard state than the soft state. Yet newborn disruption coronae show flatter spectra and softer energy spectra than long-lived active galactic nucleus counterparts. Thermal event variability rises with photon energy, consistent with local temperature fluctuations boosted in the Wien tail, offering a probe of newborn accretion flow microphysics.
arxiv-2602-17068:
Xiaocai Zhang led a three-author team designing traffic signals for corridors used by many kinds of travelers, not just cars. Buses and trams deserve priority too, yet most signal control still scores vehicle flow alone. The paper presents STDSH-MARL, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework trained centrally and run locally, built around a dual-stage hypergraph attention mechanism that links signals across space and time.

A hybrid action space sets both the next signal phase and its green duration, so timing adapts to live conditions. Tests on a corridor network across five traffic scenarios cut tram waiting time substantially and consistently, while bus gains varied more by scenario. Against strong baselines the method won overall, and ablations singled out temporal hyperedges as the biggest contributor. The work maps the trade-off among network efficiency, tram priority, and bus service.
arxiv-2602-17268:
Weiyu Wu led a large team reporting sixteen early-phase type Ia supernovae from the pilot survey of the Wide Field Survey Telescope. The sample spans the survey's early months and includes three supernovae with early-excess emission features. Discovery magnitudes sat well below peak brightness, and color indices scattered widely in roughly the first ten days, signaling diverse early photometric behavior.

The early-excess objects showed relatively brighter peaks and longer rise times than their peers. The authors argue current theoretical models need further refinement to capture early photometric evolution fully. Drawing on high-cadence multi-band data, they stress that early near-ultraviolet observations are indispensable for pinning down explosion mechanisms and progenitor systems of type Ia supernovae.
arxiv-2602-17368:
Abhishek Padhy led a fourteen-author team programming polarization singularities in a photonic-crystal laser. Handling optical singularities in nanophotonic sources is usually limited by fixed resonator geometry. The team dodges that limit, showing all-optical control of such points in real space while keeping a momentum-space vortex from a symmetry-protected bound state in the continuum.

A shaped optical pump creates a smooth mesoscopic potential, changing slowly against the lattice period. That potential traps a Bloch band with negative mass into lasing states. Envelope functions, and thus far-field textures, follow the pump shape. Using a honeycomb crystal, the team gets room-temperature telecom-band lasing. The singularities sit pinned to key points of that envelope, changeable in number and place by pump shaping, while the intrinsic vortex stays fixed. Results agree in numbers with a math account joining Bloch modes with that theory.
arxiv-2602-17468:
T. C. Wilson led a four-author team on tolerances to driver-witness misalignment in a quasilinear plasma wakefield accelerator. Plasma machines can push particles to high energy with strong fields, and they can be staged or run over long distances. Proton drivers are prized because one stage alone may reach very high energy. In the quasilinear case, the plasma wake is only partly cleared out.

The team looks at what happens when driver and witness beams fail to line up. Their models track sideways motion of the witness bunch and link its spread to how well emittance survives. A single measure, based on witness density after phase mixing, sums up that survival. Tests with particle-in-cell runs set to AWAKE Run 2c values match the models closely. The result gives labs a way to set limits on alignment for AWAKE and similar schemes.
arxiv-2602-17568:
Sofiane Ennadir led a five-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper warning that time series preprocessing deserves more care. Normalization and scaling are basic steps in time series modeling, yet their effect on Transformer models lacked formal analysis. The paper gives the first formal account of how instance-based and global scaling affect Transformer expressivity for time series learning. A new framework measures how well a model separates similar from dissimilar inputs in representation space.

Using that framework, the authors derive theoretical bounds for Standard and Min-Max scaling. The normalization choice can strongly affect representational capacity, depending on task and data. Tests on classification and forecasting benchmarks with Transformer models confirm the theory. No single normalization method wins consistently, and in some cases skipping normalization entirely performs best. The findings call for principled normalization choices tailored to each task and data set, rather than habit.
arxiv-2602-17768:
Boda Lin and team introduce KPM-Bench, a benchmark for fine-grained motion-centric video understanding. Video captioning models still struggle to describe fine motion details and suffer severe hallucination, above all for motion-centric videos where limb dynamics matter yet get neglected. The team attacks both the data gap and the evaluation gap.

An automated pipeline joins kinematic-based motion computation with linguistic parsing to decompose and describe complex human motions in detail. The benchmark holds fine-grained video-caption pairs on limb-level dynamics, diverse question-answer pairs on motion understanding, and a curated set to assess hallucination in motion descriptions. A linguistically grounded extraction algorithm, MoPE, yields a precise hallucination metric independent of large vision-language models, and folding MoPE into GRPO post-training cuts hallucination markedly.
arxiv-2602-17868:
Vasilii Feofanov and team introduce MantisV2, closing the zero-shot gap in time series sorting with fake data and test-time tricks. Base models for time series sorting can serve as universal feature tools for varied later tasks, yet a large gap remained between frozen and fine-tuned nets in early models such as Mantis. The paper strengthens zero-shot feature extraction through three moves.

First, Mantis+, a version of Mantis pre-trained fully on fake time series, is introduced. Second, careful cut-out studies refine the design into MantisV2, an improved and light encoder. Third, an enhanced test-time method leverages mid-layer codes and refines output-token pooling, with self-mixing and cross-model vector fusion adding further gains. Tests on UCR, UEA, human activity recognition and EEG sets show MantisV2 and Mantis+ always beating prior time series base models, reaching state-of-the-art zero-shot scores.
arxiv-2602-17968:
Robert Parker and team propose a method for solving Karush-Kuhn-Tucker systems that exploits block triangular submatrices. First, a Schur split isolates those submatrices; then a block backsolve factors only diag blocks of that form.

Standard factoring of symmetric-indefinite matrices with one-by-one or two-by-two pivots yields fill-in outside diag blocks. That differs from the proposed method. While exploiting a triangular submatrix limits fill-in, one-sided matrix factoring methods do not reveal inertia, which inner point methods need for nonconvex optimization. The team shows their target matrix has inertia known in advance, letting them compute KKT inertia by Sylvester's law. Finally, they show a speed edge on KKT systems from optimization problems with neural network stand-ins in constraints. It reaches up to fifteen times speedups over state-of-the-art symmetric indefinite methods MA57 and MA86 in a same-hardware test.
arxiv-2602-18068:
A Calabrò and colleagues investigate mergers in early-universe galaxy assembly. The team studies more than twelve hundred spectroscopic galaxies at redshifts five to fourteen in six JWST fields, finding mergers via Gini, M-20, and asymmetry measures.

The merger fraction barely changes from the present day to redshift eight. It averages about five percent for major mergers, thirteen percent with minor mergers included. After accounting for observability timescales, merger rates rise more than tenfold from redshift one to seven. Major mergers average about two per galaxy per billion years at redshifts five to ten, tripling with minor mergers included. Above redshift five, mergers boost star formation, though less than below redshift one. Over ten million years, their rates run about one point seven times higher than matched non-mergers, suggesting short bursty episodes. Mergers still contribute only five to ten percent of mass buildup.
arxiv-2602-18568:
Matthew Adiletta and two co-authors design a chip for reasoning models. Their 2026 paper notes large language model inference is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory wall: GPUs scale raw compute but struggle on memory-bandwidth-bound workloads. Reasoning applications worsen this with long outputs, low arithmetic intensity, and tight latency limits, dropping utilization and raising energy per inference.

The team presents the Reasoning Processing Unit, a chiplet-based architecture for scalable memory bandwidth. RPU introduces capacity-optimized high-bandwidth memory trading capacity for cheaper, lower-energy operation. A scalable chiplet architecture follows, with bandwidth-first power and area provisioning. A decoupled microarchitecture separates memory, compute, and communication pipelines, sustaining high bandwidth use. Simulations show up to forty-five point three times lower latency and eighteen point six times higher throughput over an H100 system at equal thermal design power on Llama3-405B.
arxiv-2602-18668:
Rooftop solar owners often make more power than they need, yet local wires still limit what they can share. Zeinab Salehi, with five co-authors, presents a 2026 market design that lets households trade both energy and reactive power with neighbours on the same distribution feeder.

Each household gets a dynamic operating envelope, a personal limit that keeps voltage and heat on the feeder within safe bounds. Trades settle at a competitive equilibrium, the market form of a Nash equilibrium in game terms, and the design is tested on the IEEE 13-node test feeder. The aim is wider use of solar and batteries without breaking the local grid.
arxiv-2602-18768:
Prime path coverage is a demanding test criterion, but listing every prime path in a program graph can explode in number. Jakub Zelek, with three co-authors, presents a 2026 method that generates prime paths without enumerating all simple paths first, by characterising them through strongly connected components.

That characterisation yields necessary conditions on valid endpoints and reduces the job to constrained cycle enumeration in an augmented graph. A streaming algorithm then outputs prime paths incrementally, using a Johnson-style traversal in a much smaller search space and pruning partial paths the moment they prove backward extendable. On real control-flow graphs from open-source C++ and Python projects, the method consistently beats existing approaches with stable delays between outputs.
arxiv-2602-18868:
Open-weight models can be fine-tuned for harmful uses after release, and no training resistance method yet offers theoretical guarantees. Domenic Rosati, with six co-authors, treats such interventions in 2026 as convergence-rate control problems. That framing links optimisation speed with the spectral structure of model weights.

From that insight, the authors develop spectral reparameterisation and derive SpecDef, an algorithm that provably and empirically slows first- and second-order optimisation in non-adversarial settings. In adversarial settings, they prove a fundamental limit for a broad class of such methods, including their own. An attacker with enough knowledge can bring back fast convergence, at the cost of a linearly larger model. Future work must therefore look beyond convergence-rate control alone.
arxiv-2602-18968:
When an agent uses many tools, trouble usually comes from how the tools fit together, not from one bad call. Tao Zhe, with eight co-authors, revisits tool invocation as orchestration in 2026. The core claim is that precise dependency graphs and fine-grained planning are not needed at all.

A coarse-grained layer structure gives enough global guidance, while mistakes at run time get fixed where they happen. The design learns a layered run structure from high-level tool links, then lets context constraints drive execution layer by layer. A schema-aware reflective correction mechanism spots and repairs errors locally, so faults stay with single calls instead of forcing a fresh plan for the whole path. The result is a light, reusable orchestration part, and tests show steady tool use with less complexity and overhead.
arxiv-2602-19268:
Edge devices for the internet of things need to run AI fast while sipping power, and vector engines are a key part of that hardware. Sonu Kumar and three colleagues present CORVET, a vector engine built around an iterative CORDIC unit for multiply-accumulate work. That classic trick computes with shifts and adds instead of costly multipliers. The design can switch at run time between approximate and accurate modes.

That flexibility lets the same chip trade a little accuracy for speed when a task allows it. Through vectorized, time-shared work and adjustable precision, it reaches up to four times the throughput on the same hardware. A shared block for activation functions plus a light pooling and normalization unit rounds out the design. The engine thus supports a wide range of edge jobs without a large resource bill.
arxiv-2602-19368:
Data cleaning is often treated as a routine chore, yet in practice it leans heavily on human judgment. Hazim AbdElazim and two co-authors report a careful survey study in which volunteers spotted errors, fixed data, imputed values, and matched entities in census-like scenarios with known validity. The study finds steady evidence for several cognitive bias patterns in these daily tasks.

Framing effects appear when surface formatting changes raise false-positive error flags despite the same meaning. Expert cues shift choices through anchoring, atypical but valid combos get flagged as odd ones out, and surface likeness drives confident false positives in entity matching. People also prefer leaving values missing over filling in plausible ones, an omission bias, while bowing to automation stays limited.
arxiv-2602-19768:
Vision-language models usually grasp a whole image at once, but people look around: their gaze traces a path, linking words to regions. A 2026 arXiv paper by Fan Yang and eight co-authors presents TraceVision, a model that builds path-aware spatial understanding into vision and language together.

A dedicated perception module fuses visual features with path information in both directions, while a simplification step extracts key points from raw gaze paths. A three-stage training pipeline lets gaze paths guide both description writing and region finding. The model extends to path-guided segmentation and video understanding, and the authors build a new reasoning-based narrative data set to strengthen it. Tests across captioning, prediction, region tasks, and segmentation show leading results.
arxiv-2602-19868:
Verified compilers must guarantee that compiling preserves what a program observably does. Loop optimizations strain the usual proof frameworks. A 2026 arXiv paper by David Knothe and Oliver Bringmann combines small-step and big-step semantics to verify such optimizations.

Small-step semantics suit local changes but sit awkwardly with structural ones. The authors therefore use big-step rules for structural changes, with an abstract behavioural layer as a shared interface. Coinductive big-step rules are extended to handle divergence with finite and infinite traces. That matches small-step expressiveness. That lets big-step changes sit inside an existing small-step pipeline without breaking top-level soundness theorems. The approach is shown in CompCert with checked loop unswitching and full loop unrolling.
arxiv-2602-20168:
Triage nurses decide fast with little information. Yet most models that predict deterioration are tested on signals unavailable at first assessment. A 2026 arXiv paper by KMA Solaiman and two co-authors benchmarks early deterioration forecasts honestly, under the time limits and sensing limits of real triage.

The cohort comes from MIMIC-IV-ED, with repeat patients removed. Two settings are compared: full triage and a vitals-only bare-bones setting. Both use only data from the first hour after arrival. Across methods, scores fall only slightly on vitals alone, showing early body signals carry strong clinical signal. Removing inputs one group at a time, and probing what models rely on, points to breathing and oxygen measures as the strongest early risk signals. Models degrade smoothly and stably as sensing shrinks.
arxiv-2602-20468:
Spotting anomalies in multivariate time series matters for industrial control, telemetry, and service monitoring, but shifting relations between variables and ever-present noise make it hard. Zhongpeng Qi and three co-authors propose CGSTA, a method with two innovations. Dynamic layered graph construction builds local, regional, and global views of variable relations per sliding window. Under this contrastive step, graphs from one viewpoint are set against each other, while matching time slices are brought into correspondence between viewpoints.

Stability-aware alignment then holds a per-scale stable reference learned from normal data, guiding fast-changing graphs toward it to suppress noise. Fused multi-scale and temporal features feed a conditional density estimator that scores each time step for anomaly. Across four benchmarks, CGSTA performs best on PSM and WADI and matches baselines on SWaT and SMAP.
arxiv-2602-20968:
Symmetries in quantum mechanics can break in fine ways when a system is nudged, yielding anomalies. Maxim Gritskov, Andrey Losev, and Saveliy Timchenko study those small-nudge anomalies with cohomology in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their start point is a Hamiltonian plus a symmetry maker, which form a unitary picture of a two-dimensional Abelian Lie algebra on a Hilbert space.

In that setup, nudges of the system match the first Chevalley-Eilenberg cohomology group, while anomalies of the symmetry match the second. The cohomology frame turns a physics question about broken symmetry into an algebra sorting problem. Readers get a tight math lens for telling when a nudge keeps a symmetry and when it spoils it.
arxiv-2603-01568:
Leyla Roksan Caglar, Pedro Mediano, and Baihan Lin compare how people and AI vision systems handle new visual conditions. Their 2026 work uses rate-distortion theory, which studies how much detail a system keeps as inputs get harder. Standard scores show who is right more often, but not how grace under strain differs.

The team turns each system record of hits and misses into a curve of cost versus error. Two numbers sum up each curve: slope for the price of holding accuracy, and curve shape for how abrupt the drop is. People and eighteen deep models face the same controlled image changes. Both groups follow one broad compression rule, yet people trade off more smoothly. Deep models sit in steeper, more brittle zones, even when base accuracy matches.
arxiv-2603-01768:
Pratik Jawahar and Maurizio Pierini propose a new building block for learning over time in this 2026 work. Current units split into two flawed camps: discrete ones with unstable gradients, and smooth ones that leak information away. Both flaws hurt memory for long sequences and physical signals.

Their unit, CHLU, borrows its structure from relativistic Hamiltonian physics, the math of energy-based motion. A symplectic integrator, a stepwise solver that respects that structure, keeps phase-space volume strictly conserved. That conservation targets stability over endless horizons, with tunable filtering of noise as a bonus. As a proof of principle, the unit learns to generate handwritten digits from a classic data set. The authors present it as a physics-grounded primitive, not a full replacement for standard stacks.
arxiv-2603-01968:
Hyeonbin Hwang and Yeachan Park argue that task symmetry drives the sudden leap from memorization to generalization. Their 2026 work studies grokking, where a network first memorizes, then abruptly learns the real rule. Low-dimensional internal structure appears at that leap, but what organizes it was unclear.

They identify a three-stage dynamic that recurs across grokking cases in their tests. Memorization comes first, then symmetry acquisition, then geometric organization of the representation space. Generalization itself emerges during the symmetry stage, before the final tidy geometry settles in. Tests span algebraic, structural, and relational reasoning tasks with the same pattern. A symmetry-based diagnostic can flag the onset of generalization early, and the team proposes ways to speed that onset up.
arxiv-2603-02168:
Sergio Davis, Catalina Ruíz, Claudia Loyola, and colleagues extend a classic heat formula in this 2026 physics paper. The classic result links swings in motion energy to how much heat a closed system can hold. It was derived for one narrow case, the sealed system at fixed energy. Many real systems sit in broader settings, though, and need a wider rule.

Their new formula holds for any steady setting and any system size. It ties motion energy swings to total energy swings and to heat capacity. The old result falls out when total energy stops changing. Tests used computer sampling of vibrating springs and exact math for a flat energy case. The rule may help study small systems with odd heat behavior.
arxiv-2603-02268:
Jeet Bandhu Lahiri, Parshva Runwal, Arvasu Kulkarni, and colleagues test brain-wave models across hospitals in this 2026 study. Foundation models for EEG, the brain's electrical signals, often train on narrow hospital archives. Strong scores on like data may reflect the recording setup, not the brain. Their model, PRISM, varies training mix and tuning style while holding the rest fixed.

Narrow training won on matched tests, while diverse training adapted better to new data. On a hard new task, telling epilepsy apart from look-alike conditions, diverse training won by a wide margin. The diverse model also matched a far larger rival trained on many more hours. The team further shows that two benchmarks rank the same models very differently, and explains why.
arxiv-2603-02368:
Alexandra Diaconu, Mădălina Vînaga, and Bogdan Alexe release a Romanian speech benchmark in this 2026 paper. Speech recognition lags for languages with little training data. Romanian systems also face new domains that differ from their training speech. Their data set, RO-N3WS, aims to test and improve generalization across such shifts.

The set holds over one hundred twenty-six hours of transcribed audio. Sources range from broadcast news and audiobooks to film speech, children's stories, and podcasts. Leading systems were tested both as-is and after fine-tuning. Fake speech from expressive text-to-speech models was also compared. Even small fine-tuning on real RO-N3WS speech cut errors sharply versus zero-shot use. All models, scripts, and splits will be released for repeatable work.
arxiv-2603-02468:
Moeen Ul Islam, Cheng Ouyang, Xinda Qi, and colleagues build a modular soft robotic arm in this 2026 paper. Rigid robots can be unsafe around people and clumsy in messy settings. Soft arms bend safely, but single-piece designs limit reach and repair. Their arm stacks cable-driven segments that each move independently.

The body is molded silicone with tendon channels built inside. A dual-helical tendon layout protects the cables during bending. Stacking three segments grew the flat workspace roughly thirteenfold over one segment. Workspace volume grew far more, by nearly forty times. Silicone stiffness trades bend against strength: softer bends better, stiffer bears load better. Tuning that stiffness lets designers balance softness and power for each task.
arxiv-2603-02568:
Sugana Chawla, Si Chen, Julia Qian, and colleagues frame a workshop on responsible AI for STEM careers in this 2026 paper. AI now shapes feedback, advising, and access to career information for students. That makes AI part of the infrastructure forming career identity and readiness. How such tools should be designed and governed at scale remains unsettled.

The half-day workshop gathers researchers, educators, practitioners, and policymakers. Four themes structure the talks and group activities. They cover readiness definitions, AI's proper role in career choices, developmental fit across school levels, and equity risks. Lightning talks and cross-sector dialogue surface design tensions and governance principles. The goal is shared language and workable frameworks for developmentally grounded, responsible career AI.
arxiv-2603-02668:
Austin Letson, Leopoldo Sarra, Auguste Poiroux, and colleagues built SorryDB, a 2026 benchmark of real unfinished proofs. The tasks come from seventy-eight live Lean formalization projects on GitHub, where a sorry marks a step still to prove. Unlike fixed contest sets, this list keeps updating as projects change.

Because the tasks track real community needs, tools that climb this benchmark should help working mathematicians directly. The team tested language models, agent systems, and dedicated provers on a snapshot of one thousand tasks. An agent built on Gemini Flash scored best overall, yet no approach won everywhere. Older provers and even a fixed tactic list each beat the leaders on some tasks.
arxiv-2603-02768:
Bin Qiu, Wenchi Cheng, and Hongxiang He secure a wireless link by flying one antenna through a planned path. Their 2026 paper builds a virtual multi-antenna channel from a single-antenna autonomous aerial vehicle. The moving craft creates a synthetic aperture, focusing signal strength toward a chosen direction and away from others.

The team jointly designs the flight node placement, the symbol plan, and the sending and receiving beam patterns. Their goals are higher channel capacity for the base station, tight limits on what eavesdroppers can pick up, and low transmit power per node. A receiver design based on constrained variance filtering suppresses jamming. Simulations show the combined method lifts capacity over prior approaches while holding the security constraints.
arxiv-2603-03268:
Yushi Hamaguchi studies the long-run behavior of stochastic Volterra equations, used for processes whose future depends on their whole past. Because such equations are not Markovian, their present state alone does not summarize them, which blocks standard tools. His 2026 paper lifts each one into a larger Markovian system, an evolution law on a rich function space, where those tools apply again.

Hamaguchi proves the lifted system is exponentially ergodic, settling toward a single steady behavior, using a general version of Harris's theorem. The proof builds a custom coupling and distance that exploit the equations' nonlocal structure despite heavy degeneracy. He also shows finite-dimensional equations can approximate the stationary law closely. The result both analyzes the original ones and justifies the embedding trick that statistical physicists already use.
arxiv-2603-03468:
Olga Avsajanishvili confronts a universe whose vacuum energy might change with time. The standard cosmology treats that energy, the cosmological constant, as fixed forever. Her 2026 paper tests the alternative, a time-varying vacuum model, in both flat and curved space. The evidence combines the newest baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from the DESI survey with cosmic chronometer data that track the expansion rate directly.

A full statistical sampling analysis quantifies how vacuum dynamics would alter the expansion history, the effective behavior of the cosmic fluid, and the universe's deceleration. A formal model comparison then judges the varying model against the standard one. The data push hard toward the standard picture: the vacuum dynamics parameter is driven close to zero. Even so, the varying model reduces parameter degeneracies and eases the Hubble tension, the persistent mismatch in expansion-rate measurements.
arxiv-2603-03568:
Matías Leizerovich and four colleagues confront a new entropy-based cosmology with real sky data for the first time. The Luciano-Saridakis entropy generalizes textbook entropy with two extra exponents. Fed through the gravity-thermodynamics link, it modifies cosmic dynamics so an effective dark energy appears from entropy itself, while the standard model returns as a limiting case. Their 2026 paper tests that entropic cosmology at the background level.

Four datasets constrain it jointly: cosmic chronometers, the Pantheon-plus supernova sample tied to local distance measurements, new DESI baryon oscillation data, and compressed early-universe information. The model fits the combination robustly and satisfies all anchors at once, something the standard model cannot do here. Its parameters stay near standard values, yet the standard limit itself is excluded at modest significance in the space studied, hinting at relief for the Hubble tension.
arxiv-2603-03668:
Weizhi Feng and five colleagues recruit language models to help theorem provers with their hardest bottleneck. Constraints involving inductive definitions, recursive data types and functions, resist today's best solvers, which offer only limited support for them. Proofs stall for want of auxiliary lemmas, the small helper claims human experts invent. Their 2026 approach uses structured prompts to make a language model propose exactly those lemmas.

The full method is neuro-symbolic. The model iteratively conjectures lemmas, and a constraint solver checks each one for validity and usefulness toward the goal, so bad guesses die fast. Benchmarks span algebraic data types and recurrence relations. The hybrid improves on state-of-the-art SMT and CHC solvers, solving about a quarter more proof tasks involving inductive definitions than the solvers manage alone.
arxiv-2605-00368:
Bjorn Nansen and 3 co-authors study how Australian children respond to the country's new social media ban, which bars under-sixteen accounts and obliges platforms to enforce the limit. The team ran five focus groups with fifteen young people aged twelve to sixteen. They asked how the children understood the ban's fairness, impact, and legitimacy as they met the platforms enforcing it.

The children widely judged the ban unfair and ineffective. Through the platforms' access controls, they learned where the system failed and how it, and their peers' accounts, could be evaded. The authors name this practice sneaking, and use it as a lens on the social encounter between children, platforms, and regulation. Their point is broader: children test and negotiate the systems that govern them, and purely technical controls struggle with social problems.
arxiv-2605-00468:
Joey Chan and 10 co-authors ask what happens when plain-language summaries of health research are personalized for each reader. Such summaries aim to open research to lay readers, but the standard one-size-fits-all style ignores differing needs and reading levels. In health, a misunderstanding can change a real decision, so the stakes of tailoring are unusually concrete.

Their dataset, ReLay, pairs fifty lay participants with summaries in two settings: fixed expert-written versions and interactive versions personalized by a language model. It records reader traits, information needs, search behavior, comprehension, interaction logs, and quality ratings. Evaluating five models under two personalization methods, they find personalization improves comprehension and perceived quality. It also raises the risk of echoing a reader's biases and of introducing invented content. That tension between help and safety frames their call for personalization that is both effective and trustworthy.
arxiv-2605-00768:
Jiaoda Li and Ryan Cotterell give a formal account of why local attention can improve transformer language models. Global attention lets each token use all earlier tokens, at quadratic cost. Local attention limits each token to a bounded window, cutting cost to linear, yet it sometimes raises quality as well. The authors explain that puzzle through recognizer expressivity, meaning which language patterns a model can in principle detect.

They prove local attention adds a second temporal operator beyond the one linked to global attention, strictly widening the regular languages that can be recognized. Neither form contains the other, and combining them gives the richest class. Tests on formal languages and natural language modeling support the theory.
arxiv-2605-01068:
Piedad J. Miranda and five co-authors study how drone vibration affects acoustic tap-testing for building tile checks, and how to correct for it. Checking tile integrity matters for public safety and urban durability over time. Mounting tap-testing on an unmanned aerial vehicle adds dynamic perturbations that can degrade sorting, so the authors build a controlled test rig to measure that effect.

A Stewart platform reproduces oscillatory conditions from drone flight characterization across several amplitudes. Wireless sound data are classified with principal component analysis. Accuracy falls significantly as perturbation grows, but an energy-based signal correction and filtering method restores performance above ninety-eight percent. The approach preserves key defect-related features while reducing data size.
arxiv-2605-01168:
Leixin Zhang and one co-author study disagreement in graded human ratings of inappropriate language, covering offensive language, hate speech, and toxicity perception. Annotators do not always agree, and such splits are now seen as inherent to many tasks. Items differ in how much divergence they elicit. The authors ask whether the degree of split can be predicted from textual features.

They propose an Opposition Index that quantifies perspective opposition among annotators on an item. They study prediction of both variance and high-opposition cases. Estimated and observed variance correlate moderately, and two prediction approaches perform comparably. Items with high opposition are harder to predict and are often underestimated by models, a warning for systems that treat labels as settled.
arxiv-2605-01568:
Wojciech Kozłowski and four co-authors unify the zoo of stochastic image enhancement methods, which restore degraded photos through a random process run over time. Many recent methods steer that process by the degraded input, and how they relate to plain diffusion models has been unclear.

The classification sorts methods into three families: unconditional diffusion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, and diffusion bridges. All three, the authors show, flow from one stochastic differential equation. They differ only in drift and diffusion terms, end distributions, and boundary conditions, while schedules and samplers are free choices on top. With that map in hand, they run a controlled study across enhancement tasks with identical architectures and training rules. No family wins outright; instead, specific design choices carry the performance. A modular library, ItoVision, ships the unified frame for fair prototyping.
arxiv-2605-01768:
Xiamiao Zhao, Yuanpei Wang, and Junpeng Zhou study a Turán-type problem in hypergraphs, where edges can join more than two points at once. They extend work by Alon and Frankl on graphs that avoid a given pattern while also keeping matchings small. Their setting uses expansions, formed by adding new points inside each edge of a graph.

The team finds the largest number of edges a hypergraph can have while avoiding both a large matching and an expanded clique, for small and for large matching limits. A key step is a rainbow version of the same problem across a family of hypergraphs. The result partly confirms a conjecture by Gerbner, Tompkins, and Zhou.
arxiv-2605-01868:
Rui Xu and colleagues work on conformal prediction, a method that gives prediction sets with a stated coverage rate. The guarantee assumes test data match the calibration data. When the distribution shifts, most fixes align overall score patterns, which can still leave single inputs badly covered in places where conditions differ.

The authors bound that single-input error by the distance between calibration and test distributions, which points to transport as a fix. Their Branched Normalizing Flow has two branches: one maps a test input toward the calibration form, and the other maps its prediction set back. Tests show the method holds conditional coverage better under shift than prior approaches.
arxiv-2605-02168:
Wenyi Wu, Sibo Zhu, Kun Zhou, and Biwei Huang split long-horizon agent work into three roles and ask which role deserves the most compute. Their framework uses a planner for high-level choices, an actor for execution, and a memory manager for context. That split is a known pattern, so the authors focus on how compute should be shared among the parts.

Their analysis finds planning dominates task performance. Execution and memory need far less compute and model size to stay competitive. Building on that, they train only the planner with reinforcement learning, using trajectory rewards from a vision-language judge, while freezing the other parts. The planner-centric design aims for strong long-horizon results at lower total cost.
arxiv-2605-02468:
D. Delicato and forty-four co-authors report background tests for BULLKID, a cryogenic detector built to search for light dark matter and for a rare neutrino scattering process. The device holds sixty small silicon blocks, each sensed by a kinetic inductance detector. For this test it ran on the surface, with modest shielding, rather than deep underground.

The team used fifteen array units, with two central units read for background and the units around them used as a veto. Over two hundred ninety hours, the low-energy counts matched simulations well down to six hundred electron volts. Below that, counts rose above the forecast, though not in the same way as a low-energy excess seen in other cryogenic work. High-energy counts also matched simulations.
arxiv-2605-02568:
Jaber Jaber and Osama Jaber present StreamIndex, a memory-saving implementation of compressed sparse attention, a method used in recent DeepSeek language models. In that method, a small learned indexer scores compressed keys and picks the top few for each query. Standard code builds the full score table first, which at long sequence lengths exceeds any single graphics card's memory.

StreamIndex avoids building that table. A chunked driver finds the top scores part by part and merges the parts, all in Triton code. On realistic test shapes, the standard path ran out of memory where StreamIndex ran, and it stretched the workable length far beyond the baseline with modest peak memory. Overlap with exact results was near perfect across design sweeps, and the driver fits with pipelined attention kernels.
arxiv-2605-02768:
David Gamarnik and three co-authors rigorously compute the free energy of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model at high temperature. The model, a disordered quantum mean-field system, is studied both for condensed matter and as a toy model of black holes. Its traits were derived by physicists with replica and path integral methods, but rigorous math lagged, even for basic quantities like the annealed free energy.

At high but fixed temperature, the authors settle both the annealed and quenched free energy limits. Their values agree numerically with the physics results. The proof route is new: it uses the component structure of sparse random graphs plus a variant of the cavity method, a tool from spin glass theory. Closing a physics-derived formula with a full proof is the contribution.
arxiv-2605-02868:
Ruichao Liang and seven co-authors present an agent system that writes working exploits for flaws in decentralized finance smart contracts. Such flaws drain billions each year, yet most disclosed bugs are never proved exploitable, because building a proof-of-concept by hand is slow, expert work. Protocols stay exposed in the gap between disclosure and proof.

The system treats exploit building as structured reasoning, not plain code generation. A hierarchical knowledge graph stores protocol meaning, failure causes, and exploit building blocks, serving as memory for guided multi-step search. Candidate exploits face two checks: a solver test that the exploit path is reachable, and an asset-level simulation that real profit is possible. Tests cover dozens of real attacks and audited contracts. The aim is faster verification of what is truly exploitable.
arxiv-2605-02968:
Ping Wang and Yan-Qi Du introduce a finite-size framework for tracking how gradients move during language model pretraining. Five measures separate cascade size, duration, total transport, and transport efficiency per unit, giving a compact state picture of training dynamics. The data are raw gradient measurements from a small model family across four scales, plus update fields from a larger public family across five scales.

The same algebraic closure holds in both families, with a shared near-unity size backbone, but their transport regimes differ. One family scales positively in duration and negatively in efficiency; the other hugs the baseline with weak efficiency scaling. Randomized controls give matched null floors, so the contrast reads as real. Compressibility into clean power laws also differs between the families.
arxiv-2605-03268:
Turan Orujlu, Jordan Matelsky, Martin V. Butz, Charley M. Wu, and Konrad P. Kording extend structural causal models to settings where hidden context shapes both the graph and the mechanisms. In many real systems, upstream conditions decide which links exist and how variables respond, yet standard models treat the graph as fixed and fully seen.

Their partially observed models allow interventions on nodes, edges, and context together, with edge effects split into local transmission channels. Identifiability theory shows which intervention sets can separate structure from mechanism. Tests in a simulated retina and a gene network analogue matched the theory's predictions closely.
arxiv-2605-03468:
Qian-Qian Hong, Zhi-Jian Zheng, Zhe-Jun Zhang, Xin-Xia Jian, and Chuan-Cun Shu build a theoretical framework for universal single-qutrit control in asymmetric-top molecules. A qutrit uses three levels instead of two, and molecules with three distinct rotation axes offer rich level structure but complex control.

The qutrit sits in three rotational states, with an auxiliary state giving independent phase control. Direct rotations plus auxiliary-mediated phases cover all gates, guided by a multilevel pulse-area theorem mapping gate targets to microwave fields. Simulations on 1,2-propanediol show clean Walsh-Hadamard gates with minimal leakage, and error sensitivity depends on the decomposition route chosen.
arxiv-2605-03668:
João Henrique Andrade and four co-authors prove quantitative stability estimates for the Trudinger-Moser inequality on smooth bounded domains in the plane. The inequality controls exponential integrals of functions by their gradient energy, and stability asks how near a near-extremal function must be to the true optimizers. The authors measure that closeness through the inequality's deficit.

They show the deficit controls distance to the optimizer set quadratically. That holds when the exponential growth rate is small enough. It also holds when the domain is a round disk, where the estimate survives even in the critical case. Both proofs use a new spectral gap, which the authors note may interest others. The estimate also holds generically in nondegenerate cases.
arxiv-2605-03768:
James R. Beattie, Isabelle Connor, and Enrico Ramirez-Ruiz measure the Strouhal number of turbulence driven by supernovae in the interstellar medium. The Strouhal number compares how long turbulent driving stays coherent with the turnover time of the largest eddies. Turbulence-box models commonly just set it to one, yet statistics such as the gas density distribution are sensitive to that choice.

Computing the number directly from two-time correlation tensors in stratified, multiphase simulations of Milky Way-like and starburst disks, they find median values near one quarter in both cases. The scale-dependent curves reach one at a nearly universal fraction of the outer scale, consistent with supernova remnants driving turbulence locally near their cooling radius.
arxiv-2605-03868:
David Mumford and Sy-David Friedman argue that the usual Zermelo-Fraenkel-Choice axioms do not settle the foundations of everyday mathematics. Set theory admits many models with different truths, and even classical questions such as the measurability of projective sets can vary between them. The core of mathematics, they contend, lies in structures built from the real numbers.

They propose a foundation for core mathematics consisting of both a system of axioms and a definite model of those axioms, in which essentially all core mathematics is incorporated. Because the model is definite, every core mathematical assertion receives a definite truth value, true or false, rather than depending on which set-theoretic universe one happens to inhabit.
arxiv-2605-04068:
Bilel Abderrahmane Benziane, Benoit Lardeux, Ayoub Mcharek, and Maher Jridi design a forecasting selection tool for supply chain demand prediction. Artificial intelligence forecasting methods abound, but choosing the right one for a given dataset is daunting because each dataset has distinct features. Their architecture acts as a double deep reinforcement learning agent that picks a forecasting model from a committee at prediction time.

A novel early-stopping approach based on average reward convergence speeds up the agent's training. The empirical study uses grocery sales datasets and snack demand datasets. Against state-of-the-art selection methods, the proposed approach proved robust, automatically matching forecasting models to the data at hand rather than forcing one method onto every demand series.
arxiv-2605-04268:
The ARA Collaboration reports how sensitive the Askaryan Radio Array, an observatory buried in Antarctic ice, is to neutrinos with extremely high energy. These rare particles should trigger brief radio pulses as they create particle cascades in the ice.

Using an improved simulation that adds data-driven detector effects and secondary particles, the team calculates the full array's trigger-level reach for its 2013 to 2023 run. They find world-leading sensitivity at the highest energies, with secondary particles adding a sizable share of the acceptance. Under the most hopeful flux models, up to thirteen neutrinos may already sit in the recorded data.
arxiv-2605-04468:
Xinyu Wang and three co-authors tackle catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning large language models, where learning a new task erodes skills the model already had. Recent evidence blames excessive drift in the model's output distribution during training.

Their anchored method controls that drift directly. Instead of pulling the model toward one fixed reference, a moving anchor blends the current model with a frozen reference. That blend forms an intermediate target. Training thus becomes a chain of small local updates. They prove a stable per-step bound on distribution change, and experiments on maths, medical calculation, and instruction tasks place the method on the best trade-off frontier.
arxiv-2605-04568:
Jonathan Spieler and Sven Behnke present a model-based reinforcement learning method that plans robot actions by imagining future trajectories inside a learned world model. Planning methods that search without gradients are reliable but expensive in high-dimensional control, while gradient-based planning has often performed worse despite its promise.

Their approach rolls out a policy to propose a few candidate trajectories. It then improves each by gradient ascent through the learned model. An uncertainty penalty discourages straying into regions the model knows poorly. Reusing previously optimised actions spreads the cost over time. Across twenty-four continuous control tasks, the method improves significantly on earlier approaches.
arxiv-2605-04668:
Haimin Li and Qing Wang classify the irreducible ordinary modules of affine vertex operator superalgebras. These algebras are built from basic classical Lie superalgebras. The work sits at a special family of levels, called boundary admissible levels. Such a list tells us exactly which modules the algebra admits at those levels. That is a basic structural question.

The answer splits sharply by type. For superalgebras of type I, the count is exact. There are as many distinct such modules as a positive integer parameter built into the level. For ordinary simple Lie algebras and type II superalgebras, the algebra is its own only such module. That strong rigidity statement is proved uniformly across the cases.
arxiv-2605-05068:
Raven Cilley and ten co-authors analyse a near-ultraviolet transit of XO-3 b, a massive hot Jupiter on an eccentric orbit, observed in 2024 with the XMM-Newton space telescope. Ultraviolet transits can reveal escaping atmospheres, cloud formation, and planetary magnetic fields. This planet was already known for an unusually large ultraviolet-absorbing atmosphere.

Combining the ultraviolet data with a ground-based optical transit and all TESS observations, they find the ultraviolet transit notably deeper than the optical one and its centre arriving late. Escape alone looks too weak to explain it, since the estimated mass loss is extremely small. A magnetic bow shock, they argue, could produce offsets of the observed size.
arxiv-2605-05168:
Pau Colomer and three co-authors close a long-standing gap in deterministic identification. That is a communication task where the receiver only needs to know which of a set of messages was sent, not decode data. For channels with continuous inputs, the best achievable and provable limits had never quite met. A recent galaxy code construction closed that gap for Gaussian noise channels.

The authors extend that approach to the Bernoulli channel. From there they handle any channel whose outputs trace a continuous curve, by reducing it to a Bernoulli subproblem. They prove the converse bound is tight for this broad class, settling its identification capacity. They also analyse the rate-reliability trade-off, improving lower bounds on the reliability function toward the converse.
arxiv-2605-05268:
M AlMasri generalises proper scoring rules, the incentive tools that reward honest probability forecasts, into the quantum domain. Probability distributions are replaced by density operators, the quantum states used to describe uncertain systems. AlMasri defines quantum value functionals from operator convex generators and builds a complete duality theory that yields proper quantum scoring rules from them.

From that theory come minimax optimal bounds for quantum state tomography under such incentives, including a quantum Cramér-Rao-McCarthy bound tying risk to the generator's curvature and quantum Fisher information. AlMasri also prices quantum resources such as coherence, entanglement, and adaptivity in forecasting tasks, finding scaling separations between classical and quantum strategies with uses for sensors and data markets.
arxiv-2605-05368:
What is information, at the level of logic? Matthew Collinson, Timo Eckhardt, and David Pym argue that the concept still lacks firm mathematical foundations. Without them, reasoning about the complex systems modern society depends on stays shaky. Their paper takes a first step toward an inferentialist theory of information.

One strand rethinks basic notions, swapping truth for inferability in Dretske's classic account. A second uses proof-theoretic semantics to define a basic unit of information, the inferon. A third applies those tools to distributed systems, giving a reasoning-based picture of how information flows through them.
arxiv-2605-05468:
TRAPPIST-1, a cool dwarf star with several planets, flares often and hard. Valeriy Vasilyev and twelve co-authors built a single flare-frequency distribution spanning four orders of magnitude in energy. They combined about eighty-seven hours of JWST spectroscopy with roughly seventy-four days of Kepler photometry, converting every event to one common energy scale.

The combined data follow one power law, with no break needed. Rare, powerful flares dominate the star's total flare energy output. Strong flares also occur about ten times more often than earlier estimates suggested, which matters for the atmospheres and habitability of the system's planets.
arxiv-2605-05668:
Vision-language models are residual transformers at heart, whatever their training recipe. Gongli Xi and seven co-authors ask what the attention and feed-forward parts each actually do inside. Earlier attribution studies lacked a shared theoretical basis, so the team builds one from information theory and geometry to measure residual updates.

The framework reveals a clean division of labor. Attention acts as a subspace-preserving operator, moving information without rotating its geometry, while other components reshape representations. The authors argue these models can get lost in attention when that preservation goes wrong, and the diagnostics point to architectural fixes.
arxiv-2605-05768:
Yuqian Cheng, Zhuo Chen, and Qian Lin study uniform error bounds for a class of kernel regression methods called kernel gradient flows. Users need to know not just average error, but the worst error across the whole input range. The authors work under a standard capacity and source condition used in kernel learning theory.

They prove convergence rates for the supremum norm error of both continuous and discrete gradient flows. Those rates match the best possible minimax rates for the problem. On that base they build simultaneous confidence bands that cover the true function as a whole. The band widths shrink at rates that can come close to the best possible rate as well.
arxiv-2605-05868:
Agent skills bundle instructions and executable resources that extend what a language-model agent can do. Jiangrong Wu and six co-authors warn that a skill can quietly exceed what the user's task requires, violating least privilege. The same action may be essential for one prompt and overreach for another, so detection must be task-conditioned.

Their framework, SkillScope, analyzes skills through a graph-based approach to flag over-privileged behavior relative to the current task. Fine-grained enforcement is the goal: permit the actions the task needs, block the rest. The work frames skill safety as contextual authorization, not blanket approval.
arxiv-2605-06068:
Keisuke Kamahori and three co-authors let AI coding agents build language model serving systems from scratch. Serving stacks are usually one general purpose system, hand tuned over many engineer years for every model and workload. The authors take the opposite bet: generate a bespoke stack for each usage scenario instead.

Their loop, VibeServe, plans a search over system designs in an outer loop. An inner loop then writes each candidate, checks it for correctness, and measures it on the target benchmark. In standard settings the generated systems matched leading tools on a mid size model. For a huge mixture of experts model they delivered 2.3 times the goodput of a tuned rival, and won in five non standard scenarios.
arxiv-2605-06168:
Tobia Filosi and nine co-authors build a scalable way to choose models for count time series with sudden structural breaks. Weekly health care counts are non negative, linked over time, and can be jolted by system wide shocks, which makes Gaussian models a poor fit. Their case study is solid organ transplant activity in the USA and Italy from 2014 to late 2024.

Poisson and negative binomial models include short term dynamics, holiday week effects, and pandemic level and slope shifts. A screened portfolio of models is picked by an information criterion inside each training window, then judged on expanding window forecasts. Deceased donor series in both countries returned toward pre pandemic baselines. The US living donor series converged more slowly, and COVID burden measures added little predictive value.
arxiv-2605-06368:
Paulo Mario Medina, Jose Marie Antonio Miñoza, and Sebastian Ibañez regularize image classifiers with contrastive pairs of visual explanations. Distribution shift breaks models through spurious correlations, and many remedies beat plain risk minimization only at times while growing hard to interpret. Their framework, eXplaining to Learn, instead decorrelates confounding features from the classifier's internal features directly, using the explanation maps of two classifiers trained side by side during learning.

One classifier predicts the label and the other predicts the confounder, and training cuts similarity between their Grad-CAM activation maps. On a rigorous synthetic many to many challenge benchmark, the method set new best marks for both average and worst group accuracy. Gains over the prior state of the art ran above five and ten points on those two measures. The authors frame the result as domain invariance enforced at group level.
arxiv-2605-06468:
Enric Florit-Simon proves that two ways of bounding the area of a minimal surface are in fact equivalent. Minimal surfaces can be measured intrinsically, from within the surface, or extrinsically, from the surrounding space. He shows the intrinsic and extrinsic area density bounds match, with the same asymptotic values, for complete smooth minimal immersions of any dimension and codimension.

Combined with a recent breakthrough by Bellettini, the result extends known curvature estimates for stable minimal hypersurfaces to dimension six. That case had stayed open for decades since the estimates were first developed. The paper closes a long-standing gap in minimal surface theory.
arxiv-2605-06568:
Reason Machete revisits statistical significance testing, tracing it from Fisher's error probabilities through the Neyman-Pearson addition of alternative hypotheses and second-kind errors.
