Significance tests powered much scientific progress but drew lasting controversy. Bayesian ideas were later folded in, and Fisher himself warned against treating any fixed threshold as a rule.

Machete examines current reform calls: dropping the standard threshold, requiring confirmatory studies before publication, abandoning the yes-no null framing, or replacing tests with confidence intervals and Bayesian decision theory. Each proposal's strengths and shortcomings are weighed. The paper gives readers a compact history plus a critical map of the reform debate.
arxiv-2605-06768:
Yuval Grossman, Tony Menzo, Stefan Schacht, Chinhsan Sieng, and Jure Zupan extract a key weak-interaction angle from particle decays without binning the data. The CKM angle gamma is measured through a chain where a B meson decays to a D meson and a kaon, with the D decaying to a kaon and two pions. Normalizing flows trained on D decay data learn a continuous map of the decay amplitude and phase across the Dalitz plot.

Fitting B decay data against that learned map yields gamma plus the related hadronic parameters. Tests on simulated data recover the injected angle within uncertainties, with statistical errors propagated through an ensemble of flows. Two encodings of the phase constraint are compared, and Bayesian flows are discussed.
arxiv-2605-06968:
Michael McKinsey, Stephanie Brink, and Olga Pearce ask how well small proxy programs really represent large computing codes. High-performance computing teams use such benchmarks to test new machines and guide hardware design. Checking the match by hand is slow and hard to scale across many programs.

The authors define similarity measures based on how code uses computing hardware, then sort kernels into two broad performance groups. They test the measures on the Kripke proxy and a performance suite, on both plain and graphics-accelerated systems. Their metrics correctly match related kernels, offering a more systematic way to judge benchmark quality.
arxiv-2605-07168:
Xizhe Li and four co-authors build a faster connectivity oracle that survives vertex failures in a network. After a small set of vertices fails, the oracle must update quickly and then answer whether pairs of vertices remain connected. Earlier designs needed huge memory or update times that exploded with the failure count.

The new oracle updates in time depending only on the number of failures, not the graph size, and answers queries at the best possible speed. For a fixed failure count it uses near-linear space and preprocessing. The gains come from shortcutting a decomposition, reusing simpler oracles internally, and a new patch-set mechanism.
arxiv-2605-07268:
Hanmeng Liu and five co-authors harden multiple-choice reasoning tests in a formal, validity-preserving way. Benchmarks saturate quickly and suffer contamination, while ad hoc tricks like paraphrasing add surface difficulty without logical rigor. LogiHard transforms simple selection questions into higher-order logical judgments, demanding more reasoning steps from the test taker.

An adaptive testing layer controls difficulty precisely with fewer questions. Across twelve leading models, hardened questions cut accuracy sharply, and transfer to a general benchmark showed a similar drop. The authors blame a completeness-checking gap in training rather than missing knowledge, a failure pattern human test takers did not share.
arxiv-2605-07368:
Bikshapathi Gouda and Antti Tölli design beamforming for cell-free massive MIMO networks where access points send and receive at the same time. Full-duplex operation boosts spectrum use but creates self-interference and cross-talk between access points and users. Earlier over-the-air training schemes handled uplink and downlink separately.

Their fully distributed design trains beamformers with simultaneous pilots under a joint error criterion covering those interference terms. A projection step at user devices suppresses pilot leakage that would corrupt the needed cross terms. Simulations show faster convergence and higher effective rates than separate training, with the largest gains where user interference is strong.
arxiv-2605-07568:
Peitao Han and four co-authors ask why video language models are bad at telling whether a clip plays forward or backward. People ace this arrow-of-time test, while frontier models score barely above chance. Either the visual backbone never encodes the direction of time, or the information gets lost on its way to the language model.

By testing each stage separately, the team finds that video-centric encoders do carry strong time signals, while frame-centric ones do not. The projector is a key bottleneck: a Q-Former design scrambles the signal, while a time-preserving projection passes it through. Their rebuilt system reached 98.1 percent accuracy on the test, above human performance, and also improved on broader temporal reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-07668:
Shuo Zhang and three co-authors propose a yardstick for how hard a quantum operation is to carry out on an analog quantum simulator. These machines use global control fields and promise access to many-body physics beyond classical computers, but there was no clear quantitative measure of the synthesis cost of a given operation.

They adapt Krylov complexity, a notion from operator growth dynamics, building the block Krylov basis from the simulator's native Hamiltonians and their nested commutators. In test systems including Rydberg atom arrays, the Krylov complexity of a target operation strongly predicted the minimum time needed to realize it. The measure gives designers an intuitive tool for planning efficient control protocols.
arxiv-2605-07768:
Erik Börve and three co-authors plan trajectories for one agent among others whose decisions are uncertain, a core problem for autonomous driving and robotics. Their route is to learn the distribution of surrounding agents' decisions and then solve a stochastic model predictive control problem. The catch is that the learned distribution is itself wrong in unknown ways.

They combine probably-approximately-correct learning bounds with robust optimization, so the controller hedges exactly against the errors the learning step could have made. The resulting framework sits between a fully robust controller and an all-knowing stochastic one, depending on how many samples are available. More data buys less caution in a measured way.
arxiv-2605-07868:
Shinichi Inoue and six co-authors tackle frequency crowding, a scaling bottleneck for fixed-frequency transmon quantum processors. The workhorse cross-resonance gate is normally operated in a straddling regime that tightly constrains which qubit frequencies can sit near each other, making collisions likely as chips grow. The team instead analyzes the gate far outside that regime.

Using a numerical method that stays accurate under strong, smoothly ramped drives, they sweep parameters systematically and derive collision-free conditions defining assignable frequency regions. Frequency allocation is then cast as a linear program on a unit-cell lattice. Far-detuned designs cut collisions significantly against straddling ones. A yield analysis for a thousand-qubit lattice suggests the needed frequency precision is within about a factor of two of the current state of the art.
arxiv-2605-08168:
Ayoub Agouzoul compares four fixes for a timing problem in robot control with vision-language-action models. These models are slow, so by the time an action runs, the robot's view of the world is stale. Recent methods attack the delay in different places: patching at inference time, simulating delay during training, conditioning on future states, or adding a light residual correction.

Agouzoul rebuilds all four in two shared codebases with matched versions and benchmarks them on the Kinetix suite and on LIBERO manipulation tasks, sweeping delays up to twenty control steps. The controlled comparison shows how each method holds up as latency grows.
arxiv-2605-08268:
Xiaolin Sun, Zixuan Liu, Yibin Hu, and Zizhan Zheng study a saboteur inside a team of language model agents. Groups of agents increasingly reach decisions by exchanging messages until they agree, and most frameworks assume every member shares the group's goal. A malicious insider can instead pose as a normal member while secretly working to delay or block consensus.

The authors formalize the attack as a sequential decision problem. To optimize it, they learn a world model that mimics the latent behavior of the honest agents, then train the attacker against that surrogate. The study maps how fragile multi-agent agreement can be from the inside.
arxiv-2605-08368:
Yuhao Li and Shengchao Liu draw a line that post-training debates often blur: does fine-tuning or reinforcement learning merely surface skills a model already had, or does it create new ones? Calling the first elicitation and the second creation, the authors argue the distinction should guide research claims.

They make the idea operational with accessible support, the set of behaviors a model can realistically produce within finite budgets. Training that reweights behavior inside that set is elicitation; shifting the set itself is creation. A free-energy view shows supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning both reweight a pretrained reference distribution, which reframes several standing arguments about what each method can do.
arxiv-2605-08568:
Hengyi Zhu, Zhendong Mi, Grace Li Zhang, and Shaoyi Huang shrink large language models by choosing compression levels per prompt. Standard singular value methods cut every input at the same fixed rank, yet the best rank shifts from prompt to prompt and depends heavily on the calibration data. Their framework, PARSE, trains a small router to pick ranks ahead of time.

Similar prompts share rank patterns that stay stable while answers generate, so chosen ranks can be served from a cache for speed. Added to four existing compression methods, PARSE lifts task accuracy and speeds both prompt reading and answer generation. Model deployment gains quality and speed from treating each prompt on its own terms.
arxiv-2605-08668:
Yuxuan Chen, Shuo Dai, Ruoyi Xu, and Haipeng Xie forecast electricity load by enriching time series with text and image knowledge instead of recycled copies of the same data. Prior multi modal methods mostly rework the series itself, adding redundancy rather than new knowledge, which hurts when data is scarce. Their KEMM-Net builds textual and visual embeddings that widen what the model can draw on.

A decomposition guided contrastive step then balances redundant, shared, and unique information across the modes before forecasting. On real public datasets, the method beats strong deep and multi modal baselines, with the clearest gains in few shot settings common in power systems. Grid forecasting gains accuracy from genuinely added knowledge.
arxiv-2605-08968: Feihu Liu and Jinlong Tang prove four growth line claims set by Chapoton. The claims are on arbor polytopes, shapes tied to a set line of tree like arbors. Two claims give closed forms for the growth lines of the linked poset. One is its Zeta count. One is its M-triangle. Two claims are on the shape's Ehrhart count and its volume Laplace form. All four close one pack of asks that tie poset counts to shape math.
arxiv-2605-09068:
Dong-Hui Yang and Bao-Zhu Guo study vibration-like modes, called eigenfunctions, for a class of differential operators that degenerate at part of the boundary. In such problems a weight stays positive inside the region but drops to zero on part of the edge, and many pleasant properties of standard operators are lost.

The authors prove a version of Courant's nodal domain theorem for this degenerate setting, a classic result about how the region splits into zones where a mode keeps one sign. They also show that a generic property survives: for almost every added bounded term, in a precise topological sense, the operator's eigenvalues are all simple. The work extends core spectral theory to a harder class of operators.
arxiv-2605-09168:
Fabio Rovai, writing alone, argues that a valid tool call by a language agent is not the same as a valid action in the world. Guards that check form, policy, and origin cannot certify that a state-changing step will actually help. His 2026 paper presents CIVeX, a checker that turns each proposed action into a causal question over a stored graph of actions and states.

CIVeX returns one of four verdicts: carry out the action, refuse it, test it, or hold off. Approval needs a causal certificate with a lower bound on benefit plus records of origin and risk. On a bench of nearly two thousand cases, the system made no false executions under moderate or hostile confounding. It also matched near-perfect choices on two sets of real logs.
arxiv-2605-09268:
Sinha and three colleagues stress test multi turn understanding in LLMs, where users routinely refine requests or pivot mid conversation. Models often miss these shifts and drag irrelevant context from earlier turns, producing inaccurate responses. The team studies two sub tasks: shortlisting relevant context from previous turns, and spotting when the user pivots or refines mid turn.

They construct synthetic benchmarks from real world data sets across varied domains, simulating context shifts of different difficulty levels. Across ten LLMs tested zero shot, only some reasoning and strongly instructed models detect pivots accurately. Open weight models struggle and often drag old context along despite clear cues, while every model shows a position bias. The results point to ways of improving long term robustness in multi turn LLM capabilities. The work shows continuity assumptions break when users change direction without starting a new session, a routine pattern.
arxiv-2605-09668:
Fisman and Meirom introduced a new way to compare infinite sets, built to capture long-run likeness rather than freak outliers. Their Asymptotic Hausdorff lifting takes a distance between single items and lifts it to a distance between sets, ignoring finite gaps. Older Hausdorff-style lifts, by contrast, let single outliers dominate and miss long-run behavior.

Formal languages are the motivating case: items are words, sets are languages, and the lift yields metric-valued distances between languages. The authors studied the groups of regular languages the lift treats as alike for normalized edit distances, pinning down their long-run essence. For the Marzal-Vidal normalized edit distance, they probed how to compute the lifted distance for regular and bounded context-free languages.
arxiv-2605-09768:
Arshad and nine colleagues built SAGE, a grounded evaluation system for crop disease diagnosis, plus the largest plant-disease image-symptom dataset to date. Labeled disease images are scarce and uneven across crops, pathogens, and field conditions, while frontier vision-language models still stumble on fine-grained disease calls for lack of structured symptom knowledge. The dataset covers 335 crops, 1,251 disease classes, and about 839,000 images.

An automated pipeline writes source-grounded symptom notes, each claim tied to a verbatim web quote, with experts validating samples and reconciling disease-name variants. The agentic baseline reads anatomy, narrows candidates by symptoms, compares reference images in sequence, and leaves a full reasoning trace. Adding symptom knowledge lifted accuracy by 16.2 points on average at full reference budget, and new crops need only reference images plus symptom notes, no retraining.
arxiv-2605-09868:
Damian, Loaiza-Brito and López-Ramos work in string theory, studying Type IIB compactifications where fluxes and the dilaton field vary across a complex two-dimensional plane. Compactification means rolling extra dimensions into a small shape, and dynamical cobordism is a framework that asks which such shapes can end consistently. From the equations of motion the authors show that End-of-the-World branes exist, boundaries where spacetime stops.

In cohomological language those branes appear exactly where needed to cancel a topological charge, and the paper computes the associated bordism group to show the cancellation. Extra non-perturbative objects are still required to kill the class fully, while its cohomological part survives as a subgroup. The structure suggests a link between energy scales and which physical effects, perturbative or not, show up.
arxiv-2605-09968:
Guha, working alone, proposes a unified language for adaptive learning systems, which must switch between locking in what they know and expanding into new evidence. The framework, Consolidation-Expansion Operator Mechanics, centres on the order-gap: how much the consolidation and expansion operators refuse to commute at any one knowledge state. Because it can be read from the system's own path, the gap works as a live control signal.

Large gaps mean ordering still matters and the system is unsettled, while a gap that falls and stays small means further processing will likely change little. Three results make this precise, including a stopping rule with provable promises under noise-free and bounded-noise conditions. The framework spans bandits, reinforcement learning, stochastic optimisation, continual learning and recursive language models, with the recursive-model case developed in full as a rule-based stand-in for rule-of-thumb stopping rules.
arxiv-2605-10268:
Baibei Ji and five colleagues improve how AI agents reason over very long documents. Large language models struggle when context grows, partly because attention costs rise quadratically with length. Memory-based agents read in chunks and update a running memory, but facts discarded along the way are often lost for good. Their 2026 paper presents MemReread, a fix built on streaming reading.

MemReread skips intermediate retrieval. When the final memory proves insufficient, it breaks the question down and rereads the source, recovering indirect facts that were dropped too early. A reinforcement learning framework also stretches length extrapolation and sets the number of rereading passes from task complexity. Across long-context reasoning tasks MemReread beat baseline frameworks consistently, while keeping time costs linear in context length.
arxiv-2605-10368:
Shaull Almagor and two colleagues extend Simon's factorization theorem from words to forests. Simon's theorem is a famous tool in automata theory, providing bounded-depth splits of words with respect to maps into finite semigroups. Developing an analogue for forests presents a basic difficulty: recursively splitting a forest requires tracking where each subforest fits. Their 2026 paper overcomes it by adding to the free forest algebra and building a framework for recursive splitting.

The main result identifies a new meaning limit on maps, called R-alignment, which roughly keeps different ways of cutting a forest in step at the semigroup level. Under this limit, the authors prove that every map admits bounded-depth splits. They also prove the limit is necessary: without it, some maps admit no bounded-depth split under their notion of splitting. Readers get both a positive theorem and a matching negative result.
arxiv-2605-10468:
Xingyu Qu and two colleagues ask whether Muon can fine-tune models pretrained with Adam. Muon offers an efficient pretraining alternative to Adam, yet sees little use in fine-tuning. Most open models come pretrained with Adam, and moving to Muon for fine-tuning without care degrades performance. Their 2026 paper investigates that mismatch through controlled experiments.

The authors relate the mismatch to the distinct implicit biases of Adam and Muon. Evidence shows the mismatch disrupts pretrained knowledge in proportion to update strength. That suggests constraining updates should mitigate the mismatch. The authors test it with LoRA, which freezes pretrained weights and holds updates inside a low-rank subspace. Across language and vision tasks, LoRA shrinks the performance gap between Adam and Muon seen under full fine-tuning. Studies on LoRA rank, forgetting, and LoRA variants confirm mismatch severity tracks update strength.
arxiv-2605-10568:
Yeonseok Lee proposes a self-fixing framework for CNC machine code. Language models can turn human intent into G-code. But a sound toolpath may still cause a crash, since safe runs depend on machine state, fixtures, and stock size. His 2026 paper pairs neural generation with formal checks.

The framework pulls exact boundary shapes from 3D CAD models using OpenCASCADE. An LLM writes the first code draft, while a Separation Logic prover with a Spatial Heap model checks the output. Crashes are treated as logical Spatial Data Races, breaks of the separating conjunction in Separation Logic. Proof failures turn into math feedback, packed into bounding boxes that direct the LLM's step-by-step self-fixing. The goal is safer, checked self-run manufacturing with less human oversight.
arxiv-2605-10868:
Mauricio Mendivelso-Villaquirán turns the Solar System into a classroom laboratory for Newton's law of universal gravitation. Textbooks usually hand students the finished formula as a fact from three centuries ago, with no path showing how it was earned.

A deduction built from public data from trusted sources uses planetary observations of the kind Kepler analyzed before Newton unified them. Students see how scattered measurements harden into a single law, and teachers get a worked route for teaching deduction rather than memorization. Middle- and high-school physics classes are the intended audience.
arxiv-2605-11268:
Elham Pourabbas Vafa, Sayak Saha Roy, and Shirin Nilizadeh show how public social data and generative AI can be misused to run context-aware spear-phishing campaigns. With little foe effort, a bit of public activity per target lets GenAI models extract tastes and cues, making messages matching target style while bypassing generic safeguards.

The team introduces a modular framework mixing multimodal signal pulls, style profiles, and attack-type setup across seven tactics: baiting, scareware, honey trap, tailing, impersonation, quid pro quo, and emotional exploitation. A large-scale, multi-model study covers thousands of emails and eight security criteria, set against real-world phishing mails. GenAI emails show much higher personal touch, grounding, and pull. A user study backs these results: LLM attacks beat APWG eCrimeX emails across eight angles while drawing less suspicion among human readers. Security teams get hard evidence of GenAI spear-phishing potency.
arxiv-2605-11368: Jeongchan Kim, Yunkyung Ko and Jong Chul Ye propose LPDP, a training-free operator for reward-guided DNA generation with Edit Flows. Unlike fixed-length frameworks, Edit Flows build variable-length DNA through biologically plausible insertions, deletions and substitutions. During each guided rollout, LPDP rates single-step root edits, keeps a near-best band, and re-ranks each root by working out a small bounded discrete program around its child sequence. It serves two regimes: front-loaded tilting for enhancer optimization and back-loaded tilting for exon-intron-exon inpainting.
arxiv-2605-11668: Wrobel, Barkana and Landowska compare animated emotion displays across cultures for wearables. Wearables can sense feelings nonstop, yet sending that data back quietly is hard, and lifelike avatars rarely fit small screens. Simple shape animation offers a fast, easy-to-read alternative, but cross-culture use is untested. In a study of 105 people from Poland and Turkey mapping feelings to color, shape, size and speed, color and object size proved understood everywhere. Animation speed alone showed cultural differences in range tastes, informing auto-made visuals for global use.
arxiv-2605-12168: Theresa Dahl Frehr and three colleagues ask what low-resolution data teaches. Many systems lack datasets, as sharing is limited by storage, privacy, or resources, and wearables aggregate data, losing detail. High- and low-resolution samples mix, yet low-resolution data's value on high-resolution tests is unclear. Kullback-Leibler theory shows how point influence shifts with resolution and bounds the value of high- versus low-resolution observations. Tests with a vision transformer and a convolutional net show low-resolution data lifts scores when high-resolution data is scarce.
arxiv-2605-12368: Yang removes the retraining bottleneck from machine-learning solvers for partial differential equations. His MetaColloc system first meta-trains a two-branch network on varied random fields, building a shared dictionary of basis functions. At test time the network stays frozen, and each new equation is solved by one linear least-squares step, with Newton steps for nonlinear cases. Tests on six two- and three-dimensional equations reach leading accuracy while cutting test-time compute by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2605-12568: Pronzato and Zhigljavsky study quantisation for sphere-symmetric spreads before limits take over. Zador's theorem gives the limit spread and error decay for best point sets, yet in high spaces reaching that regime needs a sample size growing super-fast with space size. For mid-size samples, they show point sets spread evenly on a sphere of suitable radius perform very well. Mean error, written as a triple integral, can be found to any detail, and the best radius follows by number or from extreme-value guesses.
arxiv-2605-12668: Rivera and Tewari propose online conformal prediction methods that keep guess sets nested across cover levels. It gives finite-sample cover promises, yet old online methods often handle one level and ignore match across levels. Different users, from weather teams to risk teams, need tuned sets across risk limits, and those sets should be nested and valid at once. Their two methods output nested sets across levels, enabling at-once doubt measure across the risk spectrum without losing truth at any level.
arxiv-2605-13068: Kachhadiya alone tackles a bind in nonlinear inverse problems: first-order steps are cheap yet brittle, while curvature-aware routes like Gauss-Newton cost more. He trains a two-way stand-in, Deceptron, that can run forward and backward. As solver D-IPG, it drags error-corrected measurement-space proposals back into latent space. A Jacobian Composition Penalty shapes the reverse Jacobian into a local left inverse of the forward one. On seven PDE problems, D-IPG tops standard baselines while solving at up to 77 times lower cost.
arxiv-2605-13768: Or Ordentlich and Yury Polyanskiy study high-rate rounded matrix multiplication with spread data, part two of a work whose part one covered tuning-free rounding. They show waterfilling lifts real GPTQ rounding, which currently allocates rate equally. A recent WaterSIC scheme using only scalar INT rounders is basis free, marked by the value of the spread matrix. GPTQ scores depend on basis choice, but with random spin and Llama-3-8B spread it sits within 0.1 bit of WaterSIC, hinting near-best at high rates.
arxiv-2605-13868: Koul and Nandakumar study dimension spectra of polynomial curves, a topic in fractal shape theory. They adapt old real root-find methods to this setting. The key result: each polynomial curve has a spectrum with at least two points. That settles a query Stull had posed. The same result yields polynomials with width past one, settling a second Stull query.
arxiv-2605-14368: Kong, Lee and Jo ask where diffusion should operate inside a pretrained model, treating hidden-state interface choice as a design question. They score interfaces with three training-free geometric proxies: local compactness, global stiffness and effective rank. The score predicts diffusion bridgeability beyond layer depth alone. Their method, DiHAL, replaces the transformer prefix below an interface with diffusion, keeping the suffix and head. Geometry-chosen interfaces stay near validation-loss oracles and beat worst-layer controls. The bridge also beats a fixed replacement.
arxiv-2605-14568: Mughal, Fatima and Bilal mine behaviour-driven test suites for repeated step subsequences worth extracting as reusable pieces. From a corpus of hundreds of Gherkin repositories they cluster paraphrase-equivalent slices and train a classifier to rank extraction-worthy candidates against three known refactoring patterns. The classifier is claimed to beat both a rule baseline and language-model judges, and most scenarios are found to carry at least one candidate.
arxiv-2605-14768: Nayak, Sharma and Mishra introduce an algebra method for eigenvalue bounds of symmetric positive definite tensors. Trace and determinant do the work as key numbers. A chain of bounds from the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality yields tighter and tighter upper and lower bounds. The bounds cover the tensor spectral radius and smallest eigenvalue. Tests claim the new approach beats older coordinate methods such as Gershgorin bounds. The bounds stay robust where Gershgorin bounds fail, including tensors with negative off-diagonal terms.
arxiv-2605-14868: Ciosek, Petrov, Felicioni and Palla introduce fast adversarial attacks with gradient prediction. Generating adversarial examples is core to robustness evaluation and red-teaming, yet even fast attacks like FGSM are limited by the backward pass. The authors eliminate the backward pass by forecasting input gradients from forward-pass hidden states via linear regression. Exact affine conditional gradient means are derived, showing optimality in the idealised NTK setting. Much of FGSM performance is recovered at a fraction of the time, a claimed five hundred and thirty-two percent increase.
arxiv-2605-15068: Giulia Murtas and five colleagues test whether magnetic reconnection at the heliospheric current sheet energizes protons and heavier ions seen by Parker Solar Probe. Solving the Parker transport equation on a large-scale reconnection simulation, they find several ion species develop power-law spectra whose slopes and cutoffs match in-situ data. The maximum energy scales with charge-to-mass ratio to a power near 0.8 to 1.1, consistent with probe measurements. The results support reconnection as the source of these high-energy heavy ions.
arxiv-2605-15168: Sayantan Kumar and three others reconstruct clinical timelines by pairing narrative text with structured health-record rows. Notes describe symptoms and course but compress or reorder events, while lab and drug rows carry timestamps but only part of the story. Their staged workflow extracts central narrative events and builds a temporal scaffold. It adds the rest and fixes time stamps against pulled structured rows. On 40 discharge notes with gold-standard timelines, multimodal tuning mostly improved temporal accuracy while event match rates held steady.
arxiv-2605-15268: Artem Belov and Andrey Morozov examine the claimed equivalence, at observable level, between the Ising minimal model and SU(2) level-2 Chern-Simons theory. On the surface the theories differ substantially: the counts of irreducible highest-weight representations and Ising anyons do not match. For tensor products of low degree, the authors inspect these discrepancies. They find that differing representation structure does not change the observables behind topological quantum computation algorithms.
arxiv-2605-15468: Trisha Solanki proposes GreenZ, a design frame for digital systems that waste less. Its three layers are ten guiding rules, five applied systems, and hands-on audit tools. At its core sit a list of eight kinds of digital waste and a choice model. That model asks if AI belongs in a step at all, before asking how to build it. The frame rests on theory but has no test data yet. An expert review is now in progress.
arxiv-2605-15568: Laszlo Wolf, Geoff L. Brennecka, and Vladan Stevanović probe why boron breaks the link between stiffness and piezoelectric reply in an aluminum-scandium nitride alloy. They run first-principles sums on 100-atom random structures across many mixes. Pair plots show boron atoms wedged off-site with three bonds, lined up along the c-axis by a scandium-driven route. Boron slowly evens out the scandium setting. Charge links show this evening-out drives the piezoelectric gain.
arxiv-2605-16068: Dutkiewicz, Misiorek, and Wrembel propose a richer ontology for tracing data lineage in relational databases. Links between database objects are often incomplete or missing. Their formal vocabulary captures structural, semantic, and change details of such data. In a knowledge-graph link test, the enriched model improved link recovery over the earlier baseline. The goal is to help analysts find where each field in a report came from and how it was changed on the way.
arxiv-2605-16268: Atreya and nine colleagues build a customer-facing triage agent that helps banks route fraud, scam, and dispute reports to the right specialist teams. Manual triage is slow and stressful for customers and staff alike. Their language-model agent holds multi-turn conversations, asks targeted questions, and classifies cases under policy-guided routing. Tested against synthetic digital twins of real customers, it improved classification accuracy on historical cases by 30.6 percent, with high satisfaction from subject-matter experts.
arxiv-2605-16568: Wu's thesis tackles reasoning under uncertainty in knowledge graphs. Such graphs may carry vague values, uncertain links, and patchy schema knowledge. Current Semantic Web standards offer no native way to reason with such uncertainty. Naive add-ons fail to scale, so the work builds a modular framework across three levels. It defines probabilistic literals with a query algebra for attributes. It compiles SPARQL provenance into usable probabilistic circuits for uncertain triples. It uses topology-aware embeddings for schema reasoning.
arxiv-2605-16668: Bresson and colleagues introduce GraViti, a graph-level variational autoencoder built on transformers that packs an entire graph into one fixed-length latent vector. The encoder stays permutation-invariant, so input order does not matter, but the rebuild loss need not be, when training data use a consistent node order. Dropping the cubic-cost matching step cuts complexity to quadratic while improving rebuild quality. The latent space allows smooth interpolation, molecular editing, property search, and direct regression of graph properties.
arxiv-2605-16768: Gao and colleagues propose ARG-Mamba, a state-space framework for segmenting optical-elevation remote-sensing images. Existing methods struggle with multi-scale context and cross-modal fusion in complex high-resolution scenes. A multi-scale state-space module captures fine local detail and global context with linear complexity, while an axial-relation fusion module models cross-modal correlations along horizontal and vertical axes. On the ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam datasets, ARG-Mamba beats state-of-the-art methods while keeping computation favorable.
arxiv-2605-17068: Ye proposes a Bayesian method for picking treatments when the best policy is uncertain. He places a Dirichlet process prior over the outcome distribution and uses its posterior both to choose policies and to judge best achievable welfare. The approach needs only simple reweighting of the data, and its welfare loss shrinks at the best possible rate while policy-class selection stays consistent. Trials on job training and bednet subsidies favor simple decision-tree rules over linear ones.
arxiv-2605-17568: Xu and colleagues propose a neural marked point process that uncovers interpretable event links while predicting well. A product-form neural influence kernel pairs a signed link network over event types with a delay-aware monotonic temporal network. That design maps excitation, inhibition and neutrality plus varied decay patterns and influence delays. A stratified Monte Carlo sampler enables efficient training. Tests on synthetic and real benchmarks validate both link discovery and predictive strength.
arxiv-2605-17668: Maren Høibø and colleagues explore deep-learning glass removal and compression for whole slide images, compared with JPEG and JPEG-XL. Digital pathology produces growing numbers of whole slide images; today JPEG yields several gigabytes per image. Deep-learning compression cut whole slide image size by 43 to 72 percent over JPEG, while glass removal cut size by under one percent to 33 percent. Combining both gave a 44 to 80 percent total reduction. On tissue patches, the best deep-learning models saved about 35 to 40 percent per patch over JPEG at similarity above 95 percent.
arxiv-2605-18068: Seyed Mohamad Moghadas and three colleagues present TEGER, a residual covariance model keeping a traffic forecaster's joint uncertainty current at test time. A fixed sensor graph gives a spatial precision factor showing which sensors' errors move together. At inference, Gaussian adjustment corrects the next forecast's mean and covariance from the latest errors, while a moving-average term rescales marginal spread to track local drift. The updates leave the backbone untouched, so the same fix turns a frozen foundation model into one with fresh, linked risk at tiny added cost.
arxiv-2605-18568: Myriam Mahaman shows in a 2026 note that the ring of differential operators on a nodal curve is neither locally projective nor a bialgebroid. An earlier paper proved local projectivity suffices for a bialgebroid structure on such rings over an affine variety. Using elementary methods, this note closes the nodal-curve case in the negative on both counts. The result separates nodal curves from varieties where the bialgebroid structure holds.
arxiv-2605-18768: Joseph Boyle and four co-authors introduce ClinQueryAgent, a 2026 agent turning population health questions into executable database queries. Cloud-based language models power the system while no patient data leaves the secure environment. Retrieval is delegated to a sub-agent to fight context rot over long dialogues. Deployed in a chat window inside a health platform, it served 128 staff from 15 practices covering 148,319 UK patients. Analysts and clinicians alike generate actionable information from health records through natural language requests, needing no programming expertise.
arxiv-2605-18868: Ye Sun and nine colleagues turn plain-language attack orders into visual tricks that fool vision and multimodal models. Their DarkLLM system trains a language model to convert an instruction into a hidden attack vector, which is then decoded as a perturbation added to an image. One small model, with about a billion parameters, thus covers targeted, untargeted, segmentation and multi-model attacks alike. Tests across many tasks, datasets and models show it working against CLIP, SAM and frontier language models, exposing a broad weakness in current foundation models.
arxiv-2605-19968: Boyd and three colleagues simulate, in a 2026 study, a simmering white dwarf before it explodes as a Type Ia supernova, focusing on the convective Urca process. Their three-dimensional MAESTROeX runs add three Urca pairs, labelled by mass numbers 21, 23 and 25, to a fuller carbon-burning network. Comparing runs with and without the process shows it weakens mixing near the edge of the convection zone without shrinking that zone, with the 23 pair mattering most.
arxiv-2605-20268: Paul Quinlan and co-workers set out Chronicle, a 324M decoder on words and time series sharing blocks, attention, stream. First on both from scratch, judged against single-domain models. Numbers alone feed time series models; mixed models bolt on text models late, with weights unshaped by time data. Training runs one kind at a time, growing mixed skill from shared weights, plus brief mixing. It ties Gemma-3-270M-PT on 19 NLU tasks, tops frozen-embedding classification on 24 UCR/UEA sets, beating fusion rivals on Time-MMD.
arxiv-2605-20468: Diaz-Rincon and three co-workers give Parkinson's dose forecasts bands that widen or narrow with confidence. Standard conformal bands treat sure and shaky calls alike, hiding how much a levodopa dose forecast can be trusted. Their CASCADE framework scales intervals for a two-stage decision: first whether a dose change is needed, then how much change. Patients the model trusts get intervals 38.9 percent narrower than standard baselines, while uncertain cases widen to hold coverage.
arxiv-2605-20568: Emmanuel Breuillard and Tsachik Gelander study dense subgroups of connected Lie groups, smooth groups of symmetries. They show any dense subgroup already contains a dense subgroup generated by twice as many elements as the group's dimension. They also give a detailed proof about contracting projective maps. It links contraction strength to the ratio of the two largest terms in the map's Cartan decomposition.
arxiv-2605-20668: Seungone Kim and fifty-six colleagues study AI reviewers through the reviews of Nature-family papers, rated by 45 expert scientists. AI reviewers are entering peer review, yet their skill and credibility remain disputed. Earlier tests asked mainly whether AI verdicts match human verdicts, which hides what AI reviewers do well or badly. In this large annotation study, experts spent 469 hours scoring 2,960 individual criticisms, each facing one specific aspect of a paper, to map strengths and limits.
arxiv-2605-20768: Wen Zhang and six colleagues demonstrate MIR single-photon temporal ghost imaging with sub-pixel detail. Ghost imaging in time recovers ultrafast signals with slow sensors, promising fast MIR sensing. Their system uses a pre-programmed near-infrared pump as a time gate to drive sum-frequency making in a nonlinear crystal. MIR waveforms at 3.4 micrometres are upconverted and caught by a room-temperature silicon sensor, with fractional-bin stepping freeing detail from pattern timescale.
arxiv-2605-20868: Dean Calver presents a tiered KV cache design for runtime-certified attention with bounded-error quantized attention. KV cache quantization cuts memory cost for long-context language-model inference but adds approximation error usually tested only empirically. Existing systems lean on average-case robustness, with no way to spot or recover from failures at runtime. His design stores INT8 keys and INT4 values on the GPU, while FP16 originals stay in system RAM for deterministic fallback, with per-head, per-step error bounds driving adaptive precision.
arxiv-2605-20968: I. Muhammad and Gerald Schuller predict energy decay curves for room impulse responses from room geometry and material properties. Predicting room echoes remains hard due to high audio size and the need for perceptual accuracy. Their neural network design predicts multi-band energy decay curves straight from geometry and materials, using a custom composite loss that optimizes both energy tiers and decay slopes in the log domain. That ensures predicted curves follow physical decay principles while staying sensitive to reverberation time and early reflections.
arxiv-2605-21068: Urosevic and six colleagues study radio emission from radiative filaments of the Cygnus Loop supernova remnant. The Cygnus Loop is an ideal lab for work on radiation ways and particle speed-up at varied shock types. To find radio spectral indices of dark and bright filaments, they observed earlier light-studied filaments via the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. At 1 and 5 GHz, they detected only bright filaments in view, while dark optical filaments present were not seen in radio.
arxiv-2605-21168: Qiyu Ruan and colleagues present ScenePilot, a tool that makes safety-critical driving scenes at the edge of what is physically possible. Most tools either make crashes that could never happen or tie what is possible to one controller. ScenePilot aims at the thin band where a scene could in principle be solved yet still beats the driving stack in use. It joins a score for physical feasibility with a learned risk predictor, plus step-level shielding that keeps new scenes near that band.
arxiv-2605-21468: Zhepei Wei and co-authors show that reward-based learning with verifiable rewards, known as RLVR, produces very low-rank and highly predictable weight trajectories in large language models. Most downstream gains are captured by a rank-one approximation of parameter deltas. The projection magnitude evolves near-linearly with training steps. They propose RELEX, which estimates the rank-one subspace from a short observation window and projects later checkpoints by linear regression, with no learned model required.
arxiv-2605-21868: Heeyun Heo and Huy Kang Kim study when to switch decks in Clash Royale, using over 926,000 matches from 34,619 players. Switching frequency runs inversely to win rate across players. This traces to a Zero Switching Cost Assumption in prior recommenders that ignore switching costs and individual propensity. Their Transition Quality Predictor runs Who, When, What. PersonaGate holds back picks for strong players. TimingGate finds when switching beats staying. ScoreFusion ranks candidates by adoptability and transition quality. It reaches a SwitchGap of plus 10.4 percentage points at a 5.4 percent recommendation rate.
arxiv-2605-21968: Saurabh Saini and co-authors improve an adaptive PID optimizer for deep learning, combining control theory with the Adam optimizer. Momentum-based stochastic gradient descent suffers noisy, varying gradients and overshoot, and Adam fixed the noise but not the overshoot. Their IAdaPID-ADG optimizer merges a PID-based extension of Adam with an adaptive gradient idea, targeting both flaws at once. Tested on MNIST, CIFAR10, and real-world IARC and AnnoCerv datasets, it substantially beats competing optimizers, and an ablation study on MNIST shows each added part contributes.
arxiv-2605-22068: Junhyub Lee, Seunghun Chae, and Hyosu Kim formalize open tree decomposition, which splits an image into hierarchical trees of visual parts with free granularity. Manual annotation for such trees is very hard, so the team builds a fully automated generation pipeline. Human checks confirm the generated annotations match human judgment well, including on complex physical assemblies. They also set a standard evaluation protocol with the Open Tree Quality metric, which jointly rates mask precision, label accuracy, and structural consistency, and they release dataset and code.
arxiv-2605-22368: Bai and colleagues build VeriScale, a tool for making code tests that can be checked by proof. Old test sets are too thin, so models look better than they are. VeriScale grows test sets with hostile code, then trims them to small sets that still tell models apart. On Verina, it makes VerinaPlus, with suites over 83 times as large, and a light VerinaLite at 14 times. Tests on eight top models show VerinaPlus lays bare flaws the old set hid. VerinaLite keeps that power at far less cost.
arxiv-2605-22568: Abdelnabi and team argue benchmarks for AI agents in high-risk roles suffer crucial flaws. Building on recent evidence, the team names three core problems that weaken safety tests: benchmark holes, aging, and run-time doubt. Benchmark holes let agents exploit flaws rather than show safety skill. Aging means benchmarks age as threats and systems change. Run-time doubt means results vary with execution conditions. The team sketches usable paths toward more robust and sound test sets.
arxiv-2605-22668: Rajabi and others tackle the drop in diffusion transformer image quality when generating above training resolution. Older training free fixes scale rotary position embeddings uniformly, trading global structure against fine detail. Their SEGA method instead scales attention across rotary parts adaptively, guided by the latent image's spatial frequency pattern at each denoising step. This scaling keeps both overall coherence and fine detail. Tests show SEGA beats top training free baselines across several target resolutions.
arxiv-2605-23168: Sun and four coauthors introduce PoisonForge, a benchmark for task poisoning of tuned models. An attacker slips pairs into tuning data, so the model inserts an entity into outputs for a task family while acting normal elsewhere. It varies bias type and poisoning mode, and tests 12 models across five families at a 1 percent budget. With 10 examples among 1,000, 11 of 12 pass 70 percent success in one setup. Leakage to tasks stays below 0.5 percent, and poison design, not model size, drives attacks.
arxiv-2605-23868: Linxiang Su revisits a quiet failure in vision transformers: patch tokens lose their local sharpness during long training even as whole image scores stay strong. Su argues the culprit is semantic diffusion, global meaning bleeding into patches beyond what local evidence warrants, not just high norm artifacts. Testing sparse attention as a light fix, swapping softmax for entmax-1.5 while keeping global links, preserves ImageNet probing and lifts segmentation markedly, with VOC mean IoU rising from 42.80 to 48.78.
arxiv-2605-24068: Carayol and Rotondo give methods for sampling profiles of uniform random maps and surjections, where only the shape matters, not the labels. A profile simply records, for each preimage size that occurs, how many preimages have that size. Their methods sample profiles directly across the whole parameter range, with no assumption linking n and k, and run near the output length up to log factors. Built on exact-size Boltzmann samplers, they also settle an open sampling question up to a log factor and yield a fast surjection sampler.
arxiv-2605-24268: Migliorelli and three co-authors extend wave-turbulence study to the alpha-FPUT lattice with site-varying spring stiffness and nonlinear factor. For constant factors, three-wave links are non-matching, but spatial shifts create a non-trivial resonant set. The authors derive a new kinetic rule hinting at much faster warming than the constant-factor case. An extra term tied to Bragg scattering promotes evening-out of the wave-action spectrum. Model runs confirm the far faster warming path under random factors.
arxiv-2605-24468: Hu and seven co-authors propose State-Adaptive Memory, a frame for reasoning consolidating interaction into compact cues. Long histories challenge agents not just by length, but because information may sit in distant steps. Existing fixes truncate, compress, or retrieve history, but none model how past access should adapt to state. Memory cues act as handles for rebuilding distant information as needs dictate. The memory module is tuned through expert-guided supervision and reinforcement learning. Across BrowseComp, BrowseComp-ZH, WideSearch, and HLE, the frame beats strong baselines across backbones.
arxiv-2605-25068: Laurence Wroe and colleagues report first tests of a trial target-moderator-reflector assembly for the VULCAN compact neutron source. VULCAN aims at an accelerator-driven neutron source for crystal studies in labs. It turns a 35 MeV electron pulse train into short neutron bursts under 20 microseconds wide, spanning 1.5 to 3.5 angstroms. The trial ran at CERN's CLEAR. Slowed pulses showed up, but measured and modelled energy spectra differed sharply, so the paper lists causes and calls for more tests.
arxiv-2605-25268: Abdul Samad Khan derives a graph network for molecular energies that keeps higher-order electron interactions instead of squashing them into simple features. The design starts from a Cholesky factorization of the electron repulsion tensor, splitting orbitals and helpers into two linked node sets. That structure cuts the theoretical cost from fourth to third power in system size while preserving interaction topology. On 132 geometries of six two-atom molecules, it reaches a mean error near 0.03 Hartree, ahead of compressed baselines, though transfer to unseen molecules varies sharply.
arxiv-2605-25368: Tae Woong Jeong and Sung Min Jo pin down atomic nitrogen radiation parameters, a major hypersonic heat source in nitrogen-rich air. Einstein and Stark values carry wide uncertainty, so the pair infers 18 parameters by Bayesian inversion of shock-tube spectra in two NASA Ames shots. A surrogate model and joint likelihood across both shots make sampling tractable in eight wavelength regions. Posterior uncertainties shrink below prior bands. Propagating the result through flow around a 3-meter sphere cuts heat-flux spread fivefold, with gains largest at top speed.
arxiv-2605-25768: Kashif and Shafique re-examine the expressibility-trainability trade-off in hybrid quantum neural networks. Highly expressive circuits are thought more prone to barren plateaus, but the hybrid link was unclear. Across depths, qubit counts, topologies and training setups, pure parameterized circuits show only a weak, regime-dependent trade-off. Hybrid architectures increasingly disrupt and can even erase the relationship under full hybrid training, as classical parts reshape the optimization landscape. They also propose a multi-objective architecture search over expressibility, trainability and task results.
arxiv-2605-26068: Xu Yao and eight colleagues' 2026 benchmark, WSADBench, is the first to judge weakly supervised anomaly detection across its three research directions together. It standardizes tests for thirty-six algorithms across four data types, varying label amount, detail, and quality over more than seven hundred thousand experiments. Four lessons emerge: the three directions correlate strongly, specialist methods win only when labels are scarcest, unlabeled data helps unevenly, and models react unevenly to label noise. The benchmark ships open with code and data.
arxiv-2605-26368: Vukasin Bozic and six colleagues lift 3D foundation models built for flat photos into the panorama world with PaGeR. From a trained transformer for 3D rebuilding, they tune one model to read flat and wraparound images alike. One pass yields two scales of depth, surface normals, and sky masks. Mixing both image kinds in training keeps the old 3D know-how intact. Indoor and outdoor tests report top scores and strong results on unseen scenes.
arxiv-2605-26468: Yuxuan Yin and six colleagues screen latent chip defects without labeled failures using a diffusion transformer. Raw test readings first pass through an autoencoder, then reshape into tokens enriched with per-device wafer-position data and sinusoidal cues. Scores come from noise-prediction error over mid-range diffusion steps, enabling fast wafer-scale screening with no manual feature work. On industrial 16-nanometer chip test data under extreme class imbalance, the method reaches state-of-the-art performance. Latent-space reconstruction residuals also point to where failures sit.
arxiv-2605-26568: Yuan-chin Ivan Chang unifies data-summary habits under target-oriented statistical compression. A useful summary keeps what matters for an inferential or choice target. The key object is the target process, the expected target given kept facts, forming a reverse martingale with a limit as kept facts shrink. Exact sufficiency means lossless compression. Rough summaries like penalized estimators yield quasi-martingale gaps gauging coherence loss. Edge degeneracy in sequential binary problems anchors the main use. Practical edge claims need joint checks of closeness, uncertainty, and path stability.

arxiv-2606-04168:
Bochen Lyu and co-authors explain in 2026 why safety training in large language models is often shallow, changing behavior mainly in the first few output words. Their culprit is autoregressive consistency: the model's drive to continue its current trajectory smoothly rather than break pattern.

Analyzing how safety training updates the model, they show this consistency concentrates the changes on early tokens. The same force predicts attacks that plant a harmful span anywhere in an otherwise safe answer, letting the model carry the harmful branch forward. Their random insertion attack did exactly that, even after long refusals. As a remedy they propose adversarial safety training built from worst-case inserted continuations, and test an initial version using random worst insertions.
arxiv-2606-04268:
Yakiv Shavidze presents ACEAPEX in 2026, a compression codec that breaks the serial bottleneck of LZ77 decompression, where each back-reference depends on data already decoded, blocking parallel work. His fix moves the bookkeeping to encode time.

All back-references are stored as absolute positions in the output, and data is organized into self-contained one-megabyte blocks that decode independently across cores. On genomic data the codec passed ten gigabytes per second on eight cores, up to about three times faster than a standard compressor setting at similar ratios. A graphics processor decoder reached far higher speeds, verified byte-for-byte against the reference. The author claims the first graphics-processor LZ77 decode at near-standard compression ratios.
arxiv-2606-04468:
Sun and colleagues present a diffusion-based method for designing objects that must balance several goals at once, in a 2026 arXiv paper. These are options where no goal can improve without hurting another. The search runs without new experiments. Recent generative methods lean on surrogate models. These stand-ins predict each goal, but they add cost and can be fooled. ParetoPilot removes the surrogate entirely. It uses the guidance already inside a pre-trained diffusion model.

Its Infer-Perturb-Guide engine works inside the denoising steps. It infers improving directions by comparing conditional and unconditional noise predictions. It builds a perturbation with a convergence pull and a diversity push. Then it steers generation through classifier-free guidance. Across 51 tasks, ParetoPilot beat 14 baselines. The rivals were surrogate-based and inverse generative methods. It won on hypervolume, a measure of Pareto front quality, and on coverage. It also avoided auxiliary training.
arxiv-2606-04668:
Baibolatov, Omel'chenko, and Rosenblum show that a more careful mathematical approximation reveals collective states in oscillator networks that the standard approximation hides, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. The standard first-order version yields the celebrated Kuramoto model. The authors compare it with second-order phase reduction, which keeps quadratic corrections.

The second-order model improves quantitative accuracy. It also reveals new dynamics. It describes bistability of synchronous states in the minimal setup of two coupled oscillators. There, in-phase and anti-phase synchrony coexist. It also explains three-cluster states. In these, the faster group splits into two clusters while the slower group forms one. The first-order theory forbids them under the Watanabe-Strogatz theorem. Agreement with numerical simulations of the full Stuart-Landau network is very good. This highlights the usefulness of higher-order phase reduction for weakly coupled oscillatory networks.
arxiv-2606-05168:
Xiangyu Wang models model collapse as an epidemic in this 2026 arXiv paper, treating synthetic data contamination as something that spreads through the AI world. Training on synthetic data degrades models, but most analyses follow one chain of self-training. In reality models ingest synthetic text from other models, generate more of it, and taint shared corpora, a cross-spreading process closer to infection dynamics.

Wang builds a coupled SIR and SIRS framework, with data corpora and AI models as two interacting populations, each split into susceptible, infected, and recovered groups. Fitting from AI text frequency data gives runaway dynamics in all three cases studied, and the model names synthetic-text spotting as the highest-leverage parameter. GPT-2 contamination chain experiments showed dose-response decline and variety loss matching the threshold picture, while multi-source mixing only slowed collapse. Detection-based filtering and herd immunity rank as the strongest remedies.
arxiv-2606-05268:
Sharon Zhang, R. Kenny Jones, Jiajun Wu, and Maneesh Agrawala build strong verifiers out of weak, model-generated ones for layout generation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generative models can produce room layouts or poster designs from a description, but checking whether an output matches it falls to fallible model judges. Their pipeline asks a language model to synthesize verifier programs in a layout verification language. Each verifier checks one imperfect aspect of the match.

Using weak learning techniques, the pipeline learns to aggregate the weak votes into a strong verifier from about ten human-labeled layouts. Across 3D room layout and 2D poster design tasks, the verifiers outperformed the status-quo panel of model judges, raising F1 scores by up to seven times. Used with natural-language feedback, the verifiers guided a layout generator to better outputs, improving layout quality by up to 66.2 percent as judged by human evaluators.
arxiv-2606-05368:
Sayan Mandal and colleagues release Biomazon in this 2026 arXiv paper, a multimodal benchmark dataset for modeling 3D forest structure and biomass in the Amazon Basin. Tropical forests hold half the world's forest carbon, so mapping their structure matters for carbon accounting. Yet machine learning pipelines usually predict scalars such as a canopy height proxy or aboveground biomass density, rather than the forest's vertical profile as a structure.

Biomazon is a 20-meter-resolution benchmark pairing GEDI lidar targets, the relative-height profile plus biomass density, with multi-sensor predictors. The predictors are Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites, ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 radar, the Copernicus elevation model, Dynamic World land cover, and AlphaEarth embeddings. All sit under spatial splits and evaluation protocols. As a baseline the authors train a shared encoder-decoder with task-specific heads and run an ablation over backbone scale, modality contributions, and embeddings, reporting single-target and joint-target results.
arxiv-2606-05568:
Yang and colleagues set out to slim the index behind a strong search model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The model, ColBERT, scores documents by comparing many small word vectors. Its indexes can take five to ten times the disk space of the raw text. The slow steps at query time are gathering and unpacking those vectors. The team asks whether a compressed index can stay accurate while acting like a classic inverted index.

Their design squeezes each vector with product quantization, a method that stores a short code in place of full numbers. In theory the result matches learned sparse search, apart from the scoring rule. In practice the new index came out fifty to seventy percent smaller than a one-bit rival index. Search quality held steady at that much smaller size. The paper appeared at the SIGIR 2026 conference on information retrieval.
arxiv-2606-05668:
Rector and colleagues map newborn star outflows across the Serpens and Aquila Rift region in a 2026 arXiv paper. Herbig-Haro objects are glowing knots where young stars blast jets into nearby gas. A sensitive survey with the DECam camera hunted them across the region. The team found eighty-eight new outflow objects. That haul more than triples the known count there.

Likely parent stars were matched to most of the outflows. Combined with dust maps and Gaia distances, the outflows mark five separate star-forming clouds. Two sit near four to five hundred parsecs away; two rift clouds lie farther, near six and seven hundred. A near cloud at about two hundred fifty parsecs appears to belong to the Local Bubble. In two clouds the outflows rim empty cavities, as if feedback shells are triggering new stars. The survey gives future young-star hunts a sharp guide.
arxiv-2606-05868:
A joint team from the Postal Savings Bank of China and Huawei squeezes financial language models for busy serving in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bank chatbots face floods of simultaneous users. The memory cache each conversation needs throttles how many can run at once. YouZhi rebuilds a model's attention layout layer by layer, shifting grouped attention toward a compressed latent form. Each layer gets its own folding size, tuned adaptively.

Distillation plus finance-specific training restore the skill the compression costs. Quality loss from the switch fell by up to thirty-five percent against uniform conversion. On Huawei Ascend hardware the savings turned into real capacity. The seven-billion model served about two point seven times as many users at once. Its finance benchmark score rose by about twelve percent. The fourteen-billion model showed the same pattern, slightly smaller. Structure surgery, the teams argue, beats buying more servers.
arxiv-2606-06068:
Antonir and Shapira count the ways to write a number as a sum of primes, with deliberately elementary tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. The prime partition function grows fast, and sharp estimates exist. Their proofs, though, are long and heavy. The authors settle for a slightly softer asymptotic: the logarithm of the count grows like two pi times a square-root term involving n and its logarithm.

The proof is short and uses no deep machinery. That simplicity is the contribution. The same recipe adapts easily to several related restricted-partition problems with long literatures. Partition asymptotics descend from Hardy and Ramanujan's celebrated formula for unrestricted partitions. Elementary routes into that landscape lower the entry barrier for students and researchers alike. Trade a little sharpness, gain a method that travels. The authors present the recipe as a template for sibling counting problems. Classical combinatorics still rewards economy of means.
arxiv-2606-06468:
Jui Hui Chung and co-authors automate mathematical proof with a planning first system in this 2026 arXiv paper. Formal theorem proving in Lean 4 demands machine checked proofs, and most AI provers decompose theorems recursively, which can loop forever on dead end strategies. Their Goedel Architect instead drafts a blueprint: a dependency graph of definitions and lemmas leading to the main theorem. A tool equipped prover then attacks each open lemma in parallel, and failures feed back to revise the blueprint itself.

Powered by an open weight DeepSeek model, the system scored ninety nine point two percent on the MiniF2F test set in a single attempt. It reached seventy five point six percent on the harder PutnamBench. Seeding the blueprint with a natural language proof closed the last two MiniF2F problems as well. Separating global planning from local proving, they argue, keeps the search from wandering.
arxiv-2606-06668:
Inside a proton, quarks are tied together by a thin tube of force that snaps when stretched too far. Carragher and March-Russell refine the theory of that tube in this 2026 arXiv paper. The standard picture treats the tube, called a QCD string, as a plain vibrating sheet. Newer work adds a heavy particle like wave that lives on the sheet, nicknamed the worldsheet axion.

The authors compute how an excited string breaks by spawning a quark and antiquark pair. The axion turns out to drive the biggest change: it makes the string's effective tension, its pulling strength, vary from place to place. Where the wave's slope is steep across space, breaking speeds up sharply; where it changes fast in time, breaking slows down. The result feeds into the collider simulations used to model how particles shower into ordinary matter.
arxiv-2606-06768:
Draw a network on a doughnut shaped surface so that every region is a disk, and you have drawn it in many possible ways. Carr and Mohar catalog those drawings for cubic graphs, networks where every point has exactly three links, in this 2026 arXiv paper, the first of a two part series. The count of drawings by genus, the number of holes in the surface, is called the genus distribution.

Their tool is the unstable dual, a subgraph of the mirror network formed by the drawing's regions. Local twists, called rotations, relate all drawings of one graph to each other, and the genus can be read back from the unstable dual. For highly connected planar cubic graphs, they characterize the duals of drawings with genus up to two and build the genus three cases from them.
arxiv-2606-07068:
Every new feature selection method claims victory over older ones, and the scoreboard may be rigged. Ebiele, Bendechache, and Brennan audit that literature in this 2026 arXiv paper. Feature selection picks the most useful variables for a model. Filter methods rank features without training the final model.

The team examined twenty eight prominent studies spanning three decades. They coded each study's data sets, baselines, and design choices. A regression then explained the new methods' win rates. Three counts alone explained a third of the variance. More data sets and more baselines lowered the win rate. More competing new methods raised it. Most methods beat several baselines yet failed to beat using all features. The authors distill five recommendations for fairer evaluation. Their warning is gentle but firm: celebrate wins only after checking the arena.
arxiv-2606-07368:
Aubreville and a consortium report the MIDOG 2025 challenge on detecting cell division in microscope images, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Counting mitotic figures, cells caught mid-division, helps grade tumors, but automated detectors often fail when tumor type, species, or scanner changes. Earlier benchmarks stressed scanner variation alone. This third challenge edition demanded generalization across far broader biological diversity, with two tracks: finding mitotic figures, and classifying them as normal or atypical.

The test set held 365 cases spanning 12 tumor types from humans, dogs, and cats, digitized on multiple scanning platforms. Teams, whose members fill the long author list, tackled both tracks under these realistic shifts. The paper describes the dataset design, the submitted methods, and how performance held up when context changed together rather than one factor at a time. It frames the challenge as a realistic rehearsal for clinical deployment, where distribution shift arrives from every direction at once.
arxiv-2606-08468:
Hyeok Kwon and colleagues learn the dependency graph of high-dimensional data without assuming a form for its distribution, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Undirected graphical models represent conditional independence among many variables: an absent edge means two variables are independent given the rest. Model selection, recovering that graph from data, is central to high-dimensional statistics. Most methods are parametric, assuming Gaussian or similar forms. The authors build a nonparametric approach on diffusion models, which build data by reversing a gradual noising process.

Recent work showed diffusion models can adapt to the unknown graph structure of the data distribution. Using them for explicit graph estimation was unexplored. The authors bridge that gap with a diffusion-based selection method. Experiments show it beats alternatives in the tests run here. That makes the method a good fit for data whose shape no one knows in advance at the start.
arxiv-2606-08568:
Abdelghani, Kaiser, and Murayama study how teenagers actually use an artificial intelligence tutor while learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These tools are now common learning companions for adolescents, yet how students regulate that use is poorly understood. Self-regulated learning and help-seeking are proposed as safeguards against passive, shortcut-oriented use. But most studies measure aggregate outcomes rather than session processes. This work-in-progress examines the process directly.

The data come from ninety-eight ninth-grade students at three German schools who used a web-based tutor built on a large language model to prepare a mathematics skill before an exam. Alongside conversation logs of more than sixteen hundred turns, the researchers collected pre- and post-tests of domain knowledge and self-reported cognitive load. They propose a turn-level codebook with two codes specific to language models: agency over the tool, and epistemic vigilance.
arxiv-2606-08768:
Kövér and colleagues explain why transformers fail to learn simple functions they can in principle represent, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A transformer is the neural network design behind modern language models. The puzzle contrasts expressivity, what settings exist that compute a function, with learnability, what training actually finds. Sensitive functions are the hard cases: one flipped input bit flips the output, as with parity, which reports whether the count of ones is even.

The authors instead study the full sensitivity profile, the spread of sensitivity across all inputs, through parameter-space geometry. They prove randomly initialized transformers almost surely compute functions with many low-sensitivity input strings. Any function lacking such strings is provably unlearnable. Sensitive functions like parity occupy a tiny region of parameter space that random starting points almost never hit. The result reframes a training failure as geometry: solutions live where training cannot reach.
arxiv-2606-08968:
Wang tests three shielding materials for a reactor neutrino detector that must hide from cosmic-ray neutrons, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The ALARM experiment will monitor reactor power by catching antineutrinos with a plastic scintillator detector. It sits about 44 meters from a reactor core at the Taishan plant, only 9.6 meters below the surface. That shallow depth lets cosmic rays generate fast neutrons that mimic the signal, so shielding is essential.

The team compared water, high-density polyethylene, and polyethylene loaded with 40 percent boron, exposing samples to an americium-beryllium neutron source. A 30-centimeter thickness of the boron-loaded plastic blocked more than 95 percent of both fast and thermal neutrons. Water and plain polyethylene performed worse at equal thickness, since boron adds neutron capture on top of slowing. Monte Carlo simulations of the test setup matched the measurements, lending confidence to their simulation of the full ALARM assembly.
arxiv-2606-09268:
Pan and colleagues give a robot one camera and the geometric discipline to know where it is and how far obstacles are, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Navigation needs global position fixes and dense, metric obstacle perception. Robots usually add LiDAR, which measures distance directly, but calibration and overhead follow. Vision-only systems are cheaper, but one camera cannot tell scale, so metric maps and consistent localization have been hard to combine.

VGP-Nav resolves monocular scale ambiguity online by anchoring visual geometry to ground-plane geometry, the constraint that the floor bears a known relation to the camera. That anchor gives a reliable metric reference, so the framework produces localization-grounded, metric obstacle representations a planner can use, from RGB alone. Experiments showed strong generalization across environments, with successful real-robot deployment: navigation needing no LiDAR or multi-sensor calibration can ship on cheap robots at scale.
arxiv-2606-09468:
Damiano Capocci, Moritz Linkmann, and Alexander Morozov ask whether polymer flow simulations must obey a physical constraint at every grid point to stay trustworthy in this 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating elastic turbulence, the chaotic motion of dilute polymer solutions, requires tracking a conformation tensor that describes how polymer molecules stretch. That tensor must stay positive-definite, yet the equations do not enforce it.

Using a standard pseudo-spectral method with no enforcement, the authors simulated a polymer solution driven through a plane channel at low Reynolds number, with a Weissenberg number of one hundred fifty. They found two resolution thresholds: below the first, runs blow up in finite time, and above the second, positivity holds everywhere. Between them, runs stayed stable and chaotic despite local violations of the constraint. Mid-plane statistics of velocity, its gradients, and polymer stretch matched the fully positive-definite simulations.
arxiv-2606-09868:
Zhijing Zhang and a large team teach a multimodal model to forget a concept it may no longer show anyone in this 2026 arXiv paper. Privacy law grants a right to be forgotten, and models can be asked to unlearn. Old unlearning needs the very images to be erased, which strict data rules often bar. Their SPACE frame works source-free, with no sight of the target data.

Stage one picks proxy anchors, stand-in features that sit near the target in the shared space, found by text cues. Stage two then works on those anchors to cut the target out by proxy. Updates are fenced inside the null space of kept knowledge, so the rest of the model stays put. Proofs bound the shake to what is kept. Across six data sets, SPACE matched top data-hungry rivals.
arxiv-2606-09968:
Baker and Liu argue that radio telescopes could double as ears for high-frequency gravitational waves, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. Waves in the megahertz to gigahertz range can convert into radio photons inside astrophysical magnetic fields, through the inverse Gertsenshtein effect. Ordinary detectors do not reach these frequencies. Radio observatories might fill the gap.

The authors show that existing radio dishes such as CHIME and FAST are strong tools for this search. They far beat many purpose-built tests at detecting mergers of primordial black holes, small black holes possibly formed in the early universe, which are the most realistic sources of brief high-frequency waves. Radio telescopes are also uniquely sensitive to steady sources, like ultralight boson clouds grown around black holes by superradiance, a process that drains spin energy. The paper maps a broad discovery space for generic high-frequency sources.
arxiv-2606-10068:
Wang and his team propose spending hyperparameter search budgets where they matter most, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning tuning. Tuning hyperparameters is needed but costly, and in high-dimensional spaces progress dilutes across many low-impact knobs. Their plan, Greedy Importance First, starts with a small warm-up sample to estimate each hyperparameter's importance. It then forms importance-based groups, allocates trials in proportion to importance, and keeps a full-space fallback for safety.

Under fixed test budgets, the method was tested on analytic functions up to fifty dimensions, the Bayesmark benchmark, and NAS-Bench-301, a thirty-three-dimensional net-design search space. On higher-dimensional benchmarks it reached better incumbents with faster progress than TPE, BOHB, random search, and sequential grouping baselines. Ablations showed the importance estimates, matched allocation, and fallback each contribute, and the importance estimator recovered the intended structure on analytic tests.
arxiv-2606-10168:
Kato and Silva pin down a generalized form of torsion in matrix groups, in a 2026 arXiv paper on algebra. An element of a group is generalized torsion if some finite product of its conjugates equals the identity. That weakens the usual torsion notion, where powers of the element itself give the identity. They study upper triangular matrix groups over commutative rings, workhorse examples in algebra. Their result connects the generalized torsion subset to torsion and exponent properties of the unit group of the underlying ring.

They also determine when these matrix groups satisfy generalized identities, equations in conjugated variables that hold for all elements.
