He implied a secret liking for the Germans and a wish for a soft peace. He spoke frankly of the Red Army's poor showing against Finland and its slow climb to a genuinely good army. On Germany he set two conditions: the physical liquidation of at least fifty thousand, perhaps a hundred thousand, of the German commanding staff, and Allied retention of the world's strong points. Roosevelt joked the figure down to forty-nine thousand; Churchill objected fiercely to cold-blooded execution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d468:
Reginald Leeper, the British ambassador to the Greek government-in-exile in Egypt, wrote to Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden on December 3, 1943. Greece was under German occupation, and its exiled government worked from Cairo. The catalog heading misspells “government,” but the parties are clear. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Leeper spoke for London to a restless exile government whose country was a battleground of resistance groups and rival claims. His reports to Eden fed British decisions about Greece at a moment when Cairo hosted both the exile court and the Allied conference. The message opens a window on the war's tangled Greek question.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d568:
Ambassador Averell Harriman recorded this memorandum on November 13, 1944, in Moscow. Harriman's memoranda often preserved his conversations and judgments about the Soviet leadership for the record in Washington. It appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

By late 1944 Harriman's tone about Moscow was hardening: the cooperation promised at Tehran was meeting the facts of Soviet power in Poland and the Balkans. His written record from this season is a key source for the alliance's turn toward friction. For readers, the memorandum shows the ambassador setting down, carefully and on paper, what a year of dealing with Stalin's government had taught him.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d68: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 29, 1943, and a second Churchill note of the same date follows it in the volume. This one is Document 68 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The last days of October were a summing-up season after Moscow and a planning season before Cairo. The catalog record gives the date and the names only. The text in the Foreign Relations series carries its errand.
frus-1944-quebec-d168:
An editors' note introduces the document printed next in the volume, the President's Log for the Quebec Conference. The Log was a booklet covering September 9 to 21, 1944, prepared by Lieutenant William Rigdon and approved by Rear Admiral Wilson Brown. The note describes its contents in detail, from the list of the president's party to the conference communiqué in an appendix.

The editors also compare the Log's party list with the one in Rigdon's later book, White House Sailor. Three names appear only in the book, and seven only in the Log, including Henry Morgenthau. Morgenthau's inclusion is explained: he accompanied Roosevelt from Washington to Hyde Park before being summoned to Quebec. The note is a small lesson in how the volume checks its own sources.
frus-1944-quebec-d268:
A draft directive to Admiral Mountbatten is proposed in C.C.S. 452/28, the British Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. His primary object would be the recapture of all Burma at the earliest date. That object must not prejudice the security of the air supply route to China, including the staging post at Myitkyina, whose protection was essential throughout.

Approved operations were the stages of Operation Capital needed for the air route, and Operation Dracula, the seaborne stroke at Rangoon. The chiefs attached the greatest importance to executing Dracula before the 1945 monsoon, with a target date of March 15. If it slipped past the monsoon, Capital would be exploited while Dracula was prepared for November 1945.
frus-1944-quebec-d68:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this memorandum on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. Stettinius remained in Washington while the leaders met in Canada. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

An opening-day memorandum from Washington shows the home government keeping pace with a traveling summit: positions restated, information supplied, and the department's interests guarded from a distance. Stettinius was also guarding the newborn United Nations project agreed at Dumbarton Oaks. For readers, the paper marks the State Department's parallel work while the conference ran.
frus-1945-50-intel-d168:
Dated 6 September 1946, this letter runs from the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) to the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy). It survives in print as document 168 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d268:
A memorandum by the Chief of the Special Procedures Group, Central Intelligence Agency (Cassady) bears the date 1 May 1948. The State Department prints it as document 268 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d368:
A memorandum from Daniel DeBardeleben reached the Acting Deputy Assistant Director for Special Operations, Central Intelligence Agency on 17 February 1949. The State Department prints it as document 368 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d68:
Byrnes, Royall, and Forrestal wrote jointly to President Truman on 7 January 1946. Three cabinet secretaries, State, War, and Navy, signed one letter to the president. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A joint letter from the three secretaries told Truman the departments had settled their fight and were ready for his order. Such unity is rare, and presidents act fast when they see it. Readers have arrived at the climax of the volume's first act: five months of memoranda, committees, and turf wars compressed into one agreed paper. The directive that followed on 22 January bears the shape these three men, with the Budget Bureau's help, had given it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d168:
Who really ran the armistice commissions in the Balkan capitals? This briefing book paper states the American position on the Allied Control Commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The commissions mirror the Allied Commission in Italy, the paper explains, but with the leading role reversed: Russia leads, as Britain and America lead in Italy. Rumania's body works under rules drawn up by the Soviet government. Washington has not objected to Soviet officers running the day-to-day work while Germany still fights. But orders to local governments must not go out in the commission's name without prior word to the other members. Otherwise the United States is tied in public to acts it never saw.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d268:
Stalin surprised Churchill on war criminals at Moscow, and this excerpt of 22 October 1944 tells how. Paragraph five of message number 801 is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The Soviet leader took what Churchill calls an unexpectedly ultra-respectable line.

There must be no executions without trial, Stalin held. Otherwise the world would say the allies were afraid to try the accused. Churchill pointed out the difficulties in international law. Stalin answered that if there were no trials, there must be no death sentences either, only lifelong confinement. Faced with that view from that quarter, Churchill tells Roosevelt, he will not press the memorandum he had given him. He asks that it be treated as withdrawn.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d368:
Matthews caught the money talk in pencil at the foreign ministers' session of February 7, 1945. His rough notes move from dismemberment to reparations. On a study commission, Molotov proposed Eden, Winant, and Gusev. Eden worried about France's absence, since France was Germany's neighbor. The three, he argued, could decide French participation themselves.

Then Ivan Maisky explained the Soviet reparations figures. Half would come at once, half in yearly payments. He set Germany's prewar national wealth at 125 billion, cut by war losses. From the mobile part, ten billion might be removed as a first payment. The shorthand shows how the famous reparations demand was built.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d468:
Victory by cable: Stettinius reported home in this top secret message to Grew of February 11, 1945. The conference had agreed on the American proposal on voting procedure. America would consult China and France on behalf of the other two powers. The United Nations conference was fixed for April 25, 1945, at San Francisco.

The communiqué, out Monday night for Tuesday's papers, would announce the substance. It would not itself say the voting plan was America's. But Washington was free, at the same moment, to state that the adopted proposal was the United States one. The wire shows the deal and the credit arranged together.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d68:
Readers opening the Malta and Yalta volume meet this editorial note before the documents of late 1944. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States explain why the volume reaches back months before the conferences themselves. Many papers printed here date from the mid-autumn of 1944.

The note says the chapter gathers key documents showing where each main subject stood before the talks. Those subjects were the problems later discussed at Malta and Yalta, and each paper shows the position the United States had taken. The editors add that the military talks had a set agenda, while the political talks did not, and that fuller coverage would wait for later volumes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d168:
Only a fragment of President Truman's June 25, 1945 message to Stalin is printed as document 168 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The extract, sent from Olympia, Washington, concerns the Belgrade agreement on Venezia Giulia, the disputed territory around Trieste that Yugoslav and Allied forces both claimed.

The surviving lines close the message. Truman tells Stalin that if any further aspect of the agreement should be considered, they will have a chance to discuss it at their early meeting. The full text appears elsewhere in the volume. Even this scrap shows the President's habit of steering hard questions toward the summit table, where the three leaders could deal with them face to face rather than by cable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d268:
A briefing paper weighed Austria's provisional government in a paper dated June 23, 1945. The paper is document 268 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the recognition of an Austrian government acceptable to all the Allied powers, an item on the American agenda.

Moscow set up Karl Renner's provisional government in Vienna in April without consulting its allies, the paper notes, a one-sided act hard to square with joint action. Yet the Renner government is, in its men and its spread of parties, as good a coalition as could be devised, the paper concedes. One worry stands out: the interior ministry, which controls the police, sits in Communist hands, and so does public instruction. The paper balances acceptance of Renner against the precedent of letting one power install governments alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d368:
Two State Department officials, Collado and Despres, drafted substitute wording on July 7, 1945, for a telegram to Pauley in Moscow. Their paragraph backs the heart of his formula for dividing reparations. The major powers, it says, would settle their own collective share among themselves, without fixing the split with the other allies before consulting them.

The draft also agrees that naming France a major power in the formula raises the sharpest difficulties, since France sat outside the talks. A closing thought notes America's odd position: its direct war damage was relatively small, even though the resources it poured into the war were vast.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d468:
Italy's ambassador calls on Grew in a memorandum of conversation dated July 6, 1945, filed under the subject of a declaration of war against Japan. Ambassador Tarchiani left with Grew a letter addressed to the President. It enclosed a memorandum setting out the present position of Italy, and her vital needs and aspirations.

Knowing how occupied the President must be at this particular moment, Tarchiani had not ventured to ask to see him personally. He sought Grew instead as an intermediary for delivering his letter. Grew replied that he would with pleasure see that the letter gets into the President's hands without delay. The extract shows Italy pleading its case in Washington on the eve of Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d568:
Belgrade charge Harold Shantz offered Washington a piece of advice on June 23, 1945. His short secret wire is document 568 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to Tito's public claim that civil rule in Venezia Giulia was still an open question.

Shantz suggests that the U.S. and British governments act through their Belgrade embassies. They should remind the Yugoslav government that article 3 of the Belgrade agreements settled the question. They should also warn that stirring up trouble in the area under Allied military government is unlikely to help the Yugoslav case. The wire is a small, sharp bid to hold Tito to a deal signed only two weeks before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d668:
Ambassador Norman Armour reported Spain's anger over the Soviet Tangier demand from Madrid on July 5, 1945. His confidential wire is document 668 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. An under secretary of the Spanish foreign ministry had spoken to him the day before.

The official, del Castillo, strongly denounced Moscow's bid for a seat at the Paris talks. Madrid had wired its London embassy to tell the Foreign Office Spain's line. Spain would welcome talks with the Americans, British, and French on restoring an international regime at Tangier. It would not discuss the matter with any other power, a phrase whose target was plainly Russia. Armour adds that Spain opposed reviving the 1923 statute as amended. It feared Russian entry into the administration and a return to French dominance.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d68:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew sent the President's naval aide a staffing plan for the Berlin trip on June 15, 1945. The letter and its enclosures form document 68 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew appends a list of State Department people whose presence, he says, would help Truman at the meeting of heads of government.

The suggested party runs to about forty names, grouped by the issues they would cover. It includes the Secretary of State, Russian interpreters Charles Bohlen and Llewellyn Thompson, and specialists on German politics, reparations, the Balkans, and the Near East. Grew notes that Secretary Stettinius had approved the list at San Francisco. The document shows the expert team Washington thought a new president would need at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1068:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh reported from Athens on July 24, 1945, on the fall of Greece's foreign minister. Ioannis Sofianopoulos came home on July 22 and resigned the next day. Fresh from talks with Molotov, he had urged a cabinet drawn in thirds from left, center, and right. The prime minister found such a government unworkable, and the Regent declared the question did not arise.

MacVeagh reads the timing darkly. The resignation was Russian-inspired, he suggests, and lands during the Potsdam talks beside a threatening Yugoslav note. Moscow may plan, he warns, to refuse election supervision by claiming a nonrepresentative Athens cannot run fair elections amid chaos. Sofianopoulos, he adds, seemed pleased with himself and hungry for the premiership.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1168:
Team to team, the Soviet delegation addressed this note straight to the United States delegation on 31 July 1945. Such messages skipped the foreign ministers and the leaders. They carried business between the staffs who ran the talks day to day.

Two days before the close, that channel still had work to do. Last points needed answers while the final text was being drafted. A direct note of this kind shows Moscow talking to Washington with no one between. It is part of the summit's working machinery, preserved because the files kept everything the channel carried.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1268:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The British chiefs wrote for their own team, in parallel with the American series across the hall.

A British paper in an American volume testifies to the allies' shared staff habits. The two machines exchanged paper as a matter of course. This memorandum is the British chiefs' view at the talks' start. Read beside the American notes of the same days, it shows two staffs framing one war and one peace in matching forms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1368:
Artemus Gates, the under secretary of the Navy, wrote to a senior plans officer of the fleet staff on 21 July 1945. The paper stayed inside the Navy's own house, moving between its civil head and its planners. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Summit volumes mostly print papers between governments or departments, so an inside-Navy paper stands out. It shows the service sorting out its own position while the talks ran in Germany. Readers get a glimpse of how one armed service thought through the questions of the hour before its views joined the wider argument in Washington. Small papers like this one keep the record honest about where policy starts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-68:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 23, 1945, record a morning session at Potsdam with two items printed here. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. The first item concerns command in Indo-China.

Admiral King read a memo on approaching Chiang Kai-shek about a boundary change. The southern part of Indo-China would be reallocated to the Southeast Asia area. General Marshall proposed amending the statement the British wanted in the final report to the President and Prime Minister. The chiefs approved Marshall's amendment and directed that it go to the Combined Chiefs. The second item printed concerns personnel shipping for allied governments. The chiefs agreed to recommend approval of the transport committee's recommendation, subject to a wording change in its enclosure. Routine in form, the minutes move real forces on paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d768:
A second American working paper bears the date July 24, 1945, as document 768. Two staff papers in one day reflect Potsdam's pace. The conference ran on paper: drafts, checks, and re-drafts. This one joined the delegation's files in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Companion papers let readers divide the work by topic and team. Each drafting group left its own trail. The document shows how a large mission organized its thinking. It also hints at the strain of the schedule. By July 24 the staff had served a week of sessions, and the hardest files were still open.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d868:
American drafters at Potsdam prepared this undated working paper as a proposed directive to the Allied commanders in Germany. It sets out the immediate economic tasks of the occupation. The paper bears no author's name. It was meant to push the commanders toward one shared program in the Control Council.

The tasks cover exports, including coal, to pay for reparations and minimum imports. They also cover fair sharing of supplies, uniform ration scales, and farm and coal output. Further items call for repair of transport, housing, and utilities. Industry would be cut back to peacetime needs. Currency, credit, public finance, and frontier controls would follow uniform rules.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d968:
J. Howard Marshall, general counsel to the reparations delegation, wrote to Edwin Pauley on July 31, 1945. He reports the firm view of two State Department men, Collado and Despres. Three subjects, they hold, must appear in the final Big Three agreement: restitution, property of Allied nationals in Germany, and German external assets.

Those men will cover the subjects through additions to the Economic Principles. Marshall still urges Pauley to push a Big Three declaration on German assets abroad, plus a vesting decree from the Control Council. On the principles themselves, he flags two deletions: the last sentence of 14(d) and all of paragraph 18, on supplies for Greater Berlin.
frus-1977-80v29-d168: Another 1977-1980 FRUS letter from President Carter on Panama. The canal diplomacy. This document preserves that letter. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gao-gaoreports-b-295968: HMR Tech doubled its May 2005 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297168: Bernard Cap Company took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297968: Project Resources took its March 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298568: Brian X. Scott took his October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. He said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Individuals get the same full hearing as the firms.
gao-gaoreports-b-299368: International Filter Manufacturing came back for more in April 2007 — a second protest and a second ruling in the same month. The firm challenged another award; the call tests these claims too. Repeat filers get repeat fairness, handled case by case.
gao-gaoreports-b-305368: An Armstrong Williams contract got a fiscal ruling in this September 2005 GAO call, which tests the Education Department's pundit deal. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the contract was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-308968: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by No-Cost Contracts for Event Planning Services. The November 27, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-310568: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Done Right Building Services, Inc. Decided December 17, 2007, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-368: The paper money's paper needed a second source in 2005, and GAO's report says more analysis would settle whether a new supplier was required. The currency's supply chain got the once-over. One mill or two was the question. The analysis had to be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-768: Short sea shipping got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the option showed the importance of systematic public investment decisions. The findings take the measure. The report shows the coastal freight was studied. The approach had to be systematic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-968: Elderly asset transfers for Medicaid got a GAO review in 2005, and the report examines the shelter-and-qualify practice. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the long-term care dollars deserved honesty. The transfers had to be understood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1068: Reserve mobilization data needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon and services had to improve the records. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the call-up lists had to be accurate. The numbers had to be right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-268: School grant awards needed tighter rules in 2006, and GAO's report says firmer steps could open the process to light. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the education dollars deserved daylight. The grant dollars deserved daylight. The education dollars deserved daylight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-368: Major weapons kept busting budgets in 2006, and GAO's report says cost and schedule problems persisted under the revised policy. The findings document the overruns. The report warns that the arsenal's price tags needed taming. The problems had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-468: National park air tour fees needed enforcing in 2006, and GAO's report says better verification and enforcement were required for compliance. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the scenic flights' fees deserved collecting. The compliance had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-568: Title insurance got a GAO first look in 2006, and the report shares preliminary views and issues for further study. The findings open the inquiry. The report warns that the closing-table fees deserved scrutiny. The study had to continue. The closing fees deserved scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-668: Oil trouble in South America threatened U.S. fuel in 2006, and GAO's report looks at what falling output there could mean. The findings map the risks. The report warns that the foreign barrels mattered to home pumps. The risk had to be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1168: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report argues that better information and a systematic process could improve how agencies allocate fuel-reduction funds and select wildfire-prevention projects. Billions were being spent thinning forests and clearing brush, but GAO found the choices were not always guided by the best risk data. The report pushes for a more strategic fight against catastrophic wildfires.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1268: This 2007 Government Accountability Office report exposes government-wide abuse of premium-class travel: internal-control weaknesses let federal employees fly business and first class improperly at taxpayer expense. GAO documents the patterns of misuse across agencies. The findings fed public outrage over bureaucrats living large on the public dime — and pressure for the tighter rules that followed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-268: The telecom switchover was funded but fuzzy in 2007, and GAO's report says the GSA had the money for new contracts but needed real cost estimates. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the dial tone of government should not go silent mid-switch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-368: The FBI's critical networks had holes in 2007 — GAO's report says the bureau had to fix weaknesses in its most sensitive systems. The findings target the digital doors. The report's irony bites: the nation's top cops could not lock their own computers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-68: First-responder grants had a cash-flow quirk in 2007, and GAO's report examines the exemption and the advance-funding rules. The findings parse the plumbing. The report asks whether the firefighters' money arrived when the fires did. The cash had to flow like the need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-868: Homeland Security's science shop filed its spending plan in 2007 — GAO's report reviews the technology directorate's budget line by line. The findings check the dollars behind the gadgets and lab work. The report asks whether the research arm was buying real breakthroughs or just burning cash.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-168: A 2007 Government Accountability Office financial audit of the Bureau of the Public Debt's schedules of federal debt for fiscal years 2007 and 2006. The audit tested the accounting behind the national debt figures the bureau reports — the official ledger of what the United States owes. GAO's opinion affirms whether those numbers fairly represent the debt, a judgment that underpins confidence in Treasury reporting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-68: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report pressing the Defense Department to tighten its handling of Global War on Terrorism spending. GAO argues DOD needed to encourage fiscal discipline and make better use of tools meant to improve cost reporting for the wars. The report documents how foggy accounting made it hard for Congress to know what the conflicts were really costing taxpayers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-768: The Government Accountability Office dug into national Response Framework: FEMA Needs Policies and Procedures to Better Integrate Non-Federal Stakeholders in the Revision Process in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
grosh-oddfellows-manual-1868:
Aaron B. Grosh was a clergyman and a leading Odd Fellow in the United States. His Odd-Fellow's Improved Manual came out in 1868. It set out the past, the rules, and the aims of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. The order was then one of the largest friendly groups in the land.

Grosh defends the order against its critics and explains its signs, degrees, and lodge work. He also gives the laws that govern local lodges and grand lodges. For the years when such groups cared for the sick and buried the dead, few books show their inner life so well.
how-to-read-character-a-new-illustrated-: How to Read Character, 1868. Another handbook. This book preserves that manual. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublin-meir-ben:
Meïr ben Gedaliah Lublin (1558–1616), known as the Maharam, was a Polish rabbi born at Lublin. A Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Solomon Schechter and M. Seligsohn profiles him. From a family of rabbis, he learned chiefly from his father-in-law, the rabbi of Cracow. Before age thirty he was called to Cracow’s rabbinate.

Lublin later served at Lemberg until 1613, arguing sharply with Joshua Falk, then returned home as rabbi until his death. Wherever he settled he ran a yeshivah, drawing pupils such as Isaiah Horowitz. The article describes his printed notes on the Talmud, still included in major Talmud editions, and his 140 published legal replies. It also describes his bold method: he corrected texts, attacked famous rivals, and rejected parts of the Shulhan Aruk. Readers get a full picture of a forceful scholar whose opinions carried across Poland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheim-10368:
Mannheim, a town in the grand duchy of Baden, receives a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It held 141,131 people in 1900, including 5,478 Jews. No Jews are known there before the mid-seventeenth century. In 1660 thirteen families won leave from Elector Karl Ludwig to settle.

The article follows the young community through fire and rebuilding. A burial ground dates from 1656, and the first rabbi, Naphtali Herz, served from 1657. By an early date seventy-eight Jews lived in town, and officials asked for no more permits. French devastation of the Palatinate then drove nearly seventy families from their burned homes. Heidelberg sheltered them until Mannheim was rebuilt by 1691. A concession of 1698 raised the community to 150 families. In 1708 a wealthy founder's Klaus, with synagogue and study house, was dedicated. The entry traces a planned court city where Jews rebuilt alongside it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-massarani-tullo:
Tullo Massarani, an Italian senator who was also an author and a painter, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar. Born at Mantua in 1826, he studied law at Pavia and threw himself into the Italian revolution of 1848. When it failed he fled abroad, lived at Paris and in Switzerland, and finally settled at Milan, sitting in Parliament from 1860 to 1867.

The entry balances his three careers. As a painter he is best known for "The Warm Baths of Alexandria" and presided over the art jury at the Paris Exposition of 1878. As a writer he made Heine popular in Italy through an 1857 essay and translations. A long list of his books on art, politics, and Italian public figures closes the sketch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-eleaza:
Meir ben Eleazar, called Meir Lombard the Preacher, was a French liturgical poet of the first half of the thirteenth century. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn entered him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His surviving work clusters around Passover. He wrote a series of poems for the seventh evening of the festival, some arranged in alphabetical order. He also wrote an alphabetical introduction, six strophes of four verses, to the Targum passage read on the seventh day.

He wrote a dirge for Zion that signs his name, “Meir Hazak,” in an acrostic at its end. The entry ends in a scholarly dispute. Landshuth credited Meir with the dirge “Ahbirah millin,” recited on the Ninth of Ab. Zunz reassigned that poem to the far more famous Meir of Rothenburg. The notice thus preserves both a small body of festival verse and the uncertainty hanging over part of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-catulle-:
Catulle Mendès was a French poet, dramatist, and critic of the Parnassian circle. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Bordeaux in 1841, he settled in Paris from 1859. In 1861 he founded the "Revue Fantaisiste." Three years later he founded the "Parnasse." From 1893 he collected his theatrical criticism for the "Journal." He gathered it in an annual volume, "L'Art au Théâtre."

The entry calls him a perfect stylist inclined to the sensual. The risk was real. His "Roman d'une Nuit" was condemned as immoral in 1867. It earned him a month's imprisonment and a fine of five hundred francs. Then comes the shelf: volumes of verse from "Philomène" to "Les Vains Amours." It holds novels of the Commune and of Parisian monsters. It holds dramas, "Gwendoline," "Isoline," and "Médée," all staged in Paris. The Legion of Honor followed in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meza-mesa-10768:
Meza, also spelled Mesa, was an Amsterdam family noted for how many of its members held rabbinic office. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling record the family in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry sketches four men of the Spanish-Portuguese community across the eighteenth century. Their surviving works are mostly sermons printed in Portuguese.

Abraham Ḥayyim preached a solemn sermon in 1747. His son David followed with sermons on liberty and sin in 1767 and 1786. David also made an edition of the Aramaic paraphrase of the Song of Songs. David de Jacob left responsa in a 1741 compilation. Solomon de Isaac was a physician and ḥakam. He co-signed the famous 1711 decision backing the Shabbethaian Nehemiah Ḥayyun, and he died in 1742.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirabeau-gabrie:
Gabriel Honoré Riqueti, Comte de Mirabeau, was a French revolutionary statesman born in 1749. He earns his Jewish Encyclopedia entry through one cause: Jewish emancipation. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote the article in 1906. A secret mission to Prussia had brought him into Berlin's Jewish circles. There he moved around Henriette Herz and the reform writer Dohm.

In London in 1787 Mirabeau published a book on Moses Mendelssohn and the political reform of the Jews. Entering the States General, he promised a Jewish friend, in the article's famous quote, I will make a human being of you. He kept the promise beside the Abbé Grégoire. He pleaded the Jewish cause in the Assembly through the debates of August 1789.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montoro-anton-d:
Anton de Montoro was born at Montoro in 1404. He was a Spanish poet who sold old clothes and wrote verses the great admired. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. El Ropero, the clothes-dealer, he called himself. Baptized in old age, he remained, the entry says plainly, a Jew at heart all his life.

His poems confess it. To a Cordova magistrate he lamented that hunger had driven him to break his ancestors' oath and buy pork. He pled with Henry IV after the Marrano houses of Carmona were plundered in 1474. At sixty-five he complained to Queen Isabella that he was still called the old, contemptible Jew. Santillana and Juan de Mena prized his verse. Poets of his own race scorned him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-botarel-f: Moses Botarel Farissol was an astronomer and mathematician of the second half of the fifteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a four-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote a work on the calendar called Meleket ha-Kebi'ah and compiled calendric tables under the title Nofet Zufim. Both works survive only in manuscript, kept in the royal library at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosessohn-aaron:
Aaron ben Moses Mosessohn was a German rabbi who died at Ansbach in 1780. Gotthard Deutsch and Louis Ginzberg wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He served first at Dessau and was elected rabbi of Berlin in 1763. His name is tied to Moses Mendelssohn, in whose circles he moved.

In 1763 Mosessohn preached a thanksgiving sermon for the Peace of Hubertsburg, and Mendelssohn put the rabbi's name on its title page. He edited the He-Aruk mi-ShaK, his great-grandfather Shabbethai Cohen's commentary on the Yoreh De'ah, adding notes of his own. About 1771 he became rabbi of Schwabach and chief rabbi of Ansbach. It was on his word that Berlin's congregation made Mendelssohn an honorary member.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagasaki-11268:
Nagasaki, a commercial seaport of Japan, had about one hundred Jews in 1904. Joseph Jacobs and N. E. B. Ezra wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the community. Most of its members had emigrated from Russia. In 1894 they founded the synagogue Beth Israel and bought a burial ground.

The article names the founders: Goldenberg, who married a Japanese widow who entered Judaism with her children, and Lessner. Lessner also started a benevolent society in 1901 for poor Jews at home and abroad. About 1902 the community formed a branch of the Anglo-Jewish Association. Two Christians of Nagasaki had lately embraced Judaism of their own accord.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-armin-1:
Armin Neumann was a Hungarian lawyer and deputy. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Grosswardein on Feb. 14, 1845. He first prepared for the rabbinate at Breslau. Then he turned to law at Berlin and Vienna.

He took his degree at Budapest in 1868. His law office at Papa opened the next year. Budapest made him a teacher of commercial law in 1887. That same year his district sent him to Parliament. His speeches on money and tax reform won attention. In 1898 he joined the commission codifying the laws. The emperor named him aulic councilor for his services. His books expound trade, insurance, and patent law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-offenbach-11668:
Offenbach is a town in Hesse, a state in Germany. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews cast out of Frankfurt came there in 1614. They came up the river with an armed guard. Crowds met them with hate at each bridge. Offenbach was the one place that fired on them.

The town is best known for Jacob Frank and his court. Frank bought its castle in the year 1786. He took the title Baron of Offenbach for himself. He held court there till his death in 1791. He was laid to rest with great pomp in the town. For sixteen years the town drew Polish Jews in throngs. Frank's kin sent out their famed red letters from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orlah-foreskin-:
Orlah is a tract on the fruit of young trees. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means the foreskin of the trees, in Hebrew. The law stands in the book of Leviticus. Fruit of a new tree is held as orlah for three years.

In those three years the fruit may not be eaten. The tract is the tenth in the order Zeraim. That order treats seeds and the fruits of the earth. It holds three chapters and thirty-five parts in all. The first part sets which trees fall under the law. It sets which parts of a tree count as fruit. Leaves, blooms, and sap do not count as fruit here. So they are not barred by the law of orlah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palestine-laws-:
The laws of Palestine are rules that hold in that land alone. The board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such laws bear a Hebrew name that means land-bound laws. The piece sorts those laws in a set of groups. Each group ties to a part of life in the land.

One group held in the days of the Temple at Jerusalem. It held the lamb of Passover and the first fruits. It held the three feasts of the year's great trek. One group dealt with rule, with kings, and with wars. One dealt with the fruits of the soil and fields. It held tithes, gifts to priests, and the poor man's rights. It held the year of rest for the land's soil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peacock-11968:
The peacock reached Israel by ship in Solomon's day. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word tukkiyyim is read as peacocks. They came among the goods from Tarshish. The entry is brief but draws on Talmud passages.

The bird is native to India, not to Palestine. Its name may echo a Tamil word for its tail. The Talmud knows the bird under a Greek name. It bars crossing the peacock with a hen. One passage shows the bird counted as clean food then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peter-12068:
Peter was a Jewish scholar of the twelfth century. The Executive Committee and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied under Samuel ben Meir and Jacob Tam. His notes survive inside the Tosafot on the Talmud. He belonged to the tosafist circle of France.

Peter died a martyr in the Second Crusade. He was walking with a funeral party for a community leader. Crusaders attacked the group and killed him on the road. Ephraim of Bonn recorded the killing for later readers. A later writer garbled the place and the facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinkes-from-a-b:
A pinkes is the register book of a Jewish community. The Executive Committee and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In it the community recorded its acts and affairs. The word first meant a simple writing tablet.

The Greek word pinax gives the term its root. The Mishnah knows three kinds of such tablets. One bore dust for quick sums in figures. One bore wax, cut by a sharp stylet. One was smooth and took ink directly. From tablets the word passed to bound books. The open pinkes became a byword for God's record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontremoli-benj: Benjamin Pontremoli was a Turkish writer on rabbinic law who lived at Smyrna. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the end of the eighteenth century. His one work is called Shebet Binyamin. It came out at Salonica in 1824. The book treats the drawing up of trade papers. He had two sons, Hayyim Isaiah and Hiyya. Both sons became writers on Jewish law as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-printers-marks-:
Printers' marks are signs or pictures printed in a book by its maker. Joseph Jacobs and A. Freimann wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such a mark may be a seal or a coat of arms. It stood at the end of a book at first. Later it moved to the title page. Its use began soon after printing itself began.

A mark often plays on the printer's own name. A deer, for instance, stands for the name Zebi. Town arms and printers' seals were used as well. The first known marks come from Spain and Portugal. A lion on a black shield marks one book of 1485. A lion on a red shield marks a book of 1487. The article shows how Hebrew printers used the custom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raba-properly-r:
Raba, more rightly Rabba ben Ulla, was a Babylonian teacher of the third set. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The time at which he lived is not fixed with care. He was a friend of Ulla, the pupil of Johanan. His words are named before those of younger men.

Rabba was a teller of tales and wise sayings as well. Some of his maxims have come down to us in the Talmud. His words stand in the tractate Shabbat in two places at least. The article picks out those sayings for the reader. It weighs where his name stands in the chains of teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapa-porto-mena:
Menahem Abraham Rapa was an Italian rabbi who died on December 30, 1596. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Porto and later at Cremona. From his new home he took the name Rapoport.

The article says he studied Hebrew, medicine, and Talmud at Venice. He also proofread Hebrew books printed there. In 1553 he saw the Talmud burned by papal order. He kept that date as a fast for life. In 1574 he became rabbi of Cremona. His works include a study of secret writing and a Pentateuch commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reitlinger-fred:
Frederick Reitlinger was a French jurist born on June 18, 1836. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Ichenhausen in Bavaria. He attended Saint Anna College at Augsburg.

The article says he studied Talmud under Abraham Geiger at Breslau. He then read law at Munich and Heidelberg. His criminal pleading won him fame across Germany. In 1866 Napoleon III asked him to write on cooperative societies. That book won him full French naturalization after one year. He practiced law in Paris from 1867. During the siege he escaped Paris by balloon on a mission. He later wrote a lively book about that voyage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rintel-moses-12:
Moses Rintel was an Australian rabbi born in Edinburgh in 1823. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Melbourne in 1880. His father Myer was a Hebraist and Talmud scholar.

The article says he served as reader at Brighton synagogue. In 1844 he went to Sydney in Australia. In 1849 Melbourne's East congregation elected him minister. At Sydney he founded a Hebrew academy. He also helped form a proper bet din there. In 1857 he resigned and a new synagogue formed. Mikveh Israel opened in 1860 with him officiating freely. Chief Rabbi Adler named him head of the bet din. His two printed sermons rank among Australia's earliest Jewish publications.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-isido:
Isidor Rosenthal was a German physiologist born at Labischin, near Bromberg, on July 16, 1836. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1859.

Rosenthal rose at Berlin, then became professor of physiology at Erlangen in 1872. His books study breathing and its link to the vagus nerve. Others treat electricity in medicine and heat control in warm-blooded animals. His general work on muscles and nerves reached a second edition in 1898. He also edited the Biologisches Centralblatt, a biology journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabbionetta-129:
Sabbionetta is an Italian town remembered here for one Hebrew printer's career. Joseph Jacobs wrote its short entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. From 1551 to 1559 Tobias ben Eliezer Foa printed Hebrew books there.

Foa's Sabbionetta output opened with Joseph Shalit's Merkabat ha-Mishnah in 1551. It closed with the Hoshen Mishpat of the Tur in 1559. He began a prayer book there and finished it after moving to Cremona. His career was ended by force over certain anti-Christian books. A Christian printer, Vicenzo Conte, then took up his work and type.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanchez-sanches:
Herman Rosenthal and Max Rosenthal wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Antonio Ribeiro Sanchez. He was a Russian court physician, born in 1699. He died in Paris in 1783. Sanchez came from a Marano family of Penamacor, in Portugal. He fled Portuguese persecution and settled in Holland. There he studied medicine at the University of Leyden.

At Leyden, Sanchez won the friendship of the great physician Herman Boerhaave. In 1731 the Empress Anna of Russia asked Boerhaave for a learned doctor. He sent Sanchez. Sanchez rose fast at the Russian court. He joined the Imperial Academy of Science. He treated the young Princess Sophia Augusta, the future Catherine II. In 1744 he saved her from a dangerous illness. Three years later he was suddenly dismissed. He sold his property and moved to Paris. The reason for his fall was never made clear.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiff-josef-13:
Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Josef Schiff. He was an Austrian stenographer, an expert in shorthand. Schiff was born on February 25, 1848, at Ragendorf, in Hungary. In 1874 he became teacher of stenography at the Vienna Academy of Agriculture. In 1898 he lectured on Gabelsberger's system at the University of Vienna.

In 1883 Schiff founded the Centralverein for Gabelsberger business shorthand. The Emperor of Austria later gave him the title of professor. His books teach the Gabelsberger system step by step. They include a course text, an exercise book, and a reader for trade schools. He also made shorthand dictionaries with the Vienna and Dresden styles. His dictation book served writers of all German systems. The Austrian Ministry of Instruction approved several of his works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sebastus-13368:
Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sebastus. Sebastus was the harbor of Cæsarea on the Mediterranean. Herod made Cæsarea a great seaport. He named the city for Julius Cæsar. He named the harbor Sebastus to honor Augustus, called Sebastos in Greek. Coins of Nero read Cæsarea at the Port of Sebastus.

The article corrects a reading by the historian Grätz. Josephus speaks of Cæsareans and Sebasteni together. Grätz took them as citizens of two towns. The authors argue otherwise. Sebastus was never an independent city. The Sebasteni were the military troops stationed at Cæsarea. The other term covers the civil population. A single Greek phrase, they show, splits one city's people into soldiers and civilians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbat-nahamu-:
Shabbat Nahamu is the first Sabbath after the Ninth of Ab fast. Cyrus Adler and Wolf Willner wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its name comes from its prophetic reading, which opens, Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Those words stand in Isaiah chapter forty.

The reading belongs to a set series of special lessons. Three Sabbaths before the fast use warnings from the prophets. Seven after it use words of comfort. Old sources list the same order used today. Groups differ slightly on the weeks before, but all agree on this one. The entry shows how the calendar turns grief into comfort, week by week.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheshet-13568:
Sheshet was a Babylonian amora of the third generation of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He often argued points of religious law with Nahman bar Jacob. He sat in on Huna's lectures as a young scholar.

Sheshet spoke sharply about sayings of Rab that displeased him. Rab must have said that while asleep, he would remark. He studied first at Nehardea, then moved to Mahuza. Later he founded an academy of his own at Shilhe. Though blind and frail in body, he had an iron will. The entry draws a vivid portrait of a blind sage whose memory and energy outmatched his peers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-samuel-da:
Samuel da Silva was a Portuguese-born physician living at Amsterdam in the early seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He is known chiefly for his fight against Uriel da Costa. Costa questioned Pharisaic tradition in a bold new book.

Before Costa's book even appeared in print, Silva acted. He had read part of it in manuscript form. In 1623 he published a Portuguese booklet against its author. Leading members of Amsterdam's young Portuguese community directed that attack. Its title proclaims a treatise on the soul's immortality. The book ably defends that doctrine against Costa's denial. Silva mocks Costa as blind and incapable Uriel. The entry recalls a fierce print duel over the soul.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sindbad-13768:
Sindbad is a set of tales about the wiles of women. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A stepmother seeks the death of an Indian prince. His seven masters delay his execution by telling tales. Each tale warns against the tricks of women. The frame works much like the Arabian Nights.

Benfey held that the book began as an Indian story book. It likely passed from India westward in stages. It was rendered into Zend, then Syriac or Arabic, then European tongues. The Hebrew version is called Mishle Sindabar. It holds four tales found in no other version. The entry follows the book across all these forms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jud:
Solomon ben Judah ha-Babli was a liturgist of the tenth century. Joseph Jacobs and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Despite his name, he was likely not from a Muslim land. Rapoport held that ancient rabbis counted Rome as Babylon. Solomon may thus have been a native of Rome itself.

He taught Meshullam ben Kalonymus, a major figure of the age. He wrote many piyyutim and selihot for the prayer book. One yozer of his begins Or yesha, light of salvation. Rashi and Jacob Tam both mention that poem with respect. His selihot use four-line strophes without a Bible verse. Scholars must take care not to confuse him with Ibn Gabirol.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spiro-joseph-mo:
Joseph Moses Spiro was an Austrian rabbi and Talmudic author of note. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Trietsch, Moravia, about 1770. His father Abraham, rabbi in Trietsch, educated him at home. Though a sickly child, he became a fine Talmudist early.

He served as rabbi at Schafa, Habern, and finally Kanitz. He held the Kanitz post from 1824 until his death in 1830. He urged systematic instruction in religious literature for children. He condemned the pilpul method of study very severely. He edited the Sefer ha-Hinnuk at Brünn in 1799. His Mesillah le-Elohenu treated the evils of unsystematic child training.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-syria-14168:
Syria is a country of western Asia under Turkish rule. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The name Syria never appears in Hebrew scripture. It enters usage only in the Greek period. Scholars usually derive it by shortening Assyria.

Herodotus treated Syria and Assyria as one name in two tongues. Winckler instead traced Syria to a Babylonian word for the West. The Septuagint uses Syria to render the Hebrew Aram. In politics the name meant the Seleucid empire. Its capital moved from Babylon to Antioch on the Orontes. The realm shrank until Pompey made it Roman in 65 B.C.E. Strabo and Pliny fix its borders at Taurus and desert. The entry disentangles one name's shifting map.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taussig-edward-:
Edward David Taussig was an American naval officer born in 1847. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at St. Louis on November 20. He entered the Naval Academy at Annapolis in 1863. He graduated in 1867 and stayed in active service.

Taussig climbed the officer ranks over three decades. He served on Pacific and European stations for years. In 1898 he took command of the Bennington. He claimed Wake Island for the United States. When Spain ceded Guam in 1899, he took charge there. The Philippines and China saw his service next. By 1903 he commanded the Pensacola navy-yard. Though of Jewish descent, he was raised Unitarian. The entry traces a sailor who raised flags for America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thessaly-14368:
Thessaly, a province of northern Greece on the Aegean Sea, held old Jewish communities. Isidore Singer and M. Caimi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews had lived there since very early times. Those present in 1905 spoke Spanish and claimed Spanish descent.

Communities stood at Larissa, Trikala, and Volo. None had a rabbi, and Hebrew study had decayed. Jewish schools at Larissa and Trikala taught religion with state support. Larissa once grew rich and earned the name Tree of Gold. A riot of poor Jews against the rich drove many away. The Greco-Turkish war of 1897 hurt the town further. Its fine synagogue still recalled better days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trabot-trabotti:
Trabot, or Trabotti, was a family of Italian scholars from France. Schulim Ochser and Isaac Broydé wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Members bore the extra name Zarfati, meaning the Frenchman. They flourished from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century.

Several Azriels served as rabbis at Rome, Florence, and Ascoli. One list of rabbis by an Azriel runs from Rabina to his own day. Jehiel Trabot held posts at Pesaro and Ferrara. His responsa survive only in manuscript copies. Levi Trabot left France for Italy, then Jerusalem. Nathaneel of Modena ranked among Italy's most respected rabbis. The entry follows the family town by town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ventura-14668:
Ventura was a family of rabbis and scholars in Italy and Greece. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Members of the family were active for three centuries. They served towns across Italy and the Levant.

The entry sketches several of them. Eliezer ben Samuel was rabbi of Ferrara, where he died in 1534. Elijah ben Abraham wrote comments on Talmud sayings and on Elijah Mizrahi. His three part work appeared at Salonica in 1799. Isaac Hananiah and Isaac ben Moses served at Pesaro and Ancona. Their legal answers survive inside other printed collections.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wertheimer-sams:
Samson Wertheimer was an Austrian court Jew, financier, and rabbi. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Worms on January 17, 1658. He died at Vienna on August 6, 1724. He studied at the yeshibot of Worms and Frankfort. In 1684 he moved to Vienna.

Wertheimer joined Samuel Oppenheimer in serving the emperor. He won Emperor Leopold's personal trust and gifts. During the Spanish succession war he raised army funds. After Oppenheimer's fall in 1703, he kept state credit alive. In 1703 the emperor named him court factor. His privileges ran for twenty years. Joseph I confirmed them all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wogue-lazare-el:
Lazare Eliezer Wogue (1817-1897) was a French rabbi and a top teacher of Jewish study. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Fontainebleau, he trained at the rabbinical school at Metz. He took his rabbi diploma in 1843 and went back to Paris.

In Paris he preached beside the chief rabbi of the city. In 1851 he won a chair of Jewish theology at Metz. He kept that chair until he retired in 1894. When the school moved to Paris, his load grew. He taught Hebrew grammar, Bible study, and German there. For sixteen years he also ran the paper Univers Israelite. France gave him the Legion of Honor in 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zappert-bruno-1:
Bruno Zappert (1845-1892) was an Austrian playwright and news writer of Vienna. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His kin came from Bohemia and spread to two lands. His sire was a maker of goods in that realm.

He schooled at the town gym school in his youth. He wished to read at a great school of the land. In 1862 he joined a trade school to aid his sire. The death of his sire changed his plans in full. He went into the book trade at Vienna in time. In 1869 he took sole charge of a known book house. He ran that house for eight years of his life. He then turned to the stage and wrote for two houses.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume nine of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter sixty one. An event from the prior July is set in its place here. The King travels to Fontainebleau and stays till mid September.

The Duchesse de Berry, with child for the first time, falls ill. Her doctor, Fagon, begs that she put off the trip a day or two. The King grows angry and grants a boat in place of a coach. No one may go out, not even to the opera next door. Madame de Saint-Simon was ordered to watch that she obeyed. Court care here shows as strict watch over a sick lady.
nilsson-primitive-inhabitants-scandinavi:
Sven Nilsson, a Swedish sage of beasts and old times, wrote this classic on the first folk of Scandinavia. John Lubbock turned it into English in 1868. Nilsson had long taught that the north had its own stone age, rich with finds.

He sets out the stone tools, shell heaps, and graves of the first north men. He matches them with the ways of wild folk of his own day to guess their life. The book is the north's match to the French case for deep age man, and a classic of its kind.
npt-1968:
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signing in 1968, after years of fear that atomic weapons would spread to many nations. It rests on a bargain between the states that already had nuclear arms and those that did not. Nearly every country in the world has since joined, making it the widest arms control agreement in force.

States without nuclear weapons promise never to build or receive them, and they accept inspections of their atomic programs. The nuclear powers promise to work toward disarmament and to share peaceful nuclear technology. The bargain has kept the circle of nuclear-armed states small for over fifty years, even as disputes over disarmament and enforcement continue to test it.
nsa-ufo-hypothesis-1968:
Analysts at the National Security Agency weighed what UFOs might mean for human survival in 1968. UFO Hypothesis and Survival Questions sets out five hypotheses for the things seen in the sky. The paper is laid to Lambros Callimahos, a famed code man of the agency.

Each hypothesis is tried for what it would ask of mankind if it proved true. The close is a fable, the Tale of the Rattler, on how pride can blind a mind to a new fact. The monograph is philosophy from inside the most sealed of agencies. It shows cleared men wondering aloud at their own desks.
nursery-tales-zulus-callaway-1868:
Henry Callaway published Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus in 1868. Callaway, an English missionary and later bishop in Natal, took the tales down in the Zulus' own words. He prints the Zulu text with English translation and notes, so readers meet the storytellers' phrasing, not a summary.

Tricksters, ogres, and clever children fill the nursery tales, while the traditions recount chiefs and migrations. The histories preserve how Zulu elders of that generation told their own past. Callaway's method was new: record first, interpret with care, and credit the speakers. His volume became the founding English collection of Zulu oral literature. Folklorists still build on the texts he saved from vanishing.
openalex-w1979540468:
Nicolas Moiroux, Cédric Pennetier, and co-authors studied mosquito biting. The catalog record gives no author or year; the sample names them. They worked in Benin, France, Thailand, and Tanzania. Anopheles funestus is a major malaria vector in Africa. Its biting had shifted toward early morning hours.

The shift followed distribution of long-lasting insecticidal nets. Two villages in south Benin showed the change clearly. The team measured human exposure with behavior surveys and models. Net protection stayed high overall, they found. Yet much remaining exposure happened outdoors or near dawn. New control tools must target those gaps, they argue.
openalex-w2059124668:
Mark Costello, Marta Coll, Roberto Danovaro and colleagues summed up world knowledge of marine biodiversity. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2010. It drew on the Census of Marine Life. That programme ran for a decade worldwide. It was the largest study of ocean life ever.

The paper merged reviews from all major ocean regions. It counted species richness by region. It also counted endemic and alien species. Gaps in knowledge were mapped alongside the counts. Many regions remain sparsely and unevenly sampled. Numbers of experts and guides varied greatly too. The authors list future challenges for ocean science. Protecting marine life needs better basic knowledge first.
openalex-w2118672468:
Ary Teixeira de Oliveira-Filho and James Alexander Ratter traced the origins of central Brazilian forests. Their paper appeared in Edinburgh Journal of Botany in 1995. Central Brazil mixes savanna with several forest types. Where those forest plants came from was unclear. Distribution patterns can reveal ancient links.

The authors analysed over a hundred floristic checklists. They also mapped fifty-five woody species in detail. Two main distribution patterns emerged clearly. Dry forest species followed fertile soil patches southwestward. Gallery forest species followed moist river corridors. Those corridors link Amazon and Atlantic rainforests. Western galleries tied more strongly to Amazonia. Southern galleries tied more to Atlantic forests.
openalex-w2134712068:
Naoko Kozuki, Anne Lee, Mariângela Silveira, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in BMC Public Health in 2013. They asked how a mother's age and number of prior births relate to risks for her baby. Outcomes included babies born too small or too early, and deaths in the first month and first year.

The team combined fourteen cohort studies from low- and middle-income countries. First-time mothers under eighteen had the highest odds of every bad outcome studied. Risks were also raised for women with three or more prior births, including those over thirty-five. The authors urge renewed effort to delay first births and care that spans a woman's whole reproductive life.
openalex-w2229420368:
Alejandra Escobar-Zepeda, Arturo Vera-Ponce de León, and Alejandro Sánchez-Flores published this review in Frontiers in Genetics in 2015. They trace the road to metagenomics, the study of whole microbial communities through their DNA. Microbes fill every corner of the planet, yet most resist growing in a lab, which long hid them from science.

The review walks the timeline from Leeuwenhoek's first microbes and Koch's cultures to high-speed DNA sequencing. That leap remade both microbiology and computing, since community DNA data are huge and tangled. New software keeps arising to gather, clean, and mine such data. The authors stress that good experiment design, backed by real bioinformatics understanding, unlocks what a metagenome holds.
openalex-w2788640168:
Lorenzo Galluzzi, Ilio Vitale, and Stuart A. Aaronson lead the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death's 2018 recommendations in Cell Death and Differentiation. For a decade the committee has standardized how cell death is defined and described. The field keeps expanding, with new mechanisms blurring old categories. This update revises the classification around mechanism rather than appearance.

The authors give exact definitions for a dozen-plus forms of cell death. The list runs from intrinsic and extrinsic apoptosis through necroptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis. It also covers rarer forms like entotic and lysosome-dependent death, plus senescence and mitotic catastrophe. They discuss when specialized new terms help and when they confuse. A widely accepted word set keeps talk clear across labs. The paper is the reference point for naming how cells die, as of 2018.
openalex-w2797697368:
Marianna Arvanitakis, Jean-Marc Dumonceau, and Jörg Albert lead these 2018 guidelines in Endoscopy, from the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. They cover care by endoscope for acute necrotizing pancreatitis, where part of the pancreas dies. Most cases of pancreatitis clear up quickly, but this severe form strikes up to a fifth of patients. It brings organ failure, procedures, and death at high rates.

The guideline weighs radiology, endoscopy, and surgery inside step-up treatment plans, drawing on many fields. It advises acting when infected tissue death is suspected or proven. Where patients tolerate it, the first procedure should wait about four weeks. Drainage, by endoscope or through the skin, should come before surgical removal of dead tissue. Technical details of endoscopic tissue removal get careful attention. The aim is consistent, evidence-based care for a fast-moving emergency.
openalex-w3034125968:
Kern Chng, Chenhao Li, Denis Bertrand, and colleagues published this study in Nature Medicine in 2020. It draws a map, a cartography, of germs and drug resistance genes inside a large teaching hospital. Cleaning is central to infection control, yet how microbes settle and persist on hospital surfaces was little explored.

The team sampled one hundred seventy-nine sites tied to forty-five beds, some of them twice, up to a year and a half apart. Deep DNA sequencing revealed distinct niches, shaped by biofilm growth and by contact with the human body. The patterns shifted across space and time. A second sequencing method recovered thousands of microbe, virus, and plasmid genomes, most of them new, exposing how resistance genes move around the hospital.
openalex-w4206071468:
Don Husereau, Michael Drummond, Federico Augustovski, and colleagues present the CHEERS 2022 reporting standards in BMC Medicine in 2022. Health economic evaluations compare the costs and results of rival treatments or policies. Readers can judge such studies only if authors report them fully and clearly. The CHEERS checklist, first published in 2013, was written to make that happen.

The 2022 statement replaces the old guidance with a checklist of twenty-eight items. It covers newer methods and gives patients and the public a larger role in studies. The rules apply to any intervention meant to improve health, in any setting. Authors, reviewers, and editors can all check a report against the same list.
openalex-w4378349368:
Priya Chaudhary, Pracheta Janmeda, Anca Docea, and colleagues review oxidative stress and antioxidants in human disease, in Frontiers in Chemistry in 2023. Free radicals are reactive oxygen particles produced constantly by body chemistry. Healthy defence systems clear them away. When that balance breaks, radicals build up and damage cells, feeding many diseases. The review gathers recent work from the main medical databases.

The authors explain how oxidative stress drives disease processes across the body. They then survey the defences, both the body's own enzymes and protective compounds taken in from outside. Plant compounds such as flavonoids and polyphenols show strong protective activity in lab and body studies. Vitamins add to that defence. The overview helps researchers see where such therapy might help most.
openalex-w4391649568:
Joshua Welsh, Deborah Goberdhan, Lorraine O'Driscoll, and colleagues present MISEV2023, the updated minimal standards for studies of extracellular vesicles. Their guidelines appeared in the Journal of Extracellular Vesicles in 2024. Vesicles are tiny packages shed by cells, carrying cargo that can reveal the cell's state. They interest researchers as disease markers and possible therapies. Publication counts in the field climb every year, but methods vary wildly.

Loose methods have caused confusion over names, purity, and measurement. The International Society for Extracellular Vesicles first issued minimal information rules in 2014, then updated them in 2018. This third edition runs from basic to advanced practice. It tells authors exactly what to report so others can judge and repeat their work.
openalex-w4410594468:
Ayana Ezoe, Makoto Katori, and Tomoyuki Shirai test whether desert bush patterns form a hyperuniform arrangement. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. Hyperuniform patterns suppress density swings at large scales. Competing desert plants, fighting over water, might settle into such a pattern.

The team mapped bush positions and weighted each point by bush size. Treated as plain points, the pattern was not hyperuniform. Once bush sizes counted, it was. They also propose simple non-equilibrium models that grow such weighted patterns. The result shows that what counts as order depends on whether size is part of the picture.
openalex-w4412156568:
Sung-Jin Kawai, Shumpei Asamizu, Hiroaki Suzuki, and colleagues discover new antibiotics by growing bacteria together. Their paper appeared in The Journal of Antibiotics in 2025. Microbes change what they produce when neighbours are present. The team paired a Streptomyces strain with a Tsukamurella partner.

The pairing yielded three new phenazine antibiotics, the griseoluteins T, C, and D. Two related known compounds appeared as well. One new compound, griseolutein T, is unstable and needed special handling. In tests it beat several clinical antibiotics against drug-resistant staph, resistant enterococci, and Clostridioides difficile. It also showed low toxicity to human cells. Combined culture thus remains a rich route to new drug leads.
openalex-w7204195968:
Veronica Cristina Kuczmarski Gerhard led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on tearing the sinus membrane during maxillary sinus lift surgery, a bone-grafting step before dental implants in the upper jaw. This tear is the most found complication of the lateral window technique, occurring in roughly a fifth to a quarter of procedures in prior studies. The review gathers current evidence on incidence, risk factors, classification, stopping, and repair.

Thin remaining bone, sinus partitions, an unsuitable membrane thickness, smoking, and standard rotary instruments raised the risk. Cone-beam scan planning, piezoelectric instruments, and surgical guides lowered it. A tear that is recognized and repaired properly does not greatly harm implant survival, the authors conclude.
openalex-w7204266568:
Janete Aparecida Klein led a Portuguese-language study, published in Brazil in 2026, on teachers' knowledge and active learning methodologies in basic education. Drawing on thinkers such as Tardif, Freire, and Moran, the authors treat teaching as a complex activity joining disciplinary, teaching, curricular, and experiential knowledge. Their question is what teacher knowledge contributes to making active methodologies work in classroom practice.

Active methods favor participation, autonomy, collaboration, and critical thinking, the analysis shows, but only when joined to planning and skilled teacher mediation. Their effectiveness depends on initial and ongoing training, on the institutional conditions schools offer, and on teachers' capacity to integrate different kinds of knowledge. Joining the two, the authors conclude, strengthens contextualized, reflective, participatory teaching aimed at meaningful learning.
openalex-w7204789668:
Ade Mulyawan and co-authors released an English-language study in 2026 on how post-heat treatment changes the magnetic anisotropy of a lanthanum-cobalt co-substituted M-type ferrite. A hard magnetic content whose atoms occupy several distinct crystal sites. Only cobalt sitting at one particular tetrahedral site boosts the material's uniaxial anisotropy, so where the cobalt ends up matters. The team compared immediate water quenching with slow cooling.

The slowly cooled sample with the highest cobalt substitution showed an anisotropy field more than a fifth higher than the quenched one at room heat. Calculations attribute the gain to slow cooling raising the share of cobalt ions on the anisotropy-friendly site. Controlling cation distribution through heat treatment, the authors show, is a viable way to tune the functionality of multi-site compounds.
openalex-w7212191868:
Leonardo Diego Lins leads a team on gut parasites and basic sanitation in the Sao Francisco valley, in Brazil's dry northeast. The zone joins the twin towns of Petrolina and Juazeiro and holds some seven hundred thousand people. The team drew on census counts, state water data, and past parasite surveys. They set the spread of gut worms and germs by the state of pipes, drains, and trash pickup.

The gaps are stark in the counts. In Petrolina, more than four in five homes have piped water. But just two in three have sewer links. Close to one home in five still uses a crude pit, and near a thousand people have no toilet at all. Juazeiro shows a stronger town grid, with near full water reach. The team ties this patchwork to the load the public health system must bear.
openalex-w7213912068:
Eduardo Machado Dechandt leads a team counting hospitalizations for chronic sinusitis in Brazil's public system. Their 2026 ecological, time-series study covers 2015 to 2025 using hospital authorization records. Sex, age, region, stay length, deaths, and mortality were all analysed.

Over thirty-three thousand admissions were processed, with short average stays. Deaths were few, giving a low overall mortality rate.
