Outcomes span cognition, mood, sensory symptoms, and daily functioning. The authors hope to learn whether a plant extract with this profile can fill an empty treatment space.
pmc-13312968:
Wen Zhang and co-authors grade, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, the meniscus injury videos circulating on Douyin, the Chinese short-video platform. Patients increasingly learn about knee injuries from such clips, so the team asked how credible, educational, and professionally deep the supply really is.

Searching two Chinese keywords on July 31, 2025, the team sieved 300 collected clips down to 143 that truly addressed meniscal injury. Two trained raters scored each video on standard benchmarks for transparency and reliability. Overall quality, plus a meniscus-specific scale built from orthopedic academy guidance. Median scores sat low across the board, signaling thin sourcing and modest teaching value, though depth varied widely. Videos from physicians and rehabilitation therapists beat those from fitness enthusiasts and patients, and treatment pathway clips scored deepest while recovery clips most often skipped key points.
pmc-13313268:
Badypwyla Israël and colleagues report a 2026 survey of expert views on child vaccination in Lubumbashi, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The national vaccine program began in 1978 and leans on families to seek shots, yet coverage stays low, and the household factors behind that gap had not been mapped.

Experts in immunization were picked on purpose, from varied fields, with deep national and outside experience per the report. They were asked whether a study of what drives coverage in Lubumbashi, under the SCAVA and VACCIN+CONNECT-OS effort, is worth doing and how it should run. The paper grounds a planned project in that expert judgment. Its aim is to raise child coverage in a city where vaccine-preventable disease still takes a heavy toll on young lives.
pmc-13314468:
Yan Wu and colleagues survey first-year medical students on a tutorial model that blends clinical and humanities teaching, in a study printed in 2026. Joining bedside skills with humanistic literacy early is a stated goal of modern medical schools, and Zhejiang University tried a new format for it.

The study ran in the Whole Life Cycle Health I course and drew 275 students, as counted in the report. A self-report survey asked about fit with the model, learning interest, gains in joining clinical and human sides, module worth, and self-rated skill growth. Most students fit the model well, at a share of 90.9 percent as given, and most said interest rose, at 88.0 percent in the report. Male students agreed more strongly on interest and on the joining effect. The results back early, guided blending of the two sides of medicine.
pmc-13314568:
Sanjiv Kandhari and fellow experts set out advice for using the drug abrocitinib in eczema care in India, in their 2026 paper. Atopic dermatitis is a long, flaring skin disease that ruins quality of life through itch, lost sleep, and repeat flares.

Older whole-body drugs such as cyclosporine and methotrexate often give weak itch control and wear poorly over time. Abrocitinib, a pill that blocks the JAK1 signal, cut itch fast and cleared skin in big trials with a fair balance of gain and risk, as the authors report. Yet real-world guidance for Indian patients was thin. Their advice covers who should get the drug, how to dose it, and how to chase lasting calm of the skin, tuned to local practice.
pmc-13315168:
Pak Thaichana and colleagues link seasonal smoky air to lung adenocarcinoma in northern Thailand, in a 2026 study. Fine dust known as PM2.5 has tied to lung cancer worldwide, yet proof for this subtype from real registry data in Southeast Asia was thin.

The team worked across eight upper northern provinces and 103 districts, as counted in the report. Daily PM2.5 readings were matched to cancer registry rates for the years 2013 to 2017 by each patient home district. Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer subtype, as the authors note. Models that handle clustered data weighed the dose link. In a region where seasonal burning spikes the air, hard numbers on cancer risk can push cleaner air policy.
pmc-13315368:
Barbara Seliger reports in 2026 on the nineteenth Tumor Immunology Meets Oncology meeting, held in May 2025 in Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany. The gathering covered basic and applied tumor immunology, with talks on how tumors differ, their surrounding tissue, and what that means for care.

Alongside the main symposium, junior scientists and clinicians presented short talks and posters, and a linked workshop covered cancer and inflammation. Sessions stressed how host and tumor cells interact, mapped with omics tools, as a base for new immune therapies and drug combinations. Biomarkers, immune escape, and anti-tumor responses ran through the program.
pmc-13315668:
Emre Demirel and colleagues report in 2026 on long-term swallowing after laser surgery that opens the airway in people whose two vocal folds are paralyzed. The operation cuts across the back of one vocal fold with a carbon dioxide laser, easing breathing, but its lasting effects on swallowing needed mapping.

Seventeen adults were checked once, well after surgery, between January and June 2025, using a flexible camera test with thin liquid, moderately thick yogurt, and a cracker. Standard scales graded airway entry, throat residue, and oral intake ability. Patient reports and functional scores were set beside the camera findings to guide follow-up care.
pmc-13315968:
Anna C Hornbach and co-authors report in 2026 a primary pelvic Ewing sarcoma growing outside bone in a young woman, paired with a review of gene-confirmed cases in female genital organs. Such tumors are extremely rare there, and firm diagnosis needs proof of the EWSR1 fusion gene that drives growth.

A healthy 21-year-old had two weeks of malaise and pelvic symptoms, and scans showed a 10 centimeter mixed cystic and solid mid-pelvis mass seeming to arise from the front of the uterus. Wide surgery removed the mass with clear margins, and gene testing confirmed the diagnosis. Care follows bone Ewing guidelines.
pmc-13316168:
Bercin Tarlan and Onur Konuk report in 2026 an eye socket case where spread of multiple myeloma looked like ordinary age-related eyelid fat bulging. A 57-year-old man whose myeloma was in remission had three months of growing fullness in the right lower eyelid.

Examination suggested slight upward eye shift and uneven fat herniation without inflammation. CT imaging instead showed a dense mass at the front lower orbit, distinct from fat. Removal and biopsy proved a plasmacytoma, positive for CD138 and kappa light chain, meaning metastatic myeloma. New eyelid fullness in such patients deserves imaging, the authors warn.
pmc-13316268:
Manana Jikurashvili and co-authors describe, in 2026, a man whose bowel cancers returned repeatedly over eighteen years before cancer reached his pancreas. The patient had a strong family history of colorectal cancer and features pointing to Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition that raises cancer risk. Spread of bowel cancer to the pancreas is rare and hard to recognise.

Now aged 58, the man developed a mass in the body and tail of the pancreas during routine surveillance. Tissue examination showed a high-grade cancer with solid and nested growth and extensive dead tissue. Staining favoured a bowel origin and showed loss of two mismatch repair proteins. The authors stress careful clinic and pathology correlation and long-term team surveillance.
pmc-13316368:
Lena Sophie Rudolf leads a 2026 study checking whether Germany's national learning catalogue for medical students, NKLM 2.0, teaches enough about food advice for children and teens. Good early nutrition guidance can prevent later disease, so gaps in training matter.

The team first built an evidence-based list of needed skills, then coded the catalogue against it, ending with 82 codes across 1,426 segments. Knowledge for prevention and communication skills took the largest shares, while five codes found no teaching content at all. Gaps included food for breastfeeding mothers, kitchen skills, eating behavior, gentle talk about body weight, and nudging methods. The authors suggest targeted courses and clearer rules on teaching formats and time.
pmc-13316668:
Naman Jain and co-authors describe, in 2026, a fatal clotting complication after severe head injury in a 35-year-old man with chronic substance use. He arrived after an unwitnessed fall. Clotting in surface veins of both arms is uncommon after trauma and usually signals body-wide inflammation rather than a local vein injury.

On day six, discolouration spread from the left hand to the right arm. Ultrasound confirmed clots in the cephalic and basilic veins without deep vein involvement. Platelet counts fell sharply, chest imaging showed extensive lung injury, and blood thinners could not be given because of bleeding inside the skull and very low platelets. He died on day eight from refractory breathing failure.
pmc-13316868:
Donato Decarolis and a large team show, in a 2026 catalysis study, how a sponge-like metal-organic framework can freeze palladium particles in their pure metal state. Palladium normally soaks up hydrogen and changes phase during reactions, muddying which form does the work.

Trapped inside the pores of NH2-UiO-66, clusters under one nanometer wide held only surface hydrogen under reaction conditions, never shifting phase. Live X-ray probing during the reaction plus simulations backed the claim. In a test reaction turning butadiene into butenes, the locked-metal catalyst stayed active, chose the wanted product more often, and overcooked less to butane than standard catalysts. Tiny size control, the team argues, can settle long phase debates.
pmc-13317568:
Pian Yu and a large team created, in a 2026 study, a dissolving microneedle patch that plants a radioactive immune trigger inside melanoma skin tumors. Melanoma often hides from immune therapy behind a suppressive local setting, so the team combined radiation with a STING alarm signal in one material.

The polymer self-assembles from lutetium-177 and nucleotide building blocks, mimicking the body's own STING activator. Pressed into skin, the patch stayed at the tumor, switched on STING, and burst tumor cells through a fiery death that drew immune attackers in. Mouse tumors shrank and survival stretched; adding a PD-L1 antibody deepened the effect and left lasting immune memory against distant tumors too.
pmc-13317768:
Xinru Yang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, the HER2 growth receptor as a target in cervical cancer, where patients with returning or resistant disease run out of options. HER2 drives breast and stomach cancers and is druggable there, but its cervical role is murkier.

Changes in HER2 are uncommon across cervical cancers overall, yet they cluster in glandular subtypes, including HPV-independent forms. The review covers the receptor's biology, how often it appears, what it predicts, and how testing should be standardized. Antibody-drug conjugates, above all trastuzumab deruxtecan, have revived interest by showing activity in HER2-carrying tumors. Careful biomarker selection, the authors argue, will decide which patients truly benefit.
pmc-13317968:
Charlie Pauvert, David Wylensek, Selina Nüchtern, and Thomas Clavel release maldipickr in a 2026 software paper. The open R tool sorts bacterial isolates by their protein fingerprints to cut duplicate work in big culturing projects. Growing microbes is back in fashion, but sequencing every colony is costly and slow.

MALDI-TOF machines already fingerprint isolates cheaply in minutes, yet standard use leans on closed commercial databases. Their package clusters fresh spectra without a reference library, grouping likely clones so teams keep one of each and drop the rest. The tool is light on computing power and fully documented on CRAN. Smarter triage lets culture collections capture more diversity per dollar.
pmc-13318568:
Yidi Zhu and co-workers report a 2026 imaging study of brain waste clearance. Their patients had a narrowed middle cerebral artery. Narrowing can weaken blood flow and vessel pulsing. The team used two related diffusion MRI measures, DTI-ALPS and a redirected version.

Scans and thinking tests covered 37 patients and 41 matched healthy controls. Both clearance measures came out clearly lower in patients. That pattern suggests waste removal around blood vessels is impaired. Each measure also fell as choroid plexus volume rose. Correlation values sat near −0.54 and −0.57 in the patient group examined. The authors propose the measures as imaging markers. They might help track how the disease progresses.
pmc-13318868:
Laya Krishnan and colleagues offer a 2026 scoping review of AI applied to gut microbes for spotting dementia. A gut-brain imbalance is linked to slow decline in thinking. AI tools now hunt gut markers that set apart dementia types and stages. No full review had gathered that work.

Searches of four databases through July 2025 found 896 papers. Screening narrowed them to 28 for close reading. Models such as random forests and neural networks came up often. Alzheimer's patients showed fewer butyrate-making gut species, including Faecalibacterium and Eubacterium. Other microbes linked to inflammation were raised. Even superagers showed distinct, perhaps protective microbe patterns. The authors argue gut signatures could back earlier, mixed test approaches.
pmc-13319368:
Rauf Khan and co-authors describe a 2026 study of thin films that clean oily water with help from data models. Two flat materials, graphene oxide and MXene, were layered on a nylon base. Four film mixes with varied amounts of one layer were made and tested for how well they held back oil.

Math models were trained to guess how well each film would work from mix and pressure settings. One model type gave the closest guesses and showed that film mix and pressure mattered most. Pairing new materials with such models could cut trial and error in filter design. Larger data sets are planned to make the guesses hold up more widely.
pmc-13319668:
Tuo Lan, Yikyung Park and Natasha Tasevska present, in 2026, a method for splitting protein intake into animal and plant sources within two common diet assessment tools. Interest in protein source is growing, yet standard recalls and food records report only total protein. A practical estimation protocol was missing.

Data came from 926 adults who completed repeated automated 24-hour recalls and two four-day food records over a year. Each reported food was linked to national nutrient databases to assign its protein to animal or plant origin. Summed estimates matched original totals almost exactly, and most foods fell within a tiny margin. Animal protein supplied well over half of intake, led by red meat, poultry and cheese, while bread led plant sources. The protocol supports future diet and health studies.
pmc-13320568:
Godknows Osarhiaekhimen, Ayomide Ayo-Salami and Adeolu Morawo describe, in 2026, a treatable inflammatory brain condition that caused two episodes of rapid dementia seven years apart. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy deposits a protein in small brain vessels. In a rare variant, the immune system attacks those vessels, producing fast cognitive decline that can be hard to diagnose.

Their patient was a 76-year-old man whose first episode, with weakness and seizures, was never definitively explained despite extensive testing. During the second episode, advanced imaging showed the characteristic one-sided white matter changes. Tissue examination then confirmed amyloid angiopathy with related inflammation. The authors stress matching clinical and imaging clues, and confirming with tissue where presentations are atypical or recurrent, because treatment can reverse decline.
pmc-13320668:
Melodie E. French, Jonathan R. Delph, and Cailey B. Condit explain in a 2026 article what limits the size of the largest earthquakes at subduction zones. Earth's biggest quakes grow along the megathrust fault where one plate dives under another, yet why growth stops at depth was unsettled. The authors link that limit to how rocks deform at each depth.

In shallow zones, all rocks break by friction, letting quakes grow large. Deeper down, sediment stops breaking and instead flows slowly, so quakes stay small and shrink with depth. Those small deep events may reflect the size of uneven patches in the fault. Modelling rock behaviour this way should sharpen hazard estimates.
pmc-13323068:
Yannik M Glauser leads a team presenting Fourier pixels for two-way light control, in a 2026 optics paper. Normal pixels only sense or emit light intensity, which wastes the phase and polarisation information carried by light waves.

Their elements use surface plasmon waves running across metal toward wavy microstructures shaped by Fourier analysis. Launched that way, the waves build clean optical wavefronts with chosen amplitude, phase and polarisation. Run in reverse, the same elements read incoming light fully on those three traits. Stacking several elements yields pixels that sense and shape light together. The authors extend the idea to waveguide modes and point to uses in displays, communication and quantum work.
pmc-13323368:
Xinyue Zheng and her team uncover, in 2026, a self-reinforcing loop that coronaviruses use to keep their copying factories running. Infected cells reshape internal membranes into double-walled vesicles where the viral genome is copied. What other cell structures play a part was unclear.

Forming those vesicles tears apart contact sites between two organelles, the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria, and the mitochondria get damaged. A mitochondrial enzyme then leaks into the cell fluid and protects a key viral protein from being tagged for destruction. Shielded, that protein drives still more vesicle formation, closing the loop. Strengthening the organelle contacts or blocking the enzyme's grip on the viral protein suppressed replication in the team's tests, pointing to fresh antiviral targets.
pmc-13323568:
Yuezhong Huang and co-authors build a machine learning model for coronary artery disease risk from UK Biobank blood proteins, reported in 2026. Participants with protein and genetic data and no prior disease were split into training, internal validation and a Scotland and Wales external validation set.

A score built from 202 proteins tracked future disease in a dose-like pattern. Adding genetic scores and the protein score to standard factors lifted discrimination in both validation sets, and a compact nine-protein panel was picked for practical use. Follow-up came from linked health records. The authors argue that blood protein patterns can sharpen heart risk prediction beyond clinic measures alone.
pmc-13324668:
Najib Aziz and colleagues report an unusual HIV case in a 2026 case report. A man with high-risk sexual exposure stayed HIV negative from 1984 through May 2021, a span of about 35 years, without ever taking preventive PrEP drugs.

During those years he had several other infections, including gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis. In fall 2021 he tested positive, and a December test found 19,100 copies per mL of HIV-1 RNA. Genetic checks showed one copy of the CCR5 delta32 change plus HLA A*02 and HLA B*5701 types. The authors suggest layered genetic traits, not one factor, likely delayed infection and may shape outlook after it.
pmc-13325168:
Beth James and co-authors evaluate a ruthenium compound against drug-resistant urinary germs and their biofilms in a 2026 study. Catheter infections persist because biofilms shield bacteria from most antibiotics.

The compound, KLS-116, killed diverse resistant species at doses at or below 25 micromolar in lab tests. Mixed with standard antibiotics it never clashed, giving neutral or additive effects. In flow models of catheters it shrank mature biofilms, and in still models it cleared them fully at 16 times the base dose within a day. Over 42 days of exposure, bacteria barely shifted in sensitivity, unlike rapid ciprofloxacin resistance. Acid levels did sway its strength.
pmc-13325368:
Parimal C. Bhomick and co-authors extrude biodegradable films loaded with herbicide-carrying frameworks in a 2026 study. Slow, targeted weed killer release could cut the chemical load reaching soil and water.

Two metal-organic frameworks, UiO-66 and its amino version, were loaded with 2,4-D, MCPA, or glyphosate. The loaded powders were blended into polycaprolactone at 10, 20, and 30 percent by weight through twin-screw extrusion. Films grew stiffer as framework share rose, beating films with herbicide mixed in directly. Release tests showed a slow, sustained leak from the framework route. The solvent-light process scales well and suits farm delivery films.
pmc-13325668:
Takeru Ikenaga and colleagues report a rare racing heart circuit inside the superior vena cava in a 2026 case report. The big vein above the heart can spark atrial fibrillation, but a self-contained loop there is almost unheard of.

Their patient was an 83-year-old woman returning a year after a first ablation for repeat tachycardia. Mapping first showed a loop on the left atrial back wall, and pulsed-field ablation fixed the veins and wall. The rhythm then shifted to a new pattern traced wholly inside the vein sleeve. A ring-shaped pulsed-field catheter isolated the vein without harming the sinus node or the phrenic nerve. Tissue selectivity made the delicate site treatable.
pmc-13325868:
Jacqueline MacDonald Gibson argues in a 2026 perspective that official United States water figures hide wide insecurity. Headline statistics credit 97.6 percent of Americans with safely managed drinking water.

Her account shows the count leans on piped access and a narrow set of system violations, missing private wells, shutoffs, and missing plumbing. Adding those groups yields an estimated 37 to 55 million water-insecure residents, some 11 to 16 percent of the 2024 population. Private unregulated systems alone may leave 16 million people exposed. She calls on environmental engineers and scientists to close the gaps in measurement and service.
pmc-13326768:
Maxime Fieux, Philippe Gevaert, and Leigh J. Sowerby tested the infectious risk of biologics for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Their 2026 paper notes that biologic therapy transformed treatment of severe, resistant disease by targeting the type 2 inflammatory cascade, yet downstream immune effects remain possible. The focus is TSLP, an epithelial alarmin that drives type 2 inflammation but also supports antiviral CD8 T cell responses, so blocking it could theoretically impair local antiviral immunity.

Pooled data from the WAYPOINT trial showed an odds ratio of 2.76 for infectious adverse events, a pattern different from all other trials of biologics for this condition. Individual and serious infections did not rise significantly on their own, and exacerbations that could be inflammatory or infectious were excluded from the pooled analysis. The authors call for continued vigilance, long-term tracking, and vaccination guidance, particularly for patients with comorbidities or more immune risks.
pmc-13327668:
Soufia Charaf and team report a repeat pelvic lipoblastoma squeezing the sciatic nerve in a baby. Their 2026 case paper tells of a 17-month-old boy with a left pelvic lipoblastoma reaching into the buttock, who limped worse over six months with nerve harm in the left leg. Lipoblastoma is a rare kind tumor of baby fat, most often found before age three, and pelvic sites are rare, with squeeze harms hinging on size and spread.

MRI showed a big fatty tumor reaching past the pelvis and squeezing the sciatic nerve, and lab study of tissue confirmed lipoblastoma. Full surgery removal was done, but a local return five months later needed a second removal, with no further return during follow-up. The team stresses MRI's key role before surgery planning and after-surgery watch, tissue study for proof, and full removal as the mainstay of care for this rare growth.
pmc-13328168:
Hessah Ibrahim Al Suwaidan and co-authors build a national One Health plan for Saudi Arabia in a 2026 mixed-methods study. One Health joins human, animal, and environmental health against zoonoses, drug resistance, and ecological hazards, but Saudi policy links remain loose. A survey of 400 health professionals and students came first, then interviews on system barriers.

Awareness was low, with 81 percent reporting no prior knowledge of One Health, collaboration scored a mean of 0.51 on a zero-to-four range, and agreement on which body owns zoonotic disease roles was poor. Awareness predicted how much action respondents reported, and interviews blamed ministry silos and murky data routes. The authors propose a national structure to join the pieces.
pmc-13328568:
Ianire Astobiza and a large team report in 2026 that an enzyme in support cells around tumours can slow cancer growth signals. The enzyme, called aspartoacylase or ASPA, was often turned down in tumour stroma and in fibroblasts linked to cancer. The team studied how ASPA interacts with TGF beta signalling in these cells.

They found a two-way effect: TGF beta lowers ASPA, while ASPA limits the changes TGF beta drives in fibroblasts. Those changes include scar-like tissue building, new blood vessel growth, and immune cell states that help tumours. In human samples, low ASPA linked to worse outcomes across several tumour types. The work points to fibroblast ASPA as a brake on harmful tumour support.
pmc-13329668:
Saurav Sharma and co-authors report an exploratory Ayurvedic study in mild cognitive impairment in 2026. Mild impairment sits between normal ageing and dementia and can hinder complex daily tasks. Care ran in sequence: Trikatu powder for 7 days, then Brahmi ghee for 90 days, each taken twice daily after food.

Of 27 people enrolled, 24 finished the single-arm open study. Thinking was scored with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment before and after care. Scores improved with a large effect size in the reported results, and no adverse events were noted. The authors stress limits: no control group, no fixed lifestyle rules, and other medicines were not tracked. Controlled trials are needed before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13330468:
Xueli Quan and colleagues report a crisis from an adrenal tumour in a teenager in a 2026 case. The boy, aged 13 years and 8 months, had belly pain for three days and was first treated for gut infection. His state crashed into heart failure shock and multi-organ failure, needing breathing support and external life support.

Scans found a left adrenal mass, and blood hormone markers were far above normal ranges in the reported values, confirming pheochromocytoma. Heart pumping strength was very low. Plasma exchange, kidney support, and heart drugs ran alongside life support for 6 days, yet organ damage deepened. Surgery never became possible. Care was withdrawn by the family and the boy died soon after.
pmc-13332868:
Débora S Raposo leads a large team asking how biological databases can serve the new United Nations benefit-sharing mechanism for digital sequence information, in a 2026 policy paper. In October 2024, parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity agreed that benefits from genetic data should help fund conservation.

Databases sit at the center of the scheme, since they host the sequence data the mechanism covers. The paper walks through the COP16 decision's demands. It covers telling users and depositors about the mechanism, improving records of where samples were collected, and keeping open access. It also covers respecting the FAIR, CARE, and TRUST principles. Building from surveys, interviews, and a workshop of database managers, it proposes steps such as updating terms of use, revising submission flows, and sharpening user messages. It suggests counting non-cash benefits like training, publications, and interoperability, so databases stay open and sustainable while sharing gains.
pmc-13333368:
Malik El-Feghi and colleagues update 2026 diagnosis and treatment of IgG4-related kidney disease and retroperitoneal scarring. Kidney involvement in IgG4-related disease most often appears as tubule inflammation, but can also appear as membranous kidney inflammation and acute interstitial inflammation as a subtype of IgG4-related tubule disease. IgG4-related retroperitoneal scarring can cause obstructive kidney disease with or without active kidney parenchymal disease. Diagnosis rests on clinic plus tissue findings, requiring matching of bedside, lab, imaging, and tissue findings while ruling out mimics.

Tissue features include a dense immune-cell buildup rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells, typically with storiform scarring. Important mimics include infection, cancer, ANCA-associated disease, and Castleman disease, detailed in the full update. The paper gives clinicians a current care frame for a disease that can mimic cancer or infection. It stresses tissue proof plus clinical matching before starting therapy.
pmc-13333668:
Takafumi Hattori and Takako Matsubara report a 2026 single-arm trial of behavioral graded activity for people with knee osteoarthritis who had not improved with standard exercise. The study asked whether pain sensitization, a possible reason for poor response, changes alongside symptoms.

Twenty-six participants completed the 12-week program. Pain and daily activity scores on the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score improved by amounts patients would notice. Pressure pain thresholds rose at the knee and forearm, pain summation fell, and daily step counts increased. Starting step count predicted gains in daily activity, while scans and baseline sensitization measures did not predict symptom change. The results suggest sensitization can shift with treatment and may be a useful target.
pmc-13333768:
Xuemei Sun and co-authors set 24 antibiotics side by side for group A streptococcal throat infection in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Penicillin stays first-line, yet broader drugs are widely prescribed, so the team ranked options on cure and safety.

The analysis pooled 64 randomized trials with 23,287 people enrolled, comparing early and late bacterial clearing, clinical response, relapse, and adverse events against penicillin V. Cefdinir and cefpodoxime cleared bacteria early more often than penicillin V, and cefprozil led on late clearing. Azithromycin did worse than penicillin V on both clearing measures. Network rankings of this kind help prescribers reserve broad-spectrum drugs for cases where they truly add value.
pmc-13334068:
Yesli Perez-Rocha and colleagues study 2026 links between food shortage patterns and thinking performance in midlife Latina women. Food shortage has been linked to cognitive aging, yet few studies examine midlife or low-income groups or track insecurity patterns over time. The team analyzed 512 women in the CHAMACOS Maternal Cognition Study from 2018 through 2024, measuring food shortage twice about three years apart with a six-item USDA household food security survey module.

Women were grouped cross-sectionally as secure or food-short and longitudinally as always secure, always food-short, or newly food-short. Thinking performance was assessed across multiple domains with the SOL-INCA-AD assessment. Associations were estimated with linear regression adjusted for social confounders and, in a subset, APOE epsilon4 carrier status. The study asks whether lasting shortage, not just a single snapshot, tracks with poorer midlife thinking.
pmc-13336368:
Chengjian Zhou and co-authors created gene-encodable degraders called endobodies in a 2026 protein study. Current membrane protein degraders depend on specific endocytic receptors, which restricts which cells they work in.

An endobody fuses a nanobody to a cell-penetrating peptide in one compact, gene-ready package. The peptide drags the bound target inside to be destroyed. The platform removed EGFR, PD-L1, and HER2 on cancer cells, and even drained HE4, a serum ovarian cancer marker that small-molecule degraders cannot touch. A bispecific version removed a membrane protein and an outside-cell protein at once. Adding a proteasome-targeting domain caught escapees and deepened the breakdown, and EGFR loss slowed lung cancer growth in animals.
pmc-13336568:
Da Kang leads a 2026 study of colorectal cancer that looks inside T cells rather than only at tumor cells. Using bulk and single-cell RNA data, the team tracked ADAR1, an enzyme that edits RNA messages. Activity was high in T cells that had entered tumors. Those cells looked worn out yet still divided often.

Lab tests showed ADAR1 pushes T cells toward exhaustion and weakens their killing power. In mice, added ADAR1 in T cells blunted anti-tumor effects through the TGF-beta-SMAD pathway. High T cell ADAR1 also matched poor response to anti-PD-1 therapy in patient groups. Blocking it in T cells might restore immune attack.
pmc-13336668:
Xi Yan and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of growing the alga Chlorella vulgaris with sodium acetate as a carbon source. Two axis labels in Figure 1 were wrong: panels C and E should read starch content and protein content in percent, not concentration in grams per liter. The corrected figure and caption are supplied in full.

A results paragraph on mixed feeding was also replaced. The study compares three modes: light-fed growth, acetate-fed growth, and a mix of both. It tracks cell growth plus starch, lipid, and protein content up to the sixth day of culture. Readers should use the corrected labels and wording when citing the growth findings.
pmc-13337068:
Yubin Cao, Junzhou He, and Wei Si slow proteins down inside a nanopore sensor in a 2026 study. Reading protein sequences through nanopores promises fast, cheap, portable analysis, but molecules zip through too quickly for accurate reading. Their design stacks a graphene layer over a silicon nitride membrane with a ring-shaped cavity.

Charge control plus the cavity's physical crowding and surface stickiness hold peptides longer in the sensing zone. Longer stays sharpen the signal without ruining its resolution, easing the electronics speed demands. Slowing traffic inside the pore is a key step toward practical single-molecule protein sequencing, which could transform how proteins are catalogued in health and disease.
pmc-13337368:
Julia Skibniewska and co-authors track how fat tissue fails early on a high-fat diet, separately in male and female mice, in a 2026 study. Weight alone may miss early metabolic trouble; cell swelling and inflammation in fat could warn sooner. Mice ate chow or a 60% fat diet from 6 weeks of age for as long as 16 weeks.

Both sexes expanded fat fast, but males gained more weight, grew larger fat cells, and developed insulin resistance sooner. Males also packed inflammatory macrophages into gonadal fat earlier, with stronger inflammatory gene activity. Females responded later and more mildly. The sex-specific timetable matters for predicting metabolic disease and designing prevention that fits each sex.
pmc-13338868:
Hamza Ahmed and colleagues ran a quality improvement study in 2026 on discharge delays after hip fracture surgery at a United Kingdom major trauma centre. Patients often wait in hospital after being medically ready to leave, which prolongs stays, raises complication risk, blocks acute beds, and distresses older patients and families. Discharge has drawn less attention than time to surgery.

Consecutive adults operated on for neck of femur fracture in 2025 were studied, with a new discharge process introduced in July 2025 for before and after comparison. The work tests whether fixing the discharge phase shortens stays without harming care. Hospitals with similar bottlenecks can adapt the approach to their own pathways.
pmc-13338968:
Sihan Chen and colleagues compared drug response genes in 2026 between East Asian and European populations using public genome data. Most pharmacogenomic studies skew European, yet drug response varies between people and populations. The team asked how variant patterns differ and what evolutionary forces may have shaped them.

East Asian groups generally carried fewer variants tied to reduced drug response than Europeans, and drug linked genes showed threefold higher population differentiation than the genome background, with FST of 0.18 versus 0.06. The work supports broader, more diverse drug gene studies so dosing guidance works fairly across ancestries.
pmc-13339868:
Francisca Román and a large team review thrombospondin-1, a host protein at the crossroads of infection and autoimmunity, in a 2026 article. Vaccines and drugs face resistance and limits in both fields, so host targets matter. The protein binds many immune partners, from CD36 and CD47 to growth factors.

Roles in defense against infection and in tolerance toward self tissues are weighed side by side. The protein can help clear invaders yet also calm or stir inflammation depending on context. That dual behavior shapes its promise as a drug target or drug itself. The review maps where boosting or blocking it might help most.
pmc-13339968:
Gina Hong and colleagues tested culture methods in 2026 to improve detection of Aspergillus fumigatus in sputum from adults with cystic fibrosis. Finding the fungus matters for diagnosing Aspergillus related lung disease, yet culture methods for cystic fibrosis sputum are not standardised. The team analysed 281 remotely collected sputum samples from 74 adults at two labs, Johns Hopkins and Dartmouth.

Detection rates were 74 percent at Johns Hopkins and 71 percent at Dartmouth. At Johns Hopkins, Czapek-Dox agar lowered the odds of growth compared with other media, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.78. The work points labs toward culture choices that catch more fungal disease in cystic fibrosis care.
pmc-13341468:
Guided Imagery and Music therapy for mood disorders is reviewed by Tianyi Wang and colleagues in the 2026 systematic review. The approach uses music-evoked imagery to work through emotion and thought, and the team searched PubMed and Web of Science for trials and brain imaging studies from 2000 to 2024.

The synthesis describes four affected circuits: calmer amygdala activity with stronger prefrontal links, hippocampal plasticity tied to theta rhythm syncing, and reorganized prefrontal coordination among them. Standard drugs often hit single pathways with side effects, so a multimodal therapy engaging several networks at once is attractive. Even so, the authors note the mechanism evidence remains loosely organized.
pmc-13341668:
Re-validating a national cancer awareness survey is laid out by Maja Nikšić and coauthors in their 2026 study protocol. The Cancer Research UK Cancer Awareness Measure, running since 2008 and now in a Plus version, tracks public knowledge and behavior on prevention, screening, and early diagnosis.

Four phases run from 2023 to 2026, revising the survey after each. Work includes auditing questions against the COM-B behavior framework, literature scoping, readability checks, and two rounds of cognitive interviews using think-aloud methods to catch confusing wording. Keeping the instrument honest matters because its numbers steer national cancer strategy.
pmc-13342468:
Blanca I Aldana reviews how chemokines, the immune system's signalling proteins, shift from guardians to aggressors over the course of Alzheimer's disease. In the healthy brain these signals maintain balance and communication between glia and neurons. Their 2026 review traces the network's progressive dysregulation with aging and disease.

In Alzheimer's, several chemokine groups change together: recruitment signals rise, interferon-linked signals climb, a restraining signal is lost, and vessel-related signals shift, feeding self-sustaining inflammation. These changes reprogram microglia and astrocytes into disease states, draw in peripheral immune cells, and destabilise synapses. Sex matters: females show stronger microglial aging and interferon signalling, males faster complement activation. Viruses including herpesviruses and SARS-CoV-2 also rewire the network. The authors argue chemokine targets need stage-matched, sex-stratified treatment rather than broad anti-inflammatory drugs.
pmc-13343468:
Ruslan Gryaznov and co-authors build a fully bio-based wood glue from lignin and zein protein in 2026. Panel makers mostly rely on formaldehyde glues whose fumes harm indoor air. The team dispersed corn zein protein inside a thick lignin gel, borrowing from protein-polyphenol bonding, with no synthetic cross-linkers at all.

Hot-pressed birch veneers formed three- to five-layer plywood that matched rival bio-based glues, and the water-based recipe scored 94 on the Eco-scale thanks to few steps and no organic solvents. Warm ethanol-water could also unglue the joints, letting the adhesive be recovered and reused. Water resistance remains the next hurdle for this debond-on-demand system.
pmc-13344468:
Van N. T. La and co-authors compare ways to read drug potency data against the MERS coronavirus main protease in 2026. Candidate blockers oddly switch this enzyme on at low doses and off at high ones, bending the usual dose-response curve and muddying rank order, so the team tested three analysis routes.

Fitting just the inhibition leg of the curve, in two variants, gave potencies that tracked live-virus results in cells. A fuller kinetic model that builds in enzyme pairing and ligand binding, then projects to cell-like enzyme levels, forecast the cellular ranking most accurately. The comparison hands antiviral hunters a surer way to judge compounds against this and similar enzymes.
pmc-13347368:
Adaeze R. Osakwe and colleagues test solubility numbers as an early screen for amorphous drug mixes, in a formulation study from 2026. Many new drugs dissolve poorly in water, so holding them in a glassy polymer can help. Yet loading limits and weak release are common, and the team measured Hansen values for ten polymers and three drugs by direct screening.

A straight link emerged between the energy gap measure and the most drug a mix could hold in glassy form. Lower gaps allowed loads up to 45 percent in the reported mixes. Tiny hot-melt batches using just 2 to 7 g of drug confirmed the guide. One drug released up to 235 percent more from low-interaction mixes than from its crystal form.
pmc-13348168:
Thijs Vangeel, Yannick Matt, Lukas Becker, Kai Oliver Siegenthaler, and Michael Sander test how polyester makeup steers enzyme breakdown, in a study from 2026. Thirty mixed polyesters varied in parts, most using a plant-based furan acid and some a fossil acid for contrast. Two enzymes were timed against each film, since surface chewing is often the slow step in full decay.

More aromatic acid slowed chewing for both acids, yet furan versions always broke faster than fossil twins at equal load in the reported rates. One enzyme worked across all films while the other only managed low-aromatic films, and short alcohol parts paired with longer acid parts favoured breakdown, rules designers can use.
pmc-13350168:
Caleb Rivera and colleagues traced Native Hawaiian relationships with land across past, present, and future in a 2026 paper. Colonial systems worked to cut Kanaka 'Ōiwi people off from 'āina, the land that feeds, weakening community health and self-rule.

Drawing on stories, proverbs, chants, and scholarship, the authors show land knowledge carried through family lines, hands-on practice, and place-based learning. They describe colonisation's disruption alongside today's efforts to reclaim land and water and restore those bonds. The paper closes by picturing futures where Hawaiian ways of knowing are honoured and control of land returns, treating the relationship itself as a source of wellbeing.
pmc-13350968:
Fang Shi and colleagues developed a smart plugging gel in 2026 for blocking water channels deep in oil reservoirs. Their gel joins two networks: a chemically linked scaffold built from three monomers and a physical network of graphene quantum dots with ascorbic acid, locked together by reaction and hydrogen bonds.

The double structure proved far denser than single-network gels. Under the best recipe it lost under 20 percent of its thickness after repeated shearing over 56 days and kept over 80.6 percent of its mass after 60 days in hot, salty conditions. Core flooding tests followed, probing whether the gel can plug the large pores that waste injected water.
pmc-13352168:
Frode Eick and Synnøve Økland Jahnsen examine homelessness and migrant health within a Nordic welfare system in 2026. Homeless people face higher rates of heart disease, infection, and mental illness, and migrant status can deepen each risk. Shelters and low-threshold services often form the bridge into care.

Their analysis centres on precarious citizenship, where weak legal standing narrows access to housing and health services. Short projects and charity responses carry severe limits, since help ends when funding ends. The authors argue for joined-up, rights-based housing responses instead. Findings speak to welfare systems that promise universal care yet leave homeless migrants at the edge.
pmc-13353168:
Paola Ferri leads a 2026 survey of work ability among nurses at an Italian teaching hospital. Keeping nurses able to work matters amid global staff shortages and an ageing population. Data came from 182 nurses at required health checks from August to October 2022, using the Work Ability Index plus home and job burden details.

Inadequate work ability affected 44.5 percent of nurses, whose mean age was 45.8 years. Muscle and joint disorders burdened 41.8 percent. Each added year of age cut the odds of adequate ability, with an odds ratio of 0.93, and heavy home burdens also hurt. Satisfaction with working conditions stood out as the top changeable protector, guiding retention efforts.
pmc-13354768:
Shaohua Xu and co-authors built a gene-based risk score for liver cancer in a 2026 study tied to 5mC, a chemical mark on DNA. Liver cancer is often found late and has poor survival, so better ways to sort patients by risk are needed. The team grouped tumors by mark patterns and used machine learning to pick key genes.

Their three-gene score split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups with clear gaps in survival. High scores linked to later stage, more gene errors, and a distinct immune mix in tumors. Lab tests showed two of the genes help cancer cells grow and move, backing the score as a care tool.
pmc-13355168:
Xiuju Chen led a 2026 phase I/II trial of NGGT001 gene care for Bietti crystalline wasting, a rare inherited retinal disease. The trial enrolled twelve adults with by genes shown disease and relatively preserved vision, testing safety and early working results across dose levels. Gene care for this illness had no set medical track record.

People received a single subretinal injection at one of three doses, with three extra people in a mid-dose growth group, and were followed for twelve months at two tertiary centres in China. Safety, vision, and retinal tests were tracked by dose. The study gives people and doctors the first guided glimpse of whether this gene care can be delivered safely and help vision.
pmc-13355268:
Weigang Ren and co-authors traced in 2026 how bladder cancer cells resist cisplatin, a key chemotherapy drug. Resistance is a major reason treatment fails in advanced disease. The team screened gene readers that sense a chemical tag on RNA and tested how they change drug response in cells.

A reader called YTHDC1 was much lower in resistant cells. Its loss steadied a partner gene's message, which raised a protein that destroys a protective factor, making cells shrug off the drug. Blocking this chain, or adding curcumin, made cells sensitive again in tests. The authors propose the chain as a target to restore drug response.
pmc-13355368:
Aidin Baghbani and others told of a reinforced double-layer vein patch for carotid surgery, in 2026. Patch angioplasty with carotid endarterectomy is the usual care for symptomatic carotid narrowing, but prosthetic patches risk illness, a particular worry in people with recent endocarditis. A vein patch avoids foreign stuff, yet a single layer may weaken.

A sixty-seven-year-old man with central retinal artery blockage and active mitral valve growths underwent left carotid endarterectomy, with his facial vein everted to form a reinforced double-layer patch. He awoke neurologically intact, and duplex sound scan at one month showed no left-over narrowing. Surgeons gain a method for sick or high-risk people where prosthetic stuff is best avoided.
pmc-13355668:
Weitao Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 case of hyperacute rejection, the fastest and most severe form of kidney transplant failure, in a 45-year-old man. His new kidney came from a deceased donor, matched his blood type, and passed standard antibody and crossmatch tests, with no prior signs of immune sensitization. Yet urine output fell within the first hour after surgery and kept dropping.

Later tests found preformed antibodies against two non-standard targets, proteins called HARS and STAT6, rather than the usual HLA targets. The authors argue that adding non-HLA antibody screening to standard checks could lower the risk of this rare disaster in future transplants.
pmc-13356468:
Denise Golmann and co-authors studied in 2026 what raises the risk of deep wound splitting after second-degree tears or episiotomy cuts in childbirth. Such tears are common and can lead to infection and lasting pelvic floor harm, yet deep splitting was little studied. Their single-center study compared 105 women whose wounds split within two weeks with 210 whose wounds held.

Women with splitting more often were first-time vaginal mothers and had far more episiotomy cuts. Antibiotics during labor were less common in the splitting group. After full adjustment, episiotomy raised odds about fourfold, while antibiotics during labor cut odds sharply. The authors support sparing use of episiotomy and weigh preventive antibiotics.
pmc-13357068:
Hui He and co-authors studied in 2026 whether immune patterns in lung tumor tissue can predict a dangerous lung inflammation caused by immune therapy drugs. Checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis can be fatal, and early warning signs are lacking. The team reviewed nineteen patients with lung squamous cell cancer treated from 2022 to 2024, four of whom developed the lung problem.

Before treatment, tissue from patients who later got pneumonitis held more of a signal called IL-8 and more neutrophil immune cells in the tissue around the tumor. After onset, their blood levels of IL-8 and another signal were lower than in others. The authors suggest these tissue clues could flag risk early.
pmc-13357868:
Yoo Jin Cho led a 2026 random trial comparing higher versus lower wattage e-cigarettes for smoking substitution. Higher wattage devices deliver nicotine more effectively, which might help smokers switch completely, and complete switching should lower exposure to a lung carcinogen derived from cigarettes. Whether wattage actually changes switching or carcinogen exposure was untested.

In a three-arm trial with a twelve-week care period and follow-up at twenty-six and fifty-two weeks, 372 adults were enrolled at academic medical centres. Complete substitution and urinary NNAL, a carcinogen marker, were matched across arms. The trial informs harm-cut debates with guided evidence on device power, switching, and toxicant exposure.
pmc-13361068:
Elizaveta Pyatenko and co-authors probed flaws in a clear conductive oxide in a 2026 materials study. The oxide, Ga2O3, is used in thin-film solar cells, and tiny flaws like missing oxygen atoms can help or hurt how it carries charge. The team used X-ray methods at varied energies to read the surface at different depths. Samples included a solar-grade film and a single crystal, before and after a flaw-adding ion treatment.

Computer models of the material helped the team read the complex signals. Matching model to measurement showed where flaw states sit in the energy layout of the surface. Such flaws can trap charge and cut device performance, or aid conduction when controlled. Knowing their depth and energy helps engineers tune this oxide for better solar cells and electronics.
pmc-13361168:
Thiago S Arnaud and co-authors tuned a crystal's heat and light behavior by swapping its atoms in a 2026 physics study. The crystal, alpha-MoO3, hosts special waves where light couples with lattice vibration, useful for tiny infrared devices. The team grew versions enriched with heavier molybdenum and oxygen isotopes. They measured how the swaps shifted the crystal's vibration tones and heat flow.

Heavier oxygen shifted the vibration tones about five percent toward lower frequencies. Heat flow along and across the layers was recorded for each version. Computer models matched the measurements and traced how vibrations scatter each other. Probing the coupled waves showed quality gains in some versions. Isotope tuning gives device makers a clean dial for setting infrared response without changing chemistry.
pmc-13361268:
Zhenyu Sun and others unified grip, self-healing, and oxygen permeability in a polymer hydrogel electrolyte for flexible zinc-air cells, in 2026. Hydrogel fluids promise flexibility, non-flammability, and leak pushback, but zinc dendrite growth and trade-offs among conductivity, oxygen permeability, strength, and firmness have limited useful use.

A neutral, three-sized physically cross-linked hydrogel joined a tight iron-ion linking network with a broader hydrogen-bonding network of beta-cyclodextrin, plus in situ chitosan derivative. The hierarchical design balanced the competing traits. Battery teams gain an electrolyte that supports flexible, safe zinc-air cells without sacrificing work.
pmc-13361468:
Oana Liliana Atomei and co-authors studied vaginal bacteria in late pregnancy and newborn size in a 2026 paper. A vagina dominated by Lactobacillus germs is seen as healthy, but links to newborn body measures were mostly untested outside gene studies. The team enrolled 144 mother and newborn pairs at a Romanian hospital in 2025. Simple stained smears judged whether these germs dominated.

Birth weight, length, and head size were recorded for each baby. In simple comparisons, germ dominance showed no link with birth weight or length. The team then ran adjusted models that account for the mother's traits and pregnancy length, plus extra checks of the result. Careful null findings matter: they stop clinics from over-reading a common test result in late pregnancy.
pmc-13361968:
Bruno Manuel García-García and co-authors tested AI role-play for teaching medical students hard conversations in a 2026 study. Telling a patient a diagnosis shapes understanding and trust, yet students get little repeatable practice. The team built a program where generative AI plays the patient across three scenarios: type 2 diabetes, obesity, and breast cancer. Students first faced trained human actors for a baseline score.

Each student then completed ten practice encounters with the AI at their own pace. Scores after the program were compared with the baseline. The study reports higher communication scores after the training across all three scenarios. A scalable practice partner could let every student rehearse breaking bad news many times before meeting real patients.
pmc-13362568:
Lidija Jakobek, Ivica Strelec, and Petra Matić report a 2026 lab study on chokeberry compounds and blood sugar control. Chokeberries hold phenolic compounds that can slow the gut enzymes that break down starch and sugar. The team ran a lab model of digestion, adding plain cellulose fiber at three levels, then tested how well the compounds still blocked those enzymes.

Most compounds were freed in the stomach stage, and fiber raised that share while lowering the share freed later in the gut stage. After digestion, the compounds still blocked both enzymes. Fiber boosted the block on one enzyme and left the other unchanged. Since the model is lab-only, the authors call for feeding studies to confirm the effect.
pmc-13362968:
Karin Hrovatin and colleagues present a 2026 study of the genome layout around genes linked to schizophrenia. They focused on spots where a protein-coding gene overlaps a non-coding RNA gene, since those RNA partners may tune the main gene. From 21 chosen genes, they found seven such overlaps and picked four single-letter variants inside them to test in patients and controls for illness, drug response, and symptoms.

None of the four variants held a clear link once the many tests were fairly adjusted. Two of them sit in guarded DNA stretches with signs of useful roles, so the team keeps them on the watch list. The work maps a tangled genome layout and gives future studies a short list of spots to probe with lab tests.
pmc-13363568:
Fernando Calzada and colleagues report a 2026 study on a water extract of fig leaves against type 2 diabetes, a traditional use they set out to test. Diabetic mice got the extract in short and month-long dosing, with blood sugar and fat measures tracked. Safety was checked at high doses, sugar-load tests probed how it works, and chemistry work named its main compounds.

The extract lowered blood sugar in both short and longer dosing and improved blood fats, with triglycerides roughly halving over four weeks, though long-term sugar marks did not fall. It blunted sugar spikes after sucrose and lactose loads, matching a standard drug, which points to blocking a gut sugar enzyme. The named compounds include two flavonoids and a plant sterol.
pmc-13364068:
Paulina Stańczak and colleagues present a 2026 review of experimental work on caffeine and the skeleton. Coffee's main stimulant is consumed worldwide, yet animal and cell studies disagree on whether it helps or harms bone. The team searched the literature to the end of 2025 and gathered 53 original studies. The set spans live animal dosing and bone cell cultures. They weighed the pattern narratively because the designs varied too much to pool.

Dose decided the direction: low and moderate doses in animals were mostly neutral, at times helpful, while high doses slowed bone building, cut mineralization, and raised bone loss. In estrogen-lacking animals, moderate doses even shielded bone, but high doses deepened the loss. Cell work echoed the dose split. The authors counsel dose-aware reading of the coffee-bone story.
pmc-13364268:
Jiawei Long and co-workers describe a 2026 soft gel sensor that makes its own power for wear on the body. The gel can stretch far, bear firm loads, and carry a weak electric flow. Built into a sensor, it reads a wide range of touch force and reacts in a split second.

In tests the sensor kept a steady signal through a thousand squeeze cycles. It tracked finger bends, breath, and grip, and a small pad of sensors mapped where touch fell. The work supports soft health gear that can watch the body with no battery swap.
pmc-13364668:
Zhuye Jie and co-workers build in 2026 a vast gene catalog of the microbes that live in the vagina, tied to host genes and place of birth. They merge near fourteen thousand microbe data sets from China and world banks, plus lab grown strains, into one store.

The store holds more than sixty five thousand microbe genomes, many new to science banks. Phage and host bug pairs show set patterns. Gene scans link seven host gene spots to which bugs live there, one tied to a germ that can cause harm. The store sets a base for work on birth health and gene play.
pmc-13365368:
Abudusalamu Ayoufu and co-authors combine genome-wide association data across ancestries and traits to probe genetic overlap between schizophrenia and chronic lung diseases. Their 2026 meta-analysis pools 322,321 participants of East Asian and European ancestry from major psychiatric and population datasets.

The joint analysis identified sixteen newly reported genetic variants associated with schizophrenia across ancestries. Follow-up work linking variants to gene activity in tissue, prioritised by machine learning, highlighted candidate genes including WBP1L and CNNM2 as contributors to schizophrenia biology. A drug repurposing screen based on gene expression nominated possible treatments shared across the psychiatric and pulmonary traits. The authors conclude the two disease families share part of their inherited architecture, supporting combined genetic models for understanding comorbidity, stratifying risk, and finding therapies that might serve both.
pmc-13366568:
Taher Uddin and co-workers set in 2026 a test that grades how hard it is for a cat borne germ to grow proof to new drugs. Cure for the germ is thin, and hid cyst forms dodge most drugs. Their test counts how big a germ pool must be for proof forms to show under drug press.

A drug set that blocks a germ build enzyme needs huge pools to yield proof forms, far more than a DNA block drug. Proof forms hold fresh gene faults in that enzyme, mapped to its work site. The grade helps pick leads that proof forms can not crack with ease.
pmc-13369068:
Qinghua Mu and co-workers sum up in 2026 how nerve tune care may ease nerve pain by calm of microglia, the brain's own guard cells. Nerve pain lacks good cures. Once lit, these cells pour fire marks that keep pain on. Tune care, from skin pads to spine pulses, can shift that state.

Paths run two ways: through nerve cells that then cue the guards, or straight at guard traits like charge sense. The team splits proof from lab and clinic work and notes that dose rules still lack a set form. Guard aim tune care is the path they back.
pmc-13370868:
Gioele Renzi and co-workers wed in 2026 two drug parts in one bit to hit a clear cell kidney cancer. One part is a DNA scar drug. The next blocks an acid clear enzyme the tumor leans on. Sour air round the tumor blocks the scar drug's entry. The wed bits aim to lift that block.

The new bits keep the scar arm whole while the block arm swaps in. They hit the tumor enzyme forms more than kin forms. Two picks slow tumor cell growth, stall their cycle, and cut long growth more than a lone block drug. A two in one aim shows worth.
pmc-13372068:
Martineau Louine and a large team studied spinal fluid in HIV and brain TB in a 2026 study from Kampala, Uganda. The brain form of TB kills about half of people who also live with HIV. The team read genes in spinal fluid to see what set apart those who lived.

Gene checks first cleared or changed the label for about one in seven people. In the clean group of 110, those who lived past two weeks had stronger signs of T cell and B cell work. Those who died showed a distinct immune tone. The clues may help teams spot high-risk patients early and test new add-on care.
pmc-13372668:
Jamie F Mayer and co-authors built a brain health plan with rural older adults in a 2026 study. The plan mixes habit change, mind drills, and trust in one's own skill. It was shaped with the users, step by step, to fit country life.

Forty older adults tried the plan, and views on it were strong. Users liked that lessons were one-to-one and fit daily life. Travel and fear of age loss were the main blocks. Users said their faith in their memory grew, and some changed daily habits. The team now has a base to test the plan on a larger scale.
pmc-13373268:
Merridy Grant and co-authors tested a mind health tool for village health staff in South Africa in a 2026 study. The tool helps staff spot mind ills and send people to care in their daily rounds. In South Africa the care gap is vast, with most who need help left out.

The study tracked how far the tool spread and how many staff took it up in plain care. Early finds show the tool can lift spotting and onward sends at the home tier. That tier is where most people first meet the health system. The work adds proof for like tools in other poor and middle lands.
pmc-13374268:
Xiumin Zhao and colleagues validate a small RNA, miR-4725-3p, as a cancer driver and outlook marker in liver cancer in a 2026 study. Hepatocellular carcinoma is aggressive with poor survival. The team split 117 patients by median miR-4725-3p level and followed them for five years, with death as the endpoint, and tested the RNA in liver cancer cell lines.

High miR-4725-3p was linked to poorer survival, and silencing it slowed cell growth and movement in Huh-7 and Hep3B cells. The transcription factor ATF5 was confirmed as a direct target, and ATF5 was low in tumours and cells. The work presents miR-4725-3p as both a prognostic marker and a possible therapeutic target, acting in part by suppressing ATF5.
pmc-13375268:
Yanhong Ren and co-authors built a cloaked drug pod for stroke in a 2026 mouse study. Stroke kills brain cells in two waves, the block and then a swell of harsh parts and immune fire. A drug that mops up harsh parts helps, but it fades fast and slips past the brain gate in poor rates.

The pod wraps the drug in a core, then in coats made from calm brain guard cells. The coat homes to the hot zone and calms immune acts as it goes. In mice the pods cut dead zone size, saved brain cells, and raised test scores. A coat that both homes and heals is the craft on show.
pmc-13375368:
Mika Saarenpää and colleagues test whether rewilding a sealed city square boosts microbial diversity in a 2026 study. Paved surfaces and biodiversity loss reshape urban microbes, yet little was known about how rewilding spreads microbes to nearby sealed ground. The team first sampled five green spaces at distances up to 100 metres, then rewilded a barren square with plants, compost growing medium, and decaying wood.

Bacterial richness and a key soil bacterium declined steadily with distance from green spaces. After rewilding, bacterial diversity rose above baseline, and microbial networks gained more nodes and connections. The work shows that green pockets enrich even paved surroundings, and that deliberate rewilding can restore microbial richness in the heart of a city square.
pmc-13377168:
Hussain and colleagues review how CRISPR-Cas gene editing, taken from bacteria's immune system, improves probiotic germs, in 2026 research. Probiotics are live microbes taken for health gains, and lactic acid bacteria are the mainstays of the field. Over 40 percent of those bacterial species carry CRISPR-Cas systems, giving engineers an editing tool already in the cell. The review lists uses across medicine, farming, food production, and industry that build on this machinery.

Editing strategies fall into additive, subtractive, and modulatory classes: adding new functions, deleting unwanted genes, or retuning how strongly genes are expressed. Examples include swapping slow gene promoters for efficient ones to boost output of compounds. The authors argue CRISPR's precision and speed let teams enhance acid tolerance, gut survival, and germ-killing output beyond what strain selection alone achieves. Hussain frames genome-edited probiotics as a fast-growing frontier needing safety frameworks to match.
pmc-13377868:
Richard Spehr and co-authors watch desert ants find home by scent in a 2026 study. The ants hunt dead bugs in salt flats of Tunisia. They walk home by a sum of their steps, then sniff for the nest's breath cloud at the end.

While the step sum says home is still far, the ants shun the scent, so they pass no strange nest. Once lost, they search in rings and build a new sum from that search. That new sum does not shun the scent, the team found. Heat strain did not drive the split. The ant brain weighs two sums in a next way by their source.
pmc-13378368:
Ju Yu and a large team report a 2026 study of papillary thyroid cancer in children, one of the most common cancers in that age group. They mapped which cells were present in tumours from 11 young patients, using tests that read gene activity in single cells. The mix of cells and signals differed markedly from healthy tissue.

Immune cells were plentiful inside the tumours, and some tumour cells exchanged calming signals with them that may help the cancer avoid attack. By tracking how tumour cells change over time, the team singled out a gene called FXYD5. Further tests linked it to tumour cell growth and movement, marking it as a possible driver of the disease in children.
pmc-13379668:
Duijvestijn and colleagues test outdoor domestic cats in the Netherlands for antibodies to two influenza viruses, in 2026 veterinary virology research. Cats can catch bird flu, H5, from infected birds, and the pandemic H1N1 virus from people; carrying both could let the viruses swap genes into a new threat.
