Bird flu antibodies appeared in seven cats, a seroprevalence of 2.8 percent, though confirmatory testing detected none. Pandemic H1N1 antibodies were commoner: 14 cats, or 5.5 percent, screened positive, with half confirmed by the second assay. A pair of cats, 0.79 percent of the sample, reacted to both viruses, proof that dual exposure happens in pets. Duijvestijn notes outdoor cats sit at the animal-human interface and deserve monitoring as influenza mixing vessels.
pmc-13381668:
Zain Nayyer and colleagues present a 2026 study on predicting who will benefit from a procedure that shrinks an enlarged prostate by blocking its blood supply. The procedure is a gentler alternative to surgery for urinary symptoms, but results vary. Reliable predictors before treatment are needed.

The team reviewed 76 patients and recorded scan measures of the prostate, such as its size and shape, plus bladder pressure and flow tests. Success was judged three months later by a clear drop in a symptom score or a clear rise in urine flow. Comparing patients who succeeded with those who did not shows which pre-treatment measures are worth checking. That could spare unlikely responders an ineffective procedure.
pmc-13382068:
Rohan Kubba and co-authors present a 2026 case of a blood vessel compression syndrome in a patient outside its usual group. The syndrome occurs when a ligament presses on the artery that supplies the stomach and liver, and it mostly affects young women. Their patient was a 62-year-old man who smoked and had unhealthy blood fats.

He came to the emergency department with long-standing belly pain after meals, though examination and routine tests showed little. A detailed scan found the artery pinched at its origin by the ligament's angle, with widening just beyond the pinch. No other cause for his symptoms was found. The case warns against ruling the syndrome out by age or sex.
pmc-13382268:
Celsa and colleagues pool evidence on whether a gene variant, PNPLA3 I148M, predicts bad outcomes in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction, in a 2026 meta-analysis. The variant is the largest genetic contributor to its inheritance, but its effect on events was unsettled. Searching three databases, the team gathered 21 studies covering 232,033 adults, with a median follow-up of 7.2 years, comparing outcomes by genotype: two risk copies, one copy, or none.

People with two risk copies faced higher risks of liver-related events, at a hazard ratio of 2.87 against those with no risk copy. Their liver cancer risk was raised, at a hazard ratio of 2.54 in the pooled comparison. One-copy carriers showed a smaller liver-event increase, at 1.57, without a cancer signal. Genotype showed no association with cardiovascular events, cancers outside the liver, or mortality. Celsa calls the effect liver-specific and dose-dependent, supporting risk stratification.
pmc-13382568:
Camille Karren's team studied Unna boot therapy for venous ulcers below the ankle, in a 2026 retrospective study. Inframalleolar ulcers in venous disease are awkward to treat, and healing factors plus recurrence were poorly charted. The team reviewed 71 office patients treated between May 2012 and May 2023, covering 83 limbs.

All ulcers received weekly Unna boots, with a median treatment span of 5 weeks, and more than 90 percent healing was reached in 51.8 percent of cases. Purely venous ulcers healed better than mixed arterial-venous ones, while heel location did not worsen odds. The findings support Unna boots as a workable mainstay for these low, hard-to-heal wounds.
pmc-13382668:
Alessandro Beneventi and a large team present a 2026 study adding a missing force to computer models used in drug design. Docking models predict how a drug molecule sits in its target protein. One important attraction, called pi-stacking, acts between flat ring structures and is often treated too crudely in those models.

The authors built a new term for a quantum-style optimisation model, called QUBO, that encodes docking as a discrete problem. Reference energies came from high-level calculations on pairs of benzene rings. Tests by simulated annealing used rings from common amino acids as partners. Better physics in the model should sharpen docking predictions for many real drugs.
pmc-13384068:
Karlijn Demers and co-authors relate fatigue to fitness and daily activity in bowel disease patients in a 2026 study. Fatigue is common and draining in inflammatory bowel disease, even when gut symptoms are quiet. Fifty-three patients in remission or with mild to moderate activity had body, heart, muscle, and movement measures taken.

Seventeen patients met the fatigue cutoff, and they carried more fat mass with lower heart fitness and leg endurance. Daily movement levels, measured by worn sensors, did not differ between groups. In combined models, fat mass and heart fitness each predicted fatigue on their own, which points to fitness training as a route to relief.
pmc-13386468:
Kathryn J. Wicht and a large team find that a human cancer drug candidate also kills malaria parasites in 2026 work. CHIR-124, built to block the human checkpoint kinase Chk1, was tested against the parasite Plasmodium falciparum. It worked on both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant blood stage parasites in lab tests.

Knockdown work pinned much of the killing on the parasite kinase PfArk1, one of several parasite kinases the drug binds. The compound also blocked formation of hemozoin, the parasite's waste crystal, raising toxic free heme in step with growth loss. Moderate activity against liver and transmission stages widens its interest.
pmc-13386968:
Wilt and colleagues show that two interferon-induced antiviral proteins, IFITM1 and IFITM3, work as partners inside the cell's digestive compartments rather than as guards, in 2026 virology research. IFITM proteins block viruses at entry by stiffening membranes. Textbooks placed IFITM1 at the cell surface and IFITM3 inside endosomes, the compartments where flu viruses fuse. Using protein-capture mass spectrometry on unengineered protein levels, the team found the two proteins interact and co-reside in endosomes and lysosomes.

Removing IFITM3 sent IFITM1 drifting to the plasma membrane, showing IFITM3 escorts its partner to the endolysosomal stations. Against influenza A virus, which fuses inside those compartments, knocking down either protein increased infection. Knocking down both together boosted infection to a greater extent than a knockdown, evidence of cooperation rather than redundancy. Wilt argues the partnership model, not the surface-versus-interior split, should guide thinking about this antiviral family and any drugs.
pmc-13387268:
Omar Horani and colleagues report pneumococcal meningitis with twin brain complications in a high-risk patient in a 2026 case report. A 45-year-old man with HIV and a prior spleen removal arrived with vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, and worsening headache. His HIV was treated, with immune counts preserved, yet the encapsulated bacterium still broke through.

He developed dangerous pressure inside the skull, needing a drain, plus extensive clotting in the brain's venous sinuses. The authors stress that spleen loss cripples antibody defense against coated bacteria even when other immunity looks intact. Fast recognition and pressure control anchor their management message.
pmc-13389168:
Blanca Poquet's team found that the enzymes of glycolysis, the cell's main sugar-breaking pathway, gather in fleeting clusters they call protein flocks. Whether sequential enzymes truly channel molecules between them has long been debated, and the workings behind any such clustering was unknown.

Using correlation spectroscopy and proximity labelling in yeast and human cells, the team saw assemblies lasting under ten milliseconds, tied to matching surface chemistry across glycolytic enzymes. These quinary traits may raise efficiency and specificity while keeping toxic intermediates low, a benefit that matters most in human cells.
pmc-13392068:
Steven Ceron's team built Janus swarmalators, groups whose agents take up space, carry facing, and couple through multiple in-space split internal phases, unlike earlier point-like, single-phase models. The simplest two-phase case already copied real Janus groups, and the model extends to three, four, and five phases plus three ways.

Mapping unexpected new moves, the team also solved the reverse problem with control wall functions, enabling global and local plans that steer desired spatial facing and motion. Groups could thus cross complex environments while avoiding blocks, linking swarm theory and controllable robot groups.
pmc-13392168:
Lopes Cardoso and colleagues scope the evidence linking the gum-disease bacterium Porphyromonas gingivalis to Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 thesis-format scoping review. Alzheimer's is the cause of dementia, and infections are suspected contributors. Searching databases, the review chose fourteen studies on it, a pathogen of periodontitis, the gum disease that destroys tooth support. The question was whether a microbe reaches the brain and participates in the neurodegeneration of the disease.

Some studies detected the bacterium or its virulence factors, including its enzymes called gingipains, in the brains of Alzheimer's patients. Experimental results indicate it can promote mechanisms central to the disease: brain inflammation and accumulation of amyloid-beta, the protein that aggregates in Alzheimer's plaques. The authors conclude the evidence points to a link between gum bacteria exposure and Alzheimer's risk. They stress this link is not proof of causation and the evidence remains small and heterogeneous.
pmc-13392468:
Yael Sofer and colleagues describe a man with hard-to-treat Cushing disease whose adrenal glands stayed switched off long after the drug osilodrostat was stopped. He had already had pituitary surgery twice plus focused radiation before starting the drug, which blocks a late step in cortisol production. Brief adrenal failure during dose changes is common with this medicine, but his course was very different.

After eighteen months of treatment his morning cortisol sat far below the reference range while pituitary drive ran extremely high, and salt-regulating and male hormone output were also suppressed. Replacement steroids were started, yet two and a half years later suppression persisted and the glands had shrunk. A check of ten earlier reports found nothing matching the full picture, suggesting recovery can take years.
pmc-13393068:
Liyue Jin, Xin Dong, Deo Prasad, and Bao-Jie He field-tested two kinds of shade station for city heat relief in subtropical Jiangsu, China. One was roofed with fabric. The other carried solar panels that generate power while shading. Both designs block direct sun, but they handle heat differently. Sensors tracked air conditions and comfort indices at several heights through the day, over grass and hard ground.

Both shelters cut the standard outdoor comfort index by roughly three degrees on average during daytime. Fabric shade cooled more steadily near the ground, while the panel roof radiated more heat downward at pedestrian height during the full-shade midday hours, weakening its benefit where people stand. Ground mattered too: grass cooled by evaporation, while pale hard surfaces sometimes trapped heat. The authors offer design guidance matched to each canopy type.
pmc-13396068:
Lei Wu and others test obinutuzumab beta in a nerve-cover attack illness in a 2026 multi-site early trial. This sugar-tuned anti-CD20 drug wipes B cells, and its safety, body drug levels, and early worth in this relapsing defense illness needed first human proof.

Eleven patients with aquaporin-4 defense marks took 500 or 1000 milligram shots in weeks 1 and 3, with dose lifts and keep-up shots for relapse-free patients over up to 208 weeks. Safety, worth, drug levels, B-cell wipe, and drug defense marks were tracked. The trial hands doctors early proof for a new B-cell drug choice in this illness.
pmc-13396268:
Hey-ran Choi and co-authors used South Korea's national health records to ask whether magnesium sulfate given around childbirth lowers later depression in mothers. Their 2026 study covers all women who delivered in the country between 2010 and 2014, leaving out those with earlier depression.

Magnesium sulfate is given by vein to prevent seizures in pregnancy complications, and hints from other work suggest it might lift mood. The team matched treated and untreated women five to one on background traits. Both groups were then followed for depression diagnoses over as many as 13 years, with close attention to the first 12 months after delivery. The design separates a brief hospital exposure from long-term mental health.
pmc-13396668:
Ning Li and others show live dopamine reads at a vanishing trace in a 2026 study. Tracing dopamine down to 10 to the minus 8 millimolar is key to brain work and brain illness lore, but old sense tools stall at that floor.

A camera-built fast stage used wide-band light scatter from a shaped face, where the out spectrum codes dose through glow, Mie, and Fano peaks. The stage reads dopamine live with no chem adds. Brain labs gain a super-fine tool for watching brain juice shifts as they happen.
pmc-13396768:
Ning and co-authors present, in 2026, cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Kir4.1/5.1 potassium channel, a two-subunit channel vital to brain and kidney function whose failure causes EAST/SeSAME syndrome. Inwardly rectifying channels pass potassium into cells more easily than out, a trick long blamed on blockers plugging the pore, but the details were missing. The team solved the channel alone and bound to three blockers: natural spermine, the drug VU0134992, and a new inhibitor, EHop-016.

The structures show a 2:2 alternating assembly of the two subunits around the pore. Blockers of different sizes all bind lying flat, parallel to the membrane, at an upper site in the cavity, supporting an inner-ring blockage mechanism for rectification. Electrophysiology and molecular dynamics simulations backed the interpretation. The authors say the maps clarify how polyamines shut the channel at positive voltages and offer a template for designing Kir channel drugs.
pmc-13397468:
Charmi Kanani and co-authors studied where stroke patients go when they leave acute hospital care in Virginia, and what sends them there. Their 2026 retrospective study uses the state's all-payer claims database for hospitalizations between 2017 and 2021, covering adults with ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke.

Destinations ranged from home and home health to skilled nursing and inpatient rehabilitation. Older age, more chronic illness, complications acquired in hospital, and longer stays all raised the odds of post-acute care, especially rehabilitation and nursing facilities. Sex and race also patterned the outcome: men went less often to home health or nursing care, while Black patients had higher odds of every formal care route than White patients.
pmc-13397668:
Volodymyr Maksym tells of a strength program for a child with special needs in a 2026 case tale. Resistance training stays underused in rehab for neurodevelopmental disorders, despite proof of gains beyond muscle strength.

A 13-year-old girl with global developmental delay after perinatal hypoxic brain injury finished a twelve-week tailored program, three times weekly for 45 to 60 minutes. It mixed supported squats, knee push-ups, assisted crunches, and inclined pull-ups under close watch. Functional, behavioral, and emotional shifts were seen. Therapists gain a workable adapted program for similar children in school and home settings.
pmc-13397868:
Xuening Li and fellow authors surveyed how Beijing toddlers eat and what food teaching they get at home. Their 2026 study questioned caregivers of children aged 6 to 35 months from June to September 2024, recruited through 388 community health centres. Early eating habits can last for life, yet care for the under-threes often stresses nutrients over learning to eat well.

Answers from 876 caregivers, sent in by phone survey, found picky eating in 12.7 percent of children, long mealtimes in 19.5 percent and distracted eating in 16.0 percent of the group. Unhealthy foods reached 38.9 percent of children and sweet drinks reached 20.8 percent at this young age. The results sketch where family food education in the capital needs to aim.
pmc-13397968:
Emma Kjær Pedersen and colleagues report the Danish DemTool trial, testing support for family carers of people with dementia. Their 2026 study ran across 30 municipalities from 2020 to 2023, with half offering the programme and half keeping usual care. Dementia care at home rests heavily on relatives, whose own stress, low mood and quality of life often suffer.

Trained dementia coordinators in primary care delivered the psychosocial programme to carers in the active towns. Main measures covered carer distress tied to the patient's symptoms and carers' own rated quality of life. The design lets councils judge whether a coordinator-led offer, scaled across whole towns, actually eases the load families carry.
pmc-13398668:
Jianhua Mu and colleagues report mid-term results for a 3D-printed strut prosthesis that rebuilds half the thigh bone's wall after tumour surgery. Their 2026 study treats parosteal osteosarcoma, a rare low-grade bone cancer of the distal femur. Standard fixes sacrifice the joint, or rely on grafts that unite slowly and bear load poorly.

Twelve patients treated between April 2018 and January 2021 split evenly between full distal femur replacement and the custom printed strut. The strut matches the half-cortex defect left after tumour removal, sparing the patient's own joint surfaces. Clinical outcomes over mid-term follow-up are compared group to group, testing whether printing's exact fit also buys better function.
pmc-13398868:
Allbert Velleniche de Aquino Almeida and co-authors train prediction models to flag babies at risk of low birth weight across São Paulo state. Their 2026 study draws on Brazil's live birth registry for 2019 to 2023, keeping 2,548,570 births after cleaning. Low birth weight drives newborn illness and death, so spotting risk before delivery could steer care to the right mothers.

Predictors span the mother's social profile, past pregnancies, prenatal care and newborn traits. Logistic regression and random forest models trained on 80 percent of records were graded on the rest. Grading used accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and curve area. Class weighting handled the rarity of the outcome. The authors weigh which model earns a place in screening practice.
pmc-13399568:
Katherine Pérez and co-authors describe Barcelona's injury surveillance system and what its first full analyses show, in a 2026 paper. Barcelona built one by linking records that already exist: emergency department visits, hospital discharges, death records, and police reports. The team examined nonfatal injuries in 2024, deaths in 2023, and trends back to 2018.

The system logged 123,420 emergency injury episodes and 18,749 injury hospitalizations in 2024. Among city residents the counts were 99,379 and 14,319, and 695 residents died of injuries in 2023, as the database tallies. Nonfatal injuries were slightly commoner in women, especially the old, while death rates ran higher in men. Falls led the mechanisms and concentrated in women aged 75 and above. Self-harm hospitalizations peaked in girls and young women aged 15 to 24, even though self-harm deaths were higher in males. The authors say linked routine data can steer prevention toward these distinct groups.
pmc-13399868:
Ignacio Pérez and colleagues describe a tendon-sparing biceps rerouting operation for irreparable rotator cuff tears. Their 2026 technical paper targets tears of the supraspinatus, the top rotator cuff tendon, where the humeral head can ride upward without a stable roof. Superior capsular reconstruction usually needs a graft, but this method repurposes the long head of the biceps instead.

The biceps tendon is released from its groove, rerouted over the humeral head footprint, and secured with two knotless all-suture anchors that form tensionable loops stabilizing the biceps and remaining cuff tissue. Side-to-side sutures add reduction and stability, with no graft harvest, tendon perforation, or bone tunnels. The authors present it as reproducible and minimally invasive for degenerative tendons, while careful patient selection and outcome data remain essential.
pmc-13399968:
Charlotte Blease and colleagues surveyed patients with rare diseases and parents of affected children about how they actually use generative AI chatbots, in a 2026 exploratory mixed-methods study. Recruited through United States rare disease organizations between November 2025 and January 2026, 115 adults completed the online survey. About two-thirds of them were parents or guardians. Questions covered prior use, purposes, trust, and harms.

Just over half, 54.8 percent, had already used generative AI for rare disease questions. The commonest uses were hunting for new treatments or trials, interpreting test results and clinic notes, finding specialists, and suggesting possible diagnoses. A third said AI output had influenced their medical decisions. Caution ran alongside the enthusiasm: 61.8 percent were moderately to extremely concerned about accuracy, most had never mentioned AI to a clinician, and 6.1 percent reported some harm. The authors note the well-educated sample limits generalizability.
pmc-13400468:
Naoki Kubo and many colleagues set out, in a 2026 white paper, the next aims of the International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium. The consortium has built a large resource by knocking out genes in mice and recording the effects. Yet most disease-linked variants found in human genome scans sit outside genes, in control regions.

Those control stretches, called cis-regulatory elements, are numerous and act only in certain tissues and times, making their roles hard to predict. The paper proposes three steps: pick the most disease-relevant candidates, edit them in mice to test function directly, and form cross-field working groups. Extending the program beyond coding genes could show how control regions shape whole-body traits.
pmc-13401268:
Maciej Bartos and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of chewing lice taken from the wings of migrating shorebirds, asking how diverse the lice are, how choosy they are about hosts. Whether heavy infestations track with poorer body condition. Feather-feeding lice can wear birds down during demanding migration and breeding seasons.

The team examined 1,403 birds from 20 migratory shorebird species in the plover and sandpiper families, identifying some lice by microscope and DNA barcoding. They found 26 louse species overall. Infestation ranged widely, from 9 to 94 percent of birds per host species, and first-year birds carried more lice than adults. Birds stopping at an artificial reservoir were more infested than those in a natural river valley. Heavier louse loads went with lower fat stores and body mass.
pmc-13401568:
Ramsey Ismail wrote a 2026 ethnographic article on how the English pop-psychology label Highly Sensitive Person became a everyday mental health idiom in Tokyo. The study rests on twenty months of fieldwork at Raku-no-Kai, a nonprofit supporting people dealing with social withdrawal and related distress.

Ismail argues the term works as an idiom of distress: a flexible, morally comfortable vocabulary that lets people speak about sensitivity and have it cared for without fully accepting a psychiatric diagnosis. Digital platforms, self-help publishing, and therapeutic media carried the label into common use. The COVID-19 pandemic sped the process by making strain and emotional overwhelm publicly discussable. The label's looseness cuts both ways, drawing people toward care while translating poorly into clinical categories when they arrive.
pmc-13401868:
Peng Chang and Danfeng Shen wrote a 2026 letter challenging the bioequivalence verdict of a phase one study by Panuganti and colleagues on recombinant human serum albumin. The study had compared the lab-made protein against plasma-derived albumin in healthy adults and found comparable behaviour, safety, and immune response.

The letter's core objection is a split result. The researchers had pre-planned a baseline correction to strip out each person's natural albumin and isolate the dosed protein. On corrected data, the product missed the equivalence window badly, with peak-level and total-exposure ratios far outside the accepted range. The trial team dismissed those numbers as artifacts of amplified variability and leaned on uncorrected data instead. Chang and Shen argue that move substantially weakens the equivalence claim for a product whose selling point is being a pathogen-free alternative.
pmc-13402668:
Nabamita Boruah and team compared breast cancers in women with Li-Fraumeni syndrome against sporadic premenopausal breast cancers. Their 2026 multimodal work addresses tumors driven by inherited TP53 changes, where breast cancer is the most common cancer in affected women. How inherited TP53 loss shapes tumor evolution and immunity had remained unclear.

Nearly all Li-Fraumeni breast cancers lost both TP53 copies, with no recurrent cancer-driving variants except HER2 amplification, and carried many short amplified chromosome segments. Key p53 target genes failed to switch on, unlike in sporadic cancers, and CD8 T-cell infiltration ran lower despite more proliferating killer T cells. Progression to invasive disease added chromosome instability and lost proliferating killer cells. The work maps mutant p53 tumorigenesis in breast tissue.
pmc-13403468:
Alper Güneş and Selim Gülücü compared eye scans in 2026 between women with polycystic ovary syndrome and healthy peers. The study held 41 women with the syndrome and 46 women without it. Light-based scans measured the retina and the blood-rich layer beneath it in one eye each.

Parts of that deeper layer were thicker in the syndrome group, and its vessel share was higher. The nerve fiber layer and central retina showed no clear gap between groups. Hormone and insulin measures also ran higher in the syndrome group. The vessel index may flag early eye changes that cause no symptoms yet.
pmc-13404368:
Shumaila Razzaque headed a 2026 study of porous plastic-like materials that cut oxygen without any metal at all. Oxygen cutting drives fuel cells and clean peroxide making, yet good catalysts usually rely on metals. Their materials are hyper-crosslinked polymers, knitted in solvent from simple building blocks.

Both test polymers sped the reaction along a clean two-step path. Oxygen gathered inside the catalyst film above the level in the surrounding fluid, which raised current. Meeting points of electrode, polymer, and watery film seem to be where the action happens. Computer checks found only weak oxygen grip, ideal for shuttling it through. Nitrogen-bearing units boosted the rate further.
pmc-13404568:
Gonzalo Ramírez-Guerrero, Thiago Reis and Claudio Ronco comment in 2026 on the CLEANSE trial of blood filtering in septic shock. The trial tested the HA-330 cartridge, which soaks up cytokines and similar molecules from blood. It stopped early, having enrolled 128 patients out of a planned 206.

Reported 28-day deaths were 44 percent with filtering and 58 percent without, a gap too small to rule out chance. The commentators argue that sample size assumptions, uneven timing between groups and endpoint choices leave the result hard to read either way. They praise the team for running a pragmatic randomised trial in a field full of small uncontrolled studies. Their warning is against citing the trial as proof for or against the treatment.
pmc-13404868:
Xindi Shen and team studied how AI-aided health management bears on self-rule among older adults. Their 2026 empirical ethics work surveys 312 community-dwelling older adults who use AI health tools, plus talks with 24 of them, probing privacy, algorithm reliance, and relational dynamics. Older adults face digital literacy blocks and lean on family and doctors, yet how those factors shape self-rule in practice had been little probed.

Privacy awareness and felt self-rule ran middling, while reliance on AI advice ran fairly high. Greater algorithm reliance tracked with lower felt self-rule, a link shaped by relational factors. Talks showed thin grasp of data practices led to box-ticking rather than real consent, and AI advice often felt commanding. Family and doctor backing could enable shared choices or prop up paternalism. The work urges self-rule-aware AI design.
pmc-13405068:
Jingjing Zuo and colleagues review surgery for a rare benign bone tumour in children's shoulders, reporting in 2026. Chondroblastoma at the top of the upper arm bone can damage the growing joint. The centre treated it by scooping out the tumour, burning the cavity and packing it with bone graft.

Seventeen patients treated between 2008 and 2018 were followed for at least seven years. Their average age was 10.9 years in the reported data, ranging from 8 to 14. Arms rested in splints for four weeks after surgery. Check-ups used symptoms and X-rays to hunt recurrence, while shoulder function was scored with MSTS and QuickDASH scales, and complications were recorded.
pmc-13405368:
Kunal Rajput and colleagues map machine learning tools built to defend health care from cyberattack, in a 2026 scoping review. Recent breaches halted pathology services for weeks and exposed millions of patient records. Conventional defences react slowly to new attack styles, while learning systems promise prediction in real time.

Searches of three databases in July 2025 gathered studies from 2019 to 2025 on organisational-level defence in health settings. Tools are charted against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, now in version 2.0 in the account given. Performance summaries sit beside gaps and practical barriers, so security teams can see where learning methods are proven and where evidence is thin.
pmc-13406768:
Hideaki Hasegawa and colleagues remove a stress kinase from mice to see how skin inflammation changes, in a 2026 study. The imiquimod cream model mimics psoriasis, and the kinase ASK1 sits above a known inflammation pathway. Its exact role in the skin disease was unclear.

Knockout mice developed worse lesions than normal mice, with thicker skin and higher inflammatory signals including IL-17 and TNF-alpha in the reported measures. A protective skin sensor, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, rose in the knockout lesions alongside its partner gene. Binding tests suggest ASK1 normally holds that receptor down. The authors read ASK1 as a brake on psoriasis development through that receptor.
pmc-13407568:
Josiel Ferreira and co-authors fed lambs, in a 2026 trial, a tropical shrub silage to see effects on body heat, methane output, and gut microbes. Twenty young crossbred lambs ate either sugarcane silage alone or a half-and-half mix with Tithonia diversifolia silage for the study period, under warm tropical conditions.

Lambs on sugarcane alone breathed faster and ran hotter on most body surfaces, while core rectal temperature stayed equal between groups. Methane production, a climate concern for livestock, did not differ between diets. One fibre-digesting gut microbe, Ruminococcus flavefaciens, grew more abundant in the mixed-diet lambs, while other measured populations held steady. The shrub improved comfort and fibre digestion support, the authors conclude, without cutting methane under these conditions.
pmc-13407968:
João Reboleira and team tested enzyme sugar-release to unlock edible seaweed Ulva as a fermentation base. Their 2026 work takes on a block: seaweed cell walls curb microbe growth, slowing novel food work despite seaweed's promise. Three enzyme plans were weighed: a fungal crude extract, a commercial cocktail, and their mix.

The mix freed the most fermentable sugars, with glucose and galacturonic acid leading, showing breaks in key structural polysaccharides. Later fermentations with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and Cyberlindnera jadinii grew two logs more than in untreated media, with greater acidification and nitrogen shifts apt for food work. Some cell wall sugars resisted breakdown, so further enzyme work is needed. The work positions sugar-release as a key enabling step.
pmc-13408068:
Olusanya J. Oluwole and co-authors survey, in 2026, smokers living with HIV in under-resourced communities about phones, apps, and quitting. Digital health could widen access to tobacco treatment. The study heard from 205 current smokers, mean age about 51. Most came from racial and ethnic minority groups with very low incomes, and they reported their habits, barriers, and technology.

Three quarters had tried to quit before. Cravings defeated 45.4 percent, treatment cost 28.8 percent, and limited care access 25.9 percent, while depression and risky drinking were common companions. Technology reach was high despite poverty: 91.7 percent owned a mobile phone and 63.9 percent had internet access. Plain phone calls were the most wanted digital format, ahead of texts and apps, and mindfulness and nicotine replacement were the most popular helps. Interest ran significantly higher among Black and non-heterosexual participants.
pmc-13408168:
Suzanna Powell and colleagues surveyed Montana school administrators in 2026 about student use of vaping devices. Schools sit on the front line for preventing, catching, and helping students quit nicotine vaping. The team wanted to know which prevention, discipline, and quitting strategies administrators actually use and judge effective.

Forty-two administrators answered the survey and eleven sat for interviews during 2025. Just over half had seen students vaping on school grounds that year. Education sessions, patrols, and telling parents about a first offence were rated most effective, while quitting support options were patchier and administrators wanted more of them. Interviews stressed teamwork with peers, parents, and school resource officers. Education sessions, signs, and posters, the cheapest measures, were also the most widely used.
pmc-13408668:
JiaQing He and co-authors unveil in 2026 a gel that grips, lets go, and reports its own grip strength wirelessly. Switchable adhesives serve climbing robots, smart grippers, and electronics handling, yet adapting to varied roughness while sensing the hold in real time has been elusive. Their material is a eutectogel whose adhesion switches with applied heat.

Mechanical tests and molecular characterisation explain how the phase transition flips the surface between sticky and release states. A machine-learning layer interprets sensor signals to estimate adhesion force on the spot, feeding robots awareness of their own attachment. Demonstrations covered adhesion-aware sensing, robotic grasping, and wall climbing, each relying on the grip-release cycle plus live feedback. The authors pitch the system as a step toward gripping surfaces that are adaptive and self-perceptive at once.
pmc-13408768: Ivo Verheijen, Gianpiero Di Maida, Gabriele Russo, and Thomas Terberger authored a 2026 Scientific Reports study of animal exploitation at the ancient elephant hunting site of Lehringen in Germany. The notice is a correction only. It fixes the first figure's legend, where Di Maida's first name was misspelled. It also aligns the legend's colour key with the map's dots for each chronological period. The site map and the article's findings are otherwise unchanged.
pmc-13409068:
Allison Valle-Bravo and co-authors test in 2026 whether thirty seconds in a kitchen blender changes what cactus mucilage can do to a real gold-mining waste liquid. The slimy extract of prickly pear pads can clump dissolved contaminants out of water. A cyanidation barren solution from actual mining, carrying lead, nickel, arsenic, cadmium, and zinc, supplied a harsh test bed for powders blended for zero, thirty, or sixty seconds.

Blending shrank the rehydrated particles, lowered water activity, and shifted surface charge, though not in proportion to blending time. Every version removed over ninety-eight percent of the lead, nickel, and arsenic across a range of doses. Cadmium removal depended on which powder was used, and zinc removal stayed lower and erratic. pmc-13413668:

pmc-13418068:

pmc-13419868:

pmc-13420268:

pmc-13421768:

pmc-13422368:

pmc-13423368:

pmc-13423968:

pmc-13435668:

pmc-13436468:

pmc-13436668:
Eric Boccio, Rachelle Perkins, and James Bonz test whether monitor placement slows spotting of oxygen drops during intubation in 2026. Monitors usually sit behind the operator at the head of the bed. Residents at two programs intubated a hard airway trainer under varied setups.

Each try paired direct or video scope use with one of three monitor spots. The fake patient oxygen fell one percent per second, starting ten seconds in. Time until the operator named the drop below ninety percent is the main gauge. Missed drops form the second gauge. Setup tweaks may buy seconds that matter in real airways.
pmc-13437768:
Oliveira and colleagues link brain structure to the first step problem in Parkinson's disease in this 2026 study. Freezing of gait is a sudden inability to move the feet. It often strikes at gait initiation. Starting a step requires anticipatory postural adjustments. Those are small weight shifts that prepare the body to step. The team studied 44 right-handed patients with mid-stage Parkinson's, 26 with freezing and 18 without, measuring their step preparation and brain anatomy from scans.

Patients with freezing had worse motor scores, took higher levodopa doses, and showed smaller sideways preparatory shifts but larger amygdala volumes than the comparison group. Across everyone, longer preparation times tracked with smaller putamen, thalamus, and prefrontal volumes. Within the freezing group, severity matched a mosaic of changes across movement and thinking regions, suggesting no single brain spot explains the deficit.
pmc-13438468: A 2026 correction in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences fixes how the equipment was described in a cattle genetics study of a rumen compound that lowers methane output. The notice is a correction only. Two passages named the GreenFeed system as the tool that measured emissions from thirty-one milking cows. The correct device is an automated head-chamber system. The methods text and a reference now credit that system's developers. The study's results, conclusions, and interpretations stand unchanged.
pmc-13439068:
Yonatan Gazit and colleagues introduce a 2026 imaging method that maps light responses in materials with near one-nanometre sharpness. Most probe microscopes sense mainly how a surface reacts upward, missing sideways responses that differ in layered materials. Their torsional force method twists a tiny cantilever and mixes signals to read sideways and upward heat responses apart.

Tests on mica, a mineral with direction-dependent optics, separated its sideways and upward vibration signals cleanly. The team also mapped strain around tiny bubbles and matched the maps to computer models. On twisted bilayer graphene, the method resolved features inside single moire cells, the repeating pattern formed by two offset sheets. Energy-by-energy pictures showed fine structure that hints at rival processes shaping light behaviour in such lattices.
pmc-13439368:
Minho Choi's team proposed an EEG signal in 2026 for mild cognitive impairment, the early stage before dementia where timely spotting matters most. Gentle daily-life screening tools remain scarce, so the team recorded front-brain waves during an auditory oddball task, cleaned epochs with time warping, and extracted beta-band coherency from event-related signals. Over sixteen hundred people, split between normal-thinking and impaired groups, were studied.

The signal differed strongly between groups and matched weakly with older markers, suggesting it captures fresh neural information. Clinicians get a candidate gentle screening signal for earlier spotting. Larger, diverse checks and clinic workflow tests must precede routine use.
pmc-13439568:
Saurabh Sonkusare and colleagues listen to brain rhythms between the amygdala and hippocampus as people learn and unlearn fear, reporting in 2026. Both structures handle emotional memory, yet how their signals coordinate in humans was murky. Electrodes placed inside the brains of patients recorded both regions during a two-day task. Neutral cues were first paired with an unpleasant outcome, then presented safely so the fear link could fade.

Slow theta rhythms and faster gamma rhythms in the amygdala rose during fear learning and fell as fear faded. Hippocampal patterns shifted the other way during the fading phase. Direction of influence split by theta sub-band: the amygdala led at slower frequencies, the hippocampus at faster ones. Computer modelling backed the reversal. The authors frame the two sub-bands as separate channels for building and releasing aversive memories.
pmc-13440068:
Aleksi Kasvi's team studied low-acuity ambulance conveyances in 2026 at a university hospital emergency department in Southwest Finland, where non-urgent arrivals strain acute care. Linked ambulance and hospital records from May 2019 to December 2023 yielded nearly thirty-five thousand lowest-urgency conveyances, with analysis focused on four common categories: general decline, falls, patient transport, and mental disorders. Testing, imaging, medication, and admission were modeled by age, sex, night, and weekend.

Older age raised testing odds most sharply in mental disorder conveyances, with imaging and lab odds roughly fivefold and fourfold higher for patients aged seventy and older. Emergency planners get a detailed demand profile for low-acuity arrivals. The findings argue for age-aware triage and alternative pathways rather than uniform emergency workups.
pmc-13441768:
Veerasak Punyapornwithaya and colleagues map the geography of lumpy skin disease outbreaks across Thailand in 2021, reporting a 2026 spatial study. The viral cattle disease emerged in the country that March and spread through December, hitting farm incomes and animal health. Outbreak records were analysed with nearest-neighbour distances, density estimation, space-time clustering, and interpolation that accounted for cattle numbers.

Outbreak sites sat an average of under fourteen kilometres from their nearest neighbour, a distinctly clustered pattern. Case density peaked in the northeast and west-central regions, while the south stayed sparse. Eight space-time clusters emerged, centred on the northeast, north, and centre. Interpolated maps likewise glowed hottest in the northeast and the western north. The authors offer the layered maps as targeting tools for vaccination, movement control, and surveillance in future seasons.
pmc-13442368:
Rawan AlSaad and colleagues benchmark modern vision models against classic networks for grading sperm shape under the microscope, reporting in 2026. Morphology grading is a core part of semen analysis, yet staining, image quality, and human judgement make it wobble. The test set held 7,770 microscopy images from three institutions, heavily weighted toward abnormal cells, with faults of head, neck, and tail represented. Ten transformer and foundation models faced five established convolutional networks under three training depths.

A fully tuned vision-language model and a compact convolutional network finished nearly level at the top on balanced accuracy scores. Two models shared the best ranking scores across thresholds. The fully tuned leader also held up best when entire data sources were hidden during training, the sternest generalisation test. Explanations of model decisions were checked for focus on true morphology. The authors frame pretrained vision encoders as credible tools for steadier sperm grading.
pmc-13444368:
Zexu Nie and colleagues ask how local grass growth steadiness builds regional calm in Inner Mongolia in a 2026 study. Satellite growth data ran from 2000 to 2018 across meadow, typical, and desert steppes. Three map grains let the team watch scale effects on the sums.

Regional calm owed more to local calm than to places canceling each other out in their sums. Local calm hugged drought resistance more than bounce-back, and the pair traded off in a steady tug. Fast-phase growth rate tied weather luck to calm, since quick growth on good spells lifted mean output. Grain size bent the strength of those links. The authors say broad climate caps the insurance that spread places can offer dry grasslands.
pmc-13447168:
Yu Xia and colleagues present a 2026 case of unusually long control of widespread small cell lung cancer. The disease usually spreads early and responds to treatment only briefly. A sixty-two-year-old man received an immune drug called adebrelimab with chemotherapy, then chest radiation and continued immune treatment.

His main tumour shrank greatly, and disease stayed controlled for thirty-three months without growth. Benefit came even though a common immune marker on his tumour was very low. Side effects stayed mild, at the lowest grades only. The authors argue that combining immune treatment, chemotherapy and radiation may help selected patients hold this aggressive cancer back far longer than usual. They also note that a single case cannot set a general rule.
pmc-13447268:
Jincheng Zhao and colleagues compare scent chemicals across parts of a medicinal and edible plant in 2026 work on Houttuynia cordata. Leaves, stems and underground rhizomes serve different food and medicine uses, partly due to their distinct odours. Knowing which volatile compounds, meaning chemicals that evaporate easily, mark each part could guide better use of the crop.

Two smell-profiling tools, an electronic nose and a chromatography method, measured samples from all three parts. Profiles differed clearly overall, though leaves and stems sat close together. Fifty-five volatile compounds were tentatively named, with terpene types the largest share. Statistical sorting found sixteen compounds that reliably separate the parts. The paired tools are presented as an effective route for quality checks and resource planning.
pmc-13447368:
Qingmei Huang and co-authors review an iron-driven form of cell death in a severe gut disease of premature babies in 2026. The disease, necrotizing enterocolitis, destroys intestinal tissue and still kills many affected infants. Ferroptosis, where iron fuels fat damage inside cells, has emerged as a key injury pathway that may unite several known triggers.

Premature infants face a risky mix of immature iron handling, iron supplements, transfusions and weak antioxidant defences. Lab evidence shows iron overload drains protective molecules, disables antioxidant enzymes and kills gut lining cells by this route. Barrier failure, inflammation and upset gut microbes then feed each other and speed decline. Blocking the pathway is proposed as a treatment direction, with a framework offered to guide future lab and clinical work.
pmc-13447568:
Xiaoying Xu and Qingling Lin describe an amoebic liver abscess in a 2026 case report centred on a simple microscope test. The abscess, caused by a gut parasite that invades the liver, is the most common spread of that infection beyond the bowel. Modern diagnosis leans on antibody and DNA tests, so direct sightings of moving parasites in drained fluid are now rarely documented.

A twenty-five-year-old man with fever, upper belly pain and cough had a right liver abscess on imaging, while cultures stayed sterile. Fresh fluid under the microscope readily showed moving, red-cell-eating parasite forms, later confirmed by sequencing. Early improvement on a tissue-active drug was followed by severe colon bleeding and ulceration that required partial bowel removal. A gut-clearing drug must follow tissue treatment to prevent such relapse, the authors stress.
pmc-13447668:
Noriaki Moriyama and colleagues report a defibrillator lead placed in the heart's natural wiring that stopped dangerous fast rhythms by pacing alone in a 2026 case study. Some implanted devices can end a racing heart with rapid pacing bursts instead of a shock, guided by a smart algorithm that adjusts each burst. Whether a lead in the left bundle branch area, a physiological pacing site, can deliver that therapy was unknown.

A fifty-seven-year-old man with advanced heart failure received a combined pacing and defibrillator system for prevention after prior events. During follow-up, repeated sustained fast rhythm episodes with varied shapes were all ended by the smart pacing from that lead, with no shocks or standard pacing needed. Faster engagement of the heart's wiring network may explain the success, though wider study is required.
pmc-13448068:
John O'Hara and colleagues couple ordered arrays of quantum light sources to silicon nitride waveguides in 2026 photonics work. Quantum computing with light needs many identical single-photon sources in known positions, yet the best emitters form randomly or fire unpredictably. Site-controlled quantum dots, grown at chosen spots, promise order if they can be wired into circuits efficiently.

Ten gallium arsenide dots were actively aligned and edge-coupled to ten waveguides on a chip, all at cryogenic temperatures. Tiny pillars built around each dot in a self-aligned process gave a regular, high-yield array. An on-chip beamsplitter confirmed triggered single photons entering the chip. Neighbouring emitters overlapped spectrally and could be tuned into near-exact alignment with extra laser light. Coupling efficiency near five percent leaves clear room to improve, the authors note.
pmc-13449368:
Joshua Wang writes in 2026 to challenge a study that linked a diabetes drug class to slower kidney failure in polycystic kidney disease. He argues its design could not have been run as described. The original authors said all analysis used the TriNetX platform, with a control group resting on a pseudo-index event. Wang points out that the platform lets users pick inclusion criteria as index events, a limit TriNetX staff have confirmed, so the two claims cannot both hold.

The stakes are practical, because index settings steer results. If controls were indexed at diagnosis while treated patients were indexed at prescription, early kidney failures would count against controls only. That would bend the study toward the drug, a pattern Wang sees in the published survival curve's early plunge. He proposes indexing both groups at first diagnosis, requiring treatment within twelve months, and starting outcome counts after day 366 for everyone.
pmc-13449568:
Shao Dong and Yi Lin developed a model in 2026 for reading a birch tree's daily rhythms from laser scans. Trees shift their branches and leaves through the day and change their chemistry with light, but most studies track shape and chemistry apart. Hyperspectral LiDAR combines three-dimensional mapping with color spectra, allowing non-destructive checks of plant chemistry.

The team classified point clouds from a single birch into branches and leaves, then tracked each part's sleep movements over twenty-four hours at thirty measurement times. A new sinusoidal-polynomial fitting model captured both movement rhythms and reflectance changes. The approach lets researchers watch how a whole tree coordinates its daily cycles, organ by organ.
pmc-13449668:
Michael Bakker and colleagues compared manual and automated eye-drop vaccination for poultry in 2026, focusing on dose consistency. Eye-drop vaccines are vital in poultry farming, but hand delivery varies with the user, wasting vaccine, raising labor costs, and risking animal health. A new automated dropper promised steadier dosing.

Statistical modeling of drop mass showed that dispensing angle and uneven hand pressure drove most manual variation. Bottle volume left over did not explain the differences. The automated device cut the standard deviation of drop mass by roughly one and a third milligrams to just over one milligram versus manual methods. Farms gain a case for automation where uniform dosing and less waste matter most.
pmc-13449968:
M. Naeem and colleagues feed in 2026 essential oils to broiler chickens to test whether they loosen Salmonella's grip on the flock. The bacterium persists in gut, organs, and litter, threatening safety. Twelve hundred day-old Ross 708 males were challenged with Salmonella Typhimurium on arrival. They were split across six diets, with eight replicate pens each: an unsupplemented control, two doses of a carvacrol-rich product, two of a thymol-rich premix, and a combination.

Effects proved patchy and short-lived. The lower carvacrol dose cut Salmonella counts in litter swabs on day fourteen, and the combination lowered liver prevalence that day, while the lower carvacrol dose reduced spleen prevalence. Cecal counts and prevalence after enrichment, and carcass contamination never separated the diets reliably. Links between gut counts and barn contamination were weak. The authors call the oils' protection limited and dependent on where in the bird or barn one looks.
pmc-13450468:
Yu Tian and colleagues linked fatty liver disease to heart muscle ischemia in 2026, especially in patients without blocked arteries. Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease often travels with heart risk, but its tie to reduced blood flow in the heart muscle was not settled. The team studied patients with suspected or known coronary disease.

Among 281 patients who had myocardial perfusion imaging, 140 had ischemia and 107 had fatty liver disease by CT criteria. Ischemic patients carried more epicardial fat and differed on other measures, and the liver-disease link held notably in patients without obstructive coronary narrowing. Cardiologists gain a reason to weigh liver health when ischemia appears without a major blockage.
pmc-13451868:
Jude Crener Junior Pierre and co-authors test in 2026 whether AI rewrites in set voices can grow training data for software that finds disease names in text. Hand-labeled medical text is costly and scarce, above all for rare diseases. Their frame lets a large language model rephrase whole papers in varied voices, from expert to plain, while guarding the labeled disease spans.

The rewrites were checked for sense keeping and word variety, then sorted into fidelity bands. A medical reading model was trained under many mixes, from gold data alone to voice-grown sets, on a rare disease set and a broad disease set. The work asks whether voice-led growth beats plain word swaps for a task where label drift ruins value.
pmc-13452268:
Raktim Chattopadhyay and co-authors trial in 2026 a branded root extract, SheVari4, for menopause relief in a blinded, dummy-controlled study. The root, Asparagus racemosus, is a classic herb for women's health, and its key sap compound mimics estrogen in mild ways. Sixty women across the menopause span took the extract or a dummy pill daily for eight weeks.

Quality-of-life scores for menopause fell over two fifths more in the extract group than with the dummy. Gains showed across hot flush, mind, body, and sexual domains, each by wide margins. Blood hormone shifts and safety labs were tracked as side scores. The authors present the extract as a plant route to ease the change.
pmc-13452568:
Ching-Piao Chu and eight co-authors settle a dispute over whether antiaromatic molecules, ring compounds that break the usual stability rules, carry current better than aromatic ones. Their 2026 study built matched molecular wires around two cores: an antiaromatic s indacene core and an aromatic benzodithiophene core. A scanning probe broke and remade single molecule links to measure flow through each wire.

Wired corner to corner, the antiaromatic wire passed about ten times more current than its aromatic match. Wired side to side, it still passed 2.8 times more, since its energy levels lined up better with the metal contacts. Adding fluorine rich groups pulled one energy level closer still and lifted flow by half again. The team reads the pattern as firm proof that antiaromatic cores can boost single molecule conductance.
pmc-13452968:
AlMusallam and colleagues present a 2026 case report of fibromuscular dysplasia found in both neck arteries during a stroke workup. A 52-year-old woman with high blood pressure arrived with acute confusion; brain imaging showed a fresh stroke in the left insular cortex. Vessel imaging showed no large blockage, but both internal carotid arteries ran a winding course with a string-of-beads look, the classic signature of this vessel-wall disease.

Catheter angiography confirmed bilateral fibromuscular dysplasia. The team judged the finding incidental rather than the stroke's cause, an important distinction: a striking image can mislead teams into treating the wrong lesion. Dysplasia weakens and narrows arteries in middle-aged women and raises stroke and tear risk over time, so the patient still needs vascular follow-up. The case teaches restraint in attribution when two findings compete.
pmc-13453568:
Fernandez-Camins and colleagues studied in 2026 how the age at which type 2 diabetes is diagnosed shapes heart and death risks in Catalonia, Spain. Using primary care records from 2010 to 2023, they followed 481,709 people with diabetes. Each was matched with about three people without diabetes of the same sex and birth year.

At ten years, people diagnosed before age 65 carried a higher diabetes-related excess risk of heart failure than those diagnosed later. Inside the older group, people diagnosed between 65 and 74 faced higher excess risks than those diagnosed at 75 or older. That pattern held for ischemic heart disease, heart failure, and death from any cause. The authors argue that relative harm from diabetes fades with older diagnosis age, which should inform gentler treatment targets for the oldest patients.
pmc-13454068:
Belinda Agyapong and four co-authors report a national policy dialogue on weaving supportive text messaging into Canada's mental health systems. Such programs cut depression, anxiety, and stress in trials, yet uptake varies by province. Their 2026 paper gathers senior voices from health authorities, federal agencies, community groups, crisis lines, funders, and universities in one structured virtual session.

Stakeholders broadly agreed the texts are scalable, workable, and cost effective. Prime slots for them include the days after an emergency visit or a hospital stay, suicide prevention follow up, and stepped care paths. Equity concerns ran central: northern connectivity gaps, language variety, and Indigenous co creation all demand care. Split jurisdiction and patchy evaluation were named as the chief brakes. A pan Canadian coordination path won support, with provincial control kept.
pmc-13454268:
Alexander J Kehl and others mapped rubisco kinds in 2026, and found twin forms all through the clan. Rubisco is the gate for near all plant carbon on Earth, yet lab work had covered only a thin slice of clans while gene data swelled. The team sampled and built a wide gene set, with a focus on thinly known clans.

New gene trees showed many deep-branch rubiscos pair up as twins, which backs a twin birth for the clan, unlike the famed sixteen-part form one. A strikingly large catalytic part was also found and shape-mapped from an early-branch clan. Biochemists gain a wider form-and-work map of Earth's top carbon-fixing enzyme.
pmc-13454468:
Gaurang R. Bhatt, Elliot J. Fuller, and François Léonard show, in 2026, that patterned light can run logic circuits in parallel within a single optical stage. Computing with light promises speed and low energy, and free-space diffractive optics can process many channels at once. Electronic chips chain simple steps in series, while the optical setup folds a whole chain into one pass.

The team first built every basic logic gate with the method. They then ran half and full adders and subtractors side by side, reading results in one shot. Chaining eight such adders produced a working 8-bit ripple-carry adder, a standard arithmetic block. Tests scaled to hundreds of parallel inputs and direct processing of two-dimensional images. The authors say the results clarify what optical processors can truly compute, a step toward practical light-based hardware.
pmc-13454668:
Hiroshi Suzuki, Junichi Ozawa, Yoko M. Nakao, and Koji Kawakami set out, in a 2026 study, to pin down normal heart tracing values for children as they grow. The corrected QT interval, a timing span on the heart tracing, is the key screen for long QT syndrome, a cause of sudden death in the young. The team re-read tracings from school screening programs.

Fourth graders formed the core group, with 2,753 children, joined by smaller sets of first and seventh graders. In first grade, boys and girls shared the same average values. By fourth grade, boys' values ran significantly shorter than girls' under both correction formulas. The team derived age- and sex-specific cutoffs from the top fraction of values. Their conclusion is practical: screening children demands cutoffs matched to age and sex, since one fixed line misjudges growing hearts.
pmc-13455268:
Heechul Park and colleagues report a 2026 study of blood signals that shift as people are treated for active tuberculosis. The lung disease still kills many people each year, and doctors lack a simple blood test that shows whether drugs are working, above all when sputum tests fail or labs are scarce. Twelve patients gave blood before and after treatment, and a second set of 22 samples served to check the main signals.

After six months of drugs, nine small RNA molecules had moved back toward levels seen in healthy people, and all nine fell by the end of therapy in the check set. Sequencing of longer RNA from the same blood found 75 changed messages, with 13 tied to those small RNAs through a target search tool. The authors present the nine molecules as possible markers for tracking drug response, though larger and more varied groups must test them first.
pmc-13455368:
Zhengxu Tang and colleagues map fats in a rat lungworm as it travels from brain to lungs in a 2026 study. Angiostrongylus cantonensis, a parasite that can cause eosinophilic meningitis in mammals, matures in lung arteries after a brain stage, and its fat chemistry may shape survival and host damage. The team paired genome and stage-by-stage gene activity data with mass spectrometry of fats in larvae at the brain stage and the lung-bound stage.

The worm proved a stripped-down fat maker, lacking several classic enzymes found in a free-living roundworm and keeping only faint levels of two others. Brain-stage larvae held steady fat profiles, while lung-bound larvae built up certain omega-6 fats and anti-inflammatory fat signals. Parasite scientists gain a lipid map of a key migration step, though the work describes patterns in rats and cannot yet say which fats drive disease.
pmc-13457068:
Orit Mazza and four colleagues design, in a 2026 study, a lean nerve testing protocol that catches polyneuropathy without the usual marathon of shocks and needles. Nerve conduction testing confirms the disease, yet labs vary wildly in how many nerves they test. The team mined records from a large Israeli center, comparing 259 patients with the disease against matched people with normal studies.

Two sensory nerves, the sural and the ulnar, carried the sharpest signals, while the tibial and ulnar led among motor nerves. A three-nerve package built from them scored 0.92 on a standard accuracy curve, catching about 81 percent of cases at about 90 percent specificity. Adding a fourth test on the other arm barely moved accuracy and lost sensitivity. The authors offer the trio as a faster, kinder standard that still respects diagnostic certainty.
pmc-13457268:
Emelie Nilsson and colleagues compared two operations for the earliest stage of rectal cancer using Sweden's national colorectal cancer registry. One option, transanal endoscopic microsurgery, removes the tumor through the anus and spares the rectum; the other is standard surgical resection, which removes more tissue. Their 2026 study covered patients treated from 2009 through 2022, with 228 microsurgery patients and 631 resection patients followed for a median of about five years.

Cancer returned in 11 percent of the microsurgery group compared with 5 percent of the resection group during follow-up. Five-year disease-free survival was 88 percent after microsurgery versus 95 percent after resection, a clear gap. The higher recurrence appeared in both low-risk and high-risk tumors, driven by cancer returning near the original site rather than spreading distantly. The authors urge greater caution about choosing the smaller operation.
pmc-13457368:
Ali Raza and colleagues build a mathematical model of hantavirus spillover in Europe, where rodents carry the virus and people catch it from the reservoir. Their 2026 study pairs an SIR framework for rodents with one for humans, then layers on environmental noise and time delays for incubation and survival. The team proves the model behaves sensibly, derives disease-free and endemic states, and computes reproduction numbers for the deterministic and stochastic versions.

Analysis names rodent-to-rodent transmission as the engine of persistence, with human cases arriving as spillover. Noise and delay-survival effects can lower the threshold, sometimes tipping the disease toward extinction. Three simulation methods agreed at fine time steps; a nonstandard finite difference scheme held positivity and stability best when steps grew or noise strengthened. The authors conclude that controlling infection within the reservoir best protects people, a message sharpened by a 2026 cruise-ship hantavirus cluster.
pmc-13457868:
Moonjung Choi and colleagues improve a smart glove sensor for tracking finger bends in a 2026 study. Textile strain sensors for hand rehabilitation often drift, double-peak and lose reliability when stretched repeatedly, because they rely on length change. The team built a glove sensor based instead on changing contact area, and tested slit presence, number of conductive contact points and stitch density with nonparametric statistics.

The slit sensor detected every peak on all fingers, while the slit-free sensor missed peaks unevenly. Reproducibility rose from 0.818 to 0.972, signal size grew up to fivefold, drift fell below 1 percent, double peaks were suppressed, and the fabric survived 20,000 abrasion cycles. Slit structure mattered most, giving rehabilitation gloves a steadier basis for estimating joint angles, though angle estimation itself remains future work.
pmc-13458668:
Leilei Wu and colleagues publish the protocol for a trial pairing two targeted pills before surgery in EGFR-mutant lung cancer. Single-agent EGFR inhibitors shrink such tumors on scans, yet the tissue left behind regresses little. Befotertinib, a third-generation EGFR blocker, joins vorolanib, a multi-target drug starving tumor blood vessels, on the theory that hitting both pathways deepens the kill while keeping patients operable.

The prospective single-arm phase I/II study enrolls resectable stage II to IIIB patients carrying the mutations, exon 19 deletion or L858R. Phase I escalates doses by a 3+3 design to find the tolerated dose. Phase II gives two 21-day cycles and reads the main endpoint, major pathological response, in the resected specimen, surgery four to six weeks after the last dose. Complete responses, clean margins, safety, and survival are secondary endpoints. The trial is registered in China's Clinical Trial Registry.
pmc-13459068:
Cheng and colleagues in China traced in 2026 how freed cholesterol in a stroked brain turns its guard cells to harm. A stroke bursts nerve skins, and cholesterol, their main fat, floods the zone. Guard cells gorge on it past their means. The team blocked a brain feed line in mice and read each guard cell's gene script. Fat load, flare marks, and harm size were tracked day by day. Three cures were tried: a fat wash drug, a flare switch block, and a gene hush.

One guard clan stood out, marked by a lone flag gene. Its cells packed fat drops and crystals, and peaked a week post stroke. Flare paths ran hot in the clan. All three cures cut the dead zone, spared the white tracts, and sped paw grip and gait. The fat to flare chain is a drug aim, the team shows.
pmc-13459268:
Yayun Song and co-authors tried a low cost way to teach nursing ethics: having students act out a hard case rather than lecture about it. Their 2026 study involved 102 second year nursing students at Hubei Polytechnic University in China. The students spent two and a half hours in an immersive role play built around an end of life decision, each taking stakeholder roles. They then answered anonymous survey questions about the ethical principles they used and what they felt they learned.

Autonomy, the patient's right to decide, was the principle students named most often, appearing in 50 of 102 responses. Beneficence, justice, and family obligations also figured. The analysis sorted students into three stances: distancing through principles, contextual ambivalence, and identifying with a value position. Students reported four gains: feeling principles physically rather than abstractly, moving past black and white judgments, taking others' perspectives, and sensing a professional identity forming.
pmc-13459768:
Da-Seul Choi and Myung-Min Oh grew kale in 2026 under extra ultraviolet-A and deep-blue light to see which wavelengths best boost growth and healthy compounds. Five-week-old seedlings in a vertical farm module received seven days of supplemental light at seven peak wavelengths, from ultraviolet through deep blue, at a fixed intensity. Growth, photosynthesis, stress markers, and phenolic content were all measured.

Deep blue light at 415 nanometers gave the strongest gains, raising photosynthesis and doubling the total phenolic content compared with untreated plants. Ultraviolet treatments stressed the plants, lowering a key measure of photosystem health, while peroxide levels rose under every treatment. The authors place a functional boundary between ultraviolet and visible blue near 400 nanometers and recommend deep blue for indoor kale production.
pmc-13459868:
Chen and colleagues in China followed in 2026 more than twenty six hundred mother and child pairs in Wuhan, to test two womb loads on early mind growth. The loads: a mother's weight pre pregnancy, and her sugar curve in a mid pregnancy drink test. Three sugar curve shapes came out of the tests. Mind scores came at age two, on a stock tot scale. The team split the counts by child sex, and weighed the pair of loads as one.

Each load alone did near no harm that held past hard checks. The pair told a new tale, in girls alone. Girls whose mothers bore both loads scored far down on the mind scale. Their odds of a low mark near triped. Boys showed no such dip. The authors urge care that weighs both loads, with a close eye on girls.
pmc-13461068:
Natana Chaves Rabelo leads a Brazilian team reporting in 2026 five years of next-generation sequencing at a public reference center for rare diseases. Rare conditions affect roughly six to seven percent of Brazilians, and genetic answers often arrive late where services are scarce. Between 2019 and 2024, 385 patients with suspected genetic disorders received clinical or whole-exome sequencing, guided by standard descriptions of each patient's features.

Sequencing solved about thirty-nine percent of cases, finding 249 variants across 165 genes, seventy-five of them never before reported. Extra findings with preventive value, spanning heart disease, cancer risk, and anesthesia danger, appeared in a small share of patients. Success leaned on cross-field teamwork and tight clinic-lab cooperation, while Brazil's mixed ancestry complicated interpreting uncertain variants.
pmc-13461368:
Yu-Bo Shi, Roderich Moessner, Ricard Alert, and Marin Bukov tackle in 2026 a foundational physics problem. Some systems, like bird flocks and sinking particles, interact non-reciprocally: the push one partner feels is not matched by an equal push back. No ordinary energy function then exists, and standard statistical tools fail. Their construction adds auxiliary degrees of freedom to a Hamiltonian, the energy-based framework of classical mechanics. The extra parts are arranged so a constraint forces the framework to reproduce the original one-sided dynamics.

Simulations built on the constrained Hamiltonian reproduced both settled and changing states. The test system held dissipative spins that only watch neighbors in a forward cone. The framework also let the team retune interactions with a periodic drive, morphing spin arrangements between square and chain patterns, opening non-reciprocal matter to Hamiltonian engineering.
pmc-13461668:
Sergi Coll and colleagues report a 2026 study of how the steroid drug methylprednisolone leaves the body, for sports drug testing. The drug is banned in competition when taken by mouth, injection, or other whole-body routes, yet allowed for some local uses. Testers rely on a urine reporting level to tell apart allowed and banned use. The team checked whether that level and the advised waiting time still fit the facts.

Sixteen men took one oral dose of 12 milligrams or the same dose daily for three days. Urine and blood were sampled before, during, and after dosing, with the drug and its breakdown products measured. Urine levels above the reporting line fell within 12 hours of a dose, and every sample past 24 hours sat below it. In blood, the drug peaked within two hours and was gone by 24 hours. The body's cortisol fell, then recovered within one to two days.
pmc-13461968:
Andrew Hall and a UK team report, in a 2026 randomized trial, what happens when cyclophosphamide joins a two-drug pair for myeloma that has returned. The pair, pomalidomide plus dexamethasone, is a standard option. Adding a third drug might lift results, and the team wanted to track effects on T cells. The trial ran at 26 hospitals and planned 250 patients, yet closed early as care shifted.

104 patients joined between 2016 and 2018, split evenly between the three-drug and two-drug plans. Time before the disease grew was longer with three drugs, a median near seven months against under five. The gap was not firm, because the trial was underpowered after early closure. Response rates ran higher with three drugs, and side effects matched earlier reports. Blood tests showed stronger rises in active T cell types with the drug. Starting levels of one T cell group predicted who fared better.
pmc-13462268:
Puzzovivo and colleagues surveyed olive orchards in 2026 to learn which ground plants young spittlebugs feed on, since these insects spread the bacterium Xylella fastidiosa that kills olive trees. Current control clears ground cover or tills soil, which harms soil and wildlife. The team recorded nymphs, the young stage, of two spittlebug species across 105 orchard plots in Apulia, southeast Italy.

One species was absent from several common ground plants, including a clover-like oxalis and annual mercury, while the second species grew almost only on grasses and shunned most broad-leaved plants. Choices tracked plant species rather than plant family, hinting at roles for sap chemistry or plant shape. The authors propose sowing or keeping plants the nymphs avoid, which could cut vector numbers while keeping the soil covered. They stress the approach still needs field trials and checks for side effects on other organisms.
pmc-13463068:
Rentong Lin and a large team reconstruct, in a 2026 study, the full map of electric currents flowing in Mercury's magnetosphere, the magnetic bubble the planet's field carves in the solar wind. The team used five years of magnetic field and plasma readings from NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft, which orbited Mercury. Currents matter because they couple plasma regions and reshape the bubble.

The map shows a layered system: a current on the bubble's boundary, a cross-tail current behind the planet, and ring currents around the equator. An unexpected polar ring current also appeared. The ring currents match what a plasma drift model predicts where pressure changes across space. Mercury's magnetosphere is tiny and squeezed hard by dense solar wind near the Sun, so its currents behave unlike Earth's. The authors say the ring systems reveal new routes for energy transfer around the innermost planet.
pmc-13464268:
Alec G. Miller and colleagues report a 2026 case of a rare shunt after catheter aortic valve replacement, where blood leaked from the outflow tract into the right atrium. A 74-year-old man arrived with worsening heart failure after receiving a balloon-expandable Sapien valve. Catheter pressures showed left-to-right shunting, and gullet ultrasound traced the leak to a Gerbode defect.

The hole was closed through a catheter with an Amplatzer septal occluder, though the device later needed swapping for a leak around its edge. Heavy calcium patterns may predispose to such defects, though predictors remain undefined. Operators should watch for this shunt after valve replacement, since ultrasound diagnosis and catheter closure can spare high-risk patients open surgery.
pmc-13464368:
Gyamfi and colleagues reported in 2026 two Ghanaian cases of double pylorus. In this rare condition, the stomach gains a second exit channel into the intestine. A peptic ulcer usually erodes through and creates the extra passage. The team also reviewed the scattered world literature. The finding appears in well under one in a hundred endoscopies. It is usually discovered by accident.

The first patient was a 72-year-old woman from Berekum with five months of ulcer-type symptoms. The second was a 15-year-old girl from Kumasi. She had suffered abdominal pain for six years across several facilities without a diagnosis. Endoscopy revealed the double opening in both. Biopsies confirmed benign ulcers with no cancer. Rapid testing found Helicobacter pylori, the stomach bacterium behind most ulcers. Both patients improved on a ten-day triple therapy of two antibiotics plus an acid suppressor.
pmc-13464568:
Liu and co-authors hunted in 2026 for what makes blood vessels inside metastatic colorectal cancers so twisted and leaky. Tumors grown from patient tissue in mice supplied the comparison. Cancers from patients whose disease had spread grew denser, leakier vessels. Flow was poor and supporting-cell coverage thin. A gene scan singled out dentin sialophosphoprotein, normally a tooth protein. It was the most strongly raised gene in the abnormal tumors.

High levels of the protein in patients tracked with advanced stage and poor survival across 174 clinical cases. The protein latches onto a vessel docking molecule. It fires a growth signal that keeps vessels malformed, with an inflammatory messenger upstream switching the gene on. Blocking the protein with an antibody straightened mouse tumor vessels. A selective drug blocking its docking partner did the same. Both treatments suppressed spread. Normalizing vessels this way could help other drugs reach the cancer.
pmc-13465168:
Francisco Javier Cánovas and four co-authors review water-based exercise for children and young adults with disabilities.
