Eight randomized trials covered ages three to twenty-nine across several disability groups. Water lifts body weight and resists motion gently, which suits practice that land makes hard.

Balance, trunk control, and broad motor function improved under Halliwick-style water therapy in trial after trial. Walking range, gait speed, and strength also gained, with muscle signal reads hinting at nerve-level retraining. Children tolerated the sessions well, though safety reporting ran thin. Dose details such as depth, warmth, and step-ups varied wildly between trials. The authors call for shared dosing rules and longer follow-up in future work.
pmc-13465368:
Miguel Henares and seven co-authors review methods for measuring histamine in fish, the chemical behind scombroid poisoning. Histamine builds as fish sits, and regulators need numbers they can trust. Lab chromatography, led by HPLC, remains the workhorse for its accuracy.

Newer routes trade some rigor for speed: light-based reads, enzyme assays, and sensor strips that answer on site. Adding selective catchers such as aptamers or molded polymers sharpens sensors and drops their detection floors. Steadiness, interference, and missing shared standards still hold sensors back from replacing lab benches. The authors call for rugged, cheap platforms that marry lab accuracy with dockside speed.
pmc-13465468:
Jie Shen leads a team that builds a non-invasive prenatal test for single-gene disorders from a mother's blood draw. Fetal DNA floats in maternal blood as a faint share, and the mother's own variants swamp the signal. Their platform enriches single DNA strands and tags each molecule to erase copying errors.

A fixed panel of common variants measured the fetal share with precision that matched two gold checks. Family haplotypes, the inherited letter blocks from each parent, then guided calls on the baby's variants. Both father-passed and mother-passed harmful variants surfaced reliably in tests. In thirty-five past clinical cases, calls matched invasive testing with high agreement, which supports wider trials for at-risk families.
pmc-13466668:
Ryo Tsujinaka and colleagues estimate frailty risk from household electricity use and test whether its links to health shift with the seasons, in a 2026 exploratory study. Participants were older adults living alone in Osaka apartment blocks. A year of power data, from late 2023 into 2024, yielded monthly risk scores from daily habits such as waking time and hours spent out.

In person that autumn, the team measured how far each person ranged from home, quality of life, and walking function with standard tools. Seasonal averages of the electricity score were then set against those outcomes. The approach interests public health planners because meters already running in homes could flag decline early without wearables or visits.
pmc-13466768:
Samaa Alotab and colleagues review bone metastasis as an evolutionary journey, borrowing the lens of phylogeography, which maps family trees onto places. Cancer spread to bone is usually treated as a late event, yet clones keep evolving inside their new skeletal homes.

Uneven primary tumours spawn bone-seeking subclones that squeeze through travel bottlenecks into blood vessel or bone-lining niches. There they may sleep for years or grow at once, taking on bone-mimicking, immune-evading, and shape-shifting traits. The review compares clone patterns across breast, prostate, lung, and kidney cancers, finding shared bone-adaptive states. Bone lesions may also reseed other organs, Alotab argues, so mapping their evolution could sharpen biomarkers and treatment timing.
pmc-13466968:
Sebastian Toennießen-Klein and colleagues mine a public cancer atlas for protein clues to survival in cervical carcinoma, in a 2026 study. Most of these tumors carry a normal TP53 gene, since the HPV virus disables its protein product directly instead. Data covered 162 patients, with protein levels for p53 and three proteins it controls.

Mutation status showed no link to survival, and p53 protein amounts carried little forecast value in tumors with the normal gene. One downstream protein, BAX, a driver of cell self-destruction, stood out instead as a possible survival marker. Patients were split into quarters by protein level for the survival comparisons, a design that tests gradients rather than single cutoffs.
pmc-13467168:
Li and co-authors feed laying hens an acidifier and trace the effects from gut to egg. Their 2026 study assigns sixty 52-week-old hens to a control diet or an acidifier-supplemented one for six weeks. It then measures laying performance and yolk composition. Shell structure, intestinal function, caecal microbes, blood metabolites, and antioxidant status were also measured. This design tests the whole gut-to-egg chain.

Supplemented hens laid more and heavier eggs per unit of feed. Seven yolk fatty acids rose, shells grew denser in microstructure, and the caecal lining and digestive enzyme activities improved. Gut microbe diversity stayed flat, but community structure shifted and several genera were enriched. Blood profiling found 395 changed metabolites, mostly in fat, amino acid, energy, and bile acid pathways, alongside friendlier blood lipids and stronger antioxidant capacity. The authors conclude the additive works through a microbiota-metabolic axis.
pmc-13467668:
Langlois and colleagues in Canada asked in 2026 what sets the cap length on a wild bird chick's gene strands. Is it the wild round it, or the blood it is born to? The caps, called telomeres, guard strand ends and shrink with age and stress. The team read caps in more than five hundred tree swallow chicks from near two hundred nests, across two years in Québec. Nest, brood size, and both parents' caps were weighed.

Wide wild swings left no mark on chick caps. One home mark did: chicks from big broods held caps a touch longer, against the strain guess. Blood spoke loudest. Chicks tracked their mothers' caps in a clear line, and their fathers' in a weak one. The bred share ran from a third to near half.
pmc-13468068:
Alexandra Wagner and co-authors watch, in 2026, exactly how uniform porous polymer microspheres form during their synthesis. These spheres serve as chromatography packing, sensor materials, and biomedical carriers because of their huge surface area and strong uptake. Using scanning electron microscopy and two-dimensional Raman spectroscopy over time, the team followed the particles of a glycidyl methacrylate copolymer as they emerged.

The data show the spheres form through fast-reacting, lopsided Janus-like intermediates, particles with two different faces, which gather into large agglomerates of varied shapes. Untangling the Raman spectra let the authors track how reactant concentrations shifted minute by minute. Discovering a hidden pool of these in-between particle species matters because such intermediates offer fresh handles for attaching useful chemistry later, turning a manufacturing curiosity into a design opportunity.
pmc-13468468:
Guoye Guo and co-authors work out in 2026 a laboratory propagation protocol for Dendrobium flexicaule, an endangered medicinal orchid whose wild stands have been depleted by over-collection. The species seeds are dust-like, carry no food reserves, and almost never germinate in nature. Starting from mature seeds under sterile conditions, the team systematically searched for the best culture media at each growth stage.

For first germination, a standard MS medium with a small dose of the hormone NAA plus potato homogenate reached a germination rate of 98.33 percent, with robust early plantlets. A second medium mix maximized multiplication and differentiation of the young shoots, at rates of 1.88-fold proliferation and 81.33 percent differentiation. A reliable recipe from seed to plantlet gives conservation programs and growers a way to supply demand without stripping wild cliffs and forests.
pmc-13469168:
Luo and colleagues in China scanned in 2026 the brains of drug free kids with a mild form of epilepsy. They hunted for waste flow and web shifts tied to slow thought. The brain's rinse path clears waste through fluid channels, and seizures may foul it. The team took 67 sick kids and 52 sound peers. Scans gave rinse marks: free water in white tracts, and a coupled pulse of brain waves and fluid.

Sick kids held more free water in their white tracts, and their wave to fluid pulse ran weak. The weak pulse tracked slow work speed in tests. Their brain webs ran more packed and more swift at once. One hub in the mid belt lost pull, which helped link the weak pulse to slow speed.
pmc-13469668:
Messina and co-authors wrote a 2026 literature review sparked by one woman whose migraine with visual aura and a single dilated pupil was followed days later by Takotsubo syndrome. Takotsubo is a sudden weakening of the heart, often after stress, that mimics a heart attack. The authors ask whether coincidence or shared biology links the two events.

Reviewing anatomy and stress physiology, Messina argues the autonomic nervous system, which runs automatic body functions, sits at the centre of both conditions. Migraine leans on the calming parasympathetic branch, while Takotsubo follows a flood of stress hormones from the sympathetic branch. The hypothalamus, a brain control centre, connects to pain pathways and heart regulation alike. Shared stress triggers, hormones, and possible genetic susceptibility may explain the overlap.
pmc-13471368:
Yajing Wu and colleagues catalog in 2026 the B3 gene family in alfalfa, a major forage crop that loses yield and quality under harsh conditions. B3 genes encode transcription factors, proteins that switch other genes on and off, and they guide plant growth and stress responses in many species. Their alfalfa inventory had never been mapped as a family.

The team found 146 B3 genes in one alfalfa cultivar and sorted them into four subfamilies of very unequal size. Gene shapes, shared motifs, and chromosome positions were charted, along with the duplication events that expanded the family. Expression data covered six tissues, from stems and flowers to roots and nodules. Stress tests then flagged which members answer salt, drought, cold, and low phosphorus. Salt switched on the most members, at twenty five, and low phosphorus the fewest.
pmc-13471468:
Xia and co-authors had orthopaedic experts grade three chatbots answering patient questions about rehabilitation after knee ligament surgery. Their 2026 blinded study sent 30 English questions, spanning five recovery phases after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, to GPT-5.4, Doubao, and MiniMax-M2.7 on a single day in March 2026.

Five clinicians scored all 90 responses on accuracy, safety, stage-fit, completeness, and understandability, without knowing which model wrote which answer. GPT-5.4 earned a higher overall score than Doubao, a gap rated highly significant after adjustment, while each model showed a distinct profile across the five domains. The authors warn that fluent wording is not enough for phase-sensitive rehab advice and that these benchmarks do not prove patient benefit.
pmc-13471568:
Ren and co-authors hunted for genes through which hormone-disrupting environmental chemicals might raise migraine risk, using genetics as a natural experiment. Their 2026 multi-omics study started from 181 endocrine-disrupting chemicals and 1,116 genes linked to them, then tested those genes against migraine genome data with Mendelian randomization and colocalization.

Several genes survived the causal screens: PNKP and B9D2 looked protective, with odds ratios between 0.990 and 0.994 per unit of predicted expression, while LRCH1 and OSBPL10 nudged risk upward, between 1.009 and 1.012 on the same scale. Methylation signals at PRDM16 and MEF2D also leaned protective. The effects are tiny per gene, the authors note, in a disorder affecting over a billion people with a female-to-male ratio near 3 to 1.
pmc-13471668:
Xu and co-authors ranked exercise styles for shrinking visceral fat, the deep belly fat tied to metabolic disease, and modeled how much exercise is enough. Their 2026 network meta-analysis combined 60 randomized trials with 3,308 overweight or obese adults, comparing interval training, aerobic exercise, resistance training, and combined programs, with doses converted to weekly energy units.

All four styles significantly reduced visceral fat, but high-intensity interval training ranked first with a SUCRA score of 72.5%, ahead of combined training at 69.1% and aerobic exercise at 59.0% in the ranking. Resistance training trailed the field. More was not always better: the dose-response curve bent into a U shape, with moderate-to-high weekly doses winning and extreme volumes losing their edge.
pmc-13471968:
Young Chan and colleagues synthesize in 2026 the qualitative evidence on what it feels like to work professionally with people dying of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Reviews had covered patients and family carers while largely skipping the staff who absorb the grief of this work daily. Seven databases were searched for qualitative and mixed method studies, and twelve passed appraisal for thematic synthesis.

Four themes emerged. The sheer emotional intensity of the disease challenged staff, who also absorbed the emotions of patients and families around them. Workers learned, mostly on their own, to balance involvement against self protection. Positive experiences and personal coping habits did appear in the accounts. Still, formal support systems were scarce, and the authors warn that unsupported staff may eventually deliver worse care or leave the field.
pmc-13472168:
Beladel and colleagues describe a heart-device infection that announced itself in a heel. Their 2026 case report concerns an 83-year-old man who came in with fever and a painful heel. He then developed heart failure symptoms. Blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus. Imaging found bone infection in the heel and spinal disc infection. It also found a 26-millimetre vegetation riding on his pacemaker lead at the tricuspid valve. A lung embolism complicated the picture.

Surgery was judged too risky. A multidisciplinary team chose a percutaneous route instead. The vegetation was sucked out by thromboaspiration and the whole device extracted. A temporary-permanent externalised system kept his heart paced. Once the infection cleared, a leadless pacemaker was implanted inside the heart. He recovered without recurrence on follow-up. The authors highlight leadless devices and aspiration as strategies that cut reinfection and embolism risk in frail patients.
pmc-13472568:
Carugno and colleagues report a 2026 study asking whether two high-risk melanoma groups are truly one group. Patients with multiple primary melanomas grow several separate skin cancers; familial melanoma patients carry inherited risk. Clinics often merge them, but the mix of genes and sun exposure behind each may differ. The team compared 333 high-risk patients split into the three possible groupings.

Clinical features, body traits, sun exposure history, tumor pathology, and genetics were compared, and statistical models hunted for what independently predicts the multiple-primary pattern. Age at first diagnosis was among the variables under the lens. If the two phenotypes separate cleanly, surveillance can be tailored: inherited-risk families need genetic counseling and whole-family screening, while multiple-primary patients may need exposure-focused prevention. Lumping distinct biologies together can misdirect both.
pmc-13473368:
Zhang and colleagues reported in 2026 a dangerous clotting complication in a leukaemia patient treated with sequential cell therapy and transplant. The patient had mixed phenotype acute leukaemia and received CD7-targeted CAR-T cells, engineered immune cells, as a bridge to a donor stem cell transplant. Early after transplant, the patient developed transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy, where tiny clots damage small vessels and organs.

Such stepwise therapy avoids harsh pre-transplant drugs while attacking the tumour and rebuilding blood formation. But this complication is rare, life-threatening, and tied to more non-relapse deaths. The authors aim to alert clinicians to this risk. Spotting it early and acting in time, they argue, are the levers that improve outcomes. The case gives transplant teams a reference pattern: what the complication looks like in this exact treatment sequence and when it struck.
pmc-13473468:
Diana Lucía Espinoza Castro and six colleagues ran a 2026 randomised trial of gum treatment in people with both periodontitis and urinary or prostate problems. Sixty patients, 30 men with chronic prostatitis and 30 women with recurrent urinary tract infections, were assigned to no treatment, oral hygiene instruction only, or full periodontal therapy. Checks ran at baseline and after 30 and 120 days. Gum pocket depth, bleeding, prostate antigen levels in men, and urine culture results in women were all tracked.

Men receiving gum therapy saw prostate antigen fall by 1.16 nanograms per millilitre on average, while control and instruction-only groups showed no significant change, though starting differences urge caution. In women, positive urine cultures dropped from 75 percent to 30 percent after therapy, and gum measures improved as well. Correlations linked deeper pockets with higher antigen and more bleeding with more infections, but association is not proof of cause, and larger trials are needed.
pmc-13473568:
Yi Zhang and five colleagues ran a 2026 randomised trial of combined self-management support for adults with both type 2 diabetes and gum disease. From Nanjing communities, 784 adults with diabetes and mild-to-moderate periodontitis were assigned in equal groups to standard care, gum-only support, diabetes-only support, or comprehensive support covering both. They received a three-month structured programme in autumn 2022, with follow-up to six months after.

Gum gains peaked at six months after the programme, with the comprehensive group improving pocket depth by 0.253 millimetres and attachment loss by 0.429 millimetres against standard care. Blood sugar benefits appeared earlier, with fasting glucose lower by 0.687 millimoles per litre at three months after the programme and glycated haemoglobin lower than the gum-only group. The comprehensive group also improved oral behaviours, lifestyle scores, and body mass more than the others. The trial supports treating mouth and metabolism together, not separately.
pmc-13474568:
North and Shafaat review a family of metal loaded enzymes that look like nitrogen fixers but do other jobs. They run pieces of the nitrogen, carbon, sulfur, and energy cycles. Nitrogenases turn nitrogen into ammonia, yet their cousins were filed as oddities. Their 2026 review gathers discoveries across bacteria, archaea, algae, and plants, comparing structures, cofactors, chemistry, and regulation against the nitrogenase template.

The family spans iron clusters to cofactors once thought unique to nitrogenase. Named members include the enzymes that finish chlorophyll in the dark for photosynthetic cells, and the pair that builds the F430 cofactor methane making archaea depend on. A reductase that cleaves sulfur compounds in bacteria is another. Spectroscopy tools borrowed from nitrogenase research reveal how each variant's metal core enforces its reaction. The gaps the authors flag, what sets one system's specificity apart and how cells switch them, define the next experiments.
pmc-13474868:
Kun Wang, Yanan Guo, and Xianfeng Yu study a long RNA strand in 2026 as a marker and shield in sepsis-related lung injury. Blood levels of the strand ran lower in sepsis patients than in healthy people, and lower still when lung injury set in. A partner small RNA moved in the opposite direction. Combined, the pair sorted lung injury cases with high accuracy.

The long strand soaked up the small RNA, which freed protective genes in lung cells. Raising the long strand in cells curbed death and inflammation under stress. Its levels also tracked with clinical severity scores in patients. A blood test plus a care target emerge from one molecule.
pmc-13476768:
Duncan B Clark and co-authors recount ten years in 2026 of ethics and medical oversight for the ABCD study, a huge United States youth development study. An advisory group has guided the study from planning to today. Foreseen issues ranged from keeping teen substance use private to reporting brain scan surprises and self-harm risk. Each site keeps a clinician for case-level calls.

Later protocol shifts added return of metabolic results, gene findings, and a bid to read health records. Site plans and shared procedures cover crises and required reporting of maltreatment. A data misuse event was handled with a crisis team. Teens aging into adults now raise fresh consent questions.
pmc-13478368:
John Robert Rilveria and seven colleagues tested in 2026 whether a mental health app called SAGIP improves wellbeing and distress over time in a university community. Members were randomised to the app or a waitlist and assessed monthly for three months.

App users improved wellbeing more and cut distress more than waitlist controls during the randomised phase. Distress fell fastest early, while wellbeing gains grew gradually and strengthened later. How often or long people used the app tracked their starting mental health but did not predict their trajectories. Gains largely held through month six, suggesting timing and quality of engagement matter more than quantity.
pmc-13478468:
Peijia Jiang and coauthors published a 2026 review of MLKL, a protein famous as an executioner of necroptotic cell death, and its lesser-known role in keeping cancer cells alive. MLKL punches pores in cell membranes to kill cells, yet in some settings it protects them instead. Blocking it slowed several tumor types in animals, while mice lacking it stayed healthy.

The review gathers the survival mechanisms proposed so far. MLKL can trigger autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and preserve mitochondrial function. Both actions may block a second death route called parthanatos, driven by overactive PARP1 chewing up DNA. The protein also helps tumor cells resist death-receptor signals and secrete growth-promoting cytokines. The authors argue this safety profile in normal animals makes MLKL an attractive drug target.
pmc-13479268:
Amber Boskma and coauthors published a 2025 inventory of staff well-being programs across the seven Dutch university medical centers. Stressed and dissatisfied health workers feed staff shortages and worse patient outcomes, so hospitals run many support programs with little shared oversight. The team interviewed 31 nurses, doctors, human resource staff, and occupational health staff by video call in 2021.

The centers reported 203 separate initiatives, spanning coaching, training courses, apps, and tools. Most targeted physical fitness, mental fitness, personal development, work-life balance, or team collaboration, and nearly all aimed at individual employees rather than teams or the organization itself. Almost none had been evaluated for whether they actually improve well-being. The authors call this individual focus and missing evaluation the field's main weaknesses.
pmc-13479568:
Jingru Chen and coauthors present a 2026 retrospective cohort study of remnant cholesterol and long-term outcomes after kidney transplantation. Abnormal blood fats are common after transplant and relate to graft survival, yet standard lipid measures predict inconsistently. Remnant cholesterol, the cholesterol carried in triglyceride-rich leftovers, may add information. The cohort held 1,943 living-donor transplant recipients.

Lipid exposure was averaged over the first year after surgery under a landmark design, so later events could be tied cleanly to earlier levels. Survival models compared remnant cholesterol against five conventional lipid measures, with curved dose-response checks and subgroup analyses. The study asks whether this single extra number sharpens prognosis enough to guide lipid management in transplant clinics.
pmc-13479868:
Panagiotis D. Velentzas, Fei Chai, and Eric H. Baehrecke published a 2026 study of hermes, a cell-surface pyruvate carrier, and its grip on autophagy, the cell's self-eating recycling system. The carrier normally supports a growth signal pathway and switches autophagy on during development. The team screened for genes whose change could rescue the carrier's mutant defects.

The brake on autophagy depended on pyruvate entering mitochondria and feeding the Krebs cycle. Losing the carrier raised reactive oxygen species, and merely dampening that rise restored autophagy and signaling. In adult animals, carrier loss shortened lifespan and broke autophagy in gut tissue. The work ties a membrane transport protein to mitochondrial chemistry, oxidative stress, and whole-animal health.
pmc-13480068:
Burcu Soy Telli and co-authors describe a 2026 effort to adapt a parent-report scale of early social skills for Turkish children. The scale covers joint attention, copying others, and grasp of what others think and feel. Four linked studies tested children aged 4 to 39 months, starting with 124 families and adding further groups for each check.

Unlike the English version with two parts, the Turkish form worked as a single scale. Two weak items were cut, leaving 19 items with strong internal consistency. Scores tracked closely with a known autism screening checklist, and repeat scores after one month held steady. A pooled check across 246 children showed the scale worked well across varied family backgrounds. Clinicians in Türkiye gain a tested tool for early social development research outside Western settings.
pmc-13480568:
Max Kadarauch and co-authors present a 2026 study on building handed ring molecules with help from electric attraction rather than bulk. Most handed catalysts steer reactions by blocking space, yet pull-based steering can speed reactions and widen scope. The team used a charged palladium ligand to join an aryl group and a nitrogen ring closure in one step, forming indolines, a ring pair found in many natural drugs.

Many pairings of the two partners gave products with high handed purity under gentle conditions. Trends linked the electronic pull of each partner to purity scores, which let the team retune the nitrogen shield group and rescue weaker pairings. The findings give makers a fresh dial for handed synthesis, since charge guidance can be tuned in ways that bulk alone cannot.
pmc-13482868:
Baran and team tested a light-based way to kill germs inside the belly after a burst appendix, using rabbits as stand-ins for patients. In their 2026 study, 19 rabbits developed a perforated appendix, a torn appendix leaking bacteria into the abdomen. Nine received methylene blue dye washed through the belly, followed by red laser light shone through a thin surgical scope. Ten got the dye wash without the light.

The light treatment proved workable and caused no clear harm to organs checked under the microscope afterward. Bacterial counts fell in only one treated rabbit, though, and rose in most animals in both groups. The gap between groups was not statistically clear, and Baran calculates the study had only modest power to spot a real effect. Larger trials would be needed before doctors could judge the approach.
pmc-13483668:
Abigail Helm explores how common lasting pain is among people in drug treatment courts who also have mental health conditions. Published in 2026, the secondary analysis covers participants from five courts, comparing 61 people with a chronic pain history against 109 without one. Intake data span pain, mental health, substance use, legal history, and quality of life.

Chronic pain history appeared in 36 percent of participants, a share the authors flag as high for this setting. That group reported stronger pain and more interference with enjoyment and daily tasks. Two thirds reported non-medical prescription opioid use, far above the share in the group without pain history, alongside more oxycodone misuse and overdoses yet fewer nights in jail. Mental health and quality of life scores did not differ. Courts are urged to screen for pain routinely.
pmc-13483868:
Koovekallu and co-authors examined how giant atmospheric waves traveling along the equator intensify extreme rain on India's west coast. These waves, coupled to storm clouds, circle the tropics and can pile moisture against the Western Ghats mountains. Their 2026 study compared extreme rainfall on wave-active days across all seasons, separating three wave families by their motion patterns.

Rossby waves, slow westward swirls, amplified land rainfall extremes the most among the wave types studied. Overall the waves boosted extreme rain over land by roughly 20 to 60 percent, and by over 150 percent over nearby ocean in the strongest cases. One wave family peaked sharply during the June to September monsoon, while others stayed active year-round. In winter the effect shrank to India's southern tip. Koovekallu says forecasters should track these waves when warning coastal districts.
pmc-13485668:
Bing Li reviews Piezo channels, the molecular pressure sensors that turn physical force into cell signals, as targets for physical therapies. Published in 2026, the synthesis starts from the channels' three-bladed propeller shape and tension-based opening mechanism. Roles across skeleton, heart and vessels, nerves, and immunity follow, together with disease links spanning genetic disorders, joint wear, and cancer.

Later sections survey hands-off control methods, including ultrasound and magnetic fields that nudge channel activity without contact. Piezoelectric materials that imitate the channels' trick are covered for tissue repair, nerve modulation, and drug delivery. Force-based medicine often lacked a molecular address; Piezo proteins supply one. Readers get both the mechanism grounding and the device frontier in a single map.
pmc-13486668:
Dai and colleagues used a national aging survey to test whether older Chinese adults who suffer headaches are more likely to lose hearing. Headaches rank among the world's top causes of disability, and hearing loss isolates older people, yet the pair are seldom studied together. Their 2026 analysis drew 3,872 adults aged 45 and older drawn from a national retirement survey, the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, excluding anyone already hearing-impaired at the start.

Headache sufferers showed about two thirds higher odds of later hearing impairment after the team adjusted for other health and social factors. The link ran stronger in men, whose odds were more than double in the subgroup analysis reported. The pattern persisted across the confounder adjustments the authors applied. Dai suggests treating headaches early might double as hearing protection, while calling for work on the biological pathway connecting the two conditions.
pmc-13487568:
Maria Zofia Lisiecka and Joanna Luczak give a short 2026 review of natural rubber latex allergy. It sets out causes, signs, and new test methods. The pair sift 67 papers from 2019 to 2024 across key databases. Fresh latex is 60 percent water, 35 percent polyisoprene, and 5 percent proteins and fats. Its Hev b proteins spark most of the risk.

Allergy rates run 5 to 17 percent in health staff. Plant and shop workers reach about 12 percent. Top risks are past allergy, cross-hits with tropical fruit, and many child surgeries. Skin tests, blood antibody tests, and challenge tests all scored well in the sifted work. Shared test rules and firm product rules are still weak points. Man-made swaps and faster tests can cut harm.
pmc-13487968:
Christopher A. Rock and a large imaging team present a finer way to map heart muscle structure in a 2026 methods study. Diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging tracks water movement to infer how heart cells are arranged, but standard scans give only a few measurement points across the wall. Their free-breathing method reaches submillimeter detail and groups each tiny volume by its diffusion traits and fiber angle patterns.

Healthy volunteers and patients with severe aortic valve narrowing, whose heart walls had thickened, both showed four recurring structural classes. Despite the thickening, cell organization stayed largely orderly in the patient group. Checks against tissue samples and lower-resolution scans supported the approach. The authors offer it for studying how heart muscle remodels in disease.
pmc-13488568:
Chibueze Anosike leads a large team surveying mental health among women petty traders in Nsukka, Nigeria, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Small-scale market trading brings heavy money stress, yet mental health in informal work is little studied. Structured interviews with 331 women at Ogige Market measured anxiety, depression, coping styles, and where women would turn for help, using standard screening and coping questionnaires.

Roughly a quarter of women screened in the moderate to severe range for anxiety, and a similar share for depression, in the reported figures. Emotion-focused coping was most common, while avoidant coping tracked with worse symptoms. Most women would seek help from partners, parents, or family, and most would avoid professionals or helplines. The authors call for trader-friendly community support.
pmc-13489768:
Matthew R. Wilson leads a very large international team testing preventive high-dose methotrexate in ultra high-risk large B-cell lymphoma in a 2026 combined analysis. The fear is relapse inside the brain and spinal cord, which standard treatment reaches poorly. Two earlier datasets were merged to give 1,923 patients classed as ultra high risk. Classing came from score or from spread to sites like testis, kidney, or breast. Patients were split by whether preventive drug was given.

Three-year brain relapse rates were close in both groups, at a level near nine percent without the drug against a level near eight percent with it in the raw figures. Adjusted models and a landmark check among early responders also found no clear benefit. Isolated brain relapse rates matched as well. The authors question routine use.
pmc-13490368:
Li and colleagues mapped the ancient rock layers hosting a giant gas field in China's Sichuan Basin, explaining why the reservoir performs brilliantly in some spots and poorly in others. The rocks are microbial dolomites from the Sinian period, built partly by ancient microbe mats after a global glaciation. Their 2026 study combined drill cores, microscope slides, rock physics measurements, and seismic surveys to reconstruct the original seafloor.

The seafloor formed a staircase of platforms, shaped by old north-south cliffs and east-west faults that moved while sediment settled. Three rock types arranged into three settings: microbial mounds, grain shoals, and the quieter seas between mounds. The lower part of the member stacks these settings in a distinct vertical order the team charts. Li says the step model predicts where porous, gas-friendly rock should hide.
pmc-13490468:
Xie and co-authors mined liver cancer data for genes tied to autophagy, the cell's self-recycling system, and built a four-gene risk model around them. Liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, behaves very differently between patients, and recycling pathways shape both growth and immunity. Their 2026 study clustered patients by 221 autophagy genes, trained the model on registry data, verified it on separate cohorts, and zoomed into single cells to locate the lead gene.

Two autophagy subtypes emerged with clearly different molecular profiles, immune landscapes, and survival outcomes. The four-gene model separated high-risk patients, whose tumors carried more mutations and more immune checkpoint genes, from low-risk ones across cohorts. Single-cell data showed the lead gene, ATIC, concentrated in tumor cells rather than surrounding tissue. Cell experiments supported ATIC actively promoting cancer progression. Xie offers the model for risk stratification and ATIC as a drug target.
pmc-13490968:
Choi and Kwak, food scientists in Korea, set out in 2026 to make rice snacks both healthier and still liked by buyers. Plain rice snacks are mostly refined starch, with little fiber. The pair added barley at six levels, from none up to the full mix, and then checked the snacks for plant compounds, antioxidant strength, and taste scores.

More barley raised total phenolics, flavonoids, and antioxidant scores on all four lab tests they ran. Ferulic acid was the main free phenolic found, and it grew as the barley share rose. Buyers liked the snacks most at the mid levels of barley, about two fifths to three fifths of the mix. Past that point, extra barley made the snacks harder and darker, and scores fell off.
pmc-13491668:
Martina Tosi leads a ten-author team describing in 2026 how routine colonoscopy preparation clashed with the strict diet of a woman who has phenylketonuria, an inherited disorder usually called PKU. Her body cannot handle phenylalanine, an amino acid in protein, so she lives on a tightly limited diet. Standard bowel preparation demanded low-fibre eating, then clear fluids, plus laxatives that can contain sweeteners.

The twenty-four-year-old British woman tolerated only 250 milligrams of phenylalanine daily and kept her blood levels well controlled. During preparation she dropped her amino acid supplement, then took a second laxative dose that unknowingly contained aspartame, a phenylalanine source. She became dizzy, exhausted, and confused, with a severe headache. The authors call for preparation plans and product warnings tailored to metabolic diets.
pmc-13491968:
Shiva Satija leads a twenty-two-author team unveiling in 2026 MutAIverse, an artificial intelligence platform that hunts for DNA adducts, the chemical scars that toxic substances leave on DNA before mutations form. Existing analysis tools rely on libraries of already proven adducts, missing novel ones. The platform instead simulates how the body activates toxins, building a library of chemically plausible adducts and tracing each back to its parent chemical.

Checked against experimental mass spectrometry datasets, the platform recovered known adducts and flagged new ones that older libraries missed. Applied to tissue from head and neck cancer patients who used smokeless tobacco, it found selective enrichment of several adducts, and a subset was confirmed by follow-up analysis. The authors offer the tool for toxicology and cancer exposure research.
pmc-13493868:
Li and Yu build a simple score from routine blood tests to capture oxidative stress, the imbalance where damaging oxygen by-products outpace the body's defences, and test whether it tracks inflammation. Using survey data from 6,044 Chinese adults collected in 2009, their 2026 score adds up six fasting measures. Four push oxidation up, including uric acid and ferritin, and two are protective. Scores ran from 6 to 30 points.

Each extra point came with a small but highly consistent rise in hs-CRP, a standard blood marker of body-wide inflammation, and the relationship stayed straight-line across the whole range. The score also cleanly separated groups already known to be at high risk. Stress tests that removed one component at a time barely moved the result, suggesting no single ingredient drives the link. The authors offer the score as a cheap way to flag the stress-inflammation pairing in large studies.
pmc-13493968:
Xingyu Liu and others study why farmers in Fars Province, Iran, join or avoid agricultural marketing networks such as cooperatives. In 2026, the mixed-methods study first talks thirty-two farmers to find barriers, then surveys 332 farmers and models intentions with structural equation model. Adoption remains low despite promotion of networks for market access and income.

Talks yield economic, institutional, social-informational, and mental barriers. In the model, attitude, perceived control, and social networks clearly predicted intention, while subjective norms and knowledge did not, and trust strongly shaped views. Perceived barriers slightly reduced intention. The authors recommend trust-based, socially embedded policies rather than information campaigns alone.
pmc-13494168:
Mallinson and colleagues ask whether a single long overnight fast changes how muscle handles the next meal. Repeated long fasts seem to sharpen muscle's protein-building response, but one night might do nothing. In their 2026 crossover study, nine healthy young men each completed two mornings. Once they had fasted a normal ten hours overnight, and once sixteen hours. Each time they drank a labelled milk protein and sugar meal while the team tracked the label into muscle protein.

The longer fast did not change how much meal protein got built into muscle over three hours. Nor did it change how much amino acid or glucose the forearm took up. It did trim the insulin response after the meal and lowered a gut hormone signal. The authors read those changes as early steps toward better insulin handling rather than improved sensitivity itself.
pmc-13494568:
Santucci and colleagues tested a heat-killed version of an eight-strain probiotic mixture in mice with chemically induced colon inflammation, in a 2026 study. The study concerns postbiotics, preparations of dead microbes that may be safer than live probiotics for fragile patients. Colitis was triggered with dextran sulfate sodium in drinking water for seven days, mimicking ulcerative colitis, and the preparation was given during the second half of that week.

Santucci found treated mice recovering signs quickly, with better disease activity scores and less colon shortening than untreated colitic mice. Inside the colon wall, three inflammatory messenger molecules dropped, and production of occludin, a protein sealing the gut barrier, partly recovered. Yet two measures did not budge: an enzyme marking neutrophil infiltration stayed high, and tissue damage looked no better. The authors read the result as partial protection, supporting work on heat-stabilized postbiotics toward inflammatory bowel disease studies.
pmc-13495168:
Ebuderda Günay and colleagues study, in a 2026 paper, how to freeze Aseel rooster sperm so it survives thawing in good shape. Frozen semen guards rare poultry lines and aids breeding, yet glycerol, the usual freeze shield, can harm sperm and even act against fertility in the hen. The team tried adding iodixanol, a gentle medium, so glycerol doses could drop.

They pooled semen from ten roosters and froze it in mixes with two glycerol levels and three iodixanol levels. After thawing, lab tools graded movement, membrane health, energy organelles, and DNA state. The higher glycerol mix alone gave the strongest movement and membrane scores. In the low-glycerol mixes, iodixanol lifted movement clearly, and the equal low pairing of the two agents scored best overall. The authors say the pairing could let breeders cut glycerol while keeping frozen stock sound.
pmc-13495268:
Isaac Emmanuel Omara and a large team trace, in a 2026 genomic study, how Rift Valley fever virus has changed across African outbreaks in people and animals. The virus, spread by mosquitoes and farm animals, threatens health and livestock trade, yet the forces letting it persist and adapt stayed murky. The team gathered nearly six hundred genome segment sequences from thirteen countries, spanning 1944 to 2022.

Over seven thousand protein-changing mutations turned up, with the richest variety in South Africa, Kenya, and Madagascar. Non-human hosts carried the broader mix, and family trees showed human cases sprouting from livestock lines, which the team names as the main source of human outbreaks. Seven mutations recurred across the genome, several in the copying enzyme and surface proteins, with signs of active selection at those spots. The authors flag these sites as candidates shaping how well the virus copies itself and dodges immunity.
pmc-13498968:
Zhang and colleagues looked for early brain-network signs that spinal cord stimulation will produce recovery in patients with disorders of consciousness, such as unresponsive wakefulness and minimally conscious states. Their 2026 study followed thirty-one patients receiving cervical stimulation, recording brain waves before treatment and at one week and one month. They related network features to consciousness scores six months later.

Zhang found recovery accompanied strengthening of network energy in the faster alpha and beta rhythms across five brain networks. It peaked at one month, while slower rhythms changed weakly and inconsistently. Communication architecture consolidated most in the beta band, with broader cooperation within and between networks in recovered patients. Two features stood out as predictors: alpha energy in the frontoparietal network at one month and beta energy in the cingulo-opercular network at one week. The authors propose these as monitoring markers while stimulation therapy is young.
pmc-13499068:
Henry Bair writes in 2026 about a new Medicare model that brings computer-assisted review to traditional fee-for-service coverage in the United States. Under the model, companies will use artificial intelligence tools alongside licensed clinicians to check medical necessity for selected services prone to fraud, waste, and abuse. Pre-approval systems can curb low-value care, yet they can also delay treatment, burden clinicians, and hide unfair patterns.

Bair argues that judging the model by savings alone would miss what makes such review legitimate. He asks for proof on patient-relevant outcomes, on fairness that lets decisions be contested, and on equity across groups, all at national scale. Two design features draw his focus, namely computer-shaped workflow choices and review after care is delivered but before payment, which can stall reimbursement. He offers three practical additions to strengthen the programme.
pmc-13501568:
Guiqin Liu leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 study of how high-altitude low oxygen changes the way medicines reach the brain. The blood-brain barrier normally keeps most drugs out of the central nervous system, and altitude hypoxia alters its structure. Working with rats and a human brain vessel cell line called hCMEC/D3, the team measured barrier leakiness with dye staining and microscopy. They then profiled drug transporters and metabolizing enzymes with proteomics, gene expression tests, and protein blots.

Hypoxia increased barrier permeability while raising the efflux transporter Abcb1, which pumps drugs back out of cells, and lowering the enzyme CYP2B1, which breaks drugs down. Test drugs spread differently through the brain. Their half-life lengthened while total clearance fell, showing slower handling overall. The authors argue that low-altitude drug dosing may not transfer to people living on high plateaus.
pmc-13503768:
Xuhui Feng leads a team that made a glass glowing in near-infrared light with near-perfect yield, in a 2026 study. Such emitters serve in imaging and night vision, yet bright molecular glows often die out when packed into a solid block. Clumping, shaking, and air all drain the stored light.

The team set tiny molybdenum clusters inside a hybrid glass based on cadmium chloride. Tests of three cluster salts showed that chloride tips gave the strongest glow. In the glass, the clusters spread out evenly and sat still, shielded from air. The best glass turned about 97 percent of absorbed light into glow inside, and about 91 percent escaped for use. The result suits small lamps for imaging work.
pmc-13503868:
Zhenfu Wen leads a team that found a brain pattern marking sleep loss, in a 2026 study. Lost sleep dulls thought and mood, yet brain scans have mostly been read one spot at a time. A whole-brain signature could track harm from poor sleep more reliably.

Using machine learning on large scan data sets, the team trained a pattern that split sleep-deprived brains from rested ones. It held up in fresh data sets from both lab studies and daily life. The pattern still showed traces of harm after a night of catch-up sleep, and it reacted to partial sleep loss as well. It also tracked how long people in the general public sleep. The authors map which brain links drive the signal and which recover fast.
pmc-13504968:
Colleen Cheek leads a team telling the stories of older adults with advanced chronic illness who land in emergency departments, in a 2026 study from Sydney. Such patients visit emergency care often, and demand is rising as populations age. Their own view of those visits is little known.

Twelve interviews covered older patients and family carers across three departments. Two built stories show patients growing passive as dependence deepens, yielding to a system felt as split, rigid, and process-bound rather than person-bound. A carer's story adds the pain of watching a loved one treated as a passive case and feeling unable to speak for them. The authors call for earlier illness planning and emergency care designed around older people's needs.
pmc-13505068:
Amir Hossein Barjasteh leads a team reporting a rare skin condition in an unusual place on a kidney transplant patient, in a 2026 case report. The condition leaves the skin open to wart viruses and usually shows as pale patches on sun-exposed skin. It arises in people whose immune defenses are suppressed.

The patient, a 38-year-old woman nine years past her transplant on three immune-suppressing drugs, developed pale patches confined to her genitals. The patches were first read as a fungal rash and treated as such without success. A skin biopsy showed the swollen, blue-gray cells that mark the condition. The authors stress biopsy for odd genital patches in transplant patients, plus watch for skin cancer over time.
pmc-13505168:
Maryam Gholam Tamimi and Mohammad Reza Daliri examined how brain networks reorganise while people process emotional faces. They used task-based brain scans from 100 healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project. Activity was summarised across 264 brain regions grouped into ten large networks, and connections between regions were mapped for face and shape viewing conditions.

Face viewing changed connection patterns at both region and network level compared with shapes. Higher thinking networks linked more positively with each other, while basic perceptual networks showed stronger opposing patterns. Overall measures suggested the brain's modules became more separate, a sign of greater specialisation. At the same time, key hub regions across attention, vision, movement, and deeper brain networks kept selective links, holding the system together. The results may help frame how these networks shift in mood and emotional disorders.
pmc-13505368:
Fasheng Wu leads a large team that re-examined radiation dosing for lung cancer that had spread to the brain. They reviewed 449 patients treated with focused CyberKnife radiation between 2006 and 2025. Two tools were combined: a dose-response model based on biologically effective dose, and an interpretable machine-learning method that explains which factors drive its forecasts.

Dose needs varied with tumour size, and tumours between two and three centimetres across required the highest dose for a fifty percent chance of control. The learning model predicted early decline in daily functioning well. Its explanations showed dose effects flipping with starting condition: lower doses raised decline risk in patients already weak, while higher doses protected those starting strong. Continuous targeted drug therapy paired with high dose gave the best tumour control. The authors offer the combined approach as a guide for tailoring dose to each patient.
pmc-13506668:
Gabriel C A Costa and colleagues report 2026 work on a protein from the cattle tick, a pest that drains farm output across warm regions. The protein, named RmTIL, comes from tick saliva glands and can block protein-cutting enzymes. The team made a lab copy of its active part and tested what it blocks.

The lab copy strongly blocked two human enzymes and a bacterial enzyme at very low doses. Silencing the RmTIL gene in female ticks lowered egg survival and raised bacterial levels in ovaries and eggs. Infection of ticks also raised RmTIL output. The protein seems to guard both feeding and microbe balance, making it a candidate target for tick control.
pmc-13507068:
P Bhuvaneshwari and colleagues propose, in 2026 work, a system that watches heart disease in real time by linking medical sensors, deep learning, and blockchain records. Wearable devices collect heart sound and electrical signals, which are cleaned, split into features, and sorted by a hybrid neural network. Blockchain methods guard the data against tampering.

Tests used public heart signal sets and a classic heart disease dataset. Reported scores reached about 99 percent for accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score, a combined precision and recall measure. The authors present the system as a secure and scalable option for near real-time heart checks outside hospitals. Independent clinical testing would still be needed.
pmc-13507268:
Gaurav Kumar Soni, Dinesh Yadav, Ashok Kumar, Swati Varun Yadav, and Manish Varun Yadav design, in 2026 work, a tiny flexible antenna for 5G wearables in the N77 and N78 bands. Wearable radios must bend with the body, stay light, and keep radiation exposure low. Their monopole design adds a symmetric multi-stub resonator on a thin flexible substrate.

Built and measured prototypes resonated near 3.5 gigahertz with about 1.3 gigahertz of usable bandwidth and modest peak gain. Tissue-model safety tests gave absorption values far below typical limits. On wrist, chest, and leg placements plus bending trials, performance held up well. Smart clothing and health monitors could adopt the compact, body-safe design.
pmc-13508168:
Brett Story leads a large team testing gene therapy for eye damage in sheep with Tay-Sachs disease, a fatal brain disorder, in 2026 work. Jacob sheep are the only large-animal model of this disease, yet their eye damage was poorly mapped. Groups included healthy sheep, untreated sick sheep, and sick sheep given a virus-based therapy by vein or into spinal fluid. The therapy carried working copies of two missing enzyme genes. Eye tissues were checked with microscopy, cell counts, and gene tests.

Untreated sheep showed swollen nerve cells in the retina, lost cells, and damaged optic nerve fibers. Vein delivery did not prevent that damage. Delivery into spinal fluid, though, preserved cell counts and nerve scores over the short term. It also cut the fatty storage buildup inside retinal cells. Little therapy virus reached the retina itself, a puzzle the authors flag for follow-up.
pmc-13508368:
Katarzyna Szczepanik, Paweł Kurowski, and Małgorzata Siekańska compare stress and coping in children who train in judo with peers who play no sport, in 2026 work. Ages ten to fifteen bring intense social and emotional change, yet sport-based comparisons of coping were lacking. The study covered 553 students, split almost evenly between regular judo trainees and non-training peers. A standardized coping questionnaire and a custom survey captured stress sources, symptoms, and responses.

Judo students reported far less school-related stress than their peers. Far more of them said they rarely or never feel stressed, and more felt always safe at school. Grades, teacher criticism, tests, and loneliness troubled the non-training group more often. Body stress symptoms, like poor focus, also split the groups. The authors suggest regular sport may build coping strength, and they offer the findings as targets for school prevention programs.
pmc-13508668:
Cheng and colleagues examine what happens when an American genetic screening playbook is applied in East Asia. The US CDC designates three hereditary conditions as Tier 1 for population screening because catching them early saves lives. Their 2026 study read whole genomes from nearly four thousand Taiwanese biobank participants and annotated variants in those Tier 1 genes. It added two genes tied to conditions commoner locally: a stroke-causing vessel disease and hereditary hearing loss.

Carriers of harmful variants in the Tier 1 genes made up roughly two percent of each cohort, higher than a comparable American project's rate. Inherited high cholesterol accounted for over three fifths of the findings. Soberingly, over two fifths of carriers did not know their cholesterol was high, exactly the gap screening exists to close. The authors argue screening panels must be re-derived, not just imported, for each population.
pmc-13508768:
Bishop and colleagues developed pHarmony, an algorithm that matches peaks between multidimensional NMR spectra, the magnetic resonance fingerprints used to map protein structures and screen drug fragments. Matching peaks across spectra is slow, especially where signals crowd together, and tools rarely say how confident a match is. Their 2026 method models how peak deviations arise from noise versus shifts.

Bishop used Bayesian inference to assign each match a reliability score. The method, a statistical framework that updates beliefs with evidence, considers all mappings together rather than one peak at a time. Tests included mapping between triple-resonance assignment spectra and between two- and three-dimensional spectra from a fragment-based drug discovery screen perturbed by ligand binding. The algorithm stayed accurate even when peaks vanished through exchange effects or picking errors, and it handles peak lists of any dimensionality, filling a gap left by picking-focused tools.
pmc-13509368:
İlgenli and co-authors ran a 2026 laboratory study on the safety of modified mineral trioxide aggregate, a calcium silicate material dentists use to repair teeth. Adding chitosan, a natural polymer, or an antiseptic called Octenisept might change how the material treats nearby cells. The test cells were fibroblasts from the ligament that holds teeth in place.

Extracts of five material versions were placed on the human cells at several strengths for one and three days. İlgenli measured survival with the MTT assay, counting anything under seventy percent survival as toxic by international standard. Direct exposure to the antiseptic solution was most damaging to the cells. Among material extracts, only the version with one percent chitosan stayed non-toxic at full strength after three days.
pmc-13509568:
Hu and colleagues reported in 2026 that a purified polysaccharide from goji berries, called Lycii Fructus, extends healthy life in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Complex sugars from plants are a focus of ageing research. This fraction was tested for its effect on the mitochondrial unfolded protein response, a repair program that keeps the cell's energy factories healthy. Worms got the fraction across their lives while the team tracked lifespan, movement, and stress resistance.

Hu found treated worms lived longer, stayed healthier, and resisted heat, oxidation, and ultraviolet stress better than controls. Their mitochondria stayed more plentiful and better shaped, energy output rose, and harmful reactive oxygen fell. The lifespan gain vanished in worms lacking either of two genes, ATFS-1 or UBL-5, that drive the repair program. In human skin cells, the fraction also cut a marker of cell ageing and improved mitochondrial function.
pmc-13509668:
Johanna Müller-Diesing and eight co-authors revisit patients with long-lasting dizziness whose cause stayed unclear at first testing, in 2026 work. The group first saw these patients between 2009 and 2012, when each had felt dizzy for at least a year without a firm diagnosis. Fourteen to seventeen years later, the team reached 51 of them by phone and repeated a standard handicap score for dizziness.

Scores fell sharply over the long gap, with the median total dropping from the high range to the low range. Nearly every patient, 49 of 51, reported improvement, and the largest gain came in daily functioning rather than in body symptoms or mood. Gains appeared across sex, age, and later diagnostic groups alike. The authors say the long view is reassuring, though larger groups are needed before a general forecast can be trusted.
pmc-13510568:
Xiao-Xin Liang, Haochen Wu, and Yong Wang build an electronic tongue that reads tears for eye disease screening, in 2026 work. Tears carry clues about eye health, yet lab tests for them are slow and hard to carry into clinics. The device joins a tiny fluid chip with sensors that make their own power from droplet motion, working in three modes that read droplet behavior in different ways.

Tuned settings kept readings steady within a narrow error band across all three modes. Paired with a learning method, the system sorted artificial tears by acidity with accuracy above ninety-six percent. Disease-linked markers, including an enzyme, an inflammation signal, and a germ tied to eye infection, each gave distinct electrical patterns that allowed type and level checks. The authors present the self-powered mini system as a step toward quick tear testing at the point of care.
pmc-13510968:
Bovio and colleagues build a wearable that estimates blood pressure continuously without a cuff. Their 2026 paper pairs the SOUNDI device, a multimodal sensor platform, with a neural network mixing convolutional and memory layers to read physiological signals and predict systolic and diastolic pressure. Data came from twenty healthy volunteers measured against a validated ambulatory reference device.

Two evaluations were run. Testing on entirely unseen people, the honest test of generalisation, the best subject's average error was about five millimetres of mercury for systolic and under four for diastolic pressure. Under a personalised split, where the model sees part of each person's data, errors fell to about three millimetres for both values, with correlations near 0.95 for systolic pressure. The authors present the results as feasibility evidence for cuffless monitoring, while noting the gap between personalised and person-independent performance.
pmc-13511268:
Iulia Stratulat-Chiriac and nine co-authors examine deaths among children born with gut malformations at a Romanian surgical center from 2020 to 2024, in 2026 work. Such birth defects remain a major cause of child death, above all in the newborn period and in lower-resource settings. Records covered 231 children admitted over five years, including the pandemic period, and the team compared survivors with those who died.

About one child in nine died during the first admission. More than half of deaths came within thirty days of arrival, and most followed surgery. Death rates ran highest for a severe joined outlet malformation and for a blocked upper bowel present at birth, among other types detailed in the full report. Eastern European data of this kind are scarce, and the authors say naming the baseline traits tied to death can guide earlier referral and sharper newborn care.
pmc-13512668:
Xufeng Fu, Bipeng Lai, Rongling He, Xiuji Huang, Qin Jiang, and Hui Li present a two-stream graph neural network for sorting diseases from multi-omics data, in 2026 work. Layers such as genes, RNA, and methylation differ in scale and grain, which makes joining them hard. The design builds a mixed graph of samples and features, with fast mutual information setting the prior strength of dependency edges.

One stream, built on a transformer, reads feature interplay in vector form, while a graph attention stream models structure among samples and molecular features. An uncertainty-aware ensemble steadies answers when samples are few or noisy. Five public benchmarks tested the system, covering Alzheimer data, glioma, breast cancer, colon tumor staging, and a kidney set used as a ceiling check. Sorting held competitive, and explanation tools surfaced breast cancer marker genes. The authors stress readable biomarker ranking as the real prize.
pmc-13512968:
Margaret K. Corley and co-authors trace the origins and spread of the invasive Asian tiger mosquito across the Americas through population genetics, in 2026 work. The mosquito now thrives across the continent and can carry dengue, chikungunya, and Zika viruses. Samples came from fifty sites in the invaded American range, fourteen in Europe, and twenty-eight in the native Asian range.

American populations descend from many separate introduction events drawing on several distinct native sources, not one founding wave. South American populations stood genetically apart from those in temperate North America and Europe. After arrival, American populations also mixed with each other, most likely through human transport moving eggs or adults along trade and travel routes. The authors say knowing invasion sources helps managers predict spread and target control of this disease carrier.
pmc-13514268:
Alexandru Mihai Micu and nine co-authors build a low-cost digital workflow for printing patient-specific practice teeth with layered enamel and built-in decay, in 2026 work. Standard plastic training teeth look idealized and feel uniform, while virtual simulators cost too much for large classes. Mouth scans and cone-beam images from one de-identified case were merged into a virtual patient, and a socket design lets each printed tooth be swapped by a screw through its root tip.

Two printing routes and a hybrid were compared on cost, time, and fidelity, and the hybrid pairing won for full two-jaw models. Fifty dental students handled one premium print and scored teaching value highest, with visual realism beating touch realism. Nearly all rated it at least equal to a natural extracted tooth, and most preferred it, though hardness felt off. Touch remains the priority for better materials.
pmc-13515568:
Shiquan Su and five colleagues report a field experiment in a subtropical moso bamboo forest in China, published in 2026, on how drought and nitrogen shape soil life. The team cut the rain reaching some plots and added nitrogen to others, mimicking two global changes at once. They then measured how many soil jobs, from nutrient cycling to productivity support, the soil kept performing, and profiled its bacteria and fungi by gene sequencing.

Reduced rainfall clearly lowered the soil's combined performance, and added nitrogen made that loss worse. Surprisingly, the count of microbe species barely changed, and performance did not track diversity at all. What mattered was which microbes were present and how they linked together in networks. Rising shares of three groups, among them Acidobacteriota, went with stronger soil performance. Su's team concludes that global change rewires soil communities rather than emptying them, and the rewiring drives the function loss.
pmc-13515768:
Paul Grama and colleagues review whether scope-based weight-loss treatments suit patients who have both obesity and inflammatory bowel disease. The treatments, such as stomach balloons and sleeve reshaping, sit between drugs and full bariatric surgery in intensity.

Direct trials in bowel disease patients barely exist, so the review leans on general scope studies and surgery data. The best candidates, it argues, are patients in lasting remission with stable nutrition and uncomplicated disease. Active upper-gut Crohn's disease, narrowed or penetrating disease, recent surgery, and heavy steroid use should prompt caution or avoidance. Grama calls for registries and trials split by disease type before firm advice can be given.
pmc-13517168:
Jingmin Luan and eight colleagues build an image-analysis method that reads brain blood vessels more faithfully after stroke, in a 2026 study. OCTA scans can watch the brain's smallest vessels over time, but stroke weakens the signal and blurs vessel edges, corrupting measurements. Their structure-aware segmentation was tested in mice with a clot-based stroke model, scoring overlap, boundary accuracy, centreline continuity, and branch-point survival against hand-drawn references.

The method beat plain approaches on those structural scores and held up when images were deliberately degraded. Applied across time, its vessel masks showed less detectable perfusion coverage and shorter apparent vessel length after the stroke, while average vessel width barely moved. Luan's team frames the work as exploratory and preclinical. Its point is methodological: stroke studies need segmentation judged on network structure, not just pixel overlap, before derived numbers can be trusted.
pmc-13518868:
Ruohan Zhong and four colleagues propose in 2026 a poverty clue hidden in cooking energy: the share of a household's energy spent preparing food. Money-based measures miss families who farm for themselves or trade without cash. Engel's law says poorer households devote a larger share of resources to basic needs.

Using a nationwide Chinese household survey, the team built an Energy Engel Coefficient and checked it against regional patterns, subjective experience, and asset ownership. The new measure followed Engel's law more faithfully than the classic spending version. It flagged 13.9 percent of households as poor, and 85.8 percent of those were missed by the traditional coefficient, mostly small low-income rural homes.
pmc-13519268:
Yichi Zhang and a large team dissect the vessel wall of narrowed dialysis fistulas in 2026 to learn why mature arteriovenous fistulas fail. Narrowing strikes 20 to 40 percent of mature fistulas, the go-to access for hemodialysis, yet the wall makeup of late failures was barely studied. Twenty-one removed specimens were checked with a custom machine-learning method.

Proteoglycans and collagen filled the wall more than muscle cells, with breaks along needle tracks. Narrowed segments showed compact collagen plus high levels of perlecan, versican, and its fragment versikine. Muscle cells there favored a quiet contractile state rather than growth. Zhang's team proposes the narrowing matures through phases, which may explain mixed responses to drug-coated devices.
pmc-13519768:
McDermott and co-authors issued a 2026 United Kingdom guideline on gene testing to prevent hearing loss from aminoglycoside antibiotics. These powerful drugs treat severe infections but can permanently damage hearing in people carrying certain mitochondrial variants. Three variants in the MT-RNR1 gene, found in about one in 330 people, carry that risk.

Carriers can lose hearing irreversibly after even a single dose at normal drug levels, the guideline stresses. McDermott recommends avoiding aminoglycosides at any detectable variant level and using alternatives where possible for carriers. Laboratory testing is nationally commissioned in England, while rapid bedside testing serves time critical cases such as newborn sepsis in some centres. Where results are unavailable and urgency is high, treatment should not be delayed. Early economic evidence suggests newborn bedside testing may save money.
pmc-13520168:
Shifang Tan leads a twelve-author study in 2026 testing Node-RADS, a standardized scoring system for judging lymph nodes on scans, in cervical cancer staging. Whether nodes harbor cancer decides treatment intensity, and ordinary MRI misses many deposits. Records covered 439 patients who had preoperative MRI plus node removal, with four readers of differing experience scoring preset nodes blindly.

Senior readers agreed almost perfectly and detected metastases with an area under the curve of 0.868. Junior readers agreed less and scored 0.758, needing consensus three times more often. Agreement between the senior and junior groups on node status was still substantial. Experience clearly shapes performance, the authors note.
pmc-13520268:
Donghoon Kang leads a six-author study in 2026 testing whether stomach microbes plus routine clinical facts can flag gastric growths, from precancerous adenoma to cancer. Samples from mouth, healthy stomach lining, and lesions were sequenced for 231 people: 129 with adenoma, 73 with cancer, and 29 healthy controls.

Microbial diversity thinned step by step toward cancer, and certain genera bloomed in cancer lesions while gut-friendly types faded. A combined prediction model using 33 microbial genera and six clinical variables reached a discrimination score of 0.830 at separating growths from healthy stomachs, beating microbe-only and clinical-only models. It also split adenoma from cancer well. Kang and colleagues propose the pairing as an endoscopy aid.
pmc-13520368:
Habib Daneshpajouh and colleagues present in 2026 a single map of gene control states built from 1,698 human tissue samples. A global group gathered the samples over many years. Older maps were made one cell type at a time. That method grows hard to run as cell types pile up.

The team used more than 9,500 signal tracks from the samples. Their model made 33 simple scores. The scores capture start sites, boost sites, active copying and silent zones. The scores also capture cell-specific patterns. Tests of gene activity matched or beat rival methods. A side score flags zones rich in disease-linked gene changes.
pmc-13520468:
Weikai Chen and colleagues present in 2026 a complete, gap-free genome assembly for common tobacco, a major crop formed by merging two wild species. Earlier assemblies left hundreds of gaps, especially in repetitive centre regions of chromosomes.

The new assembly spans 4.2 billion bases from end to end, with the two inherited subgenomes separated. Centre regions evolved unevenly after the merger, with frequent repositioning and distinct chemical marking patterns between subgenomes. One subgenome diverged faster in sequence. Plant scientists gain a reference for studying how merged genomes reorganise, plus a firmer base for tobacco breeding and gene work.
pmc-13522268:
Yanwen Li and Yubin Li profile in 2026 a fat-handling gene called LCAT across three kidney cancer subtypes, where molecular programmes and immune surroundings differ enough to demand subtype-by-subtype judgement. Public cancer atlas data supplied gene, survival and immune measures.

Gene levels fell in chromophobe tumours yet rose in clear cell and papillary tumours versus normal kidney. Survival links flipped by subtype, harming outlook at opposite ends of expression in two subtypes while helping one outcome in the third. Immune scores and cell mixes shifted with gene level in every subtype. Copy number, methylation and RNA editing regulator links round out the portrait.
pmc-13522368:
Saha and colleagues report a 2026 study of mango ginger, a turmeric relative used in pickles and folk medicine, tested against chemical liver poisoning in mice.  Mice received the plant extract at two doses alongside the poison, and blood markers, tissue slices, and computer models of its compounds were examined.

The extract, which chemical analysis showed holds 62 probable compounds, clearly lowered the raised liver enzymes and bilirubin that signal liver damage. Kidney markers and blood fats also fell toward normal, and tissue slices showed the poison's damage reversed. Computer docking showed its compounds bind well to targets tied to inflammation and cell protection. The results support developing mango ginger compounds into liver and kidney protectors, though human proof is still far off.
pmc-13522468:
Kipyo Kim and colleagues propose a way to estimate a patient's usual kidney blood marker from a CT scan in a 2026 study of acute kidney injury. Diagnosis depends on comparing current creatinine, a waste product measured in blood, with a prior usual value that is often missing. Features drawn from segmented kidney images at two large hospitals were fed into machine learning models.

Using the imaging features, the models estimated the usual value more closely than the standard back-calculation method. Staging of the acute injury based on predicted values agreed far better with the true staging, and cases were much less often overstated. The externally tested approach could help clinicians judge acute kidney injury when no earlier blood result exists.
pmc-13523268:
Hosein Azizi, Elham Davtalab Esmaeili, and Ali Reza Shafiee-Kandjani relate social and economic status to quality of life in older adults in northwestern Iran in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Eight hundred six adults aged sixty or older were enrolled by stratified random sampling. Quality of life was measured with a standard World Health Organization questionnaire, and status was scored with a validated short instrument.

A clear gradient appeared: each step up in status tracked a higher quality of life score, with the highest group scoring about eight points above the lowest after adjustment. Younger seniors reported better quality of life than the oldest group, while widowhood tracked notably lower scores. Sex showed no independent link after adjustment. The authors recommend stronger financial support and social services focused on disadvantaged and widowed older adults.
pmc-13523368:
Eli M Soyfer and colleagues test whether the time of day of immunotherapy infusions affects cancer outcomes in a 2026 real-world study. Nearly one thousand patients receiving checkpoint inhibitor drugs for solid tumors at one health system between 2018 and 2022 were grouped by whether infusions started before or after noon. Disease control, meaning shrinkage or stability, was the main outcome.

Early infusion was linked to higher disease control, at just under half of patients versus two fifths for later infusion. The association survived adjustment for stage, age, and ethnicity, and held across sex, age, stage, and drug subgroups, as well as in matched and sensitivity analyses. Evidence in the Hispanic subgroup was inconclusive because of small numbers. The authors call for prospective trials of treatment timing.
pmc-13523468:
Cansu Özbaş and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study from Ankara, Türkiye, on what adults believe about thirdhand smoke and on voluntary smoking bans at home and in cars. Thirdhand smoke is the residue that lingers on surfaces after tobacco smoke clears. Adults attending a university hospital in June 2023 answered a 33-item questionnaire in face-to-face interviews.

Complete bans were reported by 57.4 percent of participants at home and 63.2 percent in cars. Stronger belief scores on a validated thirdhand smoke scale were linked with bans in both settings. Homes without a resident smoker were far more likely to enforce a ban, and nonsmokers banned smoking more often than smokers. Higher education raised the odds of a car ban. The authors argue that teaching about residue risks could widen smoke-free private spaces.
pmc-13524468:
Sachiko Nishina and others analyze, in a 2026 Japanese study across many centers, the genes and medical features behind two groups of eye disorders present from birth and affecting both eyes. One group covers the front of the eye, including aniridia, while the second group has abnormally small or absent eyes. Single gene causes were likely, and families needed clearer guidance.

A total of 111 patients and family members had targeted sequencing with panels covering eleven to twelve known genes per condition. Diagnoses were reached for half of the front-eye group and 37.5 percent of the small-eye group, including eleven new variants. Distinct genes led each condition, with some variants arising new and others inherited from parents with mild or distinct features.
