Glaucoma clustered with two genes, and systemic or neurologic problems grouped with others.
pmc-13525168:
Gestiada and Ladia surveyed older university employees in the Philippines in 2026 to learn what shapes their subjective well-being, meaning how good they feel their lives are. The study covered 69 randomly chosen staff aged 50 and over at the University of the Philippines, including faculty and administrative workers, using the WHO-5 well-being questionnaire.

Almost ninety percent of respondents reported better well-being. Yet none of the tested factors showed a statistically significant link with well-being scores. Perceived health, diagnosed conditions, and being a care recipient did not track with the scores, and neither did learning new skills, growth, work value, or work environment. The authors suggest larger and qualitative studies to explore cultural and workplace factors their survey could not capture.
pmc-13525968:
Jiaxi Hu and colleagues explore, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study, whether radiation dose calculations for a targeted prostate cancer therapy can be simplified without losing clinical meaning. Standard dosimetry uses scans at several time points, yet sampling limits and model assumptions introduce error. Their outcome-driven approach judged each method by how well doses predicted side effects and tumor marker response.

Data from fifty patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer treated with lutetium-177 PSMA therapy were analyzed. Single-time-point dose estimates for bone marrow, taken one, two, or three days after treatment, tracked anemia grading about as well as multi-time-point doses. Cumulative tumor dose from early single scans also predicted prostate marker response comparably. The authors conclude the optimal single time point chosen by outcomes matches the physics-based choice within two days.
pmc-13526368:
Yue Wu and colleagues tested a compound that may shield the heart during sepsis, when infection-driven organ failure raises death risk. Published in 2026, the study used animal and cell models of sepsis, treating with 4-phenylbutyric acid, a drug known to ease endoplasmic reticulum stress. Transcript data from septic patients had pointed to that stress pathway as central to sepsis-related heart dysfunction.

The compound markedly eased heart dysfunction by curbing the formation of junctions between endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria and restoring mitochondrial balance and function. It acted by binding two catalytic sites on an enzyme called HK2, cutting glycolysis and lactate buildup, which in turn reduced a protein modification that drives junction assembly. The authors propose a new treatment chain for septic heart injury. Readers get a mechanistic lead, still preclinical.
pmc-13527268:
Henric Rydén, Ola Norbeck, Sophie Schauman, Mikael Skorpil, and Adam van Niekerk present, in a 2026 MRI methods paper, vendor-independent recipes for ordering scan views. The recipes let any chosen echo land at the center of the data space. In multi-shot sequences the echo placed centrally sets image contrast, yet commercial systems tie that choice to other parameters.

The constructions assign echo and shot positions across a chosen set of phase-encoding steps while avoiding large jumps near the center. Implementations in two RARE variants and in MPRAGE were tested in phantoms and in people. Shifting the center echo moved contrast weighting exactly as theory and simulation predicted, and artifact patterns matched the symmetry of each ordering. An interactive dashboard lets others reproduce the schemes, which fit common acceleration strategies.
pmc-13527968:
Winnie Nambi and ten colleagues survey HIV self-testing among nursing and medical students in eastern Uganda for a 2026 study. They questioned 384 university students about testing habits and preferences. The median age was 24. Self-testing lets young people check their status privately, which may raise uptake where clinic testing lags.

Fifty-five percent had used a self-test. A similar share said they would prefer self-testing in future. Privacy, confidentiality, and convenience were the main reasons given. Students who preferred clinics cited counseling and trust in result accuracy. Self-testing was linked with fourth-year study and having multiple partners, among other factors. The authors suggest tackling accuracy worries and counseling gaps to widen use.
pmc-13528068:
Diane Geindreau and four colleagues map research on the Making Every Contact Count program in a 2026 scoping review. The program trains health staff to use every patient contact for brief healthy-living advice. Searches covered three databases for work from 2010 to early 2026. From 304 records, twenty-two articles passed. All came from the United Kingdom and Ireland.

Studies looked at training, delivery, and views of staff, patients, and students. Most outcomes were attitudes and barriers, not health results. Quality and reporting varied widely. Gaps included working conditions, how much advice is enough, and cost-effectiveness. The authors warn that evidence for a cousin approach, screening plus brief referral, cannot simply transfer. They call for stronger trials in varied settings before wide claims are made.
pmc-13528168:
Xue Zhou and seven colleagues build a timed, targeted drug system for a deadly ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. The cancer is high-grade serous carcinoma. The target is PLK1, a cell division switch. Its blocker, Bi2536, halts the cycle and triggers cell death in lab tests. The team noticed PLK1 levels rise and fall with the daily clock.

They wrapped the drug in a shell fused from ginger vesicles and tumor cell skins. The shell homes to the tumor and adds chemical attack of its own. In mouse grafts the system beat free drug clearly. Giving doses at the daily PLK1 peak helped even more. The authors unite three ideas: a strong target, a smart carrier, and clock timing. They pitch the mix for cancers where gene-based options run out.
pmc-13530368:
Feabie Mendiaz and colleagues test in 2026 a combined repair for torn shoulder labrum tissue in rats. Surgeons created a Bankart tear in the right shoulder of each of 50 rats, then groups received stitching alone, a growth factor, bone marrow stimulation, or both additions. Healing checks ran over eight weeks with weekly walking analysis.

Marrow stimulation alone drew almost no repair cells to the tear. Adding the growth factor multiplied cell arrival sevenfold and improved tissue building and sugar-rich matrix staining. Walking recovery was strongest in the combined group. The pairing offers a candidate upgrade for human labral repair.
pmc-13531768:
Yan Feng and co-authors present a 2026 case of a rare bone-forming cancer growing under the skin of a Samoan man buttock. The 45-year-old noticed a painless lump growing for a year before care. Scans showed a large, well-bordered mass with no contact with bone, an unusual spot for this tumor type.

Surgery removed the mass, and microscopy found aggressive spindle cells making bone-like material, confirmed by marker staining. Cancer reached the deep cut edge, yet the patient declined further therapy and was lost to follow-up. The report stresses full testing even for harmless-looking surface lumps.
pmc-13532868:
Sophie A Rosser and colleagues tested whether parent and child reports of food allergy quality of life can swap for each other after oral immunotherapy. Published in 2026, the study pooled 86 parent-child pairs and 14 parent-teen pairs from three trials of peanut, egg, or milk immunotherapy, with scores taken twelve to twenty-four months after treatment. Questionnaires capture allergy life quality from parent, child, and teen viewpoints.

Parent and self reports correlated moderately, yet agreement stayed limited, with gaps beyond clinically acceptable thresholds. The instruments therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable, even as children age through follow-up. The authors urge trials to keep reporter types distinct when tracking life quality after immunotherapy. Readers get a methods warning: correlation alone does not license swapping scores.
pmc-13536768:
Maïva Faye-Ropaul and Carine Khalil interview French nursing home professionals about trusted persons in a 2026 study. French law lets adults name a trusted person to voice their care wishes if they become unable to speak for themselves. Fourteen directors, doctors, nurses, psychologists, and managers were interviewed between 2021 and 2022. Accounts were analyzed to build an explanatory model of daily collaboration.

Professionals described constant balancing among patient needs for safe and dignified care, family needs for support, and their own needs for legal safety and workable routines. Confusion about the system, impaired residents, and family strain at the end of life shaped that balance. Practices for informing families and involving trusted persons varied widely. The authors suggest teaching families early, before admission.
pmc-13536868:
Zhen Li and co-authors study quality of work life among bowel cancer survivors who returned to work in a 2026 survey at a Chinese hospital. A total of 290 survivors answered questionnaires between January and May 2023 covering work life quality, coping styles, and social support. Group comparisons and combined models searched for traits tied to better or worse work life after cancer treatment.

Average work life scores left clear room for gain. Higher family income, active coping, and fuller use of social support tracked with better scores, while avoidant coping tracked with worse scores. Survivors who paid costs directly, held basic resident insurance, or lived with a stoma also scored lower. The authors advise personal support that spots money strain, insurance type, and stoma needs early in return-to-work planning.
pmc-13538668:
Vijaya Bhaskar Sadu and colleagues design a deep learning model for outlining lower spine structures in MRI scans in a 2026 study. Accurate outlining of vertebrae and discs guides diagnosis and surgery, yet precision usually costs heavy computing. The network pairs multi-scale attention blocks with adaptive feature selection across pyramid levels and gated links between encoder and decoder. Training used 215 expert-labeled lumbar scan volumes.

Overlap scores beat three established rival models by clear margins, and boundary error measures improved by roughly a fifth to a quarter over the best baseline. Quality held steady across all spine levels and discs, with ablations crediting each new block. Training time and memory stayed manageable. The authors position the model for surgical planning and diagnostic support.
pmc-13540068:
Manoj P Shettigar and four colleagues test, in a 2026 imaging study, whether wavy undulations in the pigment layer at the back of the eye warn of a tear in that layer. Tears are a damaging complication of wet age-related macular degeneration, a common cause of sight loss in older adults.

Records covered 936 eyes with the disease, of which 79 had documented tears confirmed by photographs and autofluorescence imaging. The wavy sign, nicknamed the oscillatory sign, appeared in just under half the torn eyes, giving modest sensitivity. Its strength lay elsewhere: it was almost never seen in eyes without tears, and its absence predicted an intact layer with high reliability.
pmc-13540868:
Yuejia Liu and seven colleagues catalogue, in a 2026 genome study, a family of gene switches in wild jujube, a hardy tree valued in dry regions of China. The R2R3-MYB family helps plants grow and answer environmental stress, yet its membership in this species was unmapped.

Ninety-one family genes were found scattered unevenly across twelve chromosomes, mostly switched on in leaves. Family growth came mainly from segmental duplication under conservative selection. Thirteen genes tied directly to water shortage responses and to the drought hormone abscisic acid. Four genes, ZjMYB5, ZjMYB53, ZjMYB57, and ZjMYB85, emerged as core drought responders with tissue- and time-specific patterns, offering breeding targets.
pmc-13541568:
Abhinav B Anand and Ketan Rajawat surveyed AI use in the heart-rhythm lab. Published in 2026, the review covers tools that read heart signals, images, and anatomy to guide rhythm spotting and treatment. In the electrophysiology lab, AI aims to cut reader-to-reader spread and sharpen the hunt for faulty heart tissue.

Pairing AI with heart CT and MRI scans gives tissue slices, wall measures, scar maps, and channel hunts for fast lower-chamber rhythms. AI-guided maps of spread-out signals and focal drivers in atrial fibrillation showed steadier sessions and hopeful early results. Each patient's digital twin lets teams test plans and ideas without putting patients at risk. The authors flag limits too: models can falter on new centers and patient mixes, so workflows still need human care.
pmc-13541768:
Tang and co-authors test whether antibodies that mimic the human ACE2 receptor can keep neutralising SARS-CoV-2 as the virus keeps mutating. Most antibodies fail when the spike's receptor-binding region changes shape. A receptor mimic, though, grips exactly the patch the virus cannot afford to change, since it must still latch onto ACE2 to infect cells. Their 2026 study challenged a panel of such antibodies against recent variants, measuring killing power, binding strength, and the physical interface in structural detail.

One antibody, VIR-7229, held up best, potently neutralising the original strain and three major variant waves while keeping considerable activity against the newest lineages tested, KP.3.1.1, XEC, and a descendant of XEC. Binding assays and structural analysis showed its grip on the spike essentially intact despite the accumulated mutations around it.
pmc-13542168:
Jin Shao and colleagues model river flows in a 2026 hydrology study. The project is a water diversion in China. It links the Yangtze River to the Han River. The lower Hanjiang also loses water to a national transfer project. Judging each project's true effect is hard. The projects overlap on the same river.

A watershed simulation combined all the pieces. It included the new link and the national project. It also included a side diversion and the dam chain. The team then reran the system without the new link. The incoming water failed to offset the national withdrawal. Most of it served the side diversion instead. Flow steadiness in the lower river did improve.
pmc-13542268:
Jun-Eul Hwang and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study identifying a circulating protein, LGALS3BP, as an active driver of liver injury during sepsis rather than a passive marker of illness. Sepsis is the body's damaging overreaction to infection, and it frequently harms the liver. Blood levels of the protein climbed in two mouse models of sepsis, and its production rose in several organs, most notably the liver itself.

Forcing liver cells to make extra LGALS3BP worsened injury, raised liver enzyme levels, and cut survival. The protein primed liver cells for pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death, by switching on a signalling chain that activates the NLRP3 inflammasome. An antibody that neutralised the secreted protein calmed that chain and protected the cells. Blocking this protein could therefore become a treatment strategy for sepsis-related liver failure.
pmc-13543468:
Huamei Tang and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a fetus found before birth to carry a newly described duplication of part of chromosome 6, spanning bands 6p25.2 to p22.3. Duplications of this arm are rare, and about a quarter of reported cases include heart defects. This fetus had a functional single ventricle together with persistent truncus arteriosus, a severe combination where the heart's outflow fails to divide. The authors say it is the first such pairing reported with a pure duplication of this region.

Testing showed the extra segment had been inserted within the chromosome and came from the mother. Comparing published cases, the authors point to the chromosome's tip, the last bands of the p25 region, as the likely critical zone for heart and lung-artery problems. Two duplicated genes, RIPK1 and FARS2, are proposed as possible modifiers of the heart defects and flagged for future research.
pmc-13543568:
Öykü Akkaş and colleagues published a 2026 survey of what final-year medical students in Izmir, Turkey, know and feel about autism spectrum disorder. Across four universities, 748 sixth-year students described their training, information sources, and confidence, and completed validated scales for autism knowledge and societal attitudes. Two thirds had attended at least one autism training session, and a quarter had joined follow-up of autistic patients.

Despite that exposure, about thirty-nine percent said they were not confident managing a suspected case, and over eighty percent wanted more clinical observation of autism built into the curriculum. Students who had examined patients, received extra training, or simply knew someone autistic scored significantly higher on both knowledge and attitude measures. Book learning alone, the authors argue, is not enough: direct contact with autistic people is what turns information into competence.
pmc-13544868:
Anjusha and colleagues examine an overlooked burden of Wilson's disease, the inherited copper overload disorder that damages liver and brain: sexual health. Their 2026 cross-sectional study assessed 87 patients, men and women split by whether disease was active or in maintenance, alongside 63 healthy controls. It used a standard sexual experience scale plus depression and anxiety questionnaires and a Wilson's disability rating.

Men's sexual scores did not differ significantly between disease phases or against healthy men, a null the authors report plainly. Women's story differed: those in the active phase scored markedly worse than women in maintenance and healthy women alike, with both gaps statistically significant. In both sexes, worse sexual function tracked with greater overall disease disability, but not with the amount of copper spilled in urine at diagnosis, the classic toxicity marker. The authors call for registries and newer copper biomarkers.
pmc-13547168:
Ishaan Dharia and co-authors asked in 2026 whether inflammation of the defunctioned rectum during staged colon surgery predicts later inflammation of the small cuff of tissue left at the pouch join. Their review covered 281 patients with ulcerative colitis who had a three-stage pouch operation at one hospital between 2008 and 2020, all with at least one later pouch examination.

About a quarter showed diversion proctitis, the inflammation in question, on the removed rectum specimen. Those patients needed rectal treatment between stages more often than others. Rates of later cuff inflammation, the main outcome, were statistically indistinguishable between the groups, at roughly 19 percent against 14 percent. The authors conclude the early inflammation signals treatment need but not later cuff trouble.
pmc-13548668:
Elaheh Lael-monfared and colleagues analyze more than six thousand animal bite cases in Sarakhs County, Iran, in a 2026 cross-sectional study spanning 2017 to 2024. Bites threaten rabies and cluster where people live close to animals. Records from rabies prevention centers supplied the case census, and the team examined who was bitten, where, when, and by what.

The yearly rate approached eight hundred bites per hundred thousand residents. Nearly four in five victims were male, students were the largest occupational group, and most bites happened in villages during spring afternoons. Dogs caused nine in ten bites, almost all of them domestic animals, and legs took most injuries. Statistical links tied bite frequency to age, sex, job, season, time of day, animal type, and injury site. The authors target education at rural communities and schoolchildren.
pmc-13549168:
Benjamin Claytor and colleagues review the intertwined conditions of thymoma and myasthenia gravis, in a 2026 clinical article. The thymoma is a tumor of the gland behind the breastbone, the commonest in that chest compartment. Roughly a fifth to a third of patients with one develop myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune muscle weakness. Nearly all such patients carry antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, and their weakness tends to be widespread and stubborn.

Contrast CT scanning is the workhorse for finding and sizing the tumor. MRI and PET play supporting roles. Surgery is advised for every thymoma, since all are considered malignant. Keyhole approaches now match open surgery for early stages, with fewer complications. The review covers preparing stable patients, the small risk of new weakness after surgery, and added drug and radiation treatment for advanced tumors. Returning weakness, it notes, can signal recurrence.
pmc-13550268:
Yukihiko Nakajima and colleagues describe a corneal infection that hid behind the mask of a viral inflammation for months, in a 2026 case report. A forty-eight-year-old contact lens wearer arrived with a painful red eye, a cloudy swollen cornea, and inflammation inside the eye. Yet she showed none of the classic signs of Acanthamoeba keratitis, a parasitic infection of lens users. Virus tests on eye fluid were negative, so steroids were given for presumed viral endotheliitis.

Scrapings later found no microbes by microscope, culture, or genetic testing, and the cornea kept necrotizing despite revised anti-infective treatment. At thirty-four weeks, the dead corneal tissue sloughed off on its own. Under the microscope, that tissue held the double-walled cysts of Acanthamoeba, finally proving the diagnosis. The authors warn that this infection can mimic inner-eye inflammation and defeat standard sampling.
pmc-13550568:
Seyed Karim Irani Takleh and colleagues dose wheat with three organic compounds to find recipes that hold yield together under water stress, in a 2026 two-year field study. Fulvic acid, humic acid, and amino acids were combined at several rates in a split-factorial trial on the Taktaz cultivar, under both normal watering and drought. Nearly every measured trait responded to the three-way interaction of the ingredients.

Under normal irrigation, high humic acid alone or paired with a moderate amino acid rate stood out as stable winners. Under drought, the full trio at high rates, six liters of fulvic acid, three of amino acids, and twelve of humic acid per hectare, performed best. Correlation networks across both years repeatedly favored moderate fulvic acid with high humic acid. The authors say raising organic inputs helps wheat regulate its metabolism against drought.
pmc-13551868:
Jia Shi, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a rare metabolic disorder that impersonated viral brain inflammation in a young child. The six-year-old boy arrived with headache, vomiting, intermittent fever, and lethargy, and MRI showed swelling injury in white matter and the corpus callosum, the bridge between brain halves. Steroids helped briefly, yet imaging changes persisted, prompting metabolic and genetic workups.

Tests found markedly raised sarcosine levels and two different mutations in the SARDH gene, confirming hypersarcosinemia, an inherited disorder of amino acid breakdown. Folic acid and a vitamin B12 form were started, with partial imaging improvement the authors caution may not be caused by treatment. They present the case as a first report of this presentation pattern, needing confirmation.
pmc-13551968:
Emily R Edwards, leading fourteen colleagues, published a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of dialectical behavior therapy adapted for justice-involved veterans. Contact with the criminal legal system precedes a large share of suicide deaths in the United States, yet few treatments address legal involvement and suicide risk together. The adapted program, DBT-J, was built specifically for at-risk veterans facing both problems.

The multisite trial will compare treatment approaches, and the protocol was registered in July 2023 under the identifier printed in the article. Beyond the comparison, the paper details design choices around veteran culture, suicide risk assessment and management, and keeping participants engaged. The authors offer those lessons for anyone building programs for similarly at-risk groups, since the trial's results are not yet reported.
pmc-13554268:
R Nareshkumar leads a five-author team designing energy-saving routes for wireless sensor networks in a 2026 study. Sensor nodes run on small batteries, and clumsy routing drains them fast. Their framework learns when nodes should sleep or wake, based on leftover energy and position. A hybrid search method, blending whale and wolf pack strategies, picks cluster leaders and stable multi-path routes.

Simulations showed about ninety-eight percent of data packets arriving safely. Total energy use stayed low while data flow at the base station held strong. Paths were judged by stability, leftover energy, and link quality before use. The authors argue the blend beats older routing rules on lifespan, delivery, and fairness across the network.
pmc-13555868:
Yao Huang leads a nine-author team automating measurement of leaf pores in melon plants in a 2026 study. These pores, called stomata, govern how plants breathe and lose water, yet counting them by hand is slow. The team built a melon image set with more than eight thousand labelled pictures. Their model pairs a vision transformer with attention heads that swap information flexibly, plus a module sharpening channel detail.

Detection precision ran high on the melon test set, topping ninety percent at loose overlap. Oval fitting then measured pore length, width, count, and area automatically. Those measures agreed closely with hand measurements by expert counters. The model also transferred fairly to cucumber, watermelon, pumpkin, and loofah, though each test set was small.
pmc-13557868:
Joyce W. Y. Chan and four colleagues reported in 2026 the first results for a robotic bronchoscopy system that confirms, live, whether its needle truly sits inside a lung nodule. Older navigation methods reach the target area yet can drift from the scan's map. The new system updates lesion position with digital tomosynthesis during the procedure. Data were collected prospectively on 27 nodules in 25 patients treated in a hybrid operating room between late 2023 and late 2024.

A cone-beam scan afterwards confirmed that the tool was inside or touching the lesion in nearly all nodules, with the needle centred in about six of ten. Diagnosis was secured in a strong majority of cases, and no complications occurred. The authors say real-time confirmation answers the main weakness of earlier robotic systems.
pmc-13558668:
Shanmei Li and four colleagues treated in 2026 a crumbly mixture of red clay and tungsten mine tailings with two plant gums to stop it falling apart in water. Such mixed soils erode fast, and pond covers built from them fail early. Specimens dosed with xanthan or guar gum at several levels were cured for up to twenty-eight days across three moisture contents. They were then tested for disintegration. Imaging tools probed pore water, chemistry, and fabric.

Both gums stretched the time to full disintegration sharply, and guar gum at modest doses kept samples from ever fully breaking down during testing. Wetter and longer-cured amended soils resisted even better, with cumulative breakdown falling to a few percent in the best cases. Microscopy showed hydrogel networks coating grains, bridging clumps, and shrinking pores. The authors offer the treatment for stabilising tailings in place.
pmc-13559568:
Tang and colleagues ask whether clearing circulating tumor DNA from the blood can serve as an early sign that a cancer treatment works, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Circulating tumor DNA, fragments shed by tumors into blood, falls when therapy succeeds. Drug developers hope trial-level clearance rates could replace waiting years on survival data. The review pooled trial results and stress-tested the link with cross-validation, checking predictions against held-out trials rather than the data that built them.

The cross-validated association was strongest for progression-free survival, at 0.41 on the reported scale. It was weaker for overall survival at 0.26, and negative for recurrence at minus 1.66. The survival signal came from just eight palliative or metastatic trials. Post-treatment DNA status still predicted individual outcomes across endpoints. Tang concludes clearance remains an exploratory signal, not a validated endpoint for approving treatments.
pmc-13561168:
Yu and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on methods in a meta-analysis of electrical acupoint stimulation for shivering after anaesthesia. The treatment, shortened to TEAS, sends mild current through acupuncture points on the skin. Miao and colleagues had pooled trials and found far less shivering, but Yu questions how firm that evidence is.

Yu notes the search combined stimulation terms with shivering terms only, so trials reporting nausea outcomes without stressing shivering could be missed. That gap makes the nausea findings look stronger than the search can support. Most pooled trials also hid how patients were assigned or who knew their group, which can inflate benefits. With only one trial clearly blinding both patients and assessors, Yu urges more cautious conclusions.
pmc-13562068:
Marta Ruiz-Solana and colleagues report a 72-year-old man whose right hilar lung lesion, spotted on CT during follow-up after coronary surgery, proved to be a pulmonary hamartoma. It was diagnosed by needle sampling through the airway. Their 2026 case report showcases endobronchial ultrasound-guided aspiration for a centrally placed benign tumor, a spot where hamartomas, usually peripheral, rarely sit.

The scan showed a partially calcified, fat-containing mass beside the right main bronchus. Bronchoscopy found no growth inside the airway, but ultrasound displayed a well-defined, mixed-echogenicity lesion with bright punctate spots and shadowing behind it. Needle aspiration proceeded without complications. Cytology and cell block analysis confirmed hamartoma, the commonest benign lung tumor. The authors argue the ultrasound-guided technique is a safe, effective way to settle the nature of central lesions and spare patients bigger surgery.
pmc-13562268:
Rachel Trotter and three colleagues test a standard enhanced recovery protocol for metabolic bariatric surgery at a Midwestern community hospital. Their 2026 pre-post quality study weighs patients treated before and after the set pathway replaced patchy local habits. The many-part protocol unified care across the whole surgical path, from prep through discharge.

Opioid use after surgery fell sharply once the protocol began: the median need dropped from eighty morphine milligram equivalents to twenty-two and a half in the comparison. Nausea and vomiting rates and length of stay, however, did not change clearly. Use of the protocol ran high, at 89.4 percent of planned elements in the audit. The authors conclude that unified care around surgery cut opioid needs safely in a community setting, and they back wider use of such pathways in bariatric programs.
pmc-13562368:
Autumn Bertch and two colleagues report their centre's results using covered stent grafts to repair arteries torn or pierced by injury. Working from the inside of the vessel avoids large open wounds in already damaged limbs. Their 2026 case series covers nine adults treated between 2014 and 2025 at one hospital. Most injuries came from penetrating trauma, and most involved leg arteries. Records supplied injury details, procedure notes, and later outcomes.

Every repair succeeded on the day, and eight of the nine patients kept the limb. Three patients needed a further procedure, and clotting blocked the graft in two. Nobody died, bled from the repair, or developed an infection there. Among patients who could be checked at a median of two years, six of seven grafts stayed open. The authors call the approach workable while noting that nine cases cannot settle long-term durability.
pmc-13563768:
Pengli Yang and four colleagues measure a metabolic sensor protein in children sick with infectious mononucleosis, the glandular fever caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The illness throws the balance between two T-cell camps out of kilter: inflammatory Th17 cells and calming Treg cells. Their 2026 case-control study enrolled 40 child patients and 37 healthy children matched for age and sex. Blood tests for the sensor, HIF-1α, plus its partner signals and cell counts painted the picture.

Patients carried more HIF-1α and the inflammatory signal IL-17A. Their Th17 ranks swelled, their Treg ranks shrank, and the ratio between the camps jumped. The calming signal TGF-β1 fell in step. Every link in the correlation web pointed the same way: the higher the sensor, the hotter the immune tilt. The authors propose HIF-1α as a gauge of severity and a hint that metabolic pathways could be drugged to restore calm.
pmc-13563868:
Ifeoluwa Eunice Adewole and eleven colleagues ask what rural Nigerian schoolgirls know about the HPV vaccine while the national rollout is under way. Nigeria added the vaccine to routine immunisation in October 2023, delivering through schools and communities. Their 2026 survey covered 441 girls at twelve secondary schools across three rural areas of Oyo State in May and June 2024, during the rollout phase. Questionnaires measured knowledge, beliefs, and self-reported vaccination, and models hunted uptake predictors.

Awareness stayed low: under three in ten girls had heard of cervical cancer, the virus, or the vaccine, with schools the commonest source for those who had. Only 41 girls, 9.3 percent, reported being vaccinated. A favourable view of the vaccine dwarfed knowledge as a predictor of uptake and willingness. Among the unvaccinated, half lacked information; others felt at low risk or feared side effects. The authors press for school-based messaging built around trust, not facts alone.
pmc-13569268:
Piergiorgio Martella's team examined whether confidence in self-care links drug-taking to daily self-management in inflammatory bowel disease, in a 2026 multicentre study. Sticking to treatment is central to staying in remission, yet drug-taking remains stubbornly low and self-care demands are heavy. The team surveyed 452 patients across nine Italian outpatient units with validated scales for drug-taking, self-belief, and self-care.

Only about one in ten patients reported high drug-taking, and self-care monitoring and management lagged behind maintenance. Drug-taking tracked with better self-care maintenance, and statistical mediation showed confidence partly explained that link. The authors suggest routine checks of drug-taking and confidence, plus counselling and digital tools that build self-belief, to strengthen everyday disease management.
pmc-13571268:
Kevin Jacobsen and a large Danish team report an exploratory study, published in 2026. It links the look of basal cell carcinoma to its gene activity. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer. No tissue is cut out in this approach. Fifty-three confirmed tumours and control skin were scanned. A high-resolution optical imaging method was used. Adhesive tape strips sampled the tumours. The strips lift surface cells for RNA analysis.

Seven image features distinguished tumours from normal skin. Seventy-two genes differed in activity. Twenty-seven of those genes tracked with two image features. These included a honeycomb-like pattern and collagen changes. Gene links pointed to a tumour-growth gene and a collagen-making gene. Imaging and tape sampling can be combined in living skin.
pmc-13571368:
Michael Villalonga and co-authors report, in a 2026 case, a 40-year-old previously healthy man whose heart sac slowly stiffened into constrictive pericarditis, squeezing the heart and causing fluid on both lungs. Symptoms began with a stubborn cough treated as bronchitis, then progressed to breathlessness, fever, and clear constriction on imaging over about eighteen months.

An extensive workup found only one clue: positivity for HLA-B27, a gene marker tied to inflammatory spine and joint diseases with known heart effects. Medicines failed, and removing the thickened sac resolved his symptoms, with tissue confirming fibrous disease. The authors propose the marker as a possible predisposing factor worth studying.
pmc-13572368:
Alireza Keshtkar, with four colleagues, describes a 2026 study of two viroids found in mulberry trees near Shiraz, Iran. Viroids are tiny rings of RNA that infect plants but make no protein. The trees showed cleared veins and bent, deformed leaves. One viroid is known from citrus, the other from hops.

Deep sequencing of leaf RNA first flagged both viroids, and lab tests found them only in trees with symptoms. The team built copies of each viroid in plasmids and used them to infect young mulberry plants. The young plants grew the same vein and leaf signs, and viroid RNA built up over six to eight months. Gene changes sat mostly in two zones of each viroid. The citrus viroid had not been confirmed in mulberry anywhere before.
pmc-13572568:
Meghal Prajapati, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of shorter radiation courses after mastectomy in India. Radiation after breast removal cuts return of the cancer, yet long courses burden patients and clinics. Trials abroad set a 15-visit course as safe, and a 5-visit course worked in trials where few women had mastectomy.

Fifty women with stage II to IIIA cancer were assigned at random to 40 gray in 15 visits or 26 gray in 5 visits. Both courses covered the target well, above 95 percent. The short course spared the near lung, far lung, other breast, and spinal cord more. Heart dose ran a bit higher, yet stayed well within safe bounds, helped by a breath-hold trick for left-side cases. Skin harm was mild in both groups, and all women were alive and disease-free at six months.
pmc-13573468:
Chengzhi Song, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 two-stage model that reads MRI scans for a dangerous placenta condition. In placenta accreta spectrum, the placenta grips the womb wall too deep and can cause severe bleeding at birth. Fine hand labels for training are costly, so the team split the task in two.

A first network maps the placenta on each scan, and the best slices feed a second network that scores each patient. The study used 170 late-pregnancy cases at home sites and 54 at an outside site. Sorting scores landed in the moderate range, near 0.72 to 0.75 on the area measure in held-out and outside sets. The authors pitch the tool as a screening aid only. Wider prospective checks must come before clinical use.
pmc-13576168:
Xiaoyan Zhong and five colleagues interview hospital staff and patients in China about cutting needless intravenous infusions, in a 2026 qualitative study. Drips are used heavily in Chinese inpatient care, and overuse raises safety risks and wastes resources. The team asked what people think, what blocks change, and what might help.

Awareness of national guidance on sensible infusion use varied across groups. Doctors weighed clinical need against patient expectations and insurance audit pressure. Nurses mostly welcomed fewer infusions for lighter workloads and smoother flow. Pharmacists backed rational drug use yet cited staff shortages, thin training, and an unclear role in team decisions. Patients were split, some favouring drips for their fast feel and unaware of risks. The authors frame reduction as a negotiation across all four groups.
pmc-13576368:
Yang Guo leads a 2026 review of O-RADS, a standard scoring system for ovarian and related growths found on scans. The system, built by the American College of Radiology, sorts lesions into five risk bands with matched management advice, aiming to cut both missed cancers and needless surgery. Two arms exist: ultrasound, the front-line tool, and MRI for problem cases.

Studies show the ultrasound arm catches cancers well, with good agreement between readers and decent accuracy. A 2022 update sharpened some descriptors to cut false alarms. The MRI arm reaches specificity near 90 to 95 percent thanks to finer tissue detail. The review covers friction between the two arms, slow uptake in some clinics, and gaps in guidance for MRI cases. Contrast ultrasound, measured image markers, and AI tools are flagged as next steps.
pmc-13576568:
Nirav Patel leads a 2026 study of a caregiver education programme aimed at preventing hot water burns in young children in Soweto, South Africa. Burns are the leading trauma killer of children under four in the country. The programme taught prevention and first aid to caregivers in high-burden neighbourhoods, with reassessment seven months later.

The study covered 242 intervention and 52 control households. Most homes were severely overcrowded, and nearly nine in ten relied on manually boiled water for bathing. Knowledge of correct first aid rose by 30.8 percentage points from baseline. Safer habits also jumped: keeping stove tops high rose 43.3 points, checking bath water temperature rose 40.3 points, and holding hot drinks while holding a child fell. No gain appeared for child-free safe zones, a gap the authors tie to cramped housing.
pmc-13582668:
Kenny T. L. Ta and colleagues piloted an introductory AI session for first-year medical students at the University of Minnesota. AI is reshaping study and diagnosis, yet most medical curricula barely teach it, leaving students underprepared. Their 2026 pilot gave 241 students an interactive session with lectures, live demos, and hands-on exercises using ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini, covering benefits, harms, bias, and privacy.

Of the 180 students who attended, 92 answered a post-session survey. A majority saw value for study efficiency and diagnostic support, and over half felt more confident using AI in learning and future practice. Worries centred on reliability, over-reliance, and ethics. The authors back early AI literacy paired with ethical grounding, while noting the one-off design cannot prove lasting effects.
pmc-13582768:
Sara Movahed and colleagues review trial proof on glutamine supplements for inflammation and oxidative stress in chronic disease, in a 2026 paper. Glutamine is an amino acid the body leans on harder during illness, and it is sold as a guard against both harms. Three databases were searched to May 2025 under strict trial rules, and only six randomized trials made the cut.

Half the trials saw a clear drop in one inflammation marker, while the other marker fell in just one of three trials that tracked it. Oxidative stress results split too: one study improved two indices, another found no shift in a key protector. Doses and routes, mouth or vein, varied across the set. The authors call the signal patchy and ask for tighter trials at varied doses.
pmc-13584268:
Nanyangwe Siuluta and colleagues explore social support among women with HIV who joined an alcohol treatment trial in Florida. Their 2026 study rests on long interviews with 20 women, most of them Black and with a middle age of 49 years. Each woman had a history of unhealthy drinking and was testing a drug meant to help cut it down.

Family and friends came up most often as the source of support. Relatives who did not drink helped most, by urging the women to stay away from alcohol and cheering their progress. Kinds of help named most were emotional, such as listening without judgment, and practical guidance shared in plain talk. The team says strong support helped women stick with both alcohol care and HIV care.
pmc-13586168:
Xiaopan Li and colleagues found that a textbook reaction takes a different path on one zeolite catalyst. Friedel-Crafts alkylation is usually taught as electrophilic aromatic substitution, but the team observed that MCM-22 drives thiophene alkylation with styrene near room temperature, while zeolite beta stays nearly idle. Their 2026 study used infrared spectroscopy to watch how thiophene and styrene stick to each catalyst.

On both zeolites, thiophene appeared in three forms, including a protonated form, and styrene bound through its vinyl group. On MCM-22, the protonated thiophene vanished as reaction proceeded, pointing to attack by protonated thiophene on adsorbed styrene's side chain instead of the classic ring attack. The authors present this as a distinct low-temperature mechanism for zeolite catalysis.
pmc-13586368:
Balázs Kakuk and colleagues released a dog gut-germ dataset designed to expose how methods skew results. DNA pull-out, library prep, and reading choices all bias germ mixes, blocking cross-study match-ups. Their 2026 dataset tackles that problem in three parts, adding to 75.2 GB of raw reads plus quality and ID outputs.

One ultra-deep sample from a single dog was read on both short-read Illumina and long-read Nanopore platforms. Faeces from eight co-housed dogs over one year set two pull-out workflows against each other across 40 samples. Three full-length 16S primer sets were tested against lab-made mixes and human and dog samples. The authors offer the resource for testing pull-out, reading, and primer effects in dog germ mapping.
pmc-13587468:
Shan Zhang and colleagues sit with dying cancer patients in Beijing to learn how home palliative care feels from inside the family. Many Chinese patients spend their last phase at home, where services are thin and talk of death is often avoided. Their 2026 study recruited twelve urban patients with advanced cancer through clinics and community centers, using long interviews and observation of daily care.

Four threads ran through the accounts. Patients wanted to stay visible at the heart of family life rather than fade to its edge. They guarded personal limits to keep dignity and some say over visitors and routines. As illness advanced, they leaned on outside services as a final safety net that also spared their families. Lastly, they worked to affirm a life's worth, hoping to be remembered well. The authors urge care that protects personhood, not just comfort.
pmc-13587768:
Ryohei Nemoto and a large team build a patterned molecular carpet and catch a special electron state living on its edge. The pattern is a diatomic Kagome lattice, a web of corner-sharing triangles that theory says should host unusual, protected edge states like those in graphene. Working on a lead surface, the team let a three-armed molecule with a flat aromatic core assemble itself into that exact web, ending in zigzag edges.

Scanning tunneling microscope images confirmed the tidy lattice. Combined with tight-binding calculations, the measurements gave direct evidence of the predicted edge states, which are guarded by a bulk property captured in a quantity called the Zak phase. The authors present the self-assembled web as a clean test bed for quantum materials built from designed lattice shapes.
pmc-13588268:
Jaehyeong Park and Jong Kwon Choe published this 2026 commentary on a new catalyst that destroys perchlorate, a stubborn water pollutant that disrupts thyroid hormone production, at neutral pH. Perchlorate's four chlorine-oxygen bonds resist breaking, and earlier rhenium-palladium catalysts only worked in acid. The commentary discusses a study by Liu, Gao and co-workers in ACS Central Science reporting a simple fix: adding a cheap diamine to ruthenium nanoparticles.

With the diamine cis-1,2-diaminocyclohexane attached, the ruthenium particles reduced perchlorate rapidly at pH 7 and room temperature, conditions matching real water treatment. Park and Choe explain why older systems collapse above pH 4: their oxygen-removal cycle needs acid, and their active sites fall apart without it. The new catalyst abandons that cycle, using the ruthenium surface chemistry. The authors frame it as the first practical route to fast perchlorate cleanup at neutral pH, a long-standing goal for drinking water.
pmc-13589568:
Muhammad Ikram, Jian-Ying Zhao and San-Ji Gao published this 2026 commentary on how sugarcane sweetness depends on balancing two ancestries. Modern sugarcane is a hybrid of sugar-rich noble cane and a wild relative, blended by a breeding process called nobilization: repeated crossing back to noble cane while keeping wild traits. The commentary discusses a study by Wang and colleagues that assembled the complete genome of POJ2878, a key 1920s cultivar.

The assembly resolved 118 chromosomes and showed 80.5 percent of the genome descends from noble cane, with 19.5 percent from the wild species. Ikram and colleagues read this as ancestry editing: breeders kept the noble sugar system while dosing in wild segments for vigour and disease resistance. One wild segment, the SUS2 haplotype, raises sucrose at moderate dosage but disrupts sugar balance in excess. The commentary argues that copy number of ancestry, not just its presence, explains modern sugar content.
pmc-13591668:
Julia Fitzner and six colleagues report on a World Health Organization forum session about joining forces across groups that track outbreaks. The session looked at the Collaboratory, a WHO digital hub linking more than seventeen practice communities. Talks covered shared tools: a global store of outbreak parameters, AI aided pipelines for sorting research findings, an outbreak analysis toolkit, and smarter search for resources.

Panelists weighed hard parts too, such as fitting tools into national systems, who governs shared work, funding that lasts, and whether AI output can be trusted. A single message ran through the day, the authors say: fresh tools alone will not sharpen outbreak smarts. Lasting trust, shared ownership, and joint work across fields and lands matter just as much.
pmc-13594468:
Masato Okada and a thirteen-author team studied which patients with a weak heart pump regain function after ablation for atrial fibrillation, using the thickness of the left ventricle wall as the clue. Among more than five thousand ablation patients treated between 2012 and 2024, they focused on 342 whose ejection fraction, the share of blood pumped out each beat, started below half of normal.

Six months after ablation, the group's ejection fraction had risen substantially on average. Thicker walls at the start predicted bigger gains. Uneven thickness from segment to segment predicted smaller ones. Patients with thin yet uneven walls faced the most heart failure admissions and cardiovascular deaths. The authors suggest that measuring wall thickness and its patchiness before the procedure can help estimate how much recovery a given heart still has in reserve.
pmc-13595668:
Joongwon Choi and co-authors armed a cancer-killing virus with two extra weapons. They tested the combination against kidney cancer. That tumor type resists standard therapy behind a suppressive immune environment and heavy blood vessel growth. Their 2026 study used an adenovirus engineered to release interleukin-12, an immune activator, and a silencer of VEGF, the vessel growth signal.

In dishes and in a 3D bioprinted tumor model the armed virus killed kidney cancer cells better than a comparison virus. In mice with tumors growing in the kidney, adding a checkpoint inhibitor drug made the attack stronger still. Helper and killer T cells and natural killer cells drove it. New vessel growth inside the tumor was choked off. The authors describe the strategy as heating up a cold tumor so checkpoint therapy can finally work.
pmc-13612268:
Sicheng Cao leads a five-author team pooling the findings on mini-doses of exercise for people with type 2 diabetes. Single blood sugar averages miss the spikes and swings that damage vessels, while glucose sensors capture them around the clock. Short-bout activity, brief walks and sitting interruptions sprinkled through the day, is easy to adopt, but its effect on sensor metrics was unsettled. The team searched eleven sources and pooled randomized and crossover trials.

Thirteen studies qualified, and ten, covering 175 people, fed the main analysis. Short-bout activity lowered mean glucose by 0.71 mmol/L, though studies disagreed sharply and the prediction interval crossed zero. Other sensor metrics stayed inconclusive. Removing one outlier study collapsed the disagreement and kept a smaller benefit. Certainty ratings ran from moderate down to very low. The authors read the results as a cautious endorsement of movement snacks, pending bigger trials.
pmc-13612668:
Fengge Wang leads a large team reporting in 2026 on a hidden risk of mixing medicines. The question is whether benzodiazepines or related sleep drugs, taken with other medicines, raise the risk of venous thromboembolism, a dangerous blood clot in a vein. These sedative drugs are widely used for anxiety and poor sleep, and past work has linked them on their own to higher clot risk. The question here is which drug pairs may be harmful.

Working with a large sample of United States Medicaid and Medicare records, the team compared each person's clot risk during periods with and without the added drug. Hospital and emergency visits for clots were the outcome, and eye-drop pairs served as a check for false signals. The results are meant to point future studies toward the drug pairs most worth close testing.
pmc-13613168:
Sinem Ilayda Karaagac leads a team studying a bright pigment made by a soil bacterium, Micrococcus terreus strain SK34, and testing whether it can kill cancer cells. The pigment is rich in carotenoids, the natural colour compounds also found in carrots and tomatoes. The team grew the strain, collected 128 milligrams of extract per litre, and used fine chemical tools to name eight carotenoids in it, including beta-carotene and lycopene.

Tested on several cancer cell lines in the lab, the extract killed cells at doses between about 62 and 244 micrograms per millilitre. Its action was strong against neuroblastoma cells, a childhood nerve cancer. Computer docking studies helped explain which cell targets the compounds may bind, pushing the cells toward programmed death. The work is early and lab-based, yet it marks this strain as a candidate source for future cancer drug research.
pmc-13614668:
Isabel D. Hermsmeyer, Ziru Li, and Ormond A. MacDougald review in 2026 how glucocorticoids, steroid hormones used widely as medicines, cause bone loss and reshape the marrow inside bones. Extra hormone, whether from long treatment or from the body making too much, raises fracture risk. It acts on bone-building cells, bone-keeping cells, and bone-eating cells alike, and it also swells the fatty tissue in marrow.

One main route is the damping of a growth signal called Wnt, which cuts bone building and lets marrow fat grow. The review covers drugs and plant compounds that aim at these paths, plus tiny parcels called vesicles that marrow cells use to pass messages. The authors also warn that many lab studies fail to report basic details, making results hard to compare, and they urge tighter methods in bone research.
pmc-13614968:
Caloni and Hartung wrote a 2026 review on using AI against fungal toxins in food. Mycotoxins are poisons made by molds that creep into grain and other foods. Standard lab tests are accurate but slow, costly, and expert-hungry. The review covers AI tools for spotting, forecasting, and curbing these toxins.

Detection systems using AI topped 90 percent accuracy in lab settings. Forecasting models scored between 75 and 99 percent across studies reviewed. Early control strategies reached 80 to 86 percent success in trials. Pairing AI with gene-level data could sharpen risk calls further ahead. Shared standards and openness remain the hurdles the authors stress most. Fewer animal tests could follow if the models prove trustworthy.
pmc-13615268:
Matthias Voß, Rodrigo J. Velasco-Guillen, and Philipp Beckerle compare in 2026 three ways of turning muscle signals into torque for lower-leg prostheses, tested in a virtual balancing task. Sixteen volunteers used signals from opposing lower-leg muscles to steady a computer pendulum that was knocked off balance. Four controllers were tried in random order: a simple proportional map, a muscle-model controller, and two versions adding simulated stretch reflexes at different strengths.

Every participant managed all four controllers. The muscle-model version gave steadier control with less effort, because its paired virtual muscles mimic how real tissue builds force. Adding reflex feedback, which injects a quick velocity-based response like the body's own stretch reflex, was tested for further gains. For prosthesis designers chasing control that feels natural, the study ranks the options with user strain counted, not just accuracy.
pmc-13615968:
David N. Buckley leads a team introducing in 2026 a blood test called MammaTrace that watches for breast cancer's return by reading chemical tags on free-floating DNA in plasma. After curative treatment, stray cancer cells can linger unseen, called minimal residual disease, and later seed incurable spread. Most current tests need a piece of the original tumour; this one does not.

The team found tag regions tied to spread and recurrence by scanning DNA from patients with advanced cancer, healthy controls, and early patients who did or did not relapse. Those regions fed a targeted panel and a classifier, then the test was checked in 107 early-stage patients followed over time with repeated blood draws. Catching a return signal from blood alone could let doctors act months before a scan shows anything.
pmc-13616268:
Miran Joo leads a team studying how the share of ruthenium in four-metal alloy films changes their power as catalysts for splitting water to make hydrogen. The films mix gold, palladium, platinum, and ruthenium in one random crystal, and such mixed surfaces can beat single metals. A sputtered library of films covered a wide range of mixes, screened quickly for structure and for how well each drove the hydrogen-making reaction.

Three blends, carrying 4, 26, and 52 percent ruthenium, got close study. All kept the same cubic crystal pattern while their lattice spacing and defect patterns shifted with the mix. Local strain and chemistry at the surface, not just the recipe, steered performance. The map helps engineers tune cheap, mixed-metal catalysts by composition rather than by trial and error alone.
pmc-13616668:
Yehong Fang and colleagues study whether a glioma brain tumour's molecular marks and its location jointly shape a patient's thinking and feelings before surgery. Modern tumour classification runs on molecular features, yet how much they explain mood and cognition, beyond where the tumour sits, was unknown. The team enrolled 101 newly diagnosed patients and 52 matched healthy controls, all given a full battery of thinking and emotion tests.

Analysis first split patients by tumour site, then tested molecular and clinical links within each site group, and finally modelled the interplay across everyone. Early results show no simple across-the-board molecular effect, pointing instead to effects that depend on anatomy. For care teams, the message is that a tumour's address in the brain frames what its genes do to the mind, so assessments should read the two together.
pmc-13617868:
Yusuff Adebayo Adebisi and three colleagues examine long COVID among adults in Scotland through the lens of disability, asking whether people whose daily activities are already limited report the condition more often. They pooled the nationally representative Scottish Health Surveys of 2023 and 2024, covering nine thousand three hundred twelve adults with complete data. Activity limitation was graded as none, a little, or a lot.

Overall long COVID prevalence was about seven and a half percent, climbing in steps from about five percent among people with no limitation. It rose to about nine percent among those limited a little and over fourteen percent among those limited a lot. Adjustment for age, sex, education, deprivation, and smoking barely dented the gradient, which amounted to roughly nine extra cases per hundred adults in the most limited group. The authors urge surveillance that keeps disability breakdowns and services that reach people with limitations.
pmc-13617968:
Areen Tawil and three colleagues survey radiation safety for medical students attending orthopaedic surgery, where live X-ray imaging exposes everyone in the theatre to ionizing radiation. Students from two United Kingdom medical schools in their clinical years answered a nine-item questionnaire over ten days in December 2023. Seventy students responded, reporting what teaching they had received, what protective gear they actually wore, and how safe they felt.

The gaps were wide. Only half wore a lead apron that fit properly, and about two in five said their apron fit badly. Consistent thyroid shield use was reported by about two in five, while nearly half never wore one. Just sixteen percent had received formal radiation safety teaching before attending theatre, and a third felt unsafe around the imaging equipment. The authors recommend structured teaching before theatre exposure and guaranteed access to correctly fitted protective equipment.
pmc-13618168:
Zijie Gao and twenty colleagues uncover a metabolic circuit that helps glioblastoma, the deadliest brain tumor, survive chemoradiation and recur. They found palmitic acid, a common fatty acid, pooling in the tumor's oxygen-starved zones, where it pushes cancer stem cells toward an aggressive mesenchymal state. It also recruits a suppressive immune cell population, together building a recurrence-friendly niche. A fat-tagging modification on a key glycolysis enzyme sits at the circuit's center.

An enzyme called ZDHHC12 attaches the fatty tag to lactate dehydrogenase A at one specific site, boosting its activity, rewiring sugar metabolism, and conferring treatment resistance. Tagged enzyme also ships out in tiny vesicles that reprogram incoming immune cells into suppressive partners. The team identified rutin, a plant flavonoid, as an inhibitor of this tagging step, and blocking it re-sensitized the tumors to chemoradiotherapy. They propose the circuit as a target against post-treatment recurrence.
pmc-13619068:
Mohammed Bendaoued and eight colleagues design a flower-shaped, four-port antenna for 5G millimeter-wave wireless, small enough for fixed access gear. Multi-antenna systems boost speed and uptime but suffer interference between elements packed closely. Their answer is a hybrid defected ground structure: a central round slot ringed by four trapezoidal cut-outs in the ground plane, beneath four matching elliptical radiating elements set for dual-band use.

The radiator measures twenty-one millimeters square and resonates near twenty-seven and thirty-eight gigahertz, covering slices of two standard 5G millimeter-wave bands. Gain reached seven and a half decibels at the upper band. Simulations in a standard tool predicted strong isolation and diversity. The team built a prototype whose tests confirmed the results. For engineers building compact 5G terminals, the work offers a tested recipe for keeping four antennas apart.
pmc-13619768:
Kenichi Nakajima led a 2026 imaging study that cleans up a measurement problem in dual-tracer heart scans for ischemic heart disease and cardiomyopathy. Scanning fatty-acid metabolism and blood flow at once with two tracers is valuable. Their energy signals bleed into each other, muddying the washout rate that tracks how fast the fatty-acid tracer leaves heart muscle. The team built a simple correction from fixed energy spill ratios measured in phantoms and patients.

Applied to 38 scans from 36 patients, the correction used a thallium spill ratio of 0.12 and tracked uncorrected washout rates very closely, with mean differences near one percent for both flat and tomographic images. Normal-versus-abnormal calls stayed the same in 92 percent of flat-image studies and 95 percent of tomographic studies. Nuclear cardiology readers get a practical, standardized fix: uncorrected values roughly suffice, but correction matters when numbers must be trusted across datasets.
pmc-13620868:
Tetsuro Ohba and six colleagues report a frightening bleed during spine surgery on a seventy-eight-year-old woman with degenerative scoliosis, a sideways curve that develops with age. She was having multilevel side-approach fusion from the second to the fifth lumbar level. While a trial implant was placed at one level, massive vein bleeding began, with blood loss nearing four liters.

Angiography found no arterial leak, pointing to a vein. The wound was packed and heavy resuscitation stabilized her. Three days later, surgeons working with a vascular specialist found the culprit. A small vein branch near the big body veins had been torn away, most likely pulled by the stretching of the correction itself. A sealant patch and steady pressure stopped it. Staged back fixation finished later without trouble, leaving good alignment and no nerve damage. The authors urge slow distraction and early vascular help.
pmc-13623368:
Denise Saquetto leads a team translating and validating a questionnaire on genital self-image into Brazilian Portuguese. The Genital Self-Image Scale, in a twenty-item form, measures how women feel about their genitals, which shapes self-esteem, sexual confidence, and willingness to seek care. A translation must keep meaning, not just words, so the team followed a five-step adaptation method.

Two translators produced Portuguese versions, a merged draft was translated back into English by native speakers, and an expert panel checked wording and cultural fit. Fifteen women pre-tested the draft for clarity. The final version was given to 148 women in three groups, including women with severe pelvic organ prolapse and women who had never given birth. Scores separated the groups as expected, and repeat testing showed the scale was stable and consistent. The authors offer it as a tool for Brazilian clinics and research.
pmc-13626368:
Chunfeng Shi and colleagues cook soil's dark matter in a sterile flask to learn how clay steers its birth. Humic-like substances, the backbone of soil carbon, can form without life through the Maillard browning reaction, and the amino acid glycine drives it. The team varied glycine across five doses with glucose and catechol as partners, in the presence of two common clays, montmorillonite and kaolinite, whose crystal structures differ sharply.

More glycine pushed aromatic, complex fractions onto the clay surfaces, leaving simpler material in the water, and the effect ran stronger with kaolinite. Montmorillonite, by contrast, kept the reaction's turning point steadier across doses. A middle glycine dose best built up humic-like acid. Such mineral fingerprints may help predict which soils lock carbon away longest.
pmc-13626768:
Yang-Tai Lin and colleagues describe a 61-year-old man whose lung disease hid behind a misleading wash test. He had asthma, two months of growing breathlessness on effort, and a worsening wet cough, with blood eosinophils, an allergy-linked cell type, clearly raised. Scans showed the hazy patches at the lung edges that typify chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, a rare condition named for those very cells flooding lung tissue.

The wash from his airways, though, held mostly neutrophils and only six percent eosinophils, and antibiotics changed nothing. A surgical lung biopsy settled it: dense eosinophil invasion with an organizing pneumonia pattern, and steroid treatment worked well. Discordant wash results, the authors warn, should not overrule a strong clinical picture when biopsy can answer.
pmc-13627668:
Marco Túlio Pacheco Coelho and José Alexandre Felizola Diniz-Filho argue in a 2026 essay that macroecology needs both theory-first and data-first reasoning, not a contest between them. Macroecology studies broad patterns of life across space and time, from local populations to global ranges, speciation, and extinction. One tradition derives models from general principles, while another builds models around data, and the authors place these on a continuum of formalization rather than opposite poles.

Their case is that the field grows stronger when theories and models swap roles, each constraining, synthesizing, and sparking the other. That exchange matters because patterns at large scales do not simply add up from local processes, and new regularities can emerge only at broad scales.
pmc-13629568:
Yue Lang and four colleagues ran a pilot study hunting for chemical clues to Parkinson's disease. They combined blood profiling with genetic causal analysis. The first phase was small: fifteen patients and ten healthy controls. It found hundreds of differing compounds among the thousands detected.

Machine learning and pathway analysis singled out one candidate compound. Caffeine handling emerged as the top pathway. Genetic analysis using large Finnish data then suggested a link. Higher predicted levels of the candidate tied to lower Parkinson's risk. A caffeine-linked compound showed the same tie. An inflammatory protein may carry part of the link. The authors stress the work is early and idea-forming. The tiny profiling sample demands care.
pmc-13631568:
Catarina Pedro and four colleagues investigated a protein called TTF2, which helps switch genes off while a cell divides. Gene activity stops during division and must restart at the right moment afterward. The team used polymerase-specific tools and labeling of new RNA to watch what TTF2 does across division. Their focus was whether one factor can control several kinds of RNA production at once.

Removing TTF2 left extra transcripts stuck to chromosomes during the middle of division, mostly from one polymerase. A surprise followed later in division, when a different polymerase restarted too early and began making ribosomal RNA ahead of schedule. Parts of the nucleolus, the cell structure that builds ribosomes, were also pulled in too soon. That loss of timing left nucleoli broken up in the next cell stage, showing how one control protein guards orderly restart.
pmc-13635168:
Bastien Lechat and eleven colleagues published this 2026 study of a mattress-based monitor for sleep apnea used over many nights. Sleep apnea, where breathing repeatedly stalls in sleep, is usually judged from a single lab night. Severity swings between nights, so one night can mislabel patients. The team gave one hundred people with suspected apnea an under-mattress sensor that estimates breathing pauses at home for three months, alongside the standard lab test.

Ninety-two people supplied data. Nearly all reached fourteen valid nights in the first month, proving the zero-effort setup works. Against the lab test, the home device sorted moderate-to-severe disease with solid accuracy. People it flagged while the lab test did not tended to show wild night-to-night swings, short lab sleep, and little back-sleeping time in the lab. The authors say multi-night home monitoring can rescue missed diagnoses.
pmc-13635468:
Ruta Virsinskaite and ten colleagues built and validated a cheap exercise device that works inside an MRI scanner. Exercising during a heart scan reveals hidden weakness, yet commercial exercise machines for scanners are costly and rare. Their device is disarmingly simple: two half-pipes on a wooden base, with small weights tucked into knee socks. Patients alternate bending and straightening their legs to a beep that speeds up to raise the workload.

Twenty people, half healthy and half with pulmonary arterial hypertension, exercised on both the new device and a standard ergometer in random order. Peak measures on the two machines correlated well, from oxygen use to stroke volume, though the simple device reached lower peaks. Both machines cleanly separated patients from healthy volunteers on key measures. The authors present their build as an affordable, portable way to spread exercise heart scanning into more clinics and studies.
pmc-13644268:
Mary Ellen Mackesy-Amiti and three colleagues present a 2026 report on developing SRI-AVLOD, a training that fights drug use and HIV stigma among Tajik labor migrants in Moscow. Migrants who inject drugs face stigma inside their own diaspora on top of HIV risk.

Focus groups and interviews with sixty-five migrant workers and eighteen health workers shaped a four-session course for traditional community leaders, the avlod heads. Two groups of eight leaders piloted it in Tajikistan in September 2025 and rated it highly on acceptability and usefulness. Their stigmatizing attitudes fell after training, and early reports of spreading the message at home were favorable.
pmc-13649068:
Silvia de Andres Quevedo and three colleagues tell of a man in his sixties who sprang a rare leak of milky lymph into his belly days after a chest drain. The drain had been placed for pus round the lung. Scans then found liver cirrhosis that no one knew he had.

The lung pus grew two germs tied to tooth rot. The belly fluid was rich in fats, which proved the leak. Cirrhosis jacks up lymph pressure, so a small tear from the chest work could spill lymph into the belly. Low-fat food and plain support care dried the leak up for good. The authors urge teams to watch for this odd side effect in liver patients.
pmc-13649268:
Federico Cortese and five colleagues, in a 2026 review, pin down dyadic capability: how a stroke survivor and their carer, as a pair, turn facts and tools into real acts at home. Classes raise readiness, but home life is where care is won or lost.

The team searched seven databases to May 2025, screened over two thousand records, and kept 22 studies. They merged the yield with a formal concept study. Three marks define the concept: self-belief, bounce-back strength, and drive. Gains ran from more self-rule to less carer strain. No tested scale yet measures the pair trait, a gap the authors flag for nurse research.
pmc-13649468:
Hongqing Ma and six colleagues built a chart tool to predict survival for bowel cancer that has spread to both the liver and the lungs at the same time. Care choices for this group are hard, and few tools guide them. The team drew cases from a large United States registry and checked the tool on 65 patients at a Chinese hospital.

Nine facts, from age and tumour size to spread in bone and whether spread sites were cut out, fed the chart. It sorted risk well in all three groups and split patients into clear low- and high-risk bands. An early look hinted that cutting out the main tumour helped mainly the low-risk band. That hint needs proof in fresh studies.
pmc-13649968:
Feng Liu and seven colleagues built a deep learning tool that measures scarring and growth zones across whole liver tissue slides from rats dosed with a liver toxin. Hand scoring of such slides is slow and varies between experts. Their tool was trained to mark two targets: fibrous scar tissue and one pooled class of growth and tumour zones set by pathologists.

For each slide, the tool reports how much of the tissue each target fills and how many split zones it finds. A treated group dosed with the toxin plus hydrogen showed less of both lesion types than the toxin-only group. The authors are blunt about limits: training used a patch-level split with no clean audit trail, so outside proof is still owed before any care claims.
pmc-13650468:
Megan E Austin-Cherry and one colleague review fifteen years of group prenatal care around the world. In that model, eight to twelve pregnant people at similar stages meet together for health checks, interactive learning, and community building. They meet this way instead of attending brief one-to-one appointments.

Across diverse settings, women in group care consistently reported more empowerment, social support, better mental health, stronger health knowledge, and closer adherence to care, alongside lower rates of gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia. Babies gained indirectly through mothers' improved habits, including more breastfeeding and timely immunization. Providers described closer patient relationships, yet they also flagged the skill needed to run groups well, plus time and workload strains. The authors conclude that group care works broadly, provided programs fund training and resources, and they ask for long-term studies of children's health.
pmc-13650768:
David J Romano and fourteen colleagues demonstrate a method for recording X-ray scattering with energy resolution, something ordinary imaging detectors cannot do. Scattering maps how a molecule's electrons are arranged, and adding the energy each X-ray loses would merge scattering with spectroscopy, potentially filming a reaction's path through its electronic states.

Their filter is a thin zinc foil placed between the target and the detector. X-ray pulses from a free-electron laser fluctuate naturally from shot to shot, and a ghost-imaging algorithm exploits that randomness to reconstruct the full scattering pattern by energy and angle. Fluorescence from the foil itself must be corrected away. The team proved the method on a sulfur fluoride gas, whose large scattering signal suits the demanding technique. They argue that brighter future X-ray sources will widen the approach to smaller molecules and real reaction watching.
pmc-13650968:
Alexander Muacevic and six co-authors catalog the gene changes behind second-line drug resistance in tuberculosis isolates, knowledge that decides which backup drugs can still work. Fast change testing matters because multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is spreading. Its treatment hinges on fluoroquinolone antibiotics and older injectable drugs.

A commercial line-probe assay was run on 85 drug-resistant strains spanning several resistance classes. About a third carried fluoroquinolone resistance, and a smaller share shrugged off the injectables. The final sorting found a large pre-extensively drug-resistant group. Among fluoroquinolone-resistant strains, one change in the gyrA gene dominated, present in just over half, with two others trailing. Injectable resistance sat on the rrs gene. No resistance changes of the eis promoter type showed up alone. The authors argue such gene maps speed correct regimen choices.
pmc-2658868:
Excoffier, Laval, and Schneider present version three of Arlequin, a software package for the genetics of groups. The package joins basic and advanced methods for analysing genetic data from populations in one place. It computes standard measures of genetic diversity and estimates how common each gene variant and combination is.

The package also tests whether variants depart from expected patterns of independence. Such tests reveal migration, selection, and population history. By putting many analyses together in one shared design, the package became a workhorse for studies of human ancestry and species care.  Field teams use it to judge how cut off an at-risk group is.
pmc-3930868:
Abraham, Pedregosa, Eickenberg, and co-authors show how machine learning with scikit-learn can serve neuroimaging analysis. Brain imaging analysts increasingly turn to statistical machine learning methods. Their main virtue is handling high-dimensional datasets, such as brain activation images or time series recorded at rest.

Supervised learning is typically used to decode brain states or predict clinical traits from scans. The authors connect the general-purpose scikit-learn library to neuroimaging workflows.
